Source course: AWS Certified Security Specialty SCS-C03 Prep Course (Cybr, 152 videos)

About the course

Cybr’s free SCS-C03 course by Christophe Limpalair is built for the current exam version. Its goal is job-ready skills rather than memorising dumps. ▶ #1 01:44 It is not a beginner course: you’re expected to know IAM, EC2, VPC and S3 basics already. ▶ #1 03:22 It teaches in a multi-account lab setup, and the premium edition adds labs, quizzes and practice exams. ▶ #1 02:10

Answer: enable automatic (or on-demand) key rotation. The key ID/ARN stays the same and old key material is kept to decrypt old data, so the app needs zero changes. Creating a new key and repointing the alias (manual rotation) is only for keys that don’t support automatic rotation. ▶ #1 02:40

Exam at a glance
Questions 65: 50 scored + 15 unscored (unmarked, treat all as scored)
Passing score 750 / 1000, compensatory (no per-domain minimum)
Question types Multiple choice · multiple response · ordering (3–5 steps) · matching (3–7 pairs). Ordering/matching are all-or-nothing.
Guessing No penalty, so never leave a blank
Target candidate 3–5 years securing cloud workloads (a suggestion, not a prerequisite)

Out of scope: designing crypto algorithms, packet-level traffic analysis, managing end-user compute, training ML models. “Architect overall cloud deployments” is also listed as out of scope, but you will be asked how to chain services together. ▶ #2 00:52

Domain Weight Tasks
D1 Detection 16% 1.1 monitoring & alerting · 1.2 logging · 1.3 troubleshoot monitoring/logging
D2 Incident Response 14% 2.1 design & test IR plan · 2.2 respond to events
D3 Infrastructure Security 18% 3.1 edge · 3.2 compute · 3.3 network
D4 Identity & Access Management 20% 4.1 authentication · 4.2 authorization
D5 Data Protection 18% 5.1 in transit · 5.2 at rest · 5.3 secrets & key material
D6 Foundations & Governance 14% 6.1 multi-account · 6.2 secure deployment · 6.3 compliance

Skill IDs such as 1.1.3 mean Domain 1 → Task 1.1 → Skill 3 (“aggregate security and monitoring events”). Use the exam guide’s skill list as a checklist, and tick each one when you’re confident. ▶ #2 04:02 The service names in each skill’s “for example” list are strong hints of what the exam asks.

Ordering and matching questions are new too. ▶ #2 01:50

Part 1 – Identity & Organizations

AWS Organizations (and AWS SRA)

At a glance

Central management of many AWS accounts: one management account, member accounts grouped into OUs, consolidated billing, and organization policies (SCP, RCP, declarative, tag, backup, chat applications, AI opt-out). The AWS Security Reference Architecture (SRA) is AWS Prescriptive Guidance that says which account each security service should live in.

  • Exam skills: deploy Organizations (6.1.1) · delegated admin (6.1.4) · Control Tower (6.1.2) · org policies SCP/RCP/AI opt-out/declarative (6.1.3) · central logging account (1.2.2) · aggregate security events (1.1.3) · blast radius (2.1.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #3 Create and configure your AWS account · ▶ #5 Stop surprise AWS bills · ▶ #6 The AWS SRA project · ▶ #7 AWS Organizations
  • Cost: accounts and Organizations cost nothing. Paid security services bill per account per Region.

Why multi-account, and why Organizations

  • Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary in AWS. Separate accounts per environment/workload limit blast radius.
  • Deploying and managing solutions across multiple AWS accounts is “one of the important themes to understand for your exam”. ▶ #6 00:00
  • Practise in your own account (a brand-new one or a sandbox “completely removed from anything production”), with full control including AWS Organizations, not a shared corporate account. ▶ #3 00:00
  • Multi-account behaviour of AWS Config, CloudFormation (StackSets) and GuardDuty is examinable and easier to remember by doing. ▶ #3 00:41
  • Start with at least one practice account with an administrative IAM user, so you don’t use root for daily work. ▶ #3 00:59 The sign-up page asks for a “Root user email address” (used for account recovery and some administrative functions) and an “AWS account name”. ▶ #3 01:10
  • Enable Organizations even for a single account: it unlocks functionality in other services, including IAM Identity Center. Sign in as the admin user → AWS Organizations → Create an organization (one click). ▶ #7 00:11

The demo org (▶ #3 00:25): Root (r-…) with OUs Infrastructure, Sandbox, Security, Workload, and the management account cybr_demo_management, signed in via IAM Identity Center (AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_…). Separate OUs let SCPs and delegated admin roles be applied per function.

The management account and delegation

  • Management account = payer and root of trust. SCPs and RCPs do not restrict it. Keep workloads and people out of it.
  • Minimize use and resources in it. If it is compromised “you’re going to have a very, very bad day”. ▶ #6 01:10 Some security features don’t apply to it. ▶ #6 01:21 Use it only to set things up, orchestrate and delegate. ▶ #6 01:30
  • “Delegation in a nutshell is how you get things out of the management account.” ▶ #7 06:01
Delegation type What it does
Delegated administrator for AWS services Register a member account (usually Security Tooling / Audit) as admin for GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config, Macie, Inspector, Detective, Access Analyzer, Firewall Manager, IAM Identity Center, etc. The standard answer to “manage security services centrally without using the management account”. ▶ #7 06:01
Delegated administrator for AWS Organizations A resource-based delegation policy lets a member account manage organization policies of the types and actions you allow. ▶ #7 06:01
Trusted access (aws organizations enable-aws-service-access) Lets a service perform actions in your organization: create roles, read accounts, root users, policies, OUs. The Services page shows which services are enabled and when. ▶ #7 01:51 AWS recommends enabling it from the other service’s console, so the service can do its own supporting setup.
  • Multi-account deployment patterns: Config rules/conformance packs to all accounts → organization conformance packs or CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions. GuardDuty for all current and future accounts → delegated admin + auto-enable.
  • Org trail: created in the management account or the CloudTrail delegated admin. Member accounts see it but cannot modify or delete it.

AWS SRA: OUs and accounts

The SRA gives prescriptive guidance for AWS security best practices, especially in multi-account architectures. ▶ #6 00:10 Its documentation (AWS Prescriptive Guidance → The AWS Security Reference Architecture) illustrates a three-tier web app (web → application → data tier) inside a full org. The PDF and a PowerPoint diagram source (.zip) can be downloaded to customize. ▶ #6 00:00 It contains all security services at publication time, though not every workload needs every one. For each it gives an overview and security purpose, recommended placement (account/OU), links to other services, and design considerations. ▶ #6 00:55 For now, focus on the OUs and account names. ▶ #6 00:51 An OU is a grouping (like a folder), not an account. ▶ #6 02:01

OU Account What lives there
(root) Org Management Systems Manager, Artifact, IAM access advisor, Control Tower, IAM Identity Center, plus the everywhere services (Security Hub, GuardDuty, Config, IAM Access Analyzer, Organization trail). ▶ #6 01:01
Security Security Tooling Runs and configures security services for the whole org: CloudTrail (org trail admin), Private CA, Inspector, Artifact, Audit Manager, Config aggregator, EventBridge, Security Lake subscribers and sources, GuardDuty, Security Hub, Firewall Manager, Lambda (response), IAM Access Analyzer, Macie, Detective, even KMS. Where the security team gets access. ▶ #6 02:40 Control Tower calls it Audit.
Security Log Archive Central S3 bucket for the CloudTrail organization trail, VPC Flow Logs, access logs (CloudFront, WAF), DNS logs (Route 53 Resolver query logs), plus Security Lake. ▶ #6 04:12
Infrastructure Network Inbound VPC (IGW, NAT), Outbound VPC (NAT, proxy servers), each with flow logs. ▶ #6 06:52 Internet gateways, Route 53, CloudFront, WAF, Shield Advanced, ACM, RAM, Resolver DNS Firewall, Network Access Analyzer. ▶ #6 07:00 Inspection VPC (IDS/IPS) with a firewall subnet running AWS Network Firewall, which traffic passes through before reaching resources. ▶ #6 07:10
Infrastructure Shared Services IAM Identity Center (delegated), Systems Manager, Directory Service, AWS Managed Microsoft AD. ▶ #6 07:30
Workloads Application (Prod/Non-prod) The app itself. ▶ #6 05:31
Sandbox, Suspended Experimentation; closed or quarantined accounts.

  • Same logos in other accounts: the service runs in every account (collects data, monitors) and sends findings back to where it is configured, the Security Tooling account. Those accounts don’t manage it. ▶ #6 03:20
  • Log Archive: lock it down to very few people and systems. Mostly systems pull data; humans should not modify logs. ▶ #6 04:40 Make logs immutable. For incident response, copy data out (e.g. to Security Tooling) and work there, not in Log Archive. ▶ #6 04:51
  • Network pattern: Transit Gateway + centralized inspection VPC, shared with RAM.
  • Shared Services / Identity Center: otherwise you manage identities from the management account. Delegate administration of Identity Center to Shared Services so that team signs in there, never into the management account. ▶ #6 07:52 Identity Center supports one delegated admin. Some tasks stay management-account-only (e.g. permission sets assigned to the management account).

Application account: a VPC with EC2 in a private subnet behind an ALB, Aurora in a private subnet, Systems Manager Agent, VPC endpoints for KMS, Systems Manager and S3 (traffic stays private), and flow logs. ▶ #6 05:41 Supporting services: Secrets Manager (secrets read by EC2), an S3 data bucket, KMS, Private CA, CloudHSM, Cognito, Verified Permissions. ▶ #6 06:02 Some services repeat per account: you sometimes need KMS in an account even when it is centrally managed elsewhere. ▶ #6 06:12 The right-hand column (Security Hub, GuardDuty, Config, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer, Organization trail) gathers data from this account and reports to Security Tooling. ▶ #6 06:21

The SRA is “prescriptive guidance… not a requirement and not a hard rule”. Name or reshape OUs and accounts to fit your organization. ▶ #6 09:01 Its view is “baked into” the rest of the course, so don’t let the diagram overwhelm you. ▶ #6 08:41

Console tour: accounts, services, policies, settings

AWS accounts page lists the management account (ID, email) and members. Here you provision accounts, invite existing ones, and create OUs. ▶ #7 01:20 Demo org: ID o-jqbqypd27k, Root r-limh. A banner offers Centralize root access for member accounts → Enable in IAM (see the root user section).

Policies page (each type must be enabled before use; in the demo only RCPs show Enabled): ▶ #7 02:20

Policy type What it does
Service control policies (SCPs) Set the maximum allowed permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts. ▶ #7 02:31
Resource control policies (RCPs) Like SCPs but protect resources (max permissions on resources). ▶ #7 02:51
Declarative policies for EC2 Enforce a desired configuration for EC2 across the org, maintained even when EC2 adds new features/APIs. ▶ #7 03:10
AI services opt-out policies Whether AWS AI services may store and use your content (e.g. Rekognition, CodeWhisperer, Transcribe). ▶ #7 03:30
Backup policies Org-wide backup plans via AWS Backup. ▶ #7 03:51
Chatbot policies Access to accounts from chat apps (Slack, Microsoft Teams). ▶ #7 04:10
Tag policies Enforce the format of allowed tag values to classify/track resources. ▶ #7 04:21
  • Feature set must be All features (not consolidated billing only) to use SCPs, RCPs and the other policy types. ▶ #7 05:42

Settings page: org ID (used throughout the course), management account name and email, feature set, both delegated-admin sections, and Delete organization, possible only once all member accounts are removed. ▶ #7 06:11 The Get started page lists recommended steps (enable Identity Center, organize accounts into OUs, create policies, enable integrated services). ▶ #7 06:21

Creating accounts, OUs and OrganizationAccountAccessRole

  • Add an AWS account → Create an AWS account or Invite an existing AWS account. ▶ #7 07:30
  • Each account needs a unique email (it is the root recovery path). Plus-addressing helps, e.g. name+8@gmail.com. ▶ #7 07:50
  • OrganizationAccountAccessRole (default name, changeable) is created in every account the org creates, with admin rights, trusted by the management account. That’s how you jump between accounts. It is a high-privilege role. ▶ #7 08:21
  • New accounts land directly under Root. Select → Actions → Move → OU. ▶ #7 09:10
  • To create an OU you must first select Root (or the parent OU), “kind of a weird quirk”. Names up to 128 characters. ▶ #7 09:50
  • Invited accounts (by email or account ID; the owner must accept) don’t get the role, because Organizations had no access. Create it by hand. ▶ #7 10:50

Creating the role in an invited account: IAM → Roles → Create role → AWS account → Another AWS account → the management account ID → do not choose Require external ID (the accounts are internal) → attach AdministratorAccess → name it OrganizationAccountAccessRole for consistency.

Console demo: create accounts and OUs ([▶ #7](https://youtu.be/4D6yWs3ZsxI))
  1. Organizations → AWS accounts (hierarchy view) → Services → Policies → Settings → Get started. ▶ #7 01:11
  2. Add an AWS account → Create an AWS account → name network (central VPC stuff), email …+8@…, role OrganizationAccountAccessRole → Create AWS account. Creation takes up to about a minute. ▶ #7 07:30
  3. Refresh → select network → Actions → Move → Infrastructure. ▶ #7 09:30
  4. Select Root → Actions → Create new OU → Workload → Create organizational unit. ▶ #7 09:50
  5. Create dev (+9) and prod (+10) accounts → move both into Workload. ▶ #7 10:10
  6. Instructor’s full layout: OUs Infrastructure, Sandbox, Security, Workload; accounts log archive, security tooling, sandbox examples, shared services. Replicating it is optional: accounts are free but add complexity. ▶ #7 07:01

Org condition keys

Key Use
aws:PrincipalOrgID Resource policy: only principals in my org
aws:PrincipalOrgPaths Only principals from accounts in specific OUs
aws:ResourceOrgID Only resources in my org
aws:ResourceOrgPaths Only resources in specific OUs

S3 bucket policy that allows only principals from your org:

{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::corp-logs", "arn:aws:s3:::corp-logs/*"],
  "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-a1b2c3d4e5" },
                 "Bool": { "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false" } }
}

Billing guardrails: Budgets and anomaly detection

Create a budget right after securing root and before any lab in your own account. ▶ #5 00:00 Forgotten resources cause “surprise bill” stories. ▶ #5 00:41 Unexpected spend is also a security signal (e.g. crypto-mining). Alert before the limit, e.g. at about $4 for a $5 limit, so you can investigate in time. ▶ #5 01:00

Budget setup: Use a template (simplified) vs Customize (advanced) (custom period, start month, specific accounts). ▶ #5 01:31

Template Notifies when
Zero spend budget Spend exceeds $0.01, i.e. above Free Tier
Monthly cost budget Actual 85%, actual 100%, forecasted 100% of the amount ▶ #5 01:50
Daily Savings Plans coverage Coverage falls below a target
Daily reservation utilization RI utilization falls below a target

  • A budget only notifies: email (up to 10 recipients) or SNS. Template settings can be changed later via Custom.
  • Budget actions can act: apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop specific EC2/RDS instances (needs an execution role).
  • Cost Anomaly Detection = ML-based unusual-spend detection (per service, account, cost category).
  • CloudWatch billing alarm: metric EstimatedCharges, us-east-1 only, requires Receive Billing Alerts.
Console demo: $30 monthly cost budget ([▶ #5](https://youtu.be/WT2Io95rXKk))
  1. Sign in as administrator (works because root activated IAM access to Billing) → search Budgets → Create budget. ▶ #5 01:31
  2. Use a template (simplified) → Monthly cost budget. ▶ #5 01:40
  3. Name My Monthly Cost Budget, amount 30.00, email recipient your@email.com, scope All AWS services. ▶ #5 01:50
  4. Create budget. “It really is that simple.” ▶ #5 02:00
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Multi-account deployment of Config, CloudFormation (StackSets) and GuardDuty is examinable: practise it. ▶ #3 00:41
  • Don’t use root for daily work: create an administrative user. ▶ #3 01:00
  • Management account: minimize use and resources, some security features don’t apply to it, use it to set up, orchestrate and delegate. ▶ #6 01:10
  • Logs in Log Archive are immutable; analyse copies elsewhere during IR. ▶ #6 04:51
  • Delegate Identity Center administration to Shared Services. ▶ #6 08:10
  • SCPs set the maximum permissions for users/roles; RCPs are the resource-side equivalent. Both are “super important”. ▶ #7 02:31
  • OrganizationAccountAccessRole exists in created accounts, not invited ones. ▶ #7 10:40

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Centrally manage security service X across all accounts, least privilege Delegated admin in a security account, not the management account
Where to administer GuardDuty / Security Hub / Macie / Inspector / Detective / Config aggregator / Firewall Manager / Access Analyzer Security Tooling (Control Tower: Audit)
Restrict resource access to principals in our org Resource policy with aws:PrincipalOrgID
Allow access only from accounts in specific OUs aws:PrincipalOrgPaths
New accounts automatically get the control Attach the policy to the OU, not to accounts
Management account can’t switch into an invited account Create OrganizationAccountAccessRole manually there
Want SCPs but org has consolidated billing only Enable All features
Central, tamper-proof logs Log Archive bucket: restrictive bucket policy, S3 Object Lock (compliance mode), versioning, SSE-KMS, SCP stopping members from stopping/deleting the org trail
Deploy Config rules to every account Organization conformance packs / StackSets (service-managed)
Enable GuardDuty for all current and future accounts Delegated admin + auto-enable
Stop resources automatically when spend hits a threshold Budget actions
Detect unusual spend automatically Cost Anomaly Detection, not a fixed budget
Sudden cost spike, EC2 in Regions we never use Compromised credentials / crypto-mining. GuardDuty CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS, Impact:EC2/BitcoinDomainRequest. Revoke keys, check CloudTrail, Region-deny SCP
Root email is an employee’s personal mailbox Wrong: use a group-owned distribution list you control
Minimize blast radius Separate accounts

Real-world practice

  • Start with AWS Control Tower for the Security OU, Log Archive and Audit accounts, org trail and guardrails, then extend toward the SRA (Infrastructure, Sandbox, Policy Staging, Suspended OUs from the Organizing Your AWS Environment whitepaper). Companion code: aws-samples/aws-security-reference-architecture-examples.
  • Plan OUs by policy needs (Security, Infrastructure, Workloads Prod/Non-Prod, Sandbox, Suspended, Policy Staging), not by org chart.
  • Vend accounts with Control Tower Account Factory/AFT or IaC (aws_organizations_account), not console clicks.
  • Lock down OrganizationAccountAccessRole: replace it with Identity Center permission sets, or guard it with an SCP so only break-glass principals can assume it.
  • Account email aliases go to a shared, monitored mailbox. Removing an account from the org needs standalone billing info. Closed accounts stay in the org (SUSPENDED) for 90 days.
  • In Log Archive, give the security team read-only cross-account access (or query via Athena/Security Lake from Security Tooling). Writes come only from service principals. Lifecycle central logs to cheaper S3 classes.
  • Prefer IAM Identity Center users over IAM users, even for the lab admin. Long-term IAM access keys are a top source of leaks.
  • Create budgets in the management account (or a delegated billing account) per account/OU/cost-allocation tag, plus a zero-spend budget on sandbox accounts, before enabling paid security services (GuardDuty, Security Hub, Macie, Inspector bill per account per Region after trials). Pair with Region-deny SCPs and Cost Anomaly Detection.
  • Budget data lags by hours (up to ~8–24 h): budgets are not real-time controls. The first two action-enabled budgets are free.
aws organizations create-organizational-unit --parent-id r-abcd --name Security
aws organizations register-delegated-administrator \
  --account-id 111122223333 --service-principal guardduty.amazonaws.com
aws guardduty enable-organization-admin-account --admin-account-id 111122223333
Hands-on lab
  1. Create an org with OUs Security, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/Dev and Sandbox.
  2. Register a member account as delegated admin for one service.
  3. Create a $30 monthly cost budget with email alerts.
  4. Cleanup: deregister the delegated admin, move the accounts out, delete the budget, and close the test accounts.

Service Control Policies (SCPs)

At a glance

Organization policies that set the maximum permissions for IAM principals (users, roles, and the root user) in member accounts. They never grant permissions: an identity still needs an IAM policy that allows the action.

  • Exam skills: org policies SCP/RCP (6.1.3) · Organizations (6.1.1) · manage root user credentials (6.1.5) · least privilege & boundaries (4.2.3) · analyze authorization failures (4.2.4) · troubleshoot authentication (4.1.3)
  • Videos: ▶ #8 About SCPs · ▶ #9 Deploying SCPs · ▶ #10 Test SCPs so they don’t break production
  • Limits: 5 SCPs attached per root / OU / account · 5,120 characters per policy

What SCPs are (and are not)

  • Very similar to IAM policies in syntax and behaviour, with important differences. ▶ #8 00:20
  • They do not replace IAM or resource-based policies and “don’t actually grant any access. They can only limit.” ▶ #8 00:30
  • They give central control over the maximum available permissions for identities in member accounts, overriding IAM and resource-based policies set in those accounts: guardrails for IAM users and roles. ▶ #8 00:40

Applies to Does not apply to
All IAM users and roles in member accounts ▶ #8 06:30 The management account, even when attached at Root ▶ #8 06:11
The member account root user ▶ #8 06:30 Service-linked roles (used by AWS services to act in member accounts) ▶ #8 06:41
Nested OUs and accounts, including ones added later (inheritance) ▶ #8 07:21 Users/roles in external accounts accessing your resources ▶ #8 06:52
  • Hence “push things out of the management account”. ▶ #8 06:11
  • SCPs don’t affect resource-based policies directly. Example: an S3 bucket in a member account grants cross-account access to account B. The SCP doesn’t restrict account B’s identities and doesn’t protect the bucket → use RCPs. ▶ #8 07:21
  • SCP vs permissions boundary: SCP = whole account/OU, set centrally. Boundary = per IAM entity, used to safely delegate role creation.

FullAWSAccess and deny-by-default

Enable them in Organizations → Policies → Service control policies → Enable service control policies. Each policy type has its own enable button (e.g. Enable declarative policies for EC2). ▶ #8 01:11

  • AWS then creates the managed SCP FullAWSAccess (“allows access to every operation”): Effect: Allow, Action: "*", Resource: "*", an allow-all approach. ▶ #8 01:30
  • Why it exists: at least one SCP must be attached at all times to root, every OU and every account, and SCPs are deny by default. Removing FullAWSAccess without a replacement Allow blocks every action. ▶ #8 02:02
  • Its Targets tab: attached to every account and OU, kept in sync automatically as accounts/OUs are added or removed. Don’t touch it. ▶ #8 02:31
  • Start with no restrictions and add SCPs with explicit denies, which win over allows (like IAM). ▶ #8 02:50
Strategy How
Deny list (most common) Keep FullAWSAccess and add Deny statements
Allow list Remove FullAWSAccess; an Allow must then exist at every level (root → OU → account)
  • Policy name ≤ 128 chars, description ≤ 512 chars, optional tags. The console banner: “An SCP doesn’t grant permissions. You must still use IAM permission policies or resource policies to grant permissions.” ▶ #9 00:00
  • Quotas: max 5 SCPs attached to the root, per OU and per account; max document size 5,120 characters including whitespace. Combine and structure SCPs creatively, and “double check” as these may change. ▶ #8 08:51 With only 5 per target you’ll run out quickly. ▶ #9 07:00
  • Since 2025 SCPs support the full IAM policy language: Condition, NotResource and individual resource ARNs are allowed in Allow statements too.

Effective permissions

  • Effective permissions = intersection of SCPs ∩ permissions boundaries ∩ identity/resource-based policies. ▶ #8 06:01 An action outside any one circle is denied.
  • An explicit deny in the SCP wins even over an explicit allow in the member account. ▶ #8 05:50
  • A new user/role with the FullAWSAccess SCP in place still has no access until an IAM policy grants it. ▶ #8 07:51
  • IAM allows + SCP doesn’t deny → allowed. IAM allows + SCP denies or doesn’t allow → denied, even for AdministratorAccess. ▶ #8 08:11

Policy logic reminders

  • NotAction + Deny = “deny everything except these”. NotAction + Allow grants broadly. Don’t confuse them.
  • Condition operators (different keys) are ANDed. Values inside one key are ORed.
  • Exemptions can use aws:PrincipalTag/... instead of aws:PrincipalArn, so roles can be exempted by tag without editing the SCP.

Example: restrict EC2 instance types in Sandbox

Name RestrictEC2ForSandbox, description “Deny all but specific small EC2 instances”. The editor looks like the IAM policy editor. ▶ #8 03:11 It denies ec2:RunInstances unless the instance type is a micro:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "RequireMicroInstanceType",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "ec2:RunInstances",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "ec2:InstanceType": ["t3.micro", "t2.micro"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
  • Scoping Resource to instance/* is needed because RunInstances also touches subnets, volumes, ENIs, etc., which have no ec2:InstanceType key.
  • Anyone in Sandbox launching anything else (e.g. 2xlarge, even the smaller nano) is denied. ▶ #8 03:50
  • Created policy ARN arn:aws:organizations::<mgmt-acct>:policy/o-…/service_control_policy/p-…, type Service control policy (customer managed). ▶ #8 04:18
  • Targets → Attach → Sandbox OU (could be Infrastructure, Security, Workloads…). Selecting Root applies to every OU. ▶ #8 04:21
  • UI gripe: selecting Root shows the management account as ticked. That is “very deceiving”: SCPs don’t apply to it. ▶ #8 04:40
  • It trickles down to accounts and sub-OUs added later. Even an admin in a Sandbox account can’t launch other types. “That’s how powerful SCPs are.” ▶ #8 05:10

Console demo: FullAWSAccess and RestrictEC2ForSandbox ([▶ #8](https://youtu.be/vQ7PLTvQCIk))
  1. Organizations → Policies → Service control policies (already Enabled) → open FullAWSAccess → Content (Allow * *) → Targets (all OUs/accounts). ▶ #8 01:11
  2. Back → Create policy → name RestrictEC2ForSandbox, description “Deny all but specific small EC2 instances” → paste the JSON → Create policy. ▶ #8 03:01
  3. Open the policy → Targets → Attach → tick Sandbox (untick Root/management) → Attach policy. ▶ #8 04:18
  4. Targets now shows the Sandbox OU (ou-limh-1tzth5z3). ▶ #8 05:10

Common guardrail SCPs

Typical guardrails: deny leaving the org; deny disabling CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config, Security Hub or Access Analyzer; Region restriction with aws:RequestedRegion (exempt global services with NotAction); deny root user actions (aws:PrincipalArn = arn:aws:iam::*:root); require IMDSv2 (ec2:MetadataHttpTokens); deny creating IAM access keys; restrict instance types (ec2:InstanceType); protect security roles with aws:PrincipalArn. Opt-in Regions are disabled by default, and an SCP can deny account:EnableRegion to keep them off. SCP examples live in the Organizations user guide: reuse them. ▶ #9 03:21

1. NeverLeaveMe — “Prevent member from leaving organization”. Once an account joins, it can’t leave on its own. “That’s how basic a policy can be.” Attached at Root. ▶ #9 00:30

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "organizations:LeaveOrganization", "Resource": "*" }
  ]
}

2. Region lockdown, AWS docs version (DenyAllOutsideEU) ▶ #9 01:51

  • Uses NotAction instead of Action: the list holds global services excluded from the restriction. ▶ #9 02:10
  • Condition StringNotEquals aws:RequestedRegion = eu-central-1, eu-west-1: change to your Regions. ▶ #9 02:41
  • Plus ArnNotLike aws:PrincipalARN exempting roles allowed to bypass the SCP. ▶ #9 03:02 The two conditions are ANDed: deny only if the Region is not approved and the caller is not an exempt role.
  • Source: Organizations User Guide → SCP examples → “Deny access to AWS based on the requested AWS Region”. With Control Tower, use its Region deny control instead. ▶ #9 03:12

DenyAllOutsideEU: deny everything outside two EU Regions except global services and two roles 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyAllOutsideEU",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "NotAction": [
        "a4b:*", "acm:*", "aws-marketplace-management:*", "aws-marketplace:*",
        "aws-portal:*", "budgets:*", "ce:*", "chime:*", "cloudfront:*", "config:*",
        "cur:*", "directconnect:*", "ec2:DescribeRegions", "ec2:DescribeTransitGateways",
        "ec2:DescribeVpnGateways", "fms:*", "globalaccelerator:*", "health:*", "iam:*",
        "importexport:*", "kms:*", "…",
        "shield:*", "sts:*", "support:*", "trustedadvisor:*", "waf-regional:*",
        "waf:*", "wafv2:*", "wellarchitected:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-central-1", "eu-west-1"]
        },
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalARN": [
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/Role1AllowedToBypassThisSCP",
            "arn:aws:iam::*:role/Role2AllowedToBypassThisSCP"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

2b. LockDownUnusedRegions — the simplified version actually attached, to the Sandbox and Workload OUs: ▶ #9 04:00

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "LockDownUnusedRegions",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": ["us-east-1", "us-west-2"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

  • Conditions can be combined like IAM, e.g. only small instances in us-east-1 but larger ones elsewhere. ▶ #9 04:20
  • Region lockdown is easy in a sandbox but risky in a production org with hundreds of accounts: you must know which Regions are really used. ▶ #9 04:31

3. NoMoreRoot — “Deny all root usage!”. Deny all actions when the principal is a member-account root user. Attached at Root so it trickles down. ▶ #9 06:22 “It doesn’t matter if I have admin privileges or even if I’m the root user in one of those accounts.” ▶ #9 07:22

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "ArnLike": { "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:root"] } }
    }
  ]
}

Console demo: deploy three SCPs ([▶ #9](https://youtu.be/S18A5az5E9s))
  1. The SCP list holds FullAWSAccess and RestrictEC2ForSandbox. ▶ #9 00:00
  2. Create policy → NeverLeaveMe → paste JSON → Create → open → Targets → Attach → Root → Attach policy. ▶ #9 00:21
  3. Create policy → LockDownUnusedRegions → paste the docs example → replace it with the simple Region policy → Create → Attach to Sandbox + Workload. ▶ #9 01:41
  4. Create policy → NoMoreRoot / “Deny all root usage!” → paste JSON → Create → Attach to Root. ▶ #9 06:12
  5. Testing happens in the next lesson.

More real-world examples, a Region lock with a break-glass role and a security-baseline protection:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "DenyOutsideApprovedRegions",
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "NotAction": ["iam:*", "organizations:*", "sts:*", "cloudfront:*", "route53:*",
                  "support:*", "budgets:*", "waf:*", "globalaccelerator:*"],
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
      "StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["ap-southeast-1", "us-east-1"] },
      "ArnNotLike": { "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/BreakGlassAdmin" }
    }
  }]
}

{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Action": ["cloudtrail:StopLogging", "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail",
             "guardduty:DeleteDetector", "guardduty:DisassociateFromMasterAccount",
             "config:StopConfigurationRecorder", "organizations:LeaveOrganization"],
  "Resource": "*"
}

Testing SCPs and reading the denial

Get into the member account with OrganizationAccountAccessRole for now (Identity Center comes later). ▶ #10 00:10 From the management account: account menu → Switch role → Account ID + IAM role name, optional display name and colour. ▶ #10 00:20 Pick an account in the Sandbox OU, where most SCPs are attached. ▶ #10 00:32

The header changes to OrganizationAccountAccessRole @ <account-id>. The menu shows Currently active as the role, Signed in as the original identity (AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_… in cybr-demo-organization), Switch back and Role history. ▶ #10 01:00 Cost and usage widgets show Access denied (the role has no billing access).

Test Result
Launch t2.nano or t2.xlarge in N. Virginia (allowed Region) ▶ #10 01:30 Instance launch failed, explicit deny in an SCP ▶ #10 02:00
Switch to ap-south-1 (Mumbai) ▶ #10 02:31 Can’t even describe instances; red errors everywhere ▶ #10 02:41
Open IAM while in ap-south-1 ▶ #10 03:00 Works: IAM is global, so the Region SCP doesn’t block it ▶ #10 03:11

The error: “User: arn:aws:sts::396212980357:assumed-role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole/christophe is not authorized to perform: ec2:RunInstances on resource: arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:396212980357:instance/* with an explicit deny in a service control policy. Encoded authorization failure message: …”. Launch log: Initializing requests ✓, Launch initiation ✗. ▶ #10 02:00

Read the caller ARN, the action, the resource, the reason, and the encoded authorization failure message. It is encoded “as a security measure”; decode it for more detail. ▶ #10 02:12

AccessDenied messages name the policy type: “with an explicit deny in a service control policy”, "…in a resource control policy", "…because no identity-based policy allows…", "…in a permissions boundary", "…in a session policy". Decode with aws sts decode-authorization-message (needs sts:DecodeAuthorizationMessage).

Safe rollout: test on a Sandbox / Policy Staging OU, check CloudTrail for AccessDenied with an SCP reason, then promote OU by OU. The IAM Policy Simulator can include SCPs for member accounts. “In general you would want to test more thoroughly than this.” ▶ #10 03:31

Console demo: test the SCPs from a Sandbox account ([▶ #10](https://youtu.be/3lJoH-Q3YFo))
  1. Management account → account menu → Switch role → Sandbox account ID, role OrganizationAccountAccessRole, display name/colour → Switch Role. ▶ #10 00:20
  2. EC2 (us-east-1) → Launch instances → AMI Amazon Linux 2023 → type t2.xlarge (or t2.nano) → no key pair → existing SG → Launch instance → explicit-deny error from the SCP. ▶ #10 01:30
  3. Region → Asia Pacific (Mumbai) ap-south-1 → the Instances page fails to list (explicit deny). ▶ #10 02:31
  4. Open IAM (Global) → works normally. ▶ #10 03:00
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • SCPs “don’t actually grant any access. They can only limit.” ▶ #8 00:30
  • Never remove FullAWSAccess without a replacement Allow: everything would be blocked. ▶ #8 02:02
  • Root-level attachment still does not cover the management account. ▶ #8 04:40
  • Know: no effect on the management account, applies to root user, not to service-linked roles, not to external accounts (RCPs), inheritance, limits 5 / 5,120. ▶ #8 06:11
  • Use NotAction in Region-deny SCPs so global services aren’t blocked. ▶ #9 02:10
  • Use a principal-ARN exception so specific roles can bypass the guardrail. ▶ #9 03:02
  • The error says “explicit deny in a service control policy”: that tells you where to look. ▶ #10 02:00
  • Verify that the guardrail blocks what it should and that global services still work. ▶ #10 03:21

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Admin in a member account can’t do X though IAM allows it An SCP denies it (“explicit deny in a service control policy”)
SCP should restrict the management account Impossible: move workloads out of it
Restrict a service-linked role with an SCP Won’t work: SLRs are exempt
Everyone except the security team role must not change a guardrail SCP Deny with StringNotLike aws:PrincipalArn exception
Region-deny SCP broke IAM / STS / CloudFront / Route 53 NotAction to exempt global services; with Control Tower use its Region deny control
Prevent member accounts from leaving the org Deny organizations:LeaveOrganization at Root
Restrict member-account root users SCP with aws:PrincipalArn arn:aws:iam::*:root. Remove root credentials entirely → centralized root access
Protect OrganizationAccountAccessRole / security roles SCP deny iam:* on the role ARN except a privileged principal
We removed FullAWSAccess and everything broke SCPs are deny by default; an Allow must exist at every level
New user has FullAWSAccess SCP but can’t do anything SCPs don’t grant: add an IAM policy
External account reads our bucket via its bucket policy; SCP didn’t stop it SCPs don’t apply to external principals → RCP
Get details of an encoded AccessDenied message sts decode-authorization-message
Test a new deny SCP without risking production Staging OU or Policy Simulator
Updates since the videos
  • Since 2025 SCPs support the full IAM policy language, so Condition, NotResource and individual resource ARNs are allowed in Allow statements. “Allow statements in SCPs can’t have conditions” is outdated.
  • LockDownUnusedRegions: the narration says “deny … whenever the requested region is us-east-1 or us-west-2”, but the on-screen operator is StringNotEquals, which denies every Region except those two (an allow-list, the usual intent). To block specific Regions use StringEquals. With Action: "*" and no global-service exemption it could also break global services (IAM, STS, Organizations, CloudFront) whose calls resolve to us-east-1; here us-east-1 is allowed, so it works.
  • The RestrictEC2ForSandbox and NoMoreRoot JSON weren’t fully legible on screen. The versions above are the standard AWS-documented patterns matching the narration.

Real-world practice

  • Test SCPs in a Policy Staging OU first. A bad deny at Root can stop every workload; the management account is unaffected, so you can always roll back from there.
  • Before a Region lockdown, find which Regions each account really uses (Cost Explorer, CloudTrail Lake, IAM last accessed, Config). Roll out sandbox → non-prod → prod.
  • Always exempt break-glass and automation roles (AWSControlTowerExecution, StackSets roles, OrganizationAccountAccessRole, e.g. ArnNotLike aws:PrincipalArn arn:aws:iam::*:role/OrgAdmin) or automation breaks.
  • The 5-attachment and 5,120-char limits force consolidation: minify JSON, wildcard actions, put shared guardrails at Root and environment-specific ones at OUs.
  • Keep SCPs in Git (Terraform aws_organizations_policy + attachments) with peer review. Validate with IAM Access Analyzer policy validation.
  • Automate an SCP test suite: assume a role in a test account per OU and run expected-allow / expected-deny API calls in CI after every change.
  • After rollout, alert on CloudTrail errorCode = AccessDenied with errorMessage containing “service control policy” (metric filter or EventBridge).
  • For many accounts, use the Identity Center access portal or the console multi-session feature instead of per-browser switch-role history.
aws organizations create-policy --type SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY \
  --name deny-region --content file://deny-region.json --description "Region lock"
aws organizations attach-policy --policy-id p-xxxx --target-id ou-xxxx-sandbox
aws sts decode-authorization-message --encoded-message <msg>
Hands-on lab
  1. Attach a Region-deny SCP and an instance-type SCP (t2.micro/t3.micro only) to a Sandbox OU.
  2. Switch role into a sandbox account and try to launch a t2.xlarge.
  3. Run aws ec2 describe-instances --region eu-west-1.
  4. Read the denial in CloudTrail, decode the message, and confirm IAM still works.
  5. Cleanup: detach and delete the policies.

Resource Control Policies (RCPs)

At a glance

Organization policies that set the maximum permissions on resources in member accounts, whoever the caller is, including principals outside the org (other accounts and other organizations). The resource-side counterpart of SCPs and the basis of a data perimeter.

  • Exam skills: org policies RCP (6.1.3) · Organizations (6.1.1) · cross-account resource policies (4.2.1) · correct unintended permissions (4.2.5) · secrets management (5.3.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #11 Resource Control Policies (RCPs)
  • Limits: like SCPs, up to 5 RCPs attached per target, 5,120 characters

SCP vs RCP

SCP RCP
Caps Maximum permissions of IAM users and roles in your org ▶ #11 00:00 Maximum permissions on resources in your org ▶ #11 00:10
Question it answers “What can my principals do?” “Who can touch my resources?”
Affects external principals No Yes
Grants permissions Never Never ▶ #11 00:30
Default policy FullAWSAccess RCPFullAWSAccess (can’t be detached or modified)
  • Use case: Secrets Manager secrets that must never be accessible by external AWS accounts. ▶ #11 00:21
  • Supported at recording time: S3, STS (role trust), KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager. ▶ #11 00:51 Only these services are restricted, and the visual editor only lists them. ▶ #11 03:12
  • They don’t apply to the management account’s resources or to service-linked roles / AWS services acting on your behalf.
  • Custom RCPs are effectively Deny-only.
  • Denial message: "…with an explicit deny in a resource control policy".

The data perimeter

Perimeter Tool Key
Only trusted identities on my resources RCP aws:PrincipalOrgID
My principals only reach trusted resources SCP aws:ResourceOrgID
Only from expected networks VPC endpoint policies aws:SourceVpc / aws:SourceVpce

Typical RCPs: deny access from outside the org (aws:PrincipalOrgID, with an exception for AWS service principals via aws:PrincipalIsAWSService or aws:SourceOrgID), enforce aws:SecureTransport, require SSE-KMS on S3, confused-deputy protection (aws:SourceOrgID / aws:SourceAccount). Use …IfExists operators so calls without the key (e.g. service principals) aren’t denied by accident.

Cross-account evaluation order: explicit deny anywhere (SCP, RCP, resource, identity) → RCP allow chain → SCP allow chain → resource policy must allow → identity policy must allow (see the policy evaluation section).

Enabling RCPs and writing OrgPrincipalsOnly

Enable from the management account → Organizations → Policies: a banner “Introducing resource control policies (RCPs) — Enable RCPs” may appear; otherwise Resource control policies → Enable. ▶ #11 01:12 That attaches the AWS managed RCPFullAWSAccess: “we’re not granting access with this, we’re just not denying access”. Without it everything would be denied by default. Every account inherits it. ▶ #11 01:50

Create OrgPrincipalsOnly, “Only allow principals within our organization to access resources”. The focus is Secrets Manager, but the pattern works for S3 etc. ▶ #11 02:41 The form says: “An RCP specifies the baseline permissions for resources in your organization’s accounts. An RCP doesn’t grant permissions. Users and roles must still be granted permissions with appropriate IAM permission policies, including resource-based policies for cross-account access to resources.”

Built in the visual editor: Secrets Manager → All actions, Effect Deny, Principal *, Resource *, and two conditions:

  1. StringNotEqualsIfExists aws:PrincipalOrgID = your org ID (o-jqbqypd27k in the demo). ▶ #11 04:02
  2. BoolIfExists aws:PrincipalIsAWSService = false. ▶ #11 04:30

Meaning: deny everyone unless they belong to our organization, while not blocking AWS services (e.g. Secrets Manager rotation), which are not part of the org. ▶ #11 04:51

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnforceOrgIdentities",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "secretsmanager:*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": { "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-jqbqypd27k" },
        "BoolIfExists": { "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

The two conditions are ANDed: the deny applies only if the caller is outside the org and is not an AWS service principal.

  • Result: type Resource control policy (customer managed), ARN arn:aws:organizations::<mgmt>:policy/o-…/resource_control_policy/p-…. Not attached yet. ▶ #11 05:30
  • Targets shows Root → Infrastructure, Sandbox (Containers, Demo, Example accounts), Security, Suspended… Apply to all or to specific OUs/accounts. Don’t apply straight to production: test with one account, roll out gradually, monitor. ▶ #11 05:51

Demo: blocking a cross-org secret read

Setup ▶ #11 07:51

Account Role
A = Demo (396212980357), in our org Holds the secret
B = 272281913033, in a different organization Tries to read the secret
Management account Only creates/attaches the RCP

Create the secret in account A (N. Virginia): Store a new secret → Other type of secret → api_key = testingrcps. ▶ #11 09:02 The AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager won’t work cross-account, so a customer managed KMS key is needed. The old testrcps key was scheduled for deletion and can’t be used to encrypt your secret, so a new one was made. ▶ #11 09:11

The external account’s admins must still grant their own principals kms:Decrypt via IAM. Secret name test/ApiKey/RCP. ▶ #11 10:21 Then Resource permissions → Edit with the deliberate “misconfiguration”: ▶ #11 11:01

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AllowExternalAccountAccess",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::272281913033:root" },
      "Action": [
        "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
        "secretsmanager:DescribeSecret"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:396212980357:secret:*"
    }
  ]
}

In real life scope it to a specific secret ARN. ▶ #11 11:20

Before the RCP, account B (CLI profile sandbox = its Identity Center admin role) reads the secret: ▶ #11 11:50

aws sts get-caller-identity --profile sandbox
# "Account": "272281913033",
# "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::272281913033:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_8a29b66590b9ccb6/christophe"

aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \
  --secret-id "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:396212980357:secret:test/ApiKey/RCP-AmESHE" \
  --profile sandbox
# returns "SecretString": "{\"api_key\":\"testingrcps\"}"
  • Cross-account secrets need the full ARN as --secret-id. ▶ #11 12:22
  • Cross-account and cross-organization access works. Treat it as a misconfiguration to fix. ▶ #11 12:50

After attaching the RCP to the Demo account, the same command fails: ▶ #11 13:52

An error occurred (AccessDeniedException) when calling the GetSecretValue operation:
User: arn:aws:sts::272281913033:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_8a29b66590b9ccb6/christophe
is not authorized to perform: secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on resource:
arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:396212980357:secret:test/ApiKey/RCP-AmESHE
with an explicit deny in a resource control policy

Even though the resource policy and the KMS key policy granted the external account, the RCP denies it: an extra layer against misconfigurations, insider threats and exfiltration to attacker-controlled accounts. ▶ #11 14:02 RCPs cover limited services but probably belong in your org: start small, test, then expand. ▶ #11 14:41

Cross-account access to a KMS-encrypted resource needs the resource policy and the KMS key policy and IAM in the caller’s account.

Console demo: enable RCPs, share a secret, block it ([▶ #11](https://youtu.be/dhi3Mrp3VnI))
  1. Management account → Organizations → Policies → Enable RCPs → RCPFullAWSAccess attached everywhere. ▶ #11 01:12
  2. Create policy OrgPrincipalsOnly → Secrets Manager / All actions / Deny / Principal * / Resource * + StringNotEqualsIfExists aws:PrincipalOrgID + BoolIfExists aws:PrincipalIsAWSService false → Create (don’t attach yet). ▶ #11 02:41
  3. Account A: KMS → Create key → Symmetric, Encrypt and decrypt, alias testrcps2, default admins → Define key usage permissions → Other AWS accounts → Add another AWS account → arn:aws:iam::272281913033:root → Review (Key spec SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT, Origin AWS KMS, Single-Region) → Finish. ▶ #11 09:20
  4. Account A: Secrets Manager → Other type of secret api_key=testingrcps → refresh, pick testrcps2 → name test/ApiKey/RCP → resource policy allowing account B → no replication, no rotation → Store. Banner: “Attached resource policy to secret test/ApiKey/RCP successfully”. ▶ #11 08:50
  5. Account B (CLI, profile sandbox): aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <full ARN> → success. ▶ #11 11:50
  6. Management account → Policies → Resource control policies → OrgPrincipalsOnly → Targets → Attach → Demo account 3962… → Attach policy. ▶ #11 13:12
  7. Account B: rerun → AccessDeniedException … explicit deny in a resource control policy. ▶ #11 13:52
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • RCPs “don’t give permissions. They just set the maximum permissions that can be granted for a resource.” ▶ #11 00:42
  • Enabled and managed from the management account. ▶ #11 01:12
  • Include an AWS service exception (aws:PrincipalIsAWSService) or you’ll break services like Secrets Manager rotation. ▶ #11 05:00
  • “If you’re thinking of applying it straight to production, don’t do that. Test it first.” ▶ #11 06:00
  • Cross-account secrets require a customer managed KMS key. ▶ #11 09:11
  • RCPs protect against misconfiguration, insider threats and exfiltration. ▶ #11 14:11

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
No S3 bucket in the org may be accessed by external accounts, even with a permissive bucket policy RCP (an SCP only limits your own principals)
Enforce TLS for all S3/KMS/SQS across the org centrally RCP Deny when aws:SecureTransport = false
Secrets must never be readable externally, even if a secret policy is wrong RCP on secretsmanager:* with aws:PrincipalOrgID
Our principals must not access resources outside our org SCP with aws:ResourceOrgID, not an RCP
RCP broke Secrets Manager rotation / an AWS service Missing aws:PrincipalIsAWSService (or aws:SourceOrgID) exception
External account can’t decrypt a shared secret Secret uses the AWS managed key: re-encrypt with a CMK shared in its key policy
Updates since the videos
  • The supported-service list has grown: as of 2025 RCPs also cover Amazon ECR, OpenSearch Serverless, Cognito user pools, CloudWatch Logs and DynamoDB. Check the current list.
  • The OrgPrincipalsOnly JSON wasn’t legible on screen. The version above matches the narration and AWS’s data-perimeter example. The instructor’s “and/or” wording is loose: IAM ANDs the two condition operators.

Real-world practice

  • Typical RCP set (AWS data-perimeter-policy-examples repo): deny non-org principals on S3/KMS/Secrets Manager/SQS/STS (sts:AssumeRole* on your roles), require TLS, confused-deputy protection for service principals.
  • Before attaching, inventory legitimate external access (vendors, partner accounts, CloudFront OAC, third-party SaaS) with IAM Access Analyzer external access findings, and add exceptions (aws:PrincipalAccount or tag-based).
  • Start small: attach to one test account/OU, watch CloudTrail for errorMessage containing “resource control policy”, then expand. Validate syntax with Access Analyzer policy validation.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "EnforceOrgIdentities",
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "Principal": "*",
    "Action": ["s3:*", "sqs:*", "kms:*", "secretsmanager:*", "sts:AssumeRole"],
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
      "StringNotEqualsIfExists": { "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-a1b2c3d4e5" },
      "BoolIfExists": { "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false" }
    }
  }]
}

aws organizations enable-policy-type --root-id r-abcd --policy-type RESOURCE_CONTROL_POLICY
aws organizations create-policy --type RESOURCE_CONTROL_POLICY --name org-perimeter --content file://rcp.json
Hands-on lab
  1. Attach an RCP that enforces TLS to a sandbox OU.
  2. Call S3 through an http:// endpoint (--endpoint-url http://s3.<region>.amazonaws.com) and confirm the deny.
  3. Optional: repeat the cross-account secret test (customer managed KMS key + secret resource policy for another account) before and after an OrgPrincipalsOnly RCP.
  4. Cleanup: detach the RCP, delete the secret and schedule key deletion.

Declarative policies, AI opt-out and other organization policies

At a glance

The non-authorization Organizations policy types: declarative policies (service-enforced configuration baselines), AI services opt-out, tag, backup and chat applications policies.

  • Exam skills: org policies SCP/RCP/AI opt-out/declarative (6.1.3) · organize resources with tags (6.2.2)
  • Videos: none dedicated. The policy types are toured in ▶ #7 AWS Organizations (full notes under AWS Organizations, Part 1)

The policy types

Policy type What it does
Declarative policies (EC2 and related services) A durable baseline configuration that the service enforces itself, so it holds even when new APIs or features appear. ▶ #7 03:10 Examples: block public AMI sharing, block public EBS snapshot access, VPC Block Public Access, default IMDSv2 settings, serial console access, allowed AMIs (“Allowed Images”). Can show a custom error message.
AI services opt-out Stop AWS AI services (e.g. Rekognition, Transcribe, CodeWhisperer / Amazon Q) from storing or using your content to improve the service. ▶ #7 03:30
Backup policies Org-wide AWS Backup plans. ▶ #7 03:51
Chat applications policies (formerly Chatbot) Control access to accounts from Slack and Microsoft Teams through Amazon Q Developer in chat applications. ▶ #7 04:10
Tag policies Standardize tag keys, value case and allowed values. ▶ #7 04:21
  • Each type must be enabled separately at the root before use (the Policies page shows Enabled/Disabled per type), and needs the All features feature set.

Declarative policy vs SCP

SCP Declarative policy
Mechanism Denies API calls The service enforces a configuration state in the account
New APIs/features Need new statements Covered automatically, regardless of the API path

Control Tower preventive controls can now be implemented as declarative policies (and RCPs) as well as SCPs.

AI opt-out, tags and backups

  • AI opt-out is applied at the org root to cover all accounts. It is the answer to “ensure our data isn’t used to train AWS AI services”.
  • Tag policies report non-compliance and can enforce on supported resource types. They don’t stop untagged creation on their own: use an SCP with aws:RequestTag / aws:TagKeys for that.
  • Backup policies + AWS Backup cross-account / cross-Region copies are the ransomware-resilience pattern.

AI opt-out for every service:

{ "services": { "default": { "opt_out_policy": { "@@assign": "optOut" } } } }
Exam tips

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
No AMI or EBS snapshot can ever be shared publicly, across all accounts Declarative policy
Require IMDSv2 / block VPC public access org-wide, enforced even when EC2 adds new APIs Declarative policy for EC2
Data must not be used for AWS AI model improvement AI services opt-out policy
Enforce tag value formats across the org Tag policy
Require a CostCenter tag at creation time SCP Deny with Null: aws:RequestTag/CostCenter = true
Org-wide backup plans member accounts can’t skip Backup policy

Real-world practice

  • Enable only the policy types you use, at the root, from IaC:
aws organizations enable-policy-type --root-id r-abcd --policy-type DECLARATIVE_POLICY_EC2
aws organizations enable-policy-type --root-id r-abcd --policy-type AISERVICES_OPT_OUT_POLICY
Hands-on lab
  1. Enable the AI opt-out policy type and attach the opt-out policy at the root.
  2. Check its effect in a member account: aws organizations describe-effective-policy --policy-type AISERVICES_OPT_OUT_POLICY.
  3. Cleanup: detach it.

AWS Control Tower

At a glance

An orchestration layer over Organizations, IAM Identity Center, CloudTrail, Config, Service Catalog and CloudFormation. It sets up and governs a landing zone with best-practice guardrails, for new accounts or existing ones you enroll.

  • Exam skills: Control Tower & custom controls (6.1.2) · Organizations (6.1.1) · org policies SCP (6.1.3) · detect and remediate noncompliance (6.3.1) · central logging account (1.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #12 AWS Control Tower
  • Cost: mainly Config recording, CloudTrail and S3 storage in Log Archive, not Control Tower itself

Why Control Tower, and its four features

Dozens, hundreds or thousands of accounts become a “management nightmare” without centralized, automated governance and account compliance tooling. ▶ #12 00:00 Control Tower lets you create new accounts or enroll existing ones following recommended best practices. ▶ #12 00:21

Feature What it is
Dashboard Visibility of all your accounts and all your controls. ▶ #12 00:41
Landing zone Holds the OUs, accounts, users, etc. that you apply security controls to. ▶ #12 00:50
Controls (formerly guardrails) Rules applied to accounts, by behaviour and guidance level (below). ▶ #12 01:01
Account Factory Configurable templates that standardize and automate provisioning: the account vending machine, on demand or in batches, through Service Catalog. E.g. every new account automatically gets an admin role and a read-only role. ▶ #12 01:12

Related Account Factory options: Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) (GitOps) and Customizations for Control Tower (CfCT) for custom SCPs and StackSets.

What a landing zone sets up

  1. Two OUs: Security and Sandbox (required defaults; extend with more OUs per the SRA). ▶ #12 02:31
  2. Two shared accounts in the Security OU: Log Archive and Audit (security tooling). “Audit” can be renamed at creation, e.g. Security / Security Tooling. ▶ #12 02:51
  3. IAM Identity Center with preconfigured groups and SSO access, or a self-managed identity provider. ▶ #12 03:11
  4. Guardrail SCPs (aws-guardrails-*). From then on manage them through Control Tower, not directly in Organizations. ▶ #12 03:22 They share the 5-SCP-per-target limit with your own SCPs.
  5. All mandatory preventive controls. ▶ #12 03:32
  6. All mandatory detective controls. ▶ #12 03:42
  7. Controls apply to the whole organization except the management account, which can’t be governed that way. ▶ #12 03:42
  8. AWS resources in the accounts, e.g. AWS Config and an org CloudTrail trail. ▶ #12 03:52

Then you operate the environment from Control Tower. ▶ #12 04:02 CT aggregates CloudTrail and Config logs into Log Archive. Audit gets cross-account read/admin roles and SNS aggregate notifications for the security team.

Controls

Behaviour Implemented with Effect Example
Preventive SCPs, RCPs, and now declarative policies Stops the action Disallow changes to the CloudTrail config CT created
Detective AWS Config rules Reports non-compliance on the dashboard S3 bucket allows public read
Proactive CloudFormation Hooks Blocks non-compliant resources before provisioning RDS instance without encryption in a template

Guidance levels: mandatory, strongly recommended, elective. ▶ #12 01:01

Also: a Region deny control, data residency controls, and governed Regions.

Drift and enrolling existing accounts

  • Accounts drift from best practices within months of use. Guardrails help prevent drift and give visibility into drifted accounts. ▶ #12 02:11
  • Manual changes to CT resources cause drift: moving an account between OUs in Organizations, editing or detaching a CT SCP, deleting a CT role. Fix with Re-register OU or Repair landing zone.
  • Existing org: enroll existing accounts or OUs. Accounts need the AWSControlTowerExecution role.

Scope in this course

Control Tower is not deployed in the course: it hasn’t been “a very big part of the exam, or at least not this version”. Similar resources are built by hand for more hands-on experience. ▶ #12 04:10 Know the features, control types and guidance levels, landing-zone defaults and drift. (The video’s only frame is an empty title slide, so no diagram here.)

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Know the four features: dashboard, landing zone, controls, Account Factory. ▶ #12 00:30
  • Know the control types (preventive/detective/proactive) and guidance levels (mandatory/strongly recommended/elective). ▶ #12 01:01
  • Landing zone defaults: Security + Sandbox OUs, Log Archive + Audit accounts. ▶ #12 02:31
  • After Control Tower, manage its SCPs through Control Tower. ▶ #12 03:22

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Prevent non-compliant resources from being created via CloudFormation Proactive control
Least operational effort for a multi-account baseline Control Tower, not hand-built Organizations, CloudTrail and Config
New accounts must automatically get baseline guardrails, logging and SSO Control Tower + Account Factory
Detect, don’t block Detective control (Config rule)
Custom SCPs/StackSets applied automatically to new accounts CfCT, or AFT if Terraform
Someone moved an account / edited a CT-managed SCP and CT shows a problem Drift → Re-register OU / Repair landing zone
Restrict Regions in a CT-managed org CT Region deny control, not a hand-written SCP
Updates since the videos
  • Newer landing-zone versions let you opt out of Identity Center (self-managed IdP) and rename or skip the Sandbox OU. The Security OU + Log Archive + Audit core is unchanged.
  • Preventive controls can now be implemented as declarative policies (and RCPs) as well as SCPs.

Real-world practice

  • CT is the usual way to bootstrap an SRA-style landing zone. Enroll existing accounts by moving them into a registered OU.
  • Don’t edit CT-managed SCPs in Organizations. Add your own alongside them.
  • Apply landing-zone version updates deliberately; test in a non-prod org if possible.
  • Costs come mainly from Config recording, CloudTrail and S3 storage in Log Archive, not from Control Tower itself.
aws controltower enable-control \
  --control-identifier arn:aws:controlcatalog:::control/EXAMPLEID \
  --target-identifier arn:aws:organizations::111122223333:ou/o-xxxx/ou-xxxx-prod
aws controltower list-enabled-controls --target-identifier <ou-arn>
Hands-on lab

Read-only lab (CT is costly to tear down):

  1. Explore the Control Catalog in the console.
  2. Filter by “proactive”.
  3. Map 3 controls to the services they rely on.

Root user and centralized root access

At a glance

The root user has unrestricted access to its account. In an org, centralized root access (Nov 2024) lets you remove root credentials from member accounts and perform the few root-only tasks from a central account using short-lived root sessions.

  • Exam skills: manage root credentials, MFA, break-glass (6.1.5) · delegated admin (6.1.4) · Organizations (6.1.1) · MFA (4.1.1) · temporary credentials (4.1.2) · prepare for incidents (2.1.2) · metrics and alerts (1.1.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #4 Secure the root user · ▶ #32 Centrally managing root access
  • Root sessions last at most 15 minutes and are scoped to one of 5 task policies

Root is not a day-to-day identity

After creating an account you are signed in as root. Root should never be used beyond initial setup or in very rare circumstances. ▶ #4 00:00 AWS publishes a list of tasks that require root user credentials; outside those, don’t use root at all. ▶ #4 00:10

Root-only tasks:

  • Change account settings: account name, email, root password, root access keys.
  • Restore IAM user permissions after a lock-out.
  • Activate IAM user and role access to Billing information.
  • Close the account. Change or cancel the AWS Support plan.
  • Register as a seller in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.
  • Configure S3 bucket MFA Delete.
  • Edit/delete an S3 bucket policy or SQS queue policy that denies all principals (locked-out resource).
  • Sign up for GovCloud. Some billing and tax-invoice settings.

Root can’t be restricted by IAM policies in its own account. Only SCPs restrict root, and only in member accounts.

The 10 root hardening steps (Well-Architected Security pillar)

The AWS Well-Architected Framework has six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability). Its Security pillar gives the root guidance below. ▶ #4 00:31

# Step Detail
1 Long, strong password Set at creation or change it now; keep it in a password manager. ▶ #4 00:51
2 No root access keys A new account has none. If one was ever created, delete it immediately: “a huge no-no”. ▶ #4 01:10
3 Enable MFA Prefer hardware MFA (or passkey); software MFA still beats none. Up to 8 MFA devices on root: register backups. ▶ #4 01:34
4 Accurate contact info So AWS can reach you by phone or email if they detect something fishy. ▶ #4 02:00
5 Secure the root email and phone Anyone with access to them can reset the root password. ▶ #4 02:21
6 Alert on all root activity Not every user (too noisy), but root should never be used, so every use is worth an alert. ▶ #4 02:40
7 Two-person rule No single person holds both the credentials and the MFA. Skipped in the personal demo account. ▶ #4 03:10
8 Use root only when absolutely necessary “I know I’m a broken record… you need to listen.” ▶ #4 03:40
9 Periodically verify Root credentials still work, and alerting/monitoring wasn’t accidentally or purposely disabled. Calendar reminders or a process. ▶ #4 04:00
10 IR playbook for root misuse Covered later in the course. ▶ #4 04:20

AWS now enforces MFA for root on management and standalone accounts.

Quick check: the IAM Dashboard’s Security recommendations panel first showed 1 warning, “Add MFA for root user”, and a green “Root user has no active access keys”. ▶ #4 01:12 After MFA it shows 0. Related controls: Config/Security Hub CIS root-account-mfa-enabled, root-account-hardware-mfa-enabled, iam-root-access-key-check; GuardDuty Policy:IAMUser/RootCredentialUsage.

The account menu (top right) is where you reach Account (billing setting) and Security credentials (root MFA/keys).

Alerting on root use

The AWS sample repo aws-samples/aws-iam-root-user-activity-monitor (Terraform: hub.tf, provider.tf, root-activity-monitor-module) deploys root alerting; it is covered later in the course. ▶ #4 02:40

Its pattern: CloudTrail management events → EventBridge rule matching userIdentity.type = "Root" → SNS, deployed hub-and-spoke across accounts. EventBridge pattern for root sign-in:

{ "detail-type": ["AWS Console Sign In via CloudTrail"],
  "detail": { "userIdentity": { "type": ["Root"] } } }

Alternatives: a CloudWatch Logs metric filter + alarm on the trail (CIS, older), or a GuardDuty / Security Hub control.

Billing access and the break-glass admin user

IAM access to Billing: as a security feature, IAM identities cannot see the billing console until root activates it. ▶ #4 04:41 Account menu → Account → IAM user and role access to Billing information (Deactivated) → Edit → Activate IAM Access → Update. ▶ #4 05:00 IAM users and roles with appropriate IAM permissions can then access billing. ▶ #4 05:21

Admin / break-glass IAM user: banners recommend IAM Identity Center, which the course uses later, but an admin is needed now. ▶ #4 05:40 Keeping one IAM user in the management account is good anyway, for an outage of your IdP or Identity Center: a break-glass user (“breaking the glass to reach the fire extinguisher”), named administrator or break-glass. ▶ #4 05:51

AWS recommends IAM users only for programmatic access keys, service-specific credentials (CodeCommit/Keyspaces), or a backup credential for emergency account access. Password rules: ≥ 8 characters, at least three of upper/lower/number/symbol.

Break-glass design: a small number of emergency principals (management account root with hardware MFA in a safe, or a dedicated break-glass IAM role/user excluded from SCPs), alerting on use, and regular testing.

Console demo: harden root and create the admin user ([▶ #4](https://youtu.be/XfZDVgfpgOk))
  1. Signed in as root → IAM Dashboard: Security recommendations shows “Add MFA for root user”. ▶ #4 01:12
  2. Account menu → Security credentials → assign MFA device (fast-forwarded). Security recommendations → 0. ▶ #4 01:51
  3. Account menu → Account → IAM user and role access to Billing information → Edit → activate → Update. ▶ #4 05:00
  4. IAM → Users → Create user: name administrator, Provide user access to the AWS Management Console ✓, I want to create an IAM user (not Specify a user in Identity Center – Recommended), Autogenerated password, Users must create a new password at next sign-in ✓ (auto-attaches IAMUserChangePassword). ▶ #4 06:21
  5. Permissions: Add user to group (recommended) vs Copy permissions vs Attach policies directly. Direct would be fine for one user, but groups are a good habit → Create group administrators + AdministratorAccess (1025 policies in the picker) → Create user. ▶ #4 06:41
  6. Retrieve password page: sign-in URL https://<account-id>.signin.aws.amazon.com/console, user name, password (shown only once: Download .csv or Email sign-in instructions). ▶ #4 07:09
  7. Sign out of root, sign in as the admin: console shows administrator @ <account-id>. Root is now only for root-only tasks and periodic checks. ▶ #4 07:10
  8. Enable MFA on the admin user too (forgotten in the original recording). ▶ #4 07:40

Centralized root access: why

Root actions in member accounts should be rare, but sometimes you need them. ▶ #32 00:00 Before this feature, every member account created by Organizations got an auto-generated root password nobody knew. To use root you had to do a password reset, then set up MFA. ▶ #32 00:20 Doing (and maintaining) that for dozens or hundreds of accounts isn’t practical. ▶ #32 00:30

The central account holds the power to act as root in members, so member root users no longer need passwords or MFA.

  • Remove long-term credentials from member-account root users. That also disables the “forgot password” recovery flow and removes the need to manage their MFA. ▶ #32 00:51
  • When you need root, use a root session: short-term credentials that expire within 15 minutes, used like role credentials. ▶ #32 01:02
  • Example: you locked yourself out of an S3 bucket with a policy that denies all principals. A root session fixes it. ▶ #32 01:21
  • The management account’s root is not covered: protect it with a strong password + hardware MFA/passkey.

The two capabilities and five task policies

Enabling it (IAM → Root access management) turns on trusted access for IAM in AWS Organizations. ▶ #32 02:31

Capability What it does
Root credentials management Delete and audit root credentials (password, access keys, MFA, signing certs) of member accounts; allow password recovery for specific accounts. New accounts are created without root credentials.
Privileged root actions in member accounts Take certain root actions in members (delete misconfigured S3/SQS policies) via sts:AssumeRoot.
  • Both can be enabled later in IAM → Account settings. ▶ #32 03:01
  • Delegated administrator for centralized root access — recommended: a member account, so you don’t rely on the management account. ▶ #32 03:10
  • Banner: forgot-password recovery will be blocked for root users of all member accounts with no root credentials.

Root sessions are always scoped to one task: ▶ #32 01:30

Task policy What it allows
IAMAuditRootUserCredentials Read-only view of root credential info and account info
IAMCreateRootUserPassword Re-enable account recovery (password) without existing root credentials
IAMDeleteRootUserCredentials Remove console password, access keys, signing certificates and MFA devices
S3UnlockBucketPolicy Edit/delete an S3 bucket policy that denies all principals
SQSUnlockQueuePolicy Same for an SQS queue policy

Deleting member root credentials

The Root access management page looks like Organizations (OU tree) but lives in IAM, with a Root user credentials column (Present / Not present). ▶ #32 03:40 Accounts created before the launch (~November 15, 2024 per the instructor) show Present, and at recording time you deleted them account by account. ▶ #32 04:00

  • Select the account → Take privileged action → Delete S3 bucket policy, Delete SQS queue policy or Delete root user credentials. ▶ #32 04:30
  • The page shows Console password last used (9 months ago) and Access keys last used (Never used).
  • Warning: root keys, password, signing certificates and MFA will be deleted; you can’t sign in as root; privileged root-only actions remain possible through root sessions; no recovery through forgot-password.
  • Type confirm → Delete. ▶ #32 04:51

After deletion the column shows Not present and the third action becomes Allow password recovery: you can re-enable recovery if ever needed, but ideally use root sessions instead. ▶ #32 05:11

Console demo: enable root access management and delete credentials ([▶ #32](https://youtu.be/rlD_TxBNZNg))
  1. Management account → IAM → Root access management (New). Intro (Improved security / Better compliance / Total control) → Enable. ▶ #32 02:20
  2. Leave both capabilities checked; leave delegated admin empty (skipped in the demo) → Enable. “Root access management enabled. You can now delete root user credentials for your member accounts from the Root access management page.” ▶ #32 03:28
  3. Open Root access management: OU tree (Infrastructure, Sandbox, Security, Suspended, Workloads + management account) with the Root user credentials column. ▶ #32 03:40
  4. Select the demo account → Take privileged action → Delete root user credentials → type confirm → Delete. “Root credentials deleted for AWS Account 396212980357.” Column → Not present. ▶ #32 04:30

AssumeRoot

New STS action AssumeRoot, via API or CLI. ▶ #32 05:40

Parameter / rule Value
Prerequisite Centralized root access enabled
Endpoint Regional STS endpoint only: the global endpoint is not supported
DurationSeconds 0–900, default 900 (15 min); higher values fail
TargetPrincipal Member account ID (required)
TaskPolicyArn One of the five task policies (required)
Response Temporary access key ID, secret access key, session token
Who can call Only the management account or the delegated admin, only against member accounts. Control with IAM on sts:AssumeRoot, scoped with sts:TaskPolicyArn
Audit Logged in CloudTrail
CLI ≥ 2.21.2 (upgrade from 2.21.1, e.g. brew upgrade awscli) ▶ #32 06:10

IAMAuditRootUserCredentials (first statement, from the docs on screen):

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyAllOtherActionsOnAnyResource",
      "NotAction": [
        "iam:ListAccessKeys",
        "iam:ListSigningCertificates",
        "iam:GetLoginProfile",
        "iam:ListMFADevices",
        "iam:GetAccountSummary",
        "iam:GetUser",
        "iam:GetAccessKeyLastUsed"
      ],
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyAuditingCredentialsOnNonRootUserResource",
      …
    }
  ]
}

The pattern is Deny with NotAction: everything except the listed read calls is denied, and a second statement denies those calls on any non-root IAM user resource.

CLI demo: assume root and audit the member ([▶ #32](https://youtu.be/rlD_TxBNZNg))
  1. With management account credentials (profile cybrdemo), check aws --version (2.21.2). The first attempt failed with Error parsing parameter '--task-policy-arn': Expected: '=', received: 'EOF': the parameter is a structure and needs arn=. ▶ #32 06:30
aws sts assume-root \
  --target-principal 396212980357 \
  --task-policy-arn arn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/root-task/IAMAuditRootUserCredentials \
  --profile cybrdemo

{
  "Credentials": {
    "AccessKeyId": "ASIA…",
    "SecretAccessKey": "…",

    "Expiration": "2024-11-20T21:40:47+00:00"

}
  1. Configure a profile with the temporary credentials. ▶ #32 08:40
aws configure --profile temproot            # access key id + secret
aws configure set aws_session_token <token> --profile temproot
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile temproot
# "Arn": "arn:aws:iam::396212980357:root"

aws iam get-account-summary --profile temproot   # AccountPasswordPresent: 0, AccountAccessKeysPresent: 0
aws iam list-access-keys --profile temproot      # "AccessKeyMetadata": []

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • “Root should never be used beyond the initial setup or in very rare circumstances.” ▶ #4 00:00
  • Root access keys: “if you’ve ever created an access key for your root user, go ahead and delete it immediately.” ▶ #4 01:20
  • Prefer hardware MFA for root. ▶ #4 01:34
  • Whoever controls the root email/phone can reset the root password. ▶ #4 02:21
  • Alert on every root sign-in/action. ▶ #4 02:40
  • “Do not proceed without doing these steps and actually creating an admin account.” ▶ #4 03:51
  • Keep one IAM break-glass user in the management account for IdP / Identity Center outages. ▶ #4 05:51
  • Root session credentials last 15 minutes: “don’t wait up”. ▶ #32 09:11
  • Recommended course of action: (1) remove remaining member root credentials, (2) decide on Privileged root actions (S3/SQS), (3) delegate root management to a member account, (4) lock down access, “almost no one should have access to it”, (5) monitor it “like a hawk”. ▶ #32 10:12

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Bucket policy denies all, including admins, in a member account sts:AssumeRoot with S3UnlockBucketPolicy from the management/delegated account, not a support case
Remove long-term root credentials in 200 member accounts / stop managing root MFA at scale Centralized root access, then delete root credentials
Detect root usage EventBridge rule + SNS, a CloudWatch Logs metric filter + alarm (CIS, older), or GuardDuty / Security Hub
Prevent root in member accounts from doing X SCP with aws:PrincipalArn arn:aws:iam::*:root (never affects the management account)
IAM admins can’t see billing despite billing permissions Root must activate IAM user and role access to Billing information
Identity Center / IdP is down, admins locked out Break-glass IAM user with MFA, stored securely, monitored, tested
AssumeRoot fails against sts.amazonaws.com Use a Regional STS endpoint
Need a root task not in the five (close account, change support plan) IAMCreateRootUserPassword to re-enable recovery, then use the root password
Updates since the videos
