  • New accounts created in an org with root credentials management enabled have no root credentials. Existing ones can be cleaned up at scale by scripting sts assume-root with IAMDeleteRootUserCredentials, then DeleteLoginProfile, DeleteAccessKey, DeactivateMFADevice, etc.
  • AWS now enforces MFA for root on management and standalone accounts.

Real-world practice

  • aws-samples/aws-iam-root-user-activity-monitor deploys CloudTrail → EventBridge → SNS hub-and-spoke. Root alerts produce almost no noise, so route them to paging (PagerDuty/Slack), not email only. Also alert on AssumeRoot events.
  • Give each account a unique, group-owned root email alias (e.g. aws+prod@company) on a shared mailbox with its own MFA.
  • Two-person rule: one custodian holds the root password, another the hardware MFA. Test the break-glass user and the root alert pipeline quarterly.
  • Prefer Identity Center for humans. The break-glass IAM user has a strong password + MFA, no access keys, and an alarm on its sign-ins.
  • Centralized root access rollout: delete remaining member root credentials (scriptable), decide on privileged root actions, delegate to a security account, give almost no one access, monitor closely. Write a break-glass runbook (who, from where, approval, alerting).
  • If you also have a “deny all root” SCP, test whether it blocks the unlock tasks before relying on them for break-glass. Works alongside Control Tower: enable from the management account and delegate to the Audit account.
aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal iam.amazonaws.com
aws iam enable-organizations-root-credentials-management
aws iam enable-organizations-root-sessions

aws sts assume-root --target-principal 444455556666 \
  --task-policy-arn arn=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/root-task/S3UnlockBucketPolicy
# then, with the returned credentials:
aws s3api delete-bucket-policy --bucket locked-bucket
Hands-on lab
  1. Enable centralized root access in a test org.
  2. Delete a member’s root credentials.
  3. Audit them with IAMAuditRootUserCredentials: get-account-summary should show AccountPasswordPresent: 0.
  4. Create the EventBridge root-login alert to an SNS email.
  5. Cleanup: delete the rule and topic.

IAM policies and policy evaluation logic

At a glance

JSON documents (Effect / Action / Resource / Principal / Condition) that AWS evaluates on every request. Effective permissions are the intersection of every policy layer that applies, and an explicit Deny anywhere wins.

  • Exam skills: least privilege, boundaries, session policies (4.2.3) · analyze authorization failures (4.2.4) · cross-account resource policies (4.2.1) · ABAC/RBAC (4.2.2) · correct unintended permissions (4.2.5) · temporary credentials & identity broker (4.1.2, 4.1.1) · SCP/RCP (6.1.3)
  • Videos: ▶ #14 Managed vs inline · ▶ #15 Identity-based vs resource-based · ▶ #16 Permissions boundaries · ▶ #17 Session policies · ▶ #18 How AWS decides allow or deny

Policy types at a glance

Type Attached to Grants? Notes
Identity-based (AWS managed, customer managed, inline) User, group, role Yes What the identity may do, in its own account or cross-account ▶ #15 00:11
Resource-based S3, KMS, SQS, SNS, Lambda, Secrets Manager, role trust policy… Yes Who may access the resource and with which actions ▶ #15 00:41
Permissions boundary User or role No (cap) Max permissions for one entity
SCP / RCP Org root, OU, account No (cap) Org guardrails on principals / resources
Session policy One role or federated session No (cap) Passed at AssumeRole / federation time
ACLs S3 buckets/objects etc. Yes Legacy cross-account grants

A policy can be as simple as allow-all (full admin if nothing else restricts it) or deny-all: ▶ #14 00:10

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" }]
}

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" }]
}
  • NotAction, NotResource and NotPrincipal invert matching. NotPrincipal with Deny is error-prone. Prefer conditions on aws:PrincipalArn.
  • Groups cannot be principals in policies, can’t be nested and can’t be assumed. Roles are used for cross-account access.

Managed vs inline policies

Identities (users, groups, roles) get permissions from JSON policy documents, attached in two ways. ▶ #14 00:00

Inline Managed
Relationship Created for a single identity (users Mark and Jane each with their own), “permanently glued” to it ▶ #14 00:51 Standalone; attach to many users, groups and roles at once and detach any time (“pluggable modules”) ▶ #14 02:11
Reuse None. Two people with the same job = two identical policies to maintain ▶ #14 01:10 Edit once → applies to every attached identity, or swap one policy for another ▶ #14 03:00
Lifecycle Deleted with the principal; strict 1:1 Customer managed: versioned (5 versions), can be rolled back
Size Aggregate per user 2,048, role 10,240, group 5,120 characters Max 6,144 characters
Verdict Typically discouraged ▶ #14 01:10 Preferred
  • Instead of per-user inline policies: share one managed policy, or better, put users in an IAM group with the policy so they inherit it. ▶ #14 01:41
  • Roles are identities too, so all of this applies to roles. ▶ #14 05:01 An identity can have both managed and inline policies at once. ▶ #14 05:11
  • Quota: up to 10 managed policies per user/role/group by default (adjustable to 20). Hitting limits → consolidate into customer managed policies.

Changing or swapping the policy at the group updates both users.

Managed type Who creates it Notes
Customer managed You, in your account Do whatever you want; can be created before you know who’ll use it (e.g., a CloudTrail read-only policy) ▶ #14 04:30
AWS managed AWS, available by default in every account Listed in the AWS Managed Policy Reference Guide: AdministratorAccess, AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess, AWSCloudTrail_ReadOnlyAccess. A great starting point but rarely an exact fit: copy and modify for least privilege ▶ #14 03:41

The ARN arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AWSCloudTrail_ReadOnlyAccess has aws in the account field, which marks an AWS managed policy. Policy version v1 (default): the default version is the one AWS evaluates on a request.

  • AWS managed policies can change when AWS updates them (new actions added), which can silently broaden access. Customer managed policies change only when you change them.
  • Job-function AWS managed policies (ViewOnlyAccess, SecurityAudit, ReadOnlyAccess, PowerUserAccess, …) are common correct answers for auditors and security teams.

Identity-based vs resource-based policies

  • Any policy attached to an IAM user, group or role is identity-based. ▶ #15 00:11
  • A resource-based policy is attached to a resource (classic example: S3 bucket policy; also KMS key policies). ▶ #15 00:41
  • EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies. Typical ones: S3 bucket policies, KMS key policies, IAM role trust policies, SQS/SNS policies, Secrets Manager secret policies, Lambda function policies, ECR repository policies, API Gateway resource policies, Backup vault policies.
  • There are no managed resource-based policies. They are all inline, created by the customer, because each is designed for a specific resource. “You can expect to get tested on that on your exam.” ▶ #15 04:10
Same account ▶ #15 01:00 Cross-account ▶ #15 03:31
Needs An Allow in either the identity or the resource policy, and no explicit deny An Allow in both: identity policy in account A (plus its SCP, boundary, session policy) and resource policy in account B, or assume a role there
Example Role reads an S3 bucket: identity policy grants read; the bucket policy allows or at least doesn’t deny. Even with no bucket policy, the identity policy is enough ▶ #15 01:21 Identity in A, bucket in B. Both must allow: “an extra layer of security” ▶ #15 03:42

Evaluation walk-through ▶ #15 02:11: the identity policy allows all S3 buckets; the bucket policy denies all S3 access unless the request comes from a specific source IP range. AWS evaluates both together:

  1. Any matching explicit Deny → denied, regardless of allows. “Explicit denies always win over allows.” ▶ #15 02:31
  2. Otherwise at least one Allow in either policy → allowed. ▶ #15 02:50
  3. No allow and no deny → implicit deny. ▶ #15 03:10

So requests from outside the IP range are denied even though the identity policy allows S3.

KMS key policies and role trust policies are special: IAM policies alone are not enough unless the key or trust policy delegates to the account ("Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root"}).

Permissions boundaries

A managed policy attached to a user or role (not groups, not resources) that sets the maximum permissions its identity-based policies can grant. Like an SCP it grants nothing. Effective = identity ∩ boundary. ▶ #16 00:10 Main use: delegate responsibilities without risking privilege escalation, especially when people can create, modify or update users’ and roles’ permissions. ▶ #16 00:30

Paul has AdministratorAccess and a boundary allowing only iam:CreateAccessKey, ec2:DescribeInstances, kms:ListKeys. He can do only those three actions; anything outside the boundary is implicitly denied. “That’s how powerful IAM permission boundaries can be.” ▶ #16 01:00

Emma (delegated role creation) ▶ #16 01:41

  • Emma, a senior developer, manages a team. Asking the security team for every new permission is a bottleneck that doesn’t scale.
  • The security team lets her create roles her team can assume and attach permissions, only if DevPermissionBoundaryPolicy is attached to each new or modified role. ▶ #16 02:01
  • She can’t modify that boundary. The security team defines it, and it limits whoever assumes the roles (people or services). ▶ #16 02:30
  • Enforce this with iam:CreateRole + condition iam:PermissionsBoundary = boundary ARN. Restrict the delegate’s Resource with a path (e.g., role/app/*) so they can’t modify admin roles, and deny iam:DeleteUserPermissionsBoundary / iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion on the boundary.
Policy: delegated role creation with a mandatory boundary 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "CreateRolesOnlyWithBoundary",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["iam:CreateRole", "iam:PutRolePolicy", "iam:AttachRolePolicy", "iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/app/*",
      "Condition": { "StringEquals": {
        "iam:PermissionsBoundary": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/DevBoundary" } } },
    { "Sid": "NoBoundaryTampering",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary", "iam:DeleteUserPermissionsBoundary",
                 "iam:CreatePolicyVersion", "iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion", "iam:DeletePolicy"],
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/DevBoundary",
                   "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/*"] }
  ]
}

Boundary vs SCP: decide by scope ▶ #16 03:02

SCP Permissions boundary
Where Account/OU/org level, via Organizations Inside one account, per user/role
Use when Org-wide or account-wide mandate Delegation for one or a few IAM entities
Scenario ▶ #16 03:41 Restrict which instance types/sizes employees can launch in staging accounts, and in which Region Dev accounts: team leads let members give roles to containerized apps for testing, but must limit what they can grant. Even if a member attaches an admin policy, the boundary restricts it while keeping flexibility ▶ #16 04:12
  • Resource-based policies are not limited by the boundary when they grant access directly to the IAM user ARN (same account). If they grant to the role ARN or the account, the boundary applies (▶ #18 flow).

Session policies

Passed as a parameter when you programmatically (CLI/API) assume a role or get a federated user session. They only narrow that one session: effective = role (or federated user) identity policies ∩ session policy. They can’t elevate privileges. ▶ #17 00:00

  • Passed in AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithSAML, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity or GetFederationToken, not GetSessionToken.
  • Inline (--policy, up to 2,048 characters) and/or up to 10 managed policy ARNs (--policy-arns). ▶ #17 01:52
  • Apply only to role and federated sessions, never IAM users. Identity Center permission sets and the console’s “switch role” can’t pass them: it is a CLI/SDK feature.
  • Two use cases: (1) limit your own permissions; (2) an identity broker limits a federated user’s credentials. ▶ #17 03:20 Very different from SCPs, RCPs, boundaries, identity/resource policies. ▶ #17 03:30

Scenario: Mike and the RDS databases ▶ #17 00:40

  • Mike, a security administrator for Amazon RDS across accounts, has admin on both testing and production databases.
  • He must maintain testing-db without accidentally touching production. ▶ #17 01:01
  • He assumes the RDSSecurityManagement role and passes a session policy allowing only specific DB actions on the testing DB. ▶ #17 01:11
  • For that session he can only perform those actions, although the role has admin on both. ▶ #17 01:42
CLI: assume a role with an inline or managed session policy

Standard form (the on-screen command wasn’t captured in the video frames):

aws sts assume-role \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/RDSSecurityManagement \
  --role-session-name mike-testing-db-maintenance \
  --policy file://testing-db-session-policy.json

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "rds:DescribeDBInstances",
        "rds:ModifyDBInstance",
        "rds:RebootDBInstance",
        "rds:CreateDBSnapshot"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:111122223333:db:testing-db"
    }
  ]
}

Managed policy as the session policy ▶ #17 02:01:

aws sts assume-role --role-arn <role-arn> --role-session-name <name> \
  --policy-arns arn=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:policy/TestingDbMaintenance

Inline JSON on the command line:

aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Ops \
  --role-session-name readonly-task \
  --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::reports/*"}]}'

Classic identity broker (pre-Identity Center): the broker authenticates the user against AD, calls GetFederationToken or AssumeRole with a session policy that scopes the user (e.g., only their S3 prefix home/${user}/), and returns temporary credentials or a console sign-in URL.

How AWS decides: the evaluation flowchart

The full flow for a request made by an IAM role. You don’t need to memorize it, but it tells you which layer to check on an AccessDenied, and why effective permissions are the intersection of all layers. ▶ #18 05:00

  1. Deny evaluation: start with Deny → evaluate all applicable policies → explicit Deny in any? → final Deny. “Explicit denies always win”, no matter how many allows. ▶ #18 00:20
  2. RCP: is the resource owned by an org with an applicable RCP? Then there must be an Allow at every level from root to the resource’s account (RCPs attach at root, OUs, accounts), else implicit deny. ▶ #18 00:40 That’s why enabling RCPs/SCPs creates the default RCPFullAWSAccess / FullAWSAccess policies. ▶ #18 01:01
  3. SCP: is the principal in an org with an applicable SCP? Same rule, root → principal’s account. ▶ #18 01:22
  4. Resource-based policy (next image).
  5. Identity-based policy: does the principal have one, and does it Allow? No → implicit deny. ▶ #18 03:20
  6. Permissions boundary: if there is one, it must Allow; no boundary → skip. ▶ #18 03:41
  7. Session policy: only for federated users and role sessions; it must Allow → final Allow. Not a session → skip → Allow. ▶ #18 04:01

Resource-based layer ▶ #18 01:40

  • Different account → the resource policy must Allow (else implicit deny), then continue to the identity-based flow: cross-account still needs the identity policy too. ▶ #18 01:50
  • Same account, no Allow → is the resource an IAM role or KMS key? Yes → implicit deny (trust and key policies must allow even same-account). No → continue to identity policies. ▶ #18 02:20
  • Same account, Allow → depends on who it names: ▶ #18 02:40
Resource policy allows… Next step
The session of the calling principal Final Allow ▶ #18 02:52
The role of the calling principal Skips identity-based policies, goes to the boundary check (boundary and session policy still apply) ▶ #18 03:00
The account of the calling principal Goes through identity-based policies ▶ #18 03:10
The IAM user ARN (user chart) Final Allow

IAM user variant ▶ #18 04:30: RCPs and SCPs are the same, boundaries and identity policies about the same, the resource-based section differs slightly, and session policies are removed.

  • A same-account resource policy that allows the user principal → final Allow.
  • One that allows the account → permissions boundary → identity-based policy (must exist and allow) → Allow. ▶ #18 04:48

Footnote on the chart: “Resource-based policies for services other than IAM and KMS may also require an explicit Allow statement within the same account to grant access. For more information, see the documentation for the specific service you’re working with.”

Other rules that matter:

  • Management account principals: SCPs don’t apply. Service-linked roles: SCPs and RCPs don’t apply.
  • An explicit Deny in an SCP/RCP can’t be overridden by any allow in the account, including the member account root user.
  • If a request gets past RCPs and SCPs, the problem is likely the resource policy, identity policy, boundary or session policy. ▶ #18 05:00 AWS makes all these decisions extremely quickly. ▶ #18 05:40

Troubleshooting AccessDenied

AccessDenied although IAM allows it? Check these
  1. Read the error first: it names the layer ("…explicit deny in a service control policy / resource control policy / identity-based policy / permissions boundary / session policy", or “…because no identity-based policy allows…” / “…no resource-based policy allows…”).
  2. Establish who the caller really is: aws sts get-caller-identity, CloudTrail userIdentity.arn with the session name. Many “permission” bugs are wrong-role or wrong-account problems.
  3. Check explicit deny, SCP or RCP, resource policy (bucket, key), permissions boundary, session policy, VPC endpoint policy.
  4. Cross-account: check four places: caller identity policy, caller’s SCP/boundary, resource policy, and (if encrypted) the KMS key policy in the resource account.
  5. Tools: IAM Policy Simulator (identity + boundary + SCP; resource policies for some services), IAM Access Analyzer (policy validation, custom policy checks), CloudTrail errorCode/errorMessage, sts decode-authorization-message.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Inline policies are discouraged because they can’t be reused; prefer groups + managed policies for people with the same job. ▶ #14 01:10
  • AWS managed policies are a starting point: copy and tighten them for least privilege. ▶ #14 04:20
  • Same account: identity or resource policy allow is enough. Cross-account: both must allow. ▶ #15 02:00
  • Troubleshooting authorization questions are expected on the exam. ▶ #15 04:32
  • Boundaries don’t grant access; they cap identity-based permissions. ▶ #16 00:21
  • Decide by scope: org/account-wide → SCP; per-entity delegation inside an account → boundary. ▶ #16 03:11
  • “Session policies cannot grant more access than the identity-based policy. So you can’t use them to elevate privileges.” ▶ #17 00:32
  • RCPs and SCPs need an Allow at every level of the org. ▶ #18 01:01
  • IAM roles and KMS keys need their own resource policy to allow, even in the same account. ▶ #18 02:20
  • Session policies apply only to federated users and roles, never IAM users. ▶ #18 04:01

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
IAM allows it but still AccessDenied Explicit deny, SCP/RCP, resource policy, boundary, session policy, VPC endpoint policy. Read the error message
Let developers create roles without escalating privilege / delegate IAM admin safely iam:CreateRole with iam:PermissionsBoundary = boundary ARN + deny editing/removing the boundary
Prevent anyone in the account/OU from… SCP
Per-entity delegation inside one account Permissions boundary
Restrict a single session further / temporarily restrict a highly privileged role for one task without changing it Session policy
Policy reusable and auditable across many roles Customer managed
Strict 1:1, deleted with the identity, can’t be attached elsewhere by mistake Inline
Need control over exactly when permissions change Customer managed (AWS managed can change)
Read-only access for auditors SecurityAudit / ViewOnlyAccess job-function policies
Find over-permissive policies Access Analyzer policy generation (from CloudTrail), last accessed info, unused access findings
Find resources shared outside the account/org Access Analyzer external access findings
Boundary on a group Not possible: boundaries apply to users and roles only, and never grant
Updates since the videos
  • The video narration lists an EC2 instance as an example of a resource-based policy. EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies.
  • Earlier versions of these notes listed resource policy → boundary → session → identity. The flowchart in ▶ #18 evaluates identity-based policies before the boundary and session policy. The result (intersection) is the same, but use the flowchart order when walking through an AccessDenied.
  • As drawn in ▶ #18, a session with no session policy passed is treated as “no restriction”. AWS docs evaluate session policies only when one was passed.
  • RCPs were added to the evaluation logic in late 2024; AWS’s official flowchart (including the cross-account variant) is updated when new policy types appear.

Real-world practice

  • Manage customer managed policies as code (Terraform/CloudFormation) and attach them to Identity Center permission sets, which accept AWS managed, customer managed (by name, must exist in each account) and one inline policy.
  • Watch ReadOnlyAccess: it allows reading data in some services (e.g., s3:GetObject, DynamoDB items). For pure config viewing use ViewOnlyAccess or SecurityAudit.
  • Inline policies are easy to miss in audits and IaC drift reviews. Inventory them with aws iam get-account-authorization-details.
  • Bucket policies are the usual place for guardrails that apply to every caller: deny non-TLS (aws:SecureTransport), deny outside VPC endpoint (aws:SourceVpce), deny outside org (aws:PrincipalOrgID), deny unencrypted puts. Identity policies stay least-privilege grants.
  • Be careful with Deny + NotPrincipal/IP conditions in bucket policies: you can lock out even admins. Only root can then delete the bucket policy (or centralized root sts:AssumeRoot with the S3UnlockBucketPolicy task).
  • Boundaries in self-service platforms: CI/CD pipelines or developers create roles via IaC, and the pipeline role’s policy requires the boundary on every role it creates (CDK: PermissionsBoundary.of(stack).apply(...)). Keep the boundary broad enough for workloads (deny IAM/Organizations/billing and security-service tampering, allow app services) and version-control it: changing it affects every bounded role at once.
  • Boundaries + SCPs + Access Analyzer unused-access findings together approximate least privilege without blocking teams.
  • Session policies suit automation that assumes a broad role but should touch one resource per run, and downscoping credentials handed to a less-trusted component (e.g., an app vending S3 credentials scoped to one tenant prefix). CloudTrail AssumeRole events show requestParameters.policy/policyArns, so you can audit which sessions were downscoped. Combine with source identity and a meaningful --role-session-name.
  • Keep AWS’s official Policy evaluation logic flowchart handy.
  • Encode org guardrails as denies (SCP/RCP), grants as identity/resource allows, and delegation limits as boundaries. That separation keeps the evaluation chain predictable to debug.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create role Dev with AdministratorAccess and a permissions boundary that allows only s3:* and logs:*.
  2. Assume it and try ec2:DescribeInstances: denied.
  3. Simulate the same call in the IAM Policy Simulator.
  4. Cleanup: delete the role and the boundary policy.

IAM condition keys you actually use

At a glance

The Condition block in identity- and resource-based policies allows or restricts a request based on its context (TLS, MFA, tags, source network, org, calling service), beyond the action, resource and principal.

  • Exam skills: design authorization controls, cross-account trust (4.2.1) · ABAC/RBAC, tag conditions (4.2.2) · least-privilege policies (4.2.3) · identity solutions, MFA (4.1.1) · require encryption in transit (5.1.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #19 IAM policy conditions you’ll actually use

Why conditions

Sometimes specifying resources and principals isn’t enough: you need other favourable conditions before granting access. ▶ #19 00:12 Exam questions often ask which policy solves a problem, so you need to recognise what legitimate conditions look like. ▶ #19 00:21

Condition keys to know

Key Use
aws:PrincipalOrgID / aws:PrincipalOrgPaths Allow only callers from your org or OU
aws:ResourceOrgID Identity policy: only touch resources in your org (data perimeter)
aws:SourceArn / aws:SourceAccount / aws:SourceOrgID Confused-deputy protection when an AWS service calls on your behalf
aws:SecureTransport Deny when false → force TLS
s3:TlsVersion Deny with NumericLessThan 1.2 → minimum TLS version
aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent / aws:MultiFactorAuthAge Require MFA, or recent MFA (e.g., NumericLessThanEquals 3600). Use BoolIfExists carefully; the key is absent for long-term access keys
aws:RequestedRegion Region restriction
aws:PrincipalTag/<k> / aws:ResourceTag/<k> / aws:RequestTag/<k> / aws:TagKeys ABAC
ec2:ResourceTag/<k> e.g., launch only AMIs tagged approved=true
rds:DatabaseEngine / rds:DatabaseClass Allow only certain engines and instance classes
aws:SourceIp Public IP only. Doesn’t work for traffic through a VPC endpoint
aws:SourceVpce / aws:SourceVpc Restrict to a VPC endpoint or VPC
aws:PrincipalArn Restrict to, or make exceptions for, specific roles (ArnEquals / ArnNotEquals)
aws:PrincipalIsAWSService Exclude AWS service principals from perimeter denies
aws:CalledVia / aws:ViaAWSService Request made by a service (e.g., CloudFormation) on the user’s behalf
aws:CurrentTime / aws:EpochTime Time-window access
sts:ExternalId Third-party cross-account role (confused deputy)
kms:ViaService, kms:EncryptionContext:* Limit KMS key use to a service or context
s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption / s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id Require SSE-KMS (with a specific key) on PutObject
iam:PassedToService Limit iam:PassRole to one service
  • S3 now encrypts all new objects with SSE-S3 by default, so “deny unencrypted PUT” questions are usually about requiring SSE-KMS with a specific key.

Operators and evaluation rules

Rule Meaning
...IfExists Passes when the key is missing
Null Checks whether the key is present
Several values in one key OR
Several keys / operators AND
ForAllValues / ForAnyValue For multi-valued keys like aws:TagKeys. ForAllValues with an empty set evaluates true → add a Null check
ArnEquals / ArnLike Use ARN operators for ARNs rather than string operators where possible

The MFA trap: Bool with aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: "true" in an Allow fails closed for key-only callers. But a Deny written as Bool … "false" fails open when the key is missing (long-term access-key calls have no key). For deny statements use BoolIfExists … "false" so key-less requests are also denied.

{ "Effect": "Deny", "Action": ["iam:*", "ec2:TerminateInstances"], "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": { "BoolIfExists": { "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "false" } } }

Six common condition patterns

1. Require TLS to access an S3 bucket

The bucket policy explicitly denies all S3 actions when the request does not use secure transport (HTTPS/TLS). This is the recommended way to enforce encrypted connections. ▶ #19 00:30

Both the bucket ARN (for bucket-level actions like ListBucket) and the object ARN (/*) are needed. The other five examples were narrated over talking-head footage and weren’t on screen.

Policy: deny all S3 access without TLS (as on the slide) 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Principal": { "AWS": "*" },
      "Action": ["s3:*"],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*",
        "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>"
      ],
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Compact form for a bucket named data:

{ "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::data", "arn:aws:s3:::data/*"],
  "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" } } }

For a minimum TLS version use s3:TlsVersion (NumericLessThan 1.2), not aws:SecureTransport.

2. Restrict access to a specific IAM role

To allow only specific principals (users or roles), use ArnEquals on aws:PrincipalArn with that principal’s ARN. ▶ #19 01:01 Typical form, as a bucket-policy deny for everyone else:

{
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": "s3:*",
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>", "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*"],
  "Condition": {
    "ArnNotEquals": { "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/AppRole" }
  }
}
3. Launch only approved AMIs

Allow ec2:RunInstances only if the AMI has tag key approved with value true. AMIs without the tag are denied. ▶ #19 01:20 The second statement allows the other resources RunInstances touches.

Policy: RunInstances only from AMIs tagged approved=true 
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "ec2:RunInstances",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*::image/ami-*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": { "ec2:ResourceTag/approved": "true" }
  }
},
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "ec2:RunInstances",
  "Resource": [
    "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*", "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:network-interface/*",
    "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:subnet/*", "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:security-group/*", "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:volume/*"
  ]
}
4. Allow only certain RDS engines and instance classes

StringEquals checks that users only create MySQL or Aurora MySQL databases with instance class db.t4g.large. Any other value → creation fails. ▶ #19 01:41

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "rds:CreateDBInstance",
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "rds:DatabaseEngine": ["mysql", "aurora-mysql"],
      "rds:DatabaseClass": "db.t4g.large"
    }
  }
}
5. Assume a cross-account role only with MFA

Only allow users to assume a cross-account role if they authenticated with an MFA device. ▶ #19 02:12 Trust policy on the role:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:root" },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
  "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true" } }
}

CLI users get MFA-backed credentials with GetSessionToken (with MFA), then the aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition passes.

6. Require recent MFA (MFA age)

NumericLessThanEquals on aws:MultiFactorAuthAge = 3600 (seconds = 1 hour): the user can deactivate their MFA only if they signed in with MFA in the last hour. ▶ #19 02:31

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "iam:DeactivateMFADevice",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::*:user/${aws:username}",
  "Condition": { "NumericLessThanEquals": { "aws:MultiFactorAuthAge": "3600" } }
}

Many more condition examples exist; these six are a refresher. ▶ #19 02:51

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Expect “which policy would solve the problem” questions; recognise valid conditions. ▶ #19 00:21
  • Enforce HTTPS/TLS in S3 bucket policies. ▶ #19 00:41
  • MFA can be required for cross-account role assumption, and MFA age can be enforced for sensitive actions. ▶ #19 02:12

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
aws:SourceIp restriction breaks after adding an S3 gateway endpoint aws:SourceVpce or aws:SourceVpc
Require MFA for sensitive API calls by CLI users GetSessionToken with MFA + aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition
Deny-without-MFA statement doesn’t block access-key calls Use BoolIfExists … "false", not Bool
ForAllValues with an empty set evaluates true Add a Null check
Only allow deactivating MFA if signed in with MFA recently NumericLessThanEquals aws:MultiFactorAuthAge 3600
Third-party vendor assumes a role sts:ExternalId
AWS service writes to my bucket/queue aws:SourceArn / aws:SourceAccount
Require a minimum TLS version for S3 s3:TlsVersion, not aws:SecureTransport
Only callers from my org may access aws:PrincipalOrgID
Deny unencrypted uploads Require SSE-KMS with s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption(-aws-kms-key-id)
Limit which service a role can be passed to iam:PassedToService
Updates since the videos
  • The narration says “MySQL or MySQL” for the RDS engine example; it most likely means MySQL or Aurora MySQL.
  • The policy JSON for patterns 2–6 is the standard form; only the TLS policy was on screen.
  • S3 now encrypts all new objects with SSE-S3 by default.
  • The “approved AMI” pattern is now better done with EC2 Allowed AMIs (account/declarative-policy setting) plus Image Builder golden AMIs, but tag-condition policies still appear in exam questions.

Real-world practice

  • Put a TLS-only deny on every S3 bucket (AWS Config rule s3-bucket-ssl-requests-only, Security Hub control S3.5). Do the same for SQS/SNS with aws:SecureTransport.
  • Self-service MFA policies (iam:*MFADevice on ${aws:username}) with an MFA-required deny for everything else are the standard pattern for any remaining IAM users.
  • Use BoolIfExists in MFA deny statements so long-term access keys are covered.
Hands-on lab
  1. Add the TLS-deny statement to a test bucket.
  2. Run aws s3 ls s3://bucket --endpoint-url http://s3.<region>.amazonaws.com: denied.
  3. Run the same over HTTPS: allowed.
  4. Cleanup: delete the bucket.

IAM roles (trust policies, service roles, service-linked roles, instance profiles)

At a glance

An identity with no long-term credentials. Principals listed in its trust policy assume it through STS and get temporary credentials (access key ID + secret access key + session token). Every role has both a trust policy (who may assume it) and permissions policies (what it can do).

  • Exam skills: role trust policies (4.2.1) · temporary credentials (4.1.2) · IdP federation (4.1.1) · least privilege (4.2.3) · instance profiles, service and execution roles (3.2.2) · prepare access for incidents (2.1.2) · SCP limits (6.1.3)
  • Videos: ▶ #13 What are IAM roles? · ▶ #20 Trusted entity types · ▶ #21 Creating a service role · ▶ #22 Service-linked roles
  • AssumeRole session: default 1 hour, configurable 15 min – 12 h

IAM users vs IAM roles

  • An IAM user represents you or other people who manage resources in an account. Credentials: username + password with a sign-in link for the console, and/or an access key for the CLI, scripts and API calls. ▶ #13 00:11
  • Those are long-term credentials: they never expire unless changed manually or forced by rotation policies. Even then they typically live days to months, sometimes years, which is not ideal for security. ▶ #13 00:31
  • Roles are like users only in that you give them permissions by attaching policies. ▶ #13 01:10

IAM user IAM role
Credentials Password and/or access keys (long-term) No username/password; access keys with a session token that expires (short-term) ▶ #13 01:21
API call carries aws_access_key_id + aws_secret_access_key aws_access_key_id + aws_secret_access_key + aws_session_token. The key pair only works with its session token ▶ #13 01:41
Lifetime Until changed AssumeRole default 1 hour, 15 minutes → 12 hours ▶ #13 02:10
Used by One person Assumed by users or services ▶ #13 03:00
  • Once expired, a session token can never be reused; you must get new credentials. An attacker who steals them has limited time: credentials committed to GitHub are useless the next day, unlike an IAM user’s long-term keys. ▶ #13 02:30
  • Max session duration is a role setting (1–12 h, default 1 h). The caller requests DurationSeconds up to that max. Role chaining (a role assuming another role) is capped at 1 hour regardless. Console sessions via federation: up to 12 h.

Roles are assumed (“hats” you wear for a task) ▶ #13 04:10

  • Human: during an incident, an IR team member assumes a security analyst role with access only to services like CloudTrail and Amazon Athena. While in the role you give up your prior user’s permissions. You can switch back any time, or you fall back when the credentials expire unless renewed. ▶ #13 03:11
  • Service: an EC2 instance running a web app that needs S3 data gets a role with S3 permissions and obtains temporary credentials automatically behind the scenes. ▶ #13 03:50

Benefits ▶ #13 04:20

  1. Least privilege with task-specific roles: prevents accidental deletions/modifications and makes attackers escalate privileges to do damage. ▶ #13 04:30
  2. Clear audit trail: a user assumes the analyst role for analysis, then a break-glass role for containment and eradication. Actions are logged separately per role, so it’s easy to trace what was done, when and by whom. ▶ #13 05:11
  3. Cross-account access (delegation): in multi-account orgs, users assume roles in other accounts for day-to-day tasks. ▶ #13 04:51

Trust policy vs permissions policy

Every role has two kinds of policy: ▶ #20 02:21

  • Trust policy: a resource-based policy attached directly to the role that says who may assume it. Its Principal element names who or what. Confusing because roles are identities and resource-based policies usually aren’t associated with identities, but it is separate from the identity policies.
  • Permissions policies: identity-based, saying what the role can do. ▶ #20 02:52

Who can assume a role ▶ #20 00:31

  • IAM users.
  • IAM Identity Center users (via the AWSReservedSSO_* roles it creates in each member account).
  • Other roles: role chaining.
  • AWS accounts (principals in them) → cross-account access.
  • AWS services: EC2, CodeBuild, Lambda and many more.

The Roles page (23 roles in the demo member account) shows each role’s trusted entity: ▶ #20 01:10

  • AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_…, _ReadOnly_…, _SecurityBreakGlass_…, _SecurityDeploy_… → Identity Provider: arn:aws:iam::<acct>:saml-provider/… (Identity Center permission sets).
  • AWSServiceRoleForAccessAnalyzer, …ForCloudTrail, …ForConfig, …ForIncidentManager, …ForOrganizations, …ForSSO, …ForSupport, …ForTrustedAdvisor, …ForCloudFormationStackSetsOrgMember → AWS Service: <service> (Service-Linked Role).
  • “Last activity” helps spot unused roles.

Example: AWSServiceRoleForOrganizations (“Service-linked role used by AWS Organizations to enable integration of other AWS services with Organizations”), path role/aws-service-role/organizations.amazonaws.com/, max session 1 hour. It was created automatically with the member account. ▶ #20 01:21

The Permissions tab holds the AWS managed AWSOrganizationsServiceTrustPolicy. Despite the name it is a permissions policy (Sid, Effect, Action, Resource), e.g. iam:DeleteRole on arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws-service-role/organizations.amazonaws.com/* and iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole on *. ▶ #20 01:31

The Trust relationships tab looks similar but has a totally different purpose. No conditions here, though conditions are possible: ▶ #20 01:50

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Service": "organizations.amazonaws.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}

Trusted entity types

In Create role you first pick a trusted entity type. Each one just generates a different Principal (and action/conditions) in the trust policy. ▶ #20 04:02

Type Use it for Options shown
AWS service A service (EC2, Lambda, CodeBuild, …) assumes the role and acts in this account “Service or use case” dropdown listing all supporting services
AWS account Entities in other AWS accounts, yours or third parties (contractors, monitoring services) This account (auto-filled ID) or Another AWS account; Require external ID (“best practice when a third party will assume this role”, avoids the confused deputy) ▶ #20 05:02; Require MFA ▶ #20 05:11
Web identity Users federated by an external web IdP Login with Amazon, Amazon Cognito, Facebook, Google, OIDC; “Create new” provider; optional conditions
SAML 2.0 federation Users from a corporate directory via SAML 2.0 Provider dropdown; access: programmatic only or programmatic and AWS Management Console; attribute/condition; sign-in endpoints (Regional / Non-Regional)
Custom trust policy Edge cases, or when you just know the JSON JSON editor with “Add actions for STS”, “Add a principal”, “Add a condition”
  • Web identity: a user logs in through Amazon Cognito and assumes the role to read S3 images from your mobile app. Create/configure the identity provider first, then optionally add conditions. ▶ #20 06:10
  • SAML: a standard that lets an IdP authenticate users and pass identity information to a service provider, enabling SSO. In the demo the only provider is AWSSSO_98f792794ae8bcbc_DO_NOT_DELETE, created by IAM Identity Center in every member account. You can create a separate one. ▶ #20 06:31

  • Custom trust policy: a raw editor, sometimes faster than clicking. With CLI/API or IaC you must pass a custom trust policy anyway; the other types are console helpers that generate it. ▶ #20 08:30

The editor’s STS actions: AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithSAML, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AssumeRoot, DecodeAuthorizationMessage, SetContext, SetSourceIdentity, and (tagging) TagSession. Starting template: ▶ #20 07:41

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "Statement1",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {},
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}

Principal type ↔ STS API

Principal API
AWS account / role / user sts:AssumeRole
SAML: {"Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<acct>:saml-provider/<name>"} sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML
Web identity/OIDC: {"Federated": "cognito-identity.amazonaws.com"} or the OIDC provider ARN (GitHub Actions, EKS IRSA) sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
  • sts:TagSession must be allowed in the trust policy when session tags are passed.
  • Trusting "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root" means the whole account (any principal its admins allow). Name a specific role ARN for least privilege.
  • In trust policies, MFA = "Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}; external ID = "StringEquals": {"sts:ExternalId": "…"}.
Console demo: inspect a role and the trusted entity types ([▶ #20](https://youtu.be/kPgSsv0hFj0))
  1. Member account → IAM → Roles → filter for AWSServiceRoleForOrganizations → open it. ▶ #20 01:10
  2. Permissions tab → expand AWSOrganizationsServiceTrustPolicy (what the role can do). ▶ #20 01:31
  3. Trust relationships tab → the trust policy (who can assume it). ▶ #20 01:50
  4. Roles → Create role → step through each type: AWS service → use-case dropdown; AWS account → this/another account, external ID, MFA; Web identity → provider dropdown; SAML 2.0 → Identity Center provider, access level; Custom trust policy → editor. ▶ #20 04:02

Service roles and execution roles

A service role is a role you create and own, which an AWS service assumes to access other services on your behalf (e.g., Config, CodeBuild). An execution role is the Lambda or ECS task variant.

The service principal changes per service ▶ #21 00:20

  • Use case EC2 (other EC2 use cases exist, e.g. Spot Fleet) → "Service": ["ec2.amazonaws.com"], default description “Allows EC2 instances to call AWS services on your behalf”. ▶ #21 00:30

  • Use case Lambda → "Service": ["lambda.amazonaws.com"], “Allows Lambda functions to call AWS services on your behalf”. ▶ #21 01:01 The Organizations role had organizations.amazonaws.com: the principal is whatever service must assume the role.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole"],
      "Principal": { "Service": ["lambda.amazonaws.com"] }
    }
  ]
}

Permissions: AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole ▶ #21 01:21

  • Searching “lambda” in the 1,033 permission policies shows 21 matches: AWSLambda_FullAccess, AWSLambda_ReadOnlyAccess, AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole, AWSLambdaDynamoDBExecutionRole, AWSLambdaENIManagementAccess, AWSLambdaKinesisExecutionRole, AWSLambdaMSKExecutionRole, AWSLambdaRole, …
  • AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole (“Provides write permissions to CloudWatch Logs”): logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, logs:PutLogEvents on *. ▶ #21 01:41
  • CloudWatch Logs basics: services write to log groups containing log streams; the service needs these three actions to create the group/stream and push events. ▶ #21 02:01
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "logs:CreateLogGroup",
        "logs:CreateLogStream",
        "logs:PutLogEvents"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

Using the role from Lambda ▶ #21 02:40

  • Execution role options: Create a new role with basic Lambda permissions (default; creates myTestFunction-role-xxxx with permission to upload logs, i.e. what was just built by hand), Use an existing role, Create a new role from AWS policy templates. The console warns not to delete or edit the trust/permissions policies during creation. ▶ #21 03:00
  • With Use an existing role, the dropdown showed only 3 roles although the account has 20+: the console only lists roles whose trust policy allows Lambda to assume them. ▶ #21 03:11

  • No credentials in code: the blueprint only has console.log(...) calls and return event.key1. The function gets temporary credentials through its role at run time. ▶ #21 03:41 This removes hard-coded credentials (passwords, API keys, secret access keys), e.g. keys committed to GitHub repos, which many organizations still do. ▶ #21 04:10
  • Without the logs permissions in the role, the test would get AccessDenied. ▶ #21 05:01

  • Log group /aws/lambda/myTestFunction with one log stream. Defaults: log class Standard, retention Never expire, no KMS key, no data protection. ▶ #21 05:10
  • It works only because the trust policy lets Lambda assume the role and the permissions policy allows the Logs actions. ▶ #21 05:32
Console demo: create a Lambda service role and use it ([▶ #21](https://youtu.be/N0IjkE2-jME))
  1. IAM → Roles → Create role → AWS service → use case EC2 → pick any policy → review shows ec2.amazonaws.com in the trust policy. Cancel. ▶ #21 00:30
  2. Repeat with Lambda → Next → search and select AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole → Next → name lambda-function-role (any name, default description) → Create role. ▶ #21 01:12
  3. Lambda → Create function → Use a blueprint → “Hello world function” (nodejs18.x; runtime doesn’t matter, “this exam does not focus on code at all”) → name myTestFunction. ▶ #21 02:40
  4. Execution role Use an existing role → lambda-function-role (only 3 roles listed) → Create function. ▶ #21 03:11
  5. Code tab → Test → test event my test event with {"key1":"value1","key2":"value2","key3":"value3"} → Status Succeeded, response "value1", plus function logs. ▶ #21 04:32
  6. Monitor → View CloudWatch logs → /aws/lambda/myTestFunction → log stream with the same lines. ▶ #21 05:10
  • Lambda execution role ≠ Lambda resource-based policy: the execution role is what the function can do; the resource policy is who can invoke the function (S3, API Gateway, another account).
  • iam:PassRole is required to hand a role to a service. Restrict it with the role ARN plus iam:PassedToService:
{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "iam:PassRole",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/app/web-ec2",
  "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "iam:PassedToService": "ec2.amazonaws.com" } } }

Service-linked roles (SLRs)

A special role linked to and owned by one AWS service, which assumes it to perform actions. Not the same as a service role. ▶ #22 00:10

Service role Service-linked role
Created by You The service (e.g., automatically when you enable GuardDuty)
Permissions You choose and edit Predefined by AWS; can’t edit, can’t attach others, even as admin ▶ #22 00:20
Trust You write it Predefined; usually only that service can assume it ▶ #22 01:10
Name / path Any AWSServiceRoleFor<Service>, path /aws-service-role/<service-principal>/, label “(Service-Linked Role)”
Delete Any time Only after removing dependent resources or disabling the service ▶ #22 00:31
SCPs / RCPs Apply Don’t apply
Pick when Custom permissions needed Service needs to act with AWS-defined permissions
  • Why: predefined with all required permissions to call other services, so setup is easier. ▶ #22 00:51
  • SLRs are not meant to be reused between services or identities and can’t be, not meant for users to assume, and not for custom use cases. Their only purpose is to give that service what it needs. ▶ #22 04:41
  • Creating one requires iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole (usually implicit when you enable the service). To stop users enabling a service, deny iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole with the iam:AWSServiceName condition, or deny the service’s actions via SCP. Some services allow a custom suffix (e.g., AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling_<suffix>) for multiple SLRs.
  • Enabling a service with Organizations trusted access often creates SLRs in every member account. CloudTrail records SLR calls with userIdentity.type = AssumedRole and invokedBy = <service>.amazonaws.com.

Which services support SLRs ▶ #22 01:22

IAM docs → AWS services that work with IAM → columns Service, Actions, Resource-level permissions, Resource-based policies, ABAC, Temporary credentials, Service-linked roles (scroll right). Most services don’t; quite a few do, e.g. CloudTrail, CloudWatch Logs, AWS Config. In the frame: CloudHSM Yes, CloudTrail Yes, CloudFront Partial, CloudWatch Partial, API Gateway Yes, AppIntegrations Yes, Cloud9 Yes; CloudFormation, Cloud Map, CloudSearch, CloudShell No. ▶ #22 01:41

Recognising SLRs in the Roles list ▶ #22 02:10

  • Demo account (24 roles), mostly SLRs: AWSServiceRoleForAmazonGuardDuty, …AmazonGuardDutyMalwareProtection, …AmazonInspector2, …AmazonMacie, …Config, …ConfigRemediation, …ECS, …ElasticLoadBalancing, …NetworkFirewall, …Organizations, …SecurityHub, …SSO, …Support, …TrustedAdvisor.
  • Contrast: CloudTrailRoleForCloudWatchLogs, CloudTrailLake-us-east-1-CybrDemo, AccessAnalyzerMonitorServiceRole_… show AWS Service: cloudtrail / access-analyzer without the SLR label = ordinary service roles. ▶ #22 02:30 “Last activity” shows when each was last used.

Inspecting AWSServiceRoleForAmazonGuardDuty (“A service-linked role required for Amazon GuardDuty to access your resources”, max session 1 hour) ▶ #22 02:40

  1. ARN path: arn:aws:iam::272281913033:role/aws-service-role/guardduty.amazonaws.com/AWSServiceRoleForAmazonGuardDuty = /aws-service-role/ + service namespace + role name. ▶ #22 02:50
  2. Permissions: one AWS managed policy AmazonGuardDutyServiceRolePolicy (8 policy versions). You can’t add another policy or edit this one. ▶ #22 03:11

Summary: Allow 7 of 404 services: EC2 (Limited: List, Tagging, Write), EKS (Read, List, Tagging, Write; condition aws:TagKeys = GuardDutyManaged), ECS (ecs:account-setting = guardDutyActivate), IAM (Limited: Write; iam:AWSServiceName = malware-protection.guardduty.amazonaws.com, i.e. only creating the Malware Protection SLR), Lambda (Read), Organizations (Read, List), S3 (Read, List).

The JSON is a couple of hundred lines, starting with Sid: GuardDutyGetDescribeListPolicy, Effect: Allow, actions such as ec2:DescribeInstances, ec2:DescribeImages, ec2:DescribeVpcEndpoints, ec2:DescribeSubnets, ec2:DescribeVpcPeeringConnections, ec2:DescribeTransitGatewayAttachments, organizations:ListAccounts, organizations:DescribeAccount, organizations:DescribeOrganization, s3:GetBucketPublicAccessBlock, s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration, s3:GetBucketTagging, s3:GetAccountPublicAccessBlock, …

  1. Trust policy: only guardduty.amazonaws.com may assume it. ▶ #22 03:30
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "guardduty.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}

You could build an identical role by hand, but the SLR, authored by AWS and created automatically when you enable GuardDuty, saves a lot of time. ▶ #22 03:51 You can’t delete it without disabling GuardDuty. ▶ #22 04:20

Console demo: identify and inspect a service-linked role ([▶ #22](https://youtu.be/2EZ4yn18Np4))
  1. Docs → AWS services that work with IAM → scroll right to Service-linked roles. ▶ #22 01:22
  2. IAM → Roles → identify SLRs by the name prefix and “(Service-Linked Role)” label; compare with the CloudTrail service roles. ▶ #22 02:01
  3. Open AWSServiceRoleForAmazonGuardDuty → check the ARN path → Permissions tab (can’t add/edit) → open the AWS managed policy → Summary and JSON. ▶ #22 02:40
  4. Trust relationships tab → only guardduty.amazonaws.com can sts:AssumeRole. ▶ #22 03:30

Instance profiles, paths and session hygiene

  • Instance profile: the container that attaches a role to EC2. Credentials come from IMDS (169.254.169.254) and rotate automatically. Enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) to block SSRF credential theft. The console creates the instance profile automatically; CLI/IaC must create it explicitly.
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id i-0abc \
  --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1
  • Stolen instance credentials → GuardDuty UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS / .InsideAWS. Prevent with IMDSv2 and optionally aws:EC2InstanceSourceVPC / aws:EC2InstanceSourcePrivateIPv4 conditions.
  • IAM paths (/app/, /security/) group roles so policies can target arn:aws:iam::acct:role/app/*. Identity Center roles live under /aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/.
  • Attribution across role hops: sts:SourceIdentity (persists through role chaining) and session names; CloudTrail userIdentity.sessionContext.
  • Revoking active role sessions: temporary credentials can’t be deleted. Use Revoke active sessions (inline deny with aws:TokenIssueTime), deny via SCP/policy, or detach the instance profile and rotate. See the AWS STS section.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Long-term credentials (passwords, access keys) are the core weakness roles were designed to overcome. ▶ #13 00:50
  • Remember the numbers: 1 hour default, 15 min – 12 h for AssumeRole; expired session tokens can never be reused. ▶ #13 02:10
  • Separate roles per IR phase (analyst vs break-glass) give a clean, attributable audit trail. ▶ #13 05:20
  • Trust policy = who can assume; permissions policy = what it can do. Roles have both. ▶ #20 03:40
  • With third parties, require an external ID to avoid the confused deputy; you can also require MFA. ▶ #20 05:02
  • Service roles and service-linked roles are not the same: know the difference. ▶ #20 03:31
  • With CLI/API/IaC you always supply a custom trust policy. ▶ #20 08:30
  • Roles give temporary credentials, the fix for hard-coded keys in code and repos. ▶ #21 04:00
  • Missing execution-role permissions → AccessDenied at run time; a role won’t show in a service’s picker if its trust policy doesn’t trust that service. ▶ #21 03:22
  • SLRs can’t be edited, used by users or reused across services; delete only after removing dependents. Spot them by the AWSServiceRoleFor prefix, the label and the /aws-service-role/ path. ▶ #22 02:10

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
EC2 app needs S3 access, no keys on disk / hard-coded access keys in code Instance profile role (Lambda execution role, ECS task role). Never keys in code, env vars or AMIs
On-prem workload needs AWS credentials IAM Roles Anywhere
“Temporary credentials” STS / roles / Identity Center
“Long-term credentials” IAM users: rotate keys, use the credential report / Access Advisor to find stale ones
Stolen instance credentials used from outside AWS GuardDuty InstanceCredentialExfiltration; prevent with IMDSv2 + aws:EC2InstanceSourceVPC
User can launch EC2 with an admin role (privilege escalation) Tighten iam:PassRole
Lambda can’t write to DynamoDB Execution role permissions, not the resource policy
Lambda logs missing in CloudWatch Execution role lacks logs:CreateLogGroup/CreateLogStream/PutLogEvents
Need custom permissions for a service Service role
Service must act with AWS-defined permissions Service-linked role
Deny-all SCP but GuardDuty/Config still work SLRs aren’t restricted by SCPs
Mobile app needs AWS access Cognito identity pools (web identity), not embedded IAM user keys
Find roles trusting external accounts IAM Access Analyzer
Role chaining session longer than 1 h fails Chaining is capped at 1 hour
Updates since the videos
  • The GuardDuty SLR trust policy JSON is reconstructed from the narration; only guardduty.amazonaws.com is trusted.

Real-world practice

  • Most organizations now have zero IAM users except a break-glass user. Humans come in through IAM Identity Center (roles), workloads through service roles, CI/CD through OIDC federation (e.g., GitHub Actions → AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity). Scope OIDC trust with sub/aud conditions, or anyone using that IdP can assume the role.
  • Pre-create IR roles (SecurityAnalyst read-only with CloudTrail/Athena/Detective access, SecurityBreakGlass for containment) in every account via StackSets, with MFA and alerts on assumption.
  • Keep role session duration as short as practical. 12-hour sessions are convenient but widen the exposure window of leaked credentials.
  • Never delete the AWSSSO_…_DO_NOT_DELETE SAML provider or AWSReservedSSO_* roles by hand. Identity Center manages them; edit the permission set instead.
  • Add aws:SourceAccount / aws:SourceArn conditions to service-principal trust policies where supported (cross-service confused deputy). Use SCPs to stop member accounts creating roles that trust arbitrary external accounts, and review trust policies with Access Analyzer.
  • AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole uses Resource: "*"; for least privilege scope it to arn:aws:logs:<region>:<acct>:log-group:/aws/lambda/<fn>:*. One role per function. Set log-group retention (default Never expire) and consider a KMS key.
  • Restrict iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs and iam:PassedToService conditions.
  • Don’t delete SLRs to “clean up”: deletion fails while resources exist, and you’ll break the service. The IAM console’s Delete role check lists the resources still using it.
  • IaC for org-wide service enablement must handle SLRs that already exist (iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole errors if present): use AWS::IAM::ServiceLinkedRole or skip-if-exists logic.
  • Review AWS managed policy updates attached to SLRs (policy version history) in change management. AWS can add permissions when a service gains features.
  • Minimal service-role trust policy for EC2:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" }] }
Hands-on lab
  1. Launch a t3.micro with an instance profile whose role allows s3:ListAllMyBuckets.
  2. Require IMDSv2 (--http-tokens required).
  3. On the instance, get a token (curl -X PUT .../api/token) and fetch the role credentials with it.
  4. Cleanup: terminate the instance, delete the role and the instance profile.

Cross-account access and the confused deputy

At a glance

Giving a principal in one account access to resources in another, either by assuming a role there or through a resource-based policy, and protecting those trust relationships from being abused by a “confused deputy”.

  • Exam skills: cross-account resource policies and role trust policies (4.2.1) · temporary credentials (4.1.2) · analyze authorization failures (4.2.4) · identify and correct unintended permissions (4.2.5)
  • Videos: ▶ #23 Cross-account access with roles · ▶ #24 The confused deputy attack

Two cross-account patterns

Assume a role in the target account Resource-based policy
How Trust policy on the role (destination account B) names the source account or role; the source identity policy (account A) allows sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN Policy on the resource (S3, KMS, SQS, SNS, Lambda, Secrets Manager) allows the external principal, and its identity policy allows too
Caller’s identity Gives up its original permissions for the session Keeps its own identity and permissions
When needed Default for humans and workloads When the caller must read from A and write to B in one call (e.g., S3 copy)
Missing a side AccessDenied on sts:AssumeRole AccessDenied on the resource call
  • Cross-account KMS: the key policy must allow the external account and the external principal needs an IAM Allow. Same for Secrets Manager plus the CMK that encrypts the secret (the default aws/secretsmanager key can’t be shared, so use a CMK).
  • Within the same account, a trust policy naming the specific user ARN is enough on its own (it is a resource-based policy). Cross-account, the identity side must also allow.

Cross-account access with a role

A user in account A needs resources in account B. Creating the same user in both accounts means two sets of credentials. Instead, the user assumes a role in account B that grants access there. ▶ #23 00:11 The user gets no credentials in B; it calls STS AssumeRole and receives temporary credentials for the role. Setup order: create the role in B with the right trust policy, give the user in A permission to assume it, then test. ▶ #23 00:32

1. Create the role in account B ▶ #23 01:00

  • Trusted entity AWS account → Another AWS account (not This account, which would put the current account ID in the trust policy) → paste account A’s 12-digit ID. ▶ #23 01:10
  • Require external ID (“Best practice when a third party will assume this role”): not needed here, no third party. ▶ #23 01:31 Require MFA: the assuming entity must have authenticated with MFA. These options add Condition blocks (sts:ExternalId, aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent) to the trust policy.
  • Permissions: AWS managed AmazonECSFullAccess (demo only). Role name ECSFullAccess: remember it for the identity policy and the switch-role form. ▶ #23 01:51
  • The review screen shows the principal as AWS + account A’s ID; after creation the Trust relationships tab shows arn:aws:iam::<accountA>:root. ▶ #23 02:22 The summary also shows Maximum session duration: 1 hour (default) and a “Link to switch roles in console”.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::488075507604:root"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
      "Condition": {}
    }
  ]
}

The :root principal means any identity in account A whose own policies allow it can assume the role. Ideally be more specific: not every identity in the other account should be able to. ▶ #23 02:41

2. Allow the user in account A to assume it ▶ #23 03:01

IAM user Biscuit (arn:aws:iam::488075507604:user/Biscuit, console access “Enabled without MFA”) has no permissions. Add an inline policy allowing sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN (replace the placeholder 111122223333 with account B’s ID); the policy name doesn’t matter. ▶ #23 03:23

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": {
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::396212980357:role/ECSFullAccess"
  }
}

3. Switch role ▶ #23 04:20

  • Console multi-session support: account menu → Add session, sign in as Biscuit. Several sessions can be active side by side.
  • As Biscuit the console home shows Access denied widgets: expected, Biscuit only has sts:AssumeRole.
  • Add session → Switch role: account B’s ID, role name ECSFullAccess, a display color. ▶ #23 05:01

The header shows ECSFullAccess @ 3962…: Biscuit now operates in account B through the role and can use ECS. ▶ #23 05:31

Console demo: cross-account role and switch role ([▶ #23](https://youtu.be/yvSwNz5G5xk))
  1. Two browser windows: account B cybrdemo (3962-1298-0357) on the left, account A 4880-7550-7604 on the right, both as an admin SSO session. ▶ #23 00:40
  2. Account B: IAM → Roles → Create role → AWS account → Another AWS account → paste account A’s ID. Leave Require external ID and Require MFA unchecked → Next. ▶ #23 01:10
  3. Attach AmazonECSFullAccess, name the role ECSFullAccess, create. ▶ #23 01:51
  4. Open the role → Trust relationships to see the :root principal. ▶ #23 02:22
  5. Account A: IAM → Users → Biscuit → Add permissions → Create inline policy → JSON with sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN → name it → Create policy. ▶ #23 03:23
  6. Account menu → Add session → sign in as Biscuit in account A; switch the Region to N. Virginia. ▶ #23 04:31
  7. As Biscuit: Add session → Switch role → Account ID = B, role name = ECSFullAccess, color = blue → Switch Role. ▶ #23 05:01
  8. Header shows ECSFullAccess @ 3962…; open ECS: full access is available. ▶ #23 05:31

Recap: who needs what ▶ #23 06:02

Policy Where Says
Trust policy On the role being assumed, in the destination account (B) Who or what can assume this role: at minimum a specific user/role in the other account, at maximum the whole account (:root)
Identity-based policy On the user/role in the source account (A) Allow sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN (here an inline policy on Biscuit)

Both sides are required. “Remember the order in which this goes because you might get tested on that in your exam.” ▶ #23 06:11

What :root, sessions and CloudTrail tell you

  • :root in a Principal ≠ the root user. It means “the account”: the account delegates the decision to its own IAM policies, so any principal in A with sts:AssumeRole permission can assume the role. To restrict, name specific role ARNs, or keep :root and add conditions like aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:PrincipalArn, aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, sts:ExternalId, sts:SourceIdentity.
  • If a trusted role is deleted and recreated, the trust policy shows a unique principal ID (AROA…) and breaks: re-save the trust policy.
  • Max session duration 1–12 h (default 1 h); DurationSeconds can’t exceed it. Role chaining caps the session at 1 hour.
  • CloudTrail logs AssumeRole (event source sts.amazonaws.com) in both the caller’s account and the role’s account. Use it to trace who did what in B.
  • To revoke an assumed cross-account session: the role’s Revoke active sessions (inline deny with aws:TokenIssueTime less than now).

The confused deputy problem

A security issue where an entity without permissions coerces an entity that has them (the deputy) into performing an action it wouldn’t otherwise have performed. ▶ #24 01:30

The MonitoringCorp example ▶ #24 01:51

  1. Your account has MonitoringRole (arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/MonitoringRole) protecting your resources (GuardDuty, Lambda, S3…). A third party, MonitoringCorp, assumes it to monitor you: it is now a deputy acting on your behalf. ▶ #24 02:00
  2. MonitoringCorp signs up another, malicious customer, EvilKitty, who learns your role ARN through reconnaissance. ▶ #24 02:22
  3. During onboarding EvilKitty gives your role ARN to MonitoringCorp, claiming it is their own. ▶ #24 02:41
  4. Without an external ID, MonitoringCorp (which does have trust to your role) assumes it and shows your account’s data to EvilKitty: a complete inside look. The deputy is “confused”. ▶ #24 02:52
  5. With an external ID: legit calls use AssumeRole w/ external ID c20f49df (yours) and retrieve data. MonitoringCorp told EvilKitty “Here’s your external ID: t11a3cff. What’s your role ARN?” When it calls AssumeRole on your role with t11a3cff, the condition doesn’t match, STS refuses credentials → AccessDenied: incorrect external ID, and the vendor investigates. ▶ #24 03:22

External ID for third parties

  • Option Require external ID in Create role, added as a condition in the role’s trust policy. ▶ #24 00:00
  • Use it for third parties, typically contractors or software services, that likely work with other customers too. Not needed for roles used by your own employees. ▶ #24 00:11
  • It should be a completely random string generated by the third party, not by you, unique per customer, ideally different for each of your AWS accounts. ▶ #24 00:32
  • Flow: ask the vendor for the string → paste it when creating the role (or set it via CLI/API) → the vendor must pass it on every AssumeRole, or the call fails. ▶ #24 00:50
  • It is not a secret (not like a password, access key or API key). ▶ #24 01:11 Technically optional, but a recommended best practice because it prevents the confused deputy. ▶ #24 01:21
  • External ID applies only to sts:AssumeRole from another AWS principal. It is not used for web identity or SAML.
  • Most vendors (Datadog, Wiz, Snowflake, etc.) supply a CloudFormation template that already contains their account principal and your unique external ID.
{ "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::999988887777:root" },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
  "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "sts:ExternalId": "c7f1-unique-customer-id" } } }

aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::222233334444:role/Auditor \
  --role-session-name audit --external-id c7f1-unique-customer-id

Checking at scale ▶ #24 04:10: how do you know which of thousands of roles across dozens or hundreds of accounts are vulnerable? First build an inventory of every third-party service with access (many orgs lack one), then review the roles they assume and verify each uses an external ID. ▶ #24 04:21 (The sponsor, Sonrai Security, showed a “Third Party Access” list: Cloudflare, Databricks, FireEye, KubeCost, NETSCOUT, Palo Alto Networks, SailPoint, ServiceNow… with accounts, last IAM access and Granted/Partially Blocked status. ▶ #24 04:31)

Cross-service confused deputy (AWS services)

When an AWS service acts on your resource (SNS → SQS, CloudTrail → S3, Config → S3), add aws:SourceArn and/or aws:SourceAccount (or aws:SourceOrgID) in the resource policy, so another account can’t point the service at your resource.

{ "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "sns.amazonaws.com" },
  "Action": "sqs:SendMessage", "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-1:111122223333:alerts",
  "Condition": { "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-1:111122223333:sec-topic" } } }
Deputy Protection
Third-party SaaS assuming your role sts:ExternalId in the trust policy
AWS service writing to your resource aws:SourceArn / aws:SourceAccount / aws:SourceOrgID in the resource policy
Cross-account access failing? Check these
  • AccessDenied on sts:AssumeRole → check both the trust policy in B and the identity policy in A. Adding a resource policy to an S3 bucket in A is irrelevant for role assumption.
  • Trust policy has an sts:ExternalId or MFA condition the caller didn’t satisfy.
  • Trusted role was recreated → trust policy shows AROA…; re-save it.
  • Requested DurationSeconds above the role’s max, or above 1 hour when role chaining.
  • Cross-account KMS/Secrets Manager error → secret uses the AWS managed key; re-encrypt with a CMK and grant the key policy + IAM.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Know which policy goes where: you might get tested on the order. ▶ #23 06:11
  • The trust policy says who or what can assume the role and lives on the role in the destination account. ▶ #23 06:20
  • The identity in the source account also needs sts:AssumeRole in an identity-based policy. ▶ #23 06:30
  • Trusting the whole account (:root) works, but ideally restrict to specific principals. ▶ #23 02:41
  • External ID is for third parties, not internal employees. ▶ #24 00:11
  • It must be generated by the third party, unique per customer (ideally per account), and is not a secret. ▶ #24 00:32
  • Its purpose is to prevent the confused deputy problem. ▶ #24 01:21

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Third-party monitoring vendor needs read access to your account Cross-account role with ExternalId, not IAM user keys
Prevent another customer of the vendor from accessing your account sts:ExternalId condition
“Keep the external ID in Secrets Manager”, “rotate it like a password”, “generate it yourself” Distractors: it isn’t a secret, and the vendor generates it
Cross-account AssumeRole fails Trust policy in B and identity policy in A
S3 objects uploaded by account B unreadable by bucket owner A Object Ownership = Bucket owner enforced (ACLs disabled)
Cross-account Secrets Manager fails with a KMS error Re-encrypt with a CMK and grant the key policy
Revoke an assumed cross-account session Role’s Revoke active sessions (aws:TokenIssueTime deny)
AWS service (SNS, CloudTrail, Config) writes to your resource aws:SourceArn / aws:SourceAccount
Read from A and write to B in one call Resource-based policy (caller keeps its identity)

Real-world practice

  • In AWS Organizations, people rarely use IAM users + switch role; they use IAM Identity Center permission sets. Cross-account roles are still the standard for workloads: CI/CD pipelines, central security tooling (a security account’s role assuming read-only roles in member accounts), log shipping, backup.
  • Prefer trusting a specific role ARN over :root, also for vendors where they document it.
  • Use a permissions boundary or SCP to stop people in the source account granting themselves sts:AssumeRole on arbitrary roles.
  • Inventory third-party trust with IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzers (org zone of trust) and check each role for an sts:ExternalId condition.
  • Review vendor AssumeRole events in CloudTrail; unexpected AccessDenied from a vendor may mean misconfiguration or an attempted confused-deputy attack.
Hands-on lab
  1. In account B create role Auditor trusting account A with an sts:ExternalId condition.
  2. From account A, assume it with --external-id: succeeds.
  3. Assume it without the ID: fails with AccessDenied.
  4. Cleanup: delete the role.

ABAC and RBAC

At a glance

Two models for organizing permissions: by job function (RBAC) or by matching attributes (ABAC). In AWS the attributes are tags on the principal and on the resource.

  • Exam skills: ABAC and RBAC strategies with tags/attributes (4.2.2) · least-privilege policies (4.2.3) · tagging strategy (6.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #25 ABAC and RBAC for access control
  • Most organizations use a hybrid of the two.

RBAC: role-based access control

RBAC uses roles (job functions) to decide access. An Engineering “role” authorizes engineering activities; a Finance “role” authorizes finance activities but not engineering. A user assigned to a role gets access to that role’s resources. ▶ #25 00:23

Two rows: Engineering “Role”: Engineering User → Permissions → Resources (ECS, Secrets Manager, Lambda). Finance “Role”: Finance User → Permissions → Resources (Cost Explorer / billing). The note “(not referring to IAM roles)” stresses that the “role” is a job function.

  • “Role” means the person’s organizational role, not specifically an IAM role. In AWS you implement RBAC with IAM groups, by assuming IAM roles, or with permission sets. IAM roles are just one implementation. ▶ #25 00:40
  • RBAC predates AWS: NIST notes it was formalized in 1992 by David Ferraiolo and Rick Kuhn and became ANSI/INCITS 359-2004 (revised 359-2012). ▶ #25 01:00

Benefits ▶ #25 01:20

  • Easy to align with business logic: assign roles by department.
  • A person can have multiple roles; mix and match.
  • Easy to update: add access for a new resource to the role and everyone in it receives it.
  • Easy to audit, because role permissions are clearly defined. ▶ #25 01:50

Downside: it grows complex quickly as people are added, and the number of policies grows with every new project or resource. At large scale it becomes a “nightmare”. ▶ #25 02:00

ABAC: attribute-based access control

ABAC uses attributes instead of roles. In AWS, attributes = tags (key/value pairs) that can be added to most resources and to IAM principals. ▶ #25 02:20 Example: billing resources in S3 tagged billing = finance; users in the finance department get the same tag. On each request AWS compares the tags and allows or denies. ▶ #25 02:30

ABAC can use attributes of resources and users, and also of the environment and application state. ▶ #25 03:02

The identity policy allows three actions on *, but only when the secret’s project tag equals the principal’s project tag: ▶ #25 03:32

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": [
    "secretsmanager:GetResourcePolicy",
    "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
    "secretsmanager:UpdateSecret"
  ],
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "secretsmanager:ResourceTag/project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/project}"
    }
  }
}
Secret tag User tag Result
project = cybrlabs project = cybrlabs Allowed
project = cybrlabs project = cybrvideos Denied (no match → implicit deny) ▶ #25 04:00

Benefits ▶ #25 04:30

  • Permissions scale easily and quickly, especially with many users and teams.
  • New resources only need the right tags; access is granted automatically, with no constant updating of user permissions. ▶ #25 04:41
  • Teams move faster, not blocked by permission changes. ▶ #25 04:51
  • Granular permissions without a policy change for every new user or resource. ▶ #25 05:01
  • You can still audit attributes to determine access.
  • Tags also serve cost allocation and discovery: a user tagged project = cybrlabs and costcenter = 1234; the cost-center tag drives monthly spend reports per cost center. ▶ #25 05:21

Cost: it takes more thought and effort to set up correctly.

Condition keys and where principal tags come from

Key Matches
aws:ResourceTag/<key> Tag on the resource. Service-specific forms: secretsmanager:ResourceTag, ec2:ResourceTag
aws:PrincipalTag/<key> Tag on the calling user/role, or a session tag
aws:RequestTag/<key> Tag being set in the request (force tagging on create)
aws:TagKeys Tag keys being set in the request

Principal tags come from:

  • IAM user or role tags.
  • Session tags passed in AssumeRole, the SAML attribute https://aws.amazon.com/SAML/Attributes/PrincipalTag:<key>, or IAM Identity Center attributes for access control. TransitiveTagKeys keep tags through role chaining.
  • Cognito identity pools, which can map user attributes to principal tags.

Not every service or action supports resource-tag authorization. Check the Service Authorization Reference.

Protecting the tags

If users can change the tags, they can grant themselves access.

  • Deny iam:TagUser / TagRole / UntagRole and resource TagResource / UntagResource / ec2:CreateTags changes to the ABAC keys for non-admins.
  • Require tags at creation with aws:RequestTag.
  • Tag policies (Organizations) standardize tag keys and values but don’t enforce tagging on create by themselves. Combine them with SCP aws:RequestTag conditions.

RBAC vs ABAC

RBAC ABAC
Grants by Job function (group, role, permission set) Matching principal tags and resource tags
Setup Easier to implement initially More thought and effort to set up correctly
Growth Policy count grows with each project/resource One policy covers new tagged resources
Flexibility Less flexible Flexible and fast-moving
Auditing Easy: role permissions are clear Harder to answer “who can access X?”
Best for Small, stable orgs Many teams/projects, fast-changing environments

Most of the time use both (hybrid) to get the best of each. ▶ #25 06:02

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Don’t equate RBAC with IAM roles. RBAC is a general model; IAM roles and groups are ways to implement it. ▶ #25 01:10
  • RBAC becomes a “nightmare” at scale, and that’s where ABAC comes in. ▶ #25 02:00
  • ABAC attributes in AWS = tags. ▶ #25 02:20
