  • Hybrid is usually best: ABAC is harder to set up, RBAC is less flexible. ▶ #25 06:02

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Hundreds of projects, minimize policy updates as projects are added ABAC with aws:PrincipalTag / aws:ResourceTag
New resources created constantly, avoid updating policies each time ABAC
Department attribute from the corporate IdP should drive access Session tags via SAML or Identity Center ABAC
User could re-tag a resource (or themselves) to gain access Deny tag modification on that key
“RBAC” in the question The general model, not only IAM roles

Real-world practice

  • Typical ABAC rollout: Identity Center permission sets + IdP attributes as session tags + resource tagging enforced by IaC (CloudFormation/Terraform default tags) + SCPs that deny untagged creates.
  • ABAC cuts the policy count but makes “who can access X?” harder to answer. IAM Access Analyzer and tag inventories (Resource Groups Tagging API, AWS Config) help with auditing.
  • Cost allocation tags must be activated in the Billing console before they appear in Cost Explorer/CUR.
  • Example policy: start/stop EC2 only on instances with your project tag, and never change the project tag:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ec2:StartInstances", "ec2:StopInstances"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*",
      "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:ResourceTag/project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/project}" } } },
    { "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["ec2:CreateTags", "ec2:DeleteTags"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "ForAnyValue:StringEquals": { "aws:TagKeys": ["project"] } } }
  ]
}
  • Passing a session tag that survives role chaining:
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Dev \
  --role-session-name alice --tags Key=project,Value=alpha --transitive-tag-keys project
Hands-on lab
  1. Tag two EC2 instances project=alpha and project=beta.
  2. Attach the start/stop ABAC policy above to a role.
  3. Assume the role with session tag project=alpha and try stopping both instances. Only the alpha one stops.
  4. Cleanup: terminate the instances.

IAM auditing tools (credential report, Access Advisor, Policy Simulator)

At a glance

Built-in IAM tools to inventory credentials, see which permissions are actually used, and test policies without making real calls.

  • Exam skills: analyze authorization failures (4.2.4) · identify and correct unintended permissions (4.2.5) · troubleshoot authentication (4.1.3) · root user management (6.1.5) · audit evidence (6.3.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #33 IAM credentials report
  • A credential report is cached for 4 hours, and the CLI returns it base64-encoded.

Credential report: what it answers

A manager asks for a report of all users in an AWS account, when they were created, whether they have credentials (passwords, access keys, MFA devices), and when passwords and access keys were last used. The answer is the IAM credential report, with no third-party tools needed. ▶ #33 00:21

  • An account-wide CSV of every IAM user plus the root user: creation time, password status / last use / last change, MFA status, and status / rotation / last use of both access keys and both signing certificates.
  • It is per account, not org-wide. For many accounts, run it through a cross-account role, or use Access Analyzer.
  • Permissions: only iam:GenerateCredentialReport is needed to generate it ▶ #33 00:31; downloading also needs iam:GetCredentialReport.
  • Use it for compliance checks such as “find users without MFA or with keys older than 90 days”, and to drive the migration away from IAM users and long-term keys toward Identity Center. ▶ #33 06:20

Generating and reading the report in the console

IAM → Access reports → Credential report (also linked from the dashboard). The page says: “The credentials report lists all your IAM users in this account and the status of their various credentials. After a report is created, it is stored for up to four hours.” ▶ #33 00:41

The 4-hour rule: you can only create a new report every 4 hours. Within that window you get the existing, possibly slightly outdated report, and the CLI behaves the same; there is no way around it. If the last one is older (5–7 hours), a fresh one is generated. ▶ #33 00:50

The demo account has only the <root_account> row (arn:aws:iam::299551924423:root). ▶ #33 01:22 Columns: ▶ #33 01:30

Column(s) Demo value / note
user, arn, user_creation_time <root_account>
password_enabled TRUE: root still has a password
password_last_used, password_last_changed
password_next_rotation not_supported for root
mfa_active TRUE: important for root in a management account
access_key_1_active FALSE
access_key_1_last_rotated, _last_used_date, _last_used_region, _last_used_service same set for key 2
cert_1_active, cert_1_last_rotated, cert_2_active, cert_2_last_rotated signing certificates
  • No active access keys: good, especially for root. ▶ #33 02:02
  • The root row always appears. It is great for verifying compliance, and you’d want to automate it on a schedule. ▶ #33 02:11

Credential report from the CLI

  1. aws sts get-caller-identity --profile cybrdemo shows AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_…/christophe in 299551924423. ▶ #33 02:30
  2. aws iam generate-credential-report returns {"State": "COMPLETE"} because one exists from the past 4 hours. Otherwise it returns State: STARTED with “No report exists. Starting a new report generation task.” It takes seconds, maybe a minute or two for big accounts. ▶ #33 02:40
  3. aws iam get-credential-report returns JSON with Content (gibberish), ReportFormat: "text/csv" and GeneratedTime. Despite text/csv, Content is base64-encoded. ▶ #33 03:20
  4. Decode with --output text --query Content | base64 -D to get a readable but dense CSV. ▶ #33 03:50
  5. Pipe into awk to print one labelled line per field. Good for automation instead of downloading and processing the CSV. ▶ #33 04:32

CLI demo: generate, fetch, decode and format the report ([▶ #33](https://youtu.be/xK69zkQpEcg)) 
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile cybrdemo
aws iam generate-credential-report --profile cybrdemo
# { "State": "COMPLETE" }   (or "STARTED" + "No report exists. Starting a new report generation task.")
aws iam get-credential-report --profile cybrdemo
# { "Content": "dXNlcixhcm4s...", "ReportFormat": "text/csv", "GeneratedTime": "2024-12-10T19:48:37+00:00" }
aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content --profile cybrdemo | base64 -D   # macOS; Linux: base64 -d
# user,arn,user_creation_time,password_enabled,password_last_used,password_last_changed,password_next_rotation,mfa_active,
# access_key_1_active,access_key_1_last_rotated,access_key_1_last_used_date,access_key_1_last_used_region,
# access_key_1_last_used_service,access_key_2_active,...,cert_1_active,cert_1_last_rotated,cert_2_active,cert_2_last_rotated
# <root_account>,arn:aws:iam::299551924423:root,2023-10-26T18:21:23Z,true,2024-05-04T21:18:34Z,2023-10-26T18:21:23Z,
# not_supported,true,false,N/A,N/A,N/A,N/A,false,N/A,N/A,N/A,N/A,false,N/A,false,N/A

The awk step (partly visible on screen) is of the form:

aws iam get-credential-report --output text --query Content --profile cybrdemo | base64 -D | \
awk -F, 'NR>1 {
  print "User:", $1; print "ARN:", $2; print "Creation Time:", $3; print "Password Enabled:", $4;
  print "Password Last Used:", $5; print "Password Last Changed:", $6; print "Password Next Rotation:", $7;
  print "MFA Active:", $8; print "Access Key 1 Active:", $9; … print "Access Key 2 Active:", $14;
  print "Access Key 2 Last Rotated:", $15; print "Access Key 2 Last Used Date:", $16;
  print "Access Key 2 Last Used Region:", $17; print "Access Key 2 Last Used Service:", $18;
  print "Cert 1 Active:", $19; print "Cert 1 Last Rotated:", $20; print "Cert 2 Active:", $21;
  print "Cert 2 Last Rotated:", $22; print "-------------------"
}'

Finding unused permissions

  • Last accessed information (Access Advisor) (GenerateServiceLastAccessedDetails): per user, role, group or policy, which services and actions were last used. Use it to trim permissions. Organizations also shows last accessed data per OU or account, for SCP design.
  • IAM Access Analyzer unused access: org-wide findings for unused roles, keys, passwords and permissions (paid).
  • AWS Config managed rules: access-keys-rotated, iam-user-unused-credentials-check, mfa-enabled-for-iam-console-access, root-account-mfa-enabled, iam-root-access-key-check. Security Hub CIS/FSBP controls use the same signals.

Testing policies and troubleshooting denials

Tool Use
IAM Policy Simulator Test identity policies, permissions boundaries, SCPs and some resource policies against chosen actions and resources, without real calls. CLI: aws iam simulate-principal-policy / simulate-custom-policy
CloudTrail Filter errorCode = AccessDenied. Error messages now name the policy type that denied, e.g. “with an explicit deny in a service control policy”
Encoded authorization message aws sts decode-authorization-message for EC2 and some other services

Tool comparison

Need Tool
Who has which long-term credentials, and are they used? Credential report
Which services/actions has this principal used? Last accessed information (Access Advisor)
Unused access across the org IAM Access Analyzer unused access
Continuous evaluation of keys/MFA AWS Config rules, Security Hub
Will this policy allow the call? Policy Simulator, Access Analyzer custom policy checks
Why was this call denied? CloudTrail AccessDenied, decode-authorization-message
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • “If you need a report on users and … information related to their credentials, then you can use this IAM credentials report.” ▶ #33 06:11
  • Reports can only be regenerated every 4 hours; within that window you get the cached one. ▶ #33 00:50
  • CLI content is base64-encoded even though the format says text/csv. ▶ #33 03:30
  • Use it to help migrate off IAM users and long-term keys toward Identity Center. ▶ #33 06:20

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Report of all users, when created, whether they have passwords/keys/MFA, and when those were last used Credential report (no third-party tool)
List all IAM users with access keys older than 90 days Credential report, or Config rule access-keys-rotated for continuous evaluation
Remove unused permissions from a role Last accessed data, IAM Access Analyzer unused access, or policy generation
Test a new policy before deploying Policy Simulator or Access Analyzer custom policy checks
Why can’t I get a fresh credential report? It’s cached for 4 hours

Real-world practice

  • Automate: a scheduled Lambda (EventBridge Scheduler) assumes a read role in each account, runs generate/get, decodes, writes to S3, and alerts on old or unused keys and users without MFA.
  • With centralized root access management (Organizations) you can remove root credentials from member accounts; the report then shows root password_enabled=false.
  • A user with no password and no keys still exists as an identity. Delete unused users rather than just deactivating keys, and use the report to drive the migration from IAM users to Identity Center.
  • Useful commands:
aws iam generate-credential-report && aws iam get-credential-report \
  --query Content --output text | base64 -d > cred-report.csv
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Dev \
  --action-names s3:GetObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::reports/q1.csv
aws sts decode-authorization-message --encoded-message <msg>
aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details --arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Dev
Hands-on lab
  1. Generate the credential report, decode it, and filter for mfa_active=false.
  2. Simulate a denied call for a role with simulate-principal-policy.
  3. Make the real call, find the CloudTrail AccessDenied event and compare it with the simulator result.
  4. Cleanup: none needed.

AWS STS (temporary credentials)

At a glance

The AWS Security Token Service issues short-lived credentials (access key ID starting ASIA… + secret key + session token) for roles, federated users and MFA-protected sessions.

  • Exam skills: issue temporary credentials (4.1.2) · troubleshoot authentication (4.1.3)
  • Videos: no dedicated video. STS is covered in ▶ #13 and ▶ #20 (see IAM roles), ▶ #17 (see IAM policies and policy evaluation logic), ▶ #23 (see Cross-account access and the confused deputy), ▶ #28 and ▶ #31 (see AWS IAM Identity Center)
  • Temporary credentials can’t be revoked individually: deny by issue time or remove permissions.

STS APIs

API Who calls Notes
AssumeRole IAM user or role 15 min → the role’s max session (≤12 h, default 1 h). Role chaining is capped at 1 h
AssumeRoleWithSAML SAML IdP users Enterprise federation. Identity Center is preferred now; its roles trust a SAML provider
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity OIDC tokens (Cognito identity pool, EKS IRSA, GitHub Actions) No AWS credentials needed to call
GetSessionToken IAM user MFA-protected API access. 15 min – 36 h (default 12 h). No session policy
GetFederationToken IAM user Custom federation broker, 15 min – 36 h. A session policy is required to grant anything
AssumeRoot Management / delegated admin account Root-only tasks in member accounts, 15 min

Where the videos cover these:

  • Temporary credentials, durations and the STS API per principal type: see IAM roles. ▶ #13 ▶ #20
  • Session policies on AssumeRole / GetFederationToken: see IAM policies and policy evaluation logic. ▶ #17
  • sts:AssumeRole across accounts: see Cross-account access and the confused deputy. ▶ #23
  • AssumeRoleWithSAML, ASIA… keys and SSO profiles: see AWS IAM Identity Center. ▶ #28 ▶ #31

Recognizing temporary credentials

Key ID prefix Meaning
ASIA… Temporary STS credentials (role session, Identity Center, GetSessionToken)
AKIA… Long-term IAM user or root keys

Useful in leaked-credential and CloudTrail questions.

  • sts:SourceIdentity survives role chaining and is recorded in CloudTrail, so you can see who really acted.
  • sts:RoleSessionName can be enforced in trust policies.
  • Regional STS endpoints are preferred (lower latency, isolation). Regions that are disabled by default must be activated for STS.

Revoking sessions

Temporary credentials can’t be revoked one by one. The IAM console’s Revoke active sessions attaches an inline deny policy AWSRevokeOlderSessions with aws:TokenIssueTime DateLessThan now:

{ "Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": { "DateLessThan": { "aws:TokenIssueTime": "2026-11-18T10:00:00Z" } } }
  • Existing tokens stay valid until expiry, but every call they make is denied.
  • Deleting the role also kills them.
  • For an EC2 role compromise, also look at aws:EC2InstanceSourceVPC-style conditions, detach the instance profile and rotate.
Exam tips

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Leaked temporary credentials of a role Revoke active sessions (deny by aws:TokenIssueTime), then investigate. Rotating keys doesn’t apply
CLI user must use MFA aws sts get-session-token --serial-number ... --token-code ...
Mobile app users need direct AWS access Cognito identity pool → AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
CI/CD (GitHub) without stored keys OIDC provider + role with a token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub condition
Developers need CLI access to many accounts without long-term keys Identity Center + aws configure sso (see AWS IAM Identity Center)
Access key ID starts with ASIA Temporary STS credentials, not an IAM user key

Real-world practice

  • GitHub Actions OIDC trust policy, scoped to one repo and branch:
{ "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com" },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com" },
    "StringLike": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main" } } }
Hands-on lab
  1. Assume a role and save the temporary credentials.
  2. In the IAM console, open the role and choose Revoke active sessions.
  3. Retry a call with the old credentials: it is denied.
  4. Cleanup: remove the inline deny policy AWSRevokeOlderSessions.

AWS IAM Identity Center

At a glance

Workforce SSO (successor to AWS SSO) to all accounts in the org and to SAML/OAuth apps. Users sign in once to the AWS access portal, see every account and permission set assigned to them, and get only temporary credentials. It is the recommended replacement for IAM users (keep IAM users only for break-glass).

  • Exam skills: identity solutions, IdP integration, MFA (4.1.1) · temporary credentials (4.1.2) · troubleshoot authentication and permission sets (4.1.3) · ABAC and RBAC (4.2.2) · least privilege and boundaries (4.2.3) · deploy AWS Organizations (6.1.1) · delegated admin (6.1.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #27 IAM users vs Identity Center users · ▶ #28 Enable Identity Center · ▶ #29 Delegating administration · ▶ #30 Permission sets from delegated admin · ▶ #31 Assuming Identity Center roles
  • Two timers: permission set session (1–12 h, default 1 h) vs access portal session (default 8 h).

Why not IAM users

Up to this point the course used a single admin IAM user for console work. Before deploying resources in the multi-account setup, identity and access management must be set up properly. ▶ #27 00:00 IAM users “have a time and a place”, but they are not the best option for human identities. AWS best practice is a centralized identity provider using federation: either direct federation (IdP → IAM role via SAML/OIDC) or IAM Identity Center. ▶ #27 00:22

An IAM user works like a user on any other system: a username and password, optional MFA, and access keys for calling the AWS API. ▶ #27 01:21 Three problems:

Problem Why it hurts
Yet another set of credentials ▶ #27 01:42 Every workforce member needs a brand-new account just for AWS, although they already have one in the corporate directory (e.g. Active Directory). They remember another password or, worse, reuse the corporate one, and re-authenticate when switching apps: frustrating, error-prone, less secure. Admins manage identities “all over the place”: a nightmare. ▶ #27 02:20
Exists in only one account ▶ #27 02:30 To give one person access to 20, 100 or 1,000 accounts you’d recreate the user in every account. The work-around, roles assumed cross-account, works and many orgs still use it, but has its own challenges and limits. ▶ #27 02:50
Long-term access keys ▶ #27 03:01 Keys never expire unless deactivated or deleted. They get stolen or found and used by a threat actor, potentially years later. Many past breaches came from leaked access keys. ▶ #27 03:21

The better approach: central IdP + federation

A centralized IdP lets you centrally manage workforce users, enforce authentication policies and control authorization. Users authenticate once to the IdP, then federate into other applications with one set of credentials: single sign-on (SSO). ▶ #27 03:50 Analogy: “Sign in with Google” on an unrelated website. Google authenticates you, tells the site, and shares some attributes; no new username/password/MFA per site. ▶ #27 04:01

  1. Workforce Users → Login → Identity Provider (Entra ID, Okta, or Identity Center’s own directory). The only place users hold a password + MFA.
  2. Identity Provider → Federation → IAM Identity Center. The IdP asserts who the user is (SAML 2.0) and, typically, which groups they belong to.
  3. Identity Center → Account A, Account B … Account N. Based on assignments (user/group + permission set + account), it lets the user into each account with an IAM role it provisioned there. One identity, many accounts. ▶ #27 04:51
  • The IdP is connected to the corporate directory, usually integrated with the HR system, so joiner/mover/leaver is handled automatically in one place. ▶ #27 04:50
  • Instead of deploying users to 1,000 accounts, you assign users and groups to AWS accounts. Users see that access in a single AWS access portal and SSO into AWS accounts or other cloud apps. ▶ #27 05:20
  • Assignable cloud applications: Office 365, Salesforce, and AWS managed apps such as Amazon WorkSpaces and SageMaker Studio. ▶ #27 05:40

The portal has two tabs, Accounts and Applications. “AWS accounts (7)” has a filter box (name, ID or email) and a Create shortcut button. Accounts: Containers, cybr_demo_management, Demo, Example, Log Archive, Security Tooling, Shared Services. ▶ #27 05:36

Expanding Demo shows the permission sets the user may use there: AdministratorAccess, ReadOnly, SecurityBreakGlass, SecurityDeploy. Clicking a name opens the console as that role; Access keys gives temporary credentials (key ID, secret, session token). Identity Center users don’t get long-term access keys. ▶ #27 06:01

The course keeps using both IAM users and Identity Center users because IAM-user questions still appear on the exam. Best practice: move to Identity Center except for emergency situations (break-glass). ▶ #27 07:20

Enabling Identity Center: instances and identity sources

IAM Identity Center replaces what used to be called AWS SSO: a service with an API for managing users and groups at scale. The instructor recommends it even for individuals, because it avoids duplicate users that already exist in a corporate directory, avoids long-term access keys, and makes multiple accounts easier to manage. ▶ #28 00:21

Instance type Scope
Organization instance One per org, requires AWS Organizations, in one home Region. Lives in the management account because it provisions roles into every member account. Moving Regions means deleting and recreating it
Account instance Single account, for AWS apps only

Console → Identity Center → Enable. Without an organization, the dialog says “IAM Identity Center requires AWS Organizations” and offers Create AWS organization, which also enables Identity Center. ▶ #28 00:49 The first recommended step is Choose your identity source (Settings). ▶ #28 01:00

The warning adds: “After you create an organization, you cannot join this account to another organization until you delete its current organization.” Listed benefits: single payer / centralized cost tracking; create and invite accounts; policy-based controls; organization-wide service management.

Settings → Details: Instance ARN (arn:aws:sso:::instance/ssoins-…), Region (us-east-1), Delegated administrator (“No account registered”), Identity Center enabled applications (“Enabled in member accounts”). ▶ #28 01:00

Settings → Identity source tab: Identity source: Identity Center directory · Authentication method: Password · Provisioning method: Direct · AWS access portal URL https://d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start (unique login URL) · Identity store ID. ▶ #28 01:31 The Actions menu has Customize AWS access portal URL (custom subdomain) and Change identity source. ▶ #28 02:00

Identity source Notes
Identity Center directory Built-in. Instructor’s choice for individual accounts
Active Directory AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector (users stay on-prem, no sync)
External IdP (Okta, Entra ID…) SAML 2.0 for sign-in + SCIM for automatic user/group provisioning. SCIM tokens last 1 year

AD or an external IdP make more sense for organizations that already run one.

Settings → Management tab: delegate administration to a member account, or delete the Identity Center configuration. ▶ #28 03:52

Authentication: email OTP, MFA and sessions

  • Standard authentication → Send email OTP for users created from API. Users created with the Identity Store CreateUser API have no password; this emails a one-time password at first sign-in. ▶ #28 02:40
  • Multi-factor authentication, the instructor’s balance of security and UX: ▶ #28 03:11
Setting Recommended value
Prompt users for MFA Only when their sign-in context changes (context-aware). Alternative: every sign-in
MFA types Defaults: security keys / passkeys and built-in authenticators + authenticator apps
If a user has no registered MFA device Require them to register an MFA device at sign in (default was Allow them to sign in)
Users can add and manage their own MFA devices Greyed out (must stay on) once registration is required

  • MFA is enforced at the portal sign-in, not per account in the IAM role.
  • Session settings: maximum access portal session (default 8 hours) before re-authentication. The SSO token lasts as long as the portal session. This is separate from the permission set session duration (role session in an account, 1–12 h, default 1 h).

Users, groups and invitations

Create permission sets first, so you can assign right away. ▶ #28 04:02

  • Groups → Create group (AdministratorAccess). You can then grant the group permissions to accounts or apps. ▶ #28 05:12
  • Users → Add user: username, how the user gets the password (email, or a one-time password you share), email, first/last/display name; optional contact methods, job info, address, preferences, additional attributes → add to a group → Add. The email link is valid for up to 7 days. ▶ #28 05:51

The email “Invitation to join AWS IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS Single Sign-On)” comes from no-reply@login.awsapps.com. ▶ #28 06:32 Accept → New user sign up → set password → sign in → register an MFA device (enforced by the setting above). ▶ #28 06:40 The access portal then lists the accounts the user can access (here 1: Demo); each permission set has a Management console link and a Command line or programmatic access link. The UI has changed slightly since, but the flow is identical. ▶ #28 06:51

Console demo: enable Identity Center and give a user admin access ([▶ #28](https://youtu.be/YZUtFc3oQ9s))
  1. Console → IAM Identity Center → Enable (create an Organization if prompted).
  2. Settings → Identity source: keep Identity Center directory; note the access portal URL; optionally Actions → Customize AWS access portal URL.
  3. Settings → Authentication → Standard authentication → Configure → tick Send email OTP → Save.
  4. Settings → Authentication → Multi-factor authentication → Configure: Prompt = Only when sign-in context changes; types = security keys/built-in + authenticator apps; no device = Require them to register an MFA device at sign in → Save changes.
  5. Permission sets → Create permission set → Predefined → AdministratorAccess → session duration 1 hour, relay state blank → Create.
  6. Groups → Create group AdministratorAccess.
  7. AWS accounts → select the account → Assign users or groups → the group → permission set AdministratorAccess → Submit. Repeat for every permission set. ▶ #28 05:30
  8. Users → Add user (username, email, names) → add to the group → Add. The user receives an invite (valid 7 days).
  9. User: Accept invitation → set password → register MFA → portal shows account Demo → AdministratorAccess.
  10. Management console signs in as AdministratorAccess/Demo. ▶ #28 10:11

Permission sets

A permission set is a template: a collection of permissions, defined by policies, plus session duration and relay state, that you assign to users or groups on specific accounts. ▶ #30 01:30 Create permission set offers two types: ▶ #30 01:51

Type Contents
Predefined One AWS managed job-function policy: AdministratorAccess, Billing, DatabaseAdministrator, DataScientist, NetworkAdministrator, PowerUserAccess, ReadOnlyAccess, SecurityAudit, SupportUser, SystemAdministrator, ViewOnlyAccess
Custom Like creating an IAM role (▶ #30 02:01): AWS managed + customer managed policies (up to 10 managed combined), one inline policy, optional permissions boundary

It is the same trade-off as AWS managed vs custom IAM policies. ▶ #28 04:02

  • Customer managed policies and boundaries are referenced by name (and path) and must exist with that exact name in every target account, otherwise provisioning fails.
  • Inline policy: the console says “In most cases … we recommend that you create inline policies rather than customer managed policies”. They are identical in every account and changeable only by Identity Center admins.
  • Permissions boundary (optional): customer managed (by name) or AWS managed, attached to the roles created from the set. ▶ #30 02:21

Permission set details ▶ #30 02:41

  • Name, Description.
  • Session duration: minimum and default 1 hour; the role can go up to 12 hours.
  • Relay state: URL to redirect the user after sign-in, e.g. send an “EC2 read-only” set straight to the EC2 dashboard instead of Console Home. Optional. ▶ #30 02:51 ▶ #28 04:50

Assignment and auto-provisioning

Assigning a permission set to a user/group on an account automatically provisions the IAM role and the SAML IdP in that account. They are immutable except through Identity Center, and it works the same for one account or N. ▶ #30 04:22 A later slide contrasts this with plain IAM roles, which need CloudFormation (StackSets) to reach each account.

  • AWS accounts → organization tree (Root → Infrastructure → network, Shared Services; Sandbox; Security; Workload) → select one or more accounts → Assign users or groups. ▶ #30 03:21
  • After Submit: “We reprovisioned your AWS account successfully and applied the updated permission set to the account”. ▶ #30 04:11
  • Edits to a permission set must be re-provisioned to the accounts before users see them.

The provisioned role and SAML provider

In Shared Services (211125520673) IAM shows 0 users, 0 groups, 9 roles, 1 identity provider. ▶ #30 04:50 Roles start with AWSReservedSSO_: AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_… and AWSReservedSSO_ReadOnly_51a1842ffd23ef14. ▶ #30 05:01

  • Special path in the ARN: arn:aws:iam::211125520673:role/aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/AWSReservedSSO_ReadOnly_51a1842ffd23ef14. ▶ #30 05:11
  • Permissions: ReadOnlyAccess (AWS managed job function), auto-attached from the predefined set. ▶ #30 05:32
  • Maximum session duration: 12 hours.

The trust policy: ▶ #30 05:40

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::211125520673:saml-provider/AWSSSO_bdef2c742ae6009f_DO_NOT_DELETE"
      },
      "Action": [
        "sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML",
        "sts:TagSession"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "SAML:aud": "https://signin.aws.amazon.com/saml"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

The condition checks that the SAML audience in the SAML response matches the AWS SAML federation endpoint. ▶ #30 06:10 You could build something similar manually: IAM → Create role → trusted entity SAML 2.0 federation. ▶ #30 06:32

IAM → Identity providers shows AWSSSO_bdef2c742ae6009f_DO_NOT_DELETE, type SAML: exactly the provider named in the trust policy. ▶ #30 07:00 Its page has the ARN arn:aws:iam::211125520673:saml-provider/AWSSSO_bdef2c742ae6009f_DO_NOT_DELETE, Metadata (sign-in URL https://signin.aws.amazon.com/saml/acs/SAMLSP…, metadata URL, issuer URL https://portal.sso.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/saml/assertion/…, valid until 05/29/2124, SSO service location), Download/Replace metadata, SAML encryption settings and Tags. All auto-created (May 29 2024). ▶ #30 07:11 Because the trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML, users get temporary credentials from STS by assuming the role with SAML. ▶ #30 07:40

Identity Center roles vs regular IAM roles ▶ #30 08:51

IAM roles Identity Center–provisioned roles
Created in each account by you (ideally with IaC, e.g. CloudFormation StackSets) Deployed automatically when a permission set is assigned to an account
Modifiable via console/CLI/API Owned and managed by Identity Center; modifying them any other way errors
Trust policy can name IAM users, roles, services, IAM SAML/OIDC federated users Can only be assumed through Identity Center: not by IAM users, service accounts, or IAM-federated users (≠ Identity Center federated users)
Trust policy editable Trust policy not editable: the console looks editable but you get AccessDenied

They are still IAM roles, just with more restrictions, which is a security benefit. ▶ #30 10:01 Understanding this shapes how you grant access, when to choose Identity Center vs plain IAM roles, and how IdPs work in AWS. ▶ #30 10:10

Delegated administration

The organization instance always resides in the management account, because it must provision, deprovision and update roles across all member accounts. ▶ #29 00:10 Delegating administration to a member account lets you manage most configuration outside the management account. ▶ #29 00:22 Best practice because it limits the number of people who need management-account access and limits dangerous actions against the instance. ▶ #29 00:30

In the AWS Security Reference Architecture, AWS IAM Identity Center sits in the Org Mgmt account (with Systems Manager, Artifact, IAM access advisor, Control Tower, plus Security Hub/GuardDuty/Config/Access Analyzer/org trail), and AWS IAM Identity Center (delegated) in the Shared Services account (OU – Infrastructure, with Systems Manager, Directory Service, Managed Microsoft AD). ▶ #29 00:00 Other blocks: OU – Security with the Security Tooling account (CloudTrail, Private CA, Inspector, Artifact, Audit Manager, Config aggregator, EventBridge, Security Lake, GuardDuty, Security Hub, Firewall Manager, Lambda response, Access Analyzer, Macie, Detective, KMS) and OU – Infrastructure with the Network account (inbound / outbound / inspection VPCs, Network Firewall, Route 53, CloudFront, Shield Advanced, WAF, ACM, RAM, Resolver DNS firewall, Network Access Analyzer).

What the delegated admin can and cannot do

Can Cannot
Manage users, groups, permission sets and assignments for member accounts Modify, delete or assign permission sets provisioned to the management account ▶ #30 00:31
See the same users, groups, permission sets, accounts and OUs “just as if I’m in my management account” ▶ #29 03:10 Assign users to the management account
Delete the Identity Center configuration ▶ #29 00:51
Change the delegated admin
  • Only one delegated admin per instance, registered from the management account. If one is registered you only see Deregister account. ▶ #29 02:31
  • Trying to delete AdministratorAccess from the delegated admin gives “cannot delete permission sets provisioned in the management account”; in assignments it is greyed out with “cannot assign permission sets provisioned in management account”. To deploy admin access there you’d need a separate admin set created in the delegated admin. ▶ #30 03:41
  • That is a security benefit: the delegated admin pushes the rest of the org’s permission sets without being able to tamper with the management account’s access. ▶ #30 00:51

Recommended order ▶ #30 01:01

  1. Set up Identity Center in the management account.
  2. Create one or two admin-level permission sets for your most important users there.
  3. Delegate administration to a member account.
  4. Create, deploy and manage all remaining permission sets from the delegated admin account.

The Management tab also shows Attributes for access control (ABAC), Enable identity-aware sessions, Account instances of IAM Identity Center (lets member accounts create standalone account instances for AWS apps) and Delete IAM Identity Center instance.

Console demo: register Shared Services as delegated admin ([▶ #29](https://youtu.be/RlPA871vXYE))
  1. Sign in with the AdministratorAccess permission set, not the IAM user, via the access portal URL (e.g. https://cybrdemo.awsapps.com/start). ▶ #29 01:21 Lost the URL? Sign in with the IAM user and open Identity Center: it is in the dashboard’s Settings summary. ▶ #29 01:40
  2. The portal lists 7 accounts. Copy the Shared Services account ID (211125520673). ▶ #29 01:50
  3. Expand cybr_demo_management → AdministratorAccess for a console session. ▶ #29 02:00
  4. Identity Center → Dashboard → Register a delegated administrator → Register account → enter the account ID. Alternative: Settings → Management → Delegated administrator. ▶ #29 02:12
  5. Settings header shows Delegated administrator: Registered account: Shared Services. ▶ #29 02:50
  6. Access portal → Shared Services → AdministratorAccess → Identity Center: users, groups, permission sets, accounts and OUs are manageable from here. ▶ #29 03:00
Console demo: create and assign a ReadOnly permission set from the delegated admin ([▶ #30](https://youtu.be/xrC9KJdDuIE))
  1. In Shared Services: Identity Center → Permission sets → select AdministratorAccess → Delete → error (provisioned in the management account). ▶ #30 00:31
  2. Create permission set → look at Custom (managed / customer managed / inline / boundary) → back → Predefined → ReadOnlyAccess → Next. ▶ #30 01:40
  3. Name ReadOnly, optional description, session duration, relay state → Next → Create → “The permission set “ReadOnly” was successfully created”. ▶ #30 03:02
  4. AWS accounts → check Shared Services (could also check network) → Assign users or groups → the admin access group (contains user Christophe) → permission set ReadOnly (AdministratorAccess greyed out) → Next → Submit. Shared Services now lists AdministratorAccess and ReadOnly. ▶ #30 04:11
  5. IAM → Roles → AWSReservedSSO_ReadOnly_… → Permissions (ReadOnlyAccess) → Trust relationships. ▶ #30 05:01
  6. IAM → Identity providers → AWSSSO_…_DO_NOT_DELETE → Metadata / SAML encryption / Tags. ▶ #30 06:51

CLI access with aws configure sso

Assuming Identity Center roles from the CLI differs from assuming roles created directly in IAM, and is much easier. ▶ #31 00:00 The CLI obtains and refreshes short-term role credentials automatically.

Where to get the start URL: Identity Center dashboard Settings summary (AWS access portal URL), or run aws sso login --profile <existing-profile>, which prints Successfully logged into Start URL: https://cybrdemo.awsapps.com/start/. ▶ #31 00:30 The first time, the browser asks you to Allow access (OIDC authorization with PKCE: oidc.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/authorize … code_challenge_method=S256 … scopes=sso:account:access). ▶ #31 00:51

The portal’s credential options (Access keys / “Command line or programmatic access”):

Option What it is Verdict
AWS IAM Identity Center credentials (Recommended) aws configure sso with the SSO start URL and SSO Region. “To extend the duration of your credentials, we recommend you configure the AWS CLI to retrieve them automatically” ▶ #31 01:51 Best, most fluid. The CLI fetches and refreshes credentials (“some magic behind the scenes”)
Option 1: environment variables export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY / AWS_SESSION_TOKEN (ASIA…) ▶ #31 05:10 Short-term; move away from it
Option 2: credentials file profile ~/.aws/credentials under [211125520673_ReadOnly] ▶ #31 05:21 Short-term; move away from it
Option 3: values in an AWS service client Hard-coding “You should almost never be doing this”, even in CI/CD. Use IAM Roles Anywhere or roles ▶ #31 05:30

Dialog tabs: macOS and Linux / Windows / PowerShell. ▶ #28 07:21 Short-term credentials have an access key ID starting ASIA (temporary) instead of AKIA (long-term), plus an expiring session token. ▶ #28 10:50

aws configure sso needs AWS CLI v2 (check with aws help, exit with q). ▶ #28 07:41 Prompts: SSO session name, SSO start URL, SSO Region, SSO registration scopes (default sso:account:access). Scopes are the permissions an OAuth client requests on behalf of the user (OAuth 2.0, RFC 6749 §3.3). ▶ #28 08:21

  • The CLI opens a browser. The code in the terminal must match the code in the browser. If not, something is wrong: don’t proceed. Then Allow “botocore-client-test” access. ▶ #28 08:50
  • With one account and one role, the CLI picks them automatically. With more, it lists them (“There are 7 AWS accounts available to you”, “There are 2 roles available to you”). ▶ #31 03:31
  • You can create profiles per permission set / per role; the profile name is arbitrary. ▶ #31 02:40
  • aws s3 ls --profile … returns nothing (no buckets) and, importantly, no AccessDenied, so it works. ▶ #28 09:31
  • aws sso login --profile … re-authenticates, refreshes expired credentials and prints the start URL. ▶ #28 09:51
  • No long-term access key was ever created, yet CLI access works. You can later switch the identity source to AD or another IdP to use existing corporate identities. ▶ #28 10:20

  • --profile readonly → arn:aws:sts::211125520673:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_ReadOnly_51a1842ffd23ef14/christophe. ▶ #31 04:00
  • --profile cybrdemo → arn:aws:sts::396212980357:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_f5e2808a1e330887/christophe. The instructor first thought it was the management account, but it’s the Demo account; you could configure another profile for the management account. ▶ #31 04:21
  • The role session name is the Identity Center username (christophe).
CLI demo: SSO profiles for the Demo and Shared Services accounts ([▶ #28](https://youtu.be/YZUtFc3oQ9s), [▶ #31](https://youtu.be/9jGEOPoDL9g))

First profile (▶ #28):

aws help                       # confirm CLI v2 installed (q to exit)
aws configure sso

# The only role available to you is: AdministratorAccess

aws s3 ls --profile AdministratorAccess-396
aws sso login --profile AdministratorAccess-396

Short-term credentials shown by the portal (Option 1 / Option 2), for account Demo (3962-1298-0357):

export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="…"

ReadOnly profile in Shared Services (▶ #31 03:12):
