What aws configure sso writes to ~/.aws/config (the cached SSO token lives in ~/.aws/sso/cache/):

[profile readonly]
sso_session = readonly-sharedservices
sso_account_id = 211125520673
sso_role_name = ReadOnly
region = us-east-1

[sso-session readonly-sharedservices]
sso_start_url = https://cybrdemo.awsapps.com/start/#
sso_region = us-east-1
sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access

ABAC with attributes for access control

Attributes for access control (Settings banner → Enable) pass user attributes (department, cost center) into the session as principal tags (sts:TagSession). ▶ #28 01:20 Example from the docs: choose the Department attribute and write a permission-set policy that grants S3 access only when the user’s department matches the bucket’s department tag, using aws:PrincipalTag/... conditions. See ABAC and RBAC (Part 1).

Identity Center access failing? Check these
  • CloudTrail events from sso.amazonaws.com / signin.amazonaws.com.
  • Is the permission set provisioned? Re-provision after edits.
  • Is the SCIM token expired? Tokens last 1 year.
  • Customer managed policy or boundary missing (by exact name and path) in the target account → provisioning fails.
  • Someone edited an AWSReservedSSO_* role in IAM → it fails or reverts; change the permission set instead.
  • “Error loading SSO Token: Token … does not exist / expired” → aws sso login --profile X.
  • Wrong account or role → check sso_account_id / sso_role_name in ~/.aws/config.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • “While IAM users have a time and a place, they’re not the best option for human identities. Instead, it’s AWS best practice to rely on a centralized identity provider using federation.” ▶ #27 00:11
  • Access keys are long-term and never expire unless deactivated or deleted; leaked keys caused many breaches. ▶ #27 03:10
  • “Questions related to IAM users can still appear on the exam”: know both models. Move to Identity Center except for emergency situations. ▶ #27 07:20
  • Identity Center “prevents you from having to use long-term access keys for your users.” ▶ #28 00:31
  • Recommended MFA: context-aware prompting + require registration at sign-in, “a good balance between maximum security and user experience.” ▶ #28 03:11
  • When the device code in the terminal and the browser don’t match, “something is definitely wrong and I would not proceed.” ▶ #28 09:00
  • Temporary keys start with ASIA and have a session token; long-term keys start with AKIA. ▶ #28 10:50
  • Create permission sets before users and groups. ▶ #28 04:02
  • The instance stays in the management account; administration is delegated (Shared Services in the SRA) to reduce people in the management account and dangerous actions. ▶ #29 00:30
  • Delegated admin can’t delete the configuration or touch management-account permission sets: a good thing. ▶ #29 00:51 ▶ #30 03:50
  • Identity Center auto-provisions the IAM role and SAML IdP; they’re immutable outside Identity Center, can’t be assumed by IAM users / service accounts / IAM-federated users, and their trust policies can’t be edited. ▶ #30 09:20
  • Don’t confuse IAM federated users with Identity Center federated users. ▶ #30 09:40
  • Use aws configure sso: longer-lived, auto-refreshed credentials. Avoid env vars, the credentials file and especially hard-coding. ▶ #31 05:50

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Workforce access to 50 accounts with corporate Okta credentials, least effort Identity Center + external IdP (SAML + SCIM)
Workforce users, corporate directory, SSO to multiple accounts Identity Center
Customers / end users of a web or mobile app Amazon Cognito, not Identity Center
Eliminate long-term credentials for developers using the CLI Identity Center + aws configure sso / aws sso login
Workloads outside AWS need credentials IAM Roles Anywhere; GitHub/GitLab pipelines → OIDC federation (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity)
SAML IdP → IAM role per account (AssumeRoleWithSAML) Direct federation: still valid, but configured in every account; Identity Center centralizes it
Changed a permission set but users don’t see the change Re-provision the permission set to the accounts
Admin edits an AWSReservedSSO_* role in IAM and it fails/reverts Change the permission set instead
Delegated admin can’t edit a permission set It is assigned to the management account
Minimize management-account access while a team manages SSO users and permission sets Register a delegated administrator for Identity Center
Access based on department/cost-center attribute from the IdP Attributes for access control + aws:PrincipalTag conditions
Users from on-prem AD, no sync to cloud AD Connector as identity source
Match Identity Center roles in SCPs/resource policies aws:PrincipalArn like arn:aws:iam::*:role/aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/AWSReservedSSO_ReadOnly_* (include the path or wildcard it)
Legit remaining IAM-user use Break-glass, and tools that only accept access keys (then MFA, rotation, alert on use)
Leaked access key Deactivate it, review CloudTrail for the key ID, rotate, check for persistence (new users/keys/roles)
Updates since the videos
  • Newer CLI versions use the OAuth PKCE authorization-code flow for aws sso login by default. The device authorization flow shown in ▶ #28 (codes in terminal and browser must match) is used with --use-device-code. Device-code phishing is a real attack technique.
  • The access portal UI has changed slightly since the recording; the flow is the same.

Real-world practice

  • Enable Identity Center from the management account, then delegate administration so day-to-day admins don’t touch the management account. Assign access by groups synced from the IdP via SCIM, so HR-driven deprovisioning removes AWS access automatically.
  • Prefer an external IdP (Entra ID, Okta) + SCIM in production. With the Identity Center directory, enforce MFA and use groups exclusively for assignments.
  • Avoid assigning AdministratorAccess broadly. Build role-based permission sets (ReadOnly, Developer, SecurityAudit, BreakGlass) with short session durations for privileged sets.
  • Break-glass that doesn’t depend on Identity Center: a few IAM users or root with hardware MFA in the management account, credentials in a sealed process, every sign-in alerting via EventBridge/CloudTrail. Keep management-account permission sets managed only from the management account.
  • Protect the delegated admin account with SCPs, since it can grant admin into nearly every member account. Monitor sso.amazonaws.com / sso-directory CloudTrail events (CreatePermissionSet, CreateAccountAssignment, AttachManagedPolicyToPermissionSet) for privilege escalation.
  • Manage permission sets as code (Terraform aws_ssoadmin_*, CloudFormation AWS::SSO::PermissionSet) in the delegated admin account; drift is a common audit finding. Deploy referenced customer managed policies with StackSets first.
  • Never delete AWSSSO_*_DO_NOT_DELETE providers or AWSReservedSSO_* roles. SCPs commonly deny IAM changes on aws-reserved/* paths for non-Identity-Center principals.
  • CloudTrail attribution: sign-in shows AssumeRoleWithSAML; actions in member accounts appear as AssumedRole AWSReservedSSO_<set>_<hash>/<username> (session name = Identity Center username). Use userIdentity.sessionContext or onBehalfOf to map back to the user.
  • Tools like aws-vault, granted or saml2aws build on SSO profiles; most orgs generate sso-session profiles from the account list. Credentials copied from the portal are temporary but leak into shell history and files, and the ~/.aws/sso/cache token is itself a credential: protect developer laptops.
  • Find and remove legacy IAM users with the credential report, Access Analyzer unused-access findings, and an SCP or Config rule that blocks iam:CreateUser / iam:CreateAccessKey outside approved paths.
  • Permission sets from the CLI:
aws sso-admin create-permission-set --instance-arn $INST --name SecurityAudit \
  --session-duration PT4H
aws sso-admin attach-managed-policy-to-permission-set --instance-arn $INST \
  --permission-set-arn $PS --managed-policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/SecurityAudit
aws sso-admin create-account-assignment --instance-arn $INST --permission-set-arn $PS \
  --target-id 444455556666 --target-type AWS_ACCOUNT \
  --principal-type GROUP --principal-id <group-id>
aws configure sso   # CLI profile backed by Identity Center
Hands-on lab
  1. Enable Identity Center and create group SecOps.
  2. Assign a ReadOnlyAccess permission set to one account for that group.
  3. Sign in through the access portal.
  4. Find the AWSReservedSSO_* role and the AWSSSO_*_DO_NOT_DELETE provider in IAM of that account.
  5. Cleanup: remove the assignment and the permission set.

IAM Roles Anywhere

At a glance

Lets workloads outside AWS (on-prem servers, containers, other clouds, on-prem CI/CD) get temporary AWS credentials by presenting an X.509 certificate, instead of using long-term access keys. Released in 2022.

  • Exam skills: authorization controls incl. Roles Anywhere (4.2.1) · temporary credentials (4.1.2) · keys & certificates, Private CA (5.3.5)
  • Videos: ▶ #26 IAM Roles Anywhere

The problem it solves

Roles are the preferred way to grant access, but before 2022 workloads outside AWS had no good way to use them. The options were long-term credentials (access keys) or building a secure on-prem ↔ AWS connection. ▶ #26 00:00

Use When
IAM Roles Anywhere Workloads outside AWS that have (or can get) X.509 certificates from a PKI
IAM Identity Center Humans, not workloads
IAM role attached directly Workloads running in AWS
OIDC web identity federation (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity) CI/CD that issues OIDC tokens (GitHub Actions, GitLab); no certificates needed (see ▶ #31)

How trust works: CA, trust anchor, profile, role

Roles Anywhere uses public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and the CA that issues certificates to your on-prem workloads. The workload exchanges an X.509 certificate for temporary credentials. ▶ #26 00:31

Component What it is
Trust anchor Your CA registered in Roles Anywhere: AWS Private CA, or an external CA certificate bundle you upload ▶ #26 01:10
Profile Which roles can be assumed, session settings, optional session policies
Role Its trust policy allows the principal rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com
  • Existing PKI → reuse your own CA. No CA → create one with AWS Private CA to issue and manage private certificates. ▶ #26 01:10
  • ACM is mentioned for public TLS certificates, but Roles Anywhere needs certificates from your trust-anchor CA, typically private ones. Public ACM certificates are not used to authenticate here.

Authentication flow

  1. The application sends an authentication request to Roles Anywhere containing: ▶ #26 01:42
    • (a) its public key, encoded in the certificate
    • (b) a signature made with the matching private key
    • (c) the role it wants to assume
  2. Roles Anywhere validates the signature with the public key, then checks the certificate was issued by a trust anchor configured in the account. ▶ #26 02:11
  3. On success it creates a role session by calling AWS STS, the same as aws sts assume-role from the CLI. ▶ #26 02:20
  4. The application receives temporary credentials and uses AWS as if it were running inside AWS. ▶ #26 02:40

It is an ordinary STS session, so CloudTrail shows it like any assumed-role session. Use the source identity / session tags to trace which certificate was used.

Setup in three steps

Setup is more involved than other options. ▶ #26 02:52

  1. Initial configuration: create a trust anchor, set the trust policy of the role Roles Anywhere will assume, and define a profile (which roles can be assumed, session settings). ▶ #26 02:52
  2. Provision certificates: install the CA-signed X.509 certificate (and its private key) on the servers, applications or containers outside AWS.
  3. Use Roles Anywhere: configure the credential helper tool (aws_signing_helper) with the AWS SDK/CLI so credentials are fetched automatically. ▶ #26 03:31

Role trust policy: allow rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com with sts:AssumeRole, sts:TagSession and sts:SetSourceIdentity, narrowed by certificate attributes (aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN) or aws:SourceArn = the trust anchor ARN.

{ "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" },
  "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity"],
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "onprem-app-01" },
    "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:ap-southeast-1:111122223333:trust-anchor/TA_ID" } } }

The credential helper

aws_signing_helper credential-process takes --certificate, --private-key, --trust-anchor-arn, --profile-arn and --role-arn. It signs the request with the private key, calls the Roles Anywhere endpoint, and prints session credentials in the format the CLI/SDK credential_process expects. ▶ #26 03:41

  1. Configure the credential helper to work with the AWS SDK.
  2. It then gets credentials through Roles Anywhere automatically.
  3. It is the same process as configuring role profiles for the CLI…
  4. …except you add a credential_process line that calls aws_signing_helper. ▶ #26 03:31
Docs walkthrough: signing helper commands ([▶ #26](https://youtu.be/69smn613j2k)) 
./aws_signing_helper credential-process \
    --certificate /path/to/certificate \
    --private-key /path/to/private-key \
    --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \
    --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \
    --role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path

# ~/.aws/config
[profile onprem]
credential_process = ./aws_signing_helper credential-process --certificate /path/to/certificate --private-key /path/to/private-key --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:… --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:… --role-arn arn:aws:iam::…:role/…

Real-world variant:

[profile onprem]
credential_process = aws_signing_helper credential-process \
  --certificate /etc/pki/app.crt --private-key /etc/pki/app.key \
  --trust-anchor-arn <ta-arn> --profile-arn <profile-arn> --role-arn <role-arn>

Protecting keys and revoking access

  • “Anyone who gets access to your private keys can access your role.” The private key must be protected and reachable only by authorized people/systems. ▶ #26 04:10
  • Revocation: import a CRL into Roles Anywhere. Disabling the trust anchor or profile stops all new sessions.
  • Revoke one server: add its certificate to the CRL, or tighten the trust policy condition on its CN.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Protect the private key: whoever holds it can assume your role. ▶ #26 04:10
  • Temporary credentials needed outside AWS, e.g. for CI/CD pipelines → IAM Roles Anywhere. ▶ #26 04:21

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
On-prem app uses IAM user access keys; eliminate long-term credentials IAM Roles Anywhere
On-prem servers need AWS access without long-term access keys IAM Roles Anywhere
Workloads already have X.509 certificates from an internal PKI IAM Roles Anywhere
Hard-coded credentials in a service client / on-prem CI IAM Roles Anywhere, not IAM user keys (see ▶ #13, ▶ #27, ▶ #31)
CI/CD supports OIDC (GitHub Actions, GitLab) Web identity federation (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity), no certificates
Revoke one server’s access Add its cert to the CRL, or tighten the trust policy condition on the CN
Updates since the videos
  • Pipelines in GitHub/GitLab usually use OIDC federation (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity) rather than Roles Anywhere. Roles Anywhere fits when the workload has certificates, not OIDC tokens.
  • Public ACM certificates (mentioned in the video) are not what authenticates to Roles Anywhere. Certificates must come from your trust-anchor CA, typically private.
  • Trust policy actions, CRL import, CloudTrail tracing and certificate-attribute conditions above are additions from the AWS docs, not covered in the video.

Real-world practice

  • Store private keys in a TPM/HSM or the OS keystore where possible. aws_signing_helper supports PKCS#11 and TPM-backed keys.
  • Use short-lived certificates with automated renewal, scope each profile to specific roles, and use session policies on the profile to cap permissions further.
  • Restrict the trust policy to specific certificate subjects (CN/OU) so one leaked cert from the same CA can’t assume every role.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create a local CA with openssl.
  2. Register it as a trust anchor, create a role (trust policy above) and a profile.
  3. Issue a client certificate from the CA.
  4. Get credentials with aws_signing_helper credential-process and run aws sts get-caller-identity --profile onprem.
  5. Cleanup: delete the trust anchor, profile and role.

Amazon Cognito

At a glance

Customer identity and access management (CIAM) for the end users of your web and mobile apps: sign-up, sign-in, social login, profile and custom attributes, and access to AWS resources. Not for your workforce (that’s IAM Identity Center).

  • Exam skills: identity solutions for app users, MFA (4.1.1) · temporary credentials (4.1.2) · troubleshoot Cognito authentication (4.1.3) · ABAC and RBAC with identity pools (4.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #35 Amazon Cognito
  • Free tier: 50,000 active users per month. Federation via OIDC or SAML 2.0.

The end-user problem

So far the course covered workforce identities. Customers/end users signing up for and into your web or mobile apps need Amazon Cognito. ▶ #35 00:10 End-user management needs: ▶ #35 00:20

  • sign-up,
  • sign-in and the authentication process,
  • social login (reuse social media credentials),
  • profile management, including custom attributes,
  • permissions: control what end users can access. ▶ #35 00:40

Cognito supports all of these: it adds sign-up, sign-in and access control to web and mobile apps, and can handle tokens from external IdPs like Facebook and Google. ▶ #35 00:51 The product page: “Implement secure, frictionless customer identity and access management that scales”. ▶ #35 00:14

  1. Add sign-up: gather login and custom attributes, verify and save registration data (self-registration into a user pool).
  2. Add sign-in: local/adaptive authentication, federation through third-party login; hosted UI and SDK.
  3. Control access: federated access with OAuth2/OIDC, and credential-broker access via an identity pool.
  4. Application resources: ALB, API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB and other AWS services, with role- or attribute-based access control.

User pools vs identity pools

User pool ▶ #35 01:20 Identity pool ▶ #35 02:10
Job Authentication: a user directory Authorization to AWS: federated identities
Sign-in Directly, or via Facebook, Google, Apple, Amazon, or any OpenID Connect / SAML IdP Takes a token from a user pool, social IdP or SAML
Output JWTs: ID, access and refresh tokens Temporary AWS credentials via STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
Notes Every user gets a directory profile in the pool however they sign in ▶ #35 01:32. Hosted UI / managed login Authenticated and unauthenticated (guest) roles

User pool features ▶ #35 01:41

  • Different user pools for different types of users, to simplify permissions.
  • MFA (TOTP, SMS, email), including phone and email verification.
  • Compromised credentials checks and account takeover protection.
  • Fully customizable sign-in UI. ▶ #35 02:01
  • Protects API Gateway (Cognito authorizer) and ALB (authenticate-cognito action).

Tokens

Token Holds
ID token Identity claims
Access token Scopes, for APIs
Refresh token Gets new ID/access tokens

APIs must verify the signature, iss, aud/client_id and exp.

How they work together

  1. The user logs in to your app via social sign-in, an OIDC or SAML IdP, or a custom auth method.
  2. The user pool authenticates the user and returns authentication tokens. ▶ #35 02:31
  3. The user needs AWS services, e.g. objects in an S3 bucket.
  4. The identity pool exchanges the user pool tokens for AWS credentials. ▶ #35 02:41
  5. Those credentials access AWS services according to the assigned permissions and policies. ▶ #35 02:50

Benefits: you don’t worry about how end users securely reach AWS resources in the backend, and there are no hard-coded credentials. ▶ #35 03:01

ABAC with identity pools

Cognito reads user attributes from corporate IdPs or social sign-ins and can map them to principal tags referenced in IAM permissions policies. ▶ #35 03:31

AWS docs example (Using attributes for access control, “the Amazon Cognito identity pools implementation of ABAC”): a streaming service with free and paid memberships. Media files in S3 are tagged free or paid. At sign-in the user’s membership attribute becomes a principal tag, and the IAM policy allows premium content only when the tags match. This simplifies access control greatly. ▶ #35 03:41

RBAC with identity pools

Permissions per user are controlled through IAM roles; different users get different access depending on their role. ▶ #35 04:31

  • Guest (unauthenticated) user → identity pool → role with limited access.
  • Authenticated user → identity pool → a different role with more access. ▶ #35 04:40
  • AWS docs (Using role-based access control): you can define rules that choose the role from claims in the user’s ID token, a default authenticated role, and a role for unauthenticated guests. Roles must have a trust policy so only Cognito can assume them for your identity pool. ▶ #35 04:52

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Federated": "cognito-identity.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud": "us-east-1:12345678-corner-cafe-123456790ab"
        },
        "ForAnyValue:StringLike": {
          "cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:amr": "authenticated"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Keep both conditions:

  • cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud = your pool ID. Without it, any identity pool can assume the role.
  • cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:amr = authenticated (or unauthenticated for the guest role).

Security features and troubleshooting

  • Threat protection: compromised-credential detection, adaptive authentication (blocks or adds MFA on risky sign-ins), account-takeover protection. Requires the Plus feature tier.
  • AWS WAF web ACL on the user pool.
  • Lambda triggers: pre sign-up, pre token generation, post authentication.
  • Disable unauthenticated (guest) access unless needed; if enabled, give that role minimal permissions.
Cognito sign-in failing? Check these
  • CloudTrail logs Cognito management and some auth events.
  • App client settings: callback URL, OAuth flows, client secret.
  • Token expiry.
  • Identity pool role trust policy: aud must be the right pool ID, amr must match authenticated/unauthenticated.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Cognito = end users / customers of web and mobile apps. ▶ #35 00:10
  • User pools authenticate (directory, tokens); identity pools give temporary AWS credentials. ▶ #35 01:12
  • Identity pools avoid hard-coding credentials in apps. ▶ #35 03:11
  • Access via identity pools can be ABAC (attributes → tags) or RBAC (roles for guest vs authenticated). ▶ #35 03:20

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Mobile users upload directly to their own S3 prefix, without embedding keys Identity pool role with ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} in the resource ARN
Block sign-ins with leaked passwords Cognito threat protection (compromised credentials, Plus tier)
Authenticate users for a web app; sign-up/sign-in, social login, MFA for customers User pool
Give app users AWS credentials Identity pool
Protect API Gateway / ALB with user login User pool authorizer / ALB authenticate-cognito
Workforce SSO to AWS accounts IAM Identity Center, not Cognito
Guest access abused Disable unauthenticated access or minimize the guest role
Updates since the videos
  • What were called “advanced security features” (compromised credentials, adaptive authentication, account takeover protection) are now threat protection and require the Plus feature tier.

Real-world practice

  • Per-user S3 prefix from an identity pool role:
{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::app-uploads/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/*" }
  • Enforce TOTP MFA on a user pool:
aws cognito-idp set-user-pool-mfa-config --user-pool-id ap-southeast-1_abc \
  --software-token-mfa-configuration Enabled=true --mfa-configuration ON
  • Use separate user pools per tenant or per app tier only when isolation requires it; otherwise use groups/attributes.
  • Use Lambda triggers (pre sign-up, pre token generation, post authentication) for custom validation, claim enrichment and anti-abuse.
  • Enable CloudTrail data events / user-pool log export for auth events and feed them into security monitoring.
  • Common incident: overly broad identity pool roles (e.g. s3:* on a bucket) abused by anyone who can obtain a guest identity.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create a user pool with TOTP MFA.
  2. Create an identity pool linked to it, with an authenticated role (trust policy with aud + amr).
  3. Sign in through the hosted UI and exchange the tokens for AWS credentials.
  4. Cleanup: delete both pools.

AWS Directory Service

At a glance

Many organizations manage identities with Microsoft Active Directory. AWS Directory Service offers several ways to run or connect Microsoft AD with AWS services: a real AD hosted by AWS, a proxy to on-prem AD, or a cheap Samba-based directory.

  • Exam skills: identity solutions & IdP integration, MFA (4.1.1) · troubleshoot Directory Service (4.1.3) · hybrid communication (3.3.3)
  • Videos: ▶ #34 AWS Directory Service (slides only, no demo)

The three directory options

AWS Directory Service provides multiple ways of setting up and running Microsoft AD with AWS services. ▶ #34 00:11

Option What it is Use when
AWS Managed Microsoft AD Real Windows AD hosted by AWS (2 DCs, multi-AZ) AD-aware apps in AWS (EC2, RDS for SQL Server, WorkSpaces, FSx for Windows, Identity Center), trusts with on-prem AD, group policy, schema extensions, multi-Region replication (Enterprise), sharing to other accounts
AD Connector Proxy that redirects authentication to on-prem AD; stores nothing in the cloud Use existing on-prem identities for Identity Center, WorkSpaces, console; needs VPN/DX and a service account
Simple AD Samba 4–based, small, low cost, LDAP-compatible Basic LDAP / domain join; no trusts, no MFA

AWS Managed Microsoft AD

An actual Microsoft AD hosted in the AWS cloud. ▶ #34 00:21 Use it to:

  • create a managed Microsoft AD in your cloud environment;
  • deploy new apps or migrate existing AD-aware workloads to AWS; ▶ #34 00:42
  • integrate with directory-aware AWS services: Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS for SQL Server, Amazon WorkSpaces and IAM Identity Center; ▶ #34 00:50
  • create and manage users, groups and roles to control access to directory-aware workloads and AWS services. ▶ #34 01:00

Trusts are Managed AD only: one-way or two-way, forest or external. A typical setup is a one-way trust where the AWS domain trusts on-prem, so on-prem users access AWS resources.

aws ds create-microsoft-ad --name corp.example.com --password '***' --edition Standard \
  --vpc-settings VpcId=vpc-123,SubnetIds=subnet-a,subnet-b
aws ds create-trust --directory-id d-123 --remote-domain-name onprem.example.com \
  --trust-password '***' --trust-direction "One-Way: Outgoing" --trust-type Forest \
  --conditional-forwarder-ip-addrs 10.0.0.10

AD Connector

  • Uses your existing on-premises Microsoft AD to access AWS apps and services. ▶ #34 01:13
  • Redirects authentication requests from AWS to on-prem AD: it acts as a proxy. ▶ #34 01:21
  • Fits when you only need on-prem users to sign in to AWS apps/services with existing AD credentials. ▶ #34 01:30
  • Benefits: no directory data stored in the cloud, keep existing identity management processes, still provide SSO to the workforce, simpler control of access to AWS resources. ▶ #34 01:42

Simple AD

  • Low-scale, low-cost directory with basic AD compatibility. ▶ #34 02:02
  • Supports Samba 4–compatible applications, and LDAP for LDAP-aware apps. ▶ #34 02:11
  • Supports only a limited subset of Managed Microsoft AD features. E.g. no multi-factor authentication, which can be a deal breaker. ▶ #34 02:30

MFA and related identity services

  • MFA: Managed AD and AD Connector support RADIUS MFA. Simple AD does not.
  • Amazon Cognito: for SaaS, mobile and web apps that need a scalable directory to manage/authenticate their users, and/or social login. Covered in its own lesson. ▶ #34 02:50
  • Amazon Cloud Directory: organizes directory objects into hierarchies (reporting structure, team locations around the world, project membership), as a managed service that scales without infrastructure. ▶ #34 03:30
Directory integration failing? Check these
  • DNS and conditional forwarders.
  • Security group ports: 53, 88, 389, 445, 636…
  • Service account permissions for AD Connector.
  • Network connectivity (VPN/DX) to on-prem domain controllers.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Managed Microsoft AD = AD hosted in AWS; integrates with EC2, RDS for SQL Server, WorkSpaces, Identity Center. ▶ #34 00:31
  • AD Connector = proxy to on-prem AD; nothing stored in the cloud. ▶ #34 01:21
  • Simple AD = cheap, basic, Samba 4/LDAP, no MFA. ▶ #34 02:02
  • Customer/social identities for apps → Cognito. ▶ #34 02:50

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
On-prem AD stays the single source, no directory data in AWS AD Connector
Need a trust relationship with the on-prem forest Managed Microsoft AD (Simple AD and AD Connector can’t)
Existing on-prem AD and AWS-hosted AD-aware workloads that must keep working if the link is down Managed Microsoft AD + forest trust
Small, cheap, basic LDAP/Linux/Samba directory, no MFA or trusts Simple AD
Workforce SSO to many AWS accounts using AD identities IAM Identity Center with Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector as identity source
Add MFA to AD sign-in for WorkSpaces RADIUS on Managed AD or AD Connector
Customer / social login for a web or mobile app Amazon Cognito
Updates since the videos
  • Amazon Cloud Directory is a niche/legacy service and is unlikely to matter on SCS-C03. Focus on Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector, Simple AD, Cognito and Identity Center.

Real-world practice

  • Most enterprises connect Identity Center to an external IdP (Entra ID/Okta) via SAML + SCIM instead of AD directly. Directory Service is mostly used for Windows workloads (EC2 domain join, FSx for Windows, WorkSpaces, RDS SQL Server).
  • Use SSM AWS-JoinDirectoryServiceDomain or seamless domain join for EC2.
  • Enable directory log forwarding to CloudWatch Logs for security monitoring of Managed Microsoft AD.
Hands-on lab

Read-only, because Managed AD has an hourly cost:

  1. Open the Directory Service console’s create wizard.
  2. Compare the three options and note which features are greyed out for Simple AD.
  3. Cleanup: none, as long as you don’t create a directory.

Amazon Verified Permissions

At a glance

A managed fine-grained authorization service for your own applications. Policies are written in Cedar and stored in a policy store. The app calls IsAuthorized (or IsAuthorizedWithToken with a Cognito or OIDC token) and gets Allow or Deny.

  • Exam skills: authorization controls incl. Verified Permissions (4.2.1)
  • Videos: none in the course (knowledge-based section)

How it works

  • It decouples authorization logic from application code: central policies, an audit trail in CloudTrail, and the ability to analyze policies.
  • Cedar supports RBAC (principal in a group) and ABAC (attributes and context), with a schema for validation.
  • Integrates with Cognito user pools as the identity source and with API Gateway (Lambda authorizer).
permit (
  principal in MyApp::Group::"doctors",
  action == MyApp::Action::"viewRecord",
  resource
) when { resource.department == principal.department };

aws verifiedpermissions is-authorized --policy-store-id ps-123 \
  --principal entityType=MyApp::User,entityId=alice \
  --action actionType=MyApp::Action,actionId=viewRecord \
  --resource entityType=MyApp::Record,entityId=r-42

Verified Permissions vs IAM

IAM Verified Permissions
Controls access to AWS resources (S3, KMS, EC2…) Your app’s resources (documents, orders, patient records)
Policy language IAM JSON policies Cedar
Called by AWS services on every API call Your application (IsAuthorized)
Exam tips

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
App needs fine-grained, per-record permissions managed centrally, without hard-coding logic Verified Permissions (Cedar)
Control which IAM role can call S3 That’s IAM, not Verified Permissions

Real-world practice

  • Use the Cognito user pool as the identity source and IsAuthorizedWithToken, so the app passes the token instead of building principal entities itself.
  • Keep app authorization out of code: one policy store per application, policies versioned and reviewed like code.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create a policy store from the sample PhotoFlash template.
  2. Test allow and deny decisions in the console’s test bench.
  3. Cleanup: delete the policy store.

IAM Access Analyzer

At a glance

Uses automated reasoning to find who has access to what (external, internal and unused access) and to validate policies before you deploy them. It is detective, not preventive.

  • Exam skills: cross-account resource policies (4.2.1) · least-privilege policies (4.2.3) · analyze authorization failures (4.2.4) · correct unintended permissions (4.2.5) · delegated admin (6.1.4) · IaC with StackSets (6.2.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #135 Unused access · ▶ #136 Multi-account deployment · (▶ #55 Access Analyzer for S3 is in the S3 notes)
  • Cost: external access analysis free; unused access $0.20 per IAM user/role per month

Analyzer types

Analyzer Finds Cost
External access Resources shared outside the zone of trust (account or organization) Free
Internal access Who inside your org can reach critical resources
Unused access Unused roles, unused access keys and passwords, unused service/action permissions over a tracking period (default 90 days, range 1–365) $0.20 per IAM user/role per month
  • External access covers S3 buckets and directory buckets, IAM role trust, KMS keys, Lambda functions/layers, SQS, SNS, Secrets Manager, EBS/RDS snapshots, ECR, EFS, DynamoDB tables/streams.
  • Unused access can suggest a least-privilege policy (recommendations). Finding types: Unused IAM role, Unused IAM user access key, Unused IAM user password, Unused permission.
  • Creating any analyzer creates a service-linked role. ▶ #135 02:30

The getting-started page (IAM → Access reports → Access Analyzer, sub-items External access, Unused access, Analyzer settings) shows How it works: ▶ #135 00:11

  1. Create an analyzer to monitor external and unused access for an organization or account.
  2. Review findings: unused access granted to IAM users/roles, and external access to resources from outside your zone of trust.
  3. Take action: archive intended access, or resolve by removing unused access.

Unused access analyzer

Tracking period: default 90 days, configurable. It flags access not used for longer than the period: a role used 80 days ago isn’t flagged, one used 94 days ago is. The choice is the organization’s; the instructor prefers shorter, to catch unused roles, keys and passwords before 3 months pass. The demo uses 30 days. ▶ #135 01:10

Region: can’t be changed. “IAM Access Analyzer monitors all IAM users and roles in your accounts. Unused access findings do not change based on Region.” ▶ #135 02:00 Pricing is based on the number of IAM roles and users per analyzer per month per Region.

  • Selected accounts: the current account, or the whole AWS Organization (not shown in the demo).
  • Service access: a service-linked role is created in the current account (View permission details shows role name, trusted entity, permissions). ▶ #135 02:30
  • The initial scan takes a few minutes (~5). No findings? Check the configuration and whether any keys/credentials/roles were actually inactive for the period. ▶ #135 03:00
Console demo: create an unused access analyzer ([▶ #135](https://youtu.be/KOQXGwxLaYQ))
  1. IAM → Access Analyzer → Unused access → Create analyzer (or from the getting-started page). ▶ #135 00:40
  2. Findings type: External access analysis vs Unused access analysis → choose unused.
  3. Name: keep the pre-populated UnusedAccess-ConsoleAnalyzer-<uuid>.
  4. Tracking period: 30 days; current account; review the service-linked role; tags optional → Create analyzer.
  5. Analyzer starts with 0 findings. Wait ~5 minutes → refresh → 2 findings. ▶ #135 03:00
  6. Open the OrganizationAccountAccessRole finding → review recommendations → Export finding (JSON) → view Add archive rule options (finding type = Unused IAM role, resource owner account ≠ …) → cancel.
  7. Manage analyzer → Delete analyzer. ▶ #135 07:21

Unused access findings: delete, archive, export

Columns: Finding ID, Finding type (e.g. Unused permissions, Unused role), IAM resource (name + type), Last updated, Status (Active/Archived), with a status filter (Active). Demo findings: aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/AWSReservedSSO_Admin… (IAM role) → Unused permissions, and OrganizationAccountAccessRole → Unused role. ▶ #135 03:42

  • Definitely not needed → delete the resource (e.g. the role). ▶ #135 04:11
  • Expected to be unused for long periods → archive (checkbox → Actions → Archive, or from the finding page; the Intended unused IAM role toggle). ▶ #135 04:20

The finding page shows finding ID, type, resource name/type, ARN, Last used: 2 months ago, status, last scan, and Recommendations: Step 1 review the role’s details, Step 2 delete the IAM role. Export finding gives JSON with analyzedAt, createdAt, resource ARN, resource type (role), resource owner account, status, updatedAt, finding type and recommended steps. ▶ #135 04:11

Archive rules

Use them when many similar findings should be handled the same way. ▶ #135 05:42

Part Values
Filter keys error, finding ID, finding type, resource, resource owner account, resource type
Conditions equals / not equals / contains
Finding type values (unused) Unused IAM role, Unused IAM user access key, Unused IAM user password, Unused permission
  • Example: finding type = Unused IAM role AND resource owner account ≠ X, e.g. to exclude roles from a specific account in an org-wide analyzer. ▶ #135 05:42
  • A preview lists the findings matching the criteria before you create the rule.
  • The Analyzer settings page lists the archive rules per analyzer and has Create archive rule.

Clean-up: remediate findings, then Unused access → Manage analyzer → Delete analyzer to stop the cost. Deleting stops analysis and loses its findings. ▶ #135 07:30

Multi-account deployment and zone of trust

Following the Security Reference Architecture (SRA), delegate to the Security Tooling account, but you must start in the management account. ▶ #136 00:00

  1. Management account → IAM → Access Analyzer → Analyzer settings → Delegated administrator – optional → enter the Security Tooling account ID. (Demo: administrator = management account 299551924423; delegated admin 851725223689, with Change/Remove.) ▶ #136 00:10
  2. Sign in to the Security Tooling account and open Access Analyzer.
  3. Create analyzer → External access analysis (“scans the resources within the zone of trust”), not Unused access (“scans IAM users and roles within selected organization or account”). ▶ #136 01:10
  4. Region (US East – N. Virginia): “You should enable Access Analyzer in each Region where you use resources.” Name auto-generated ExternalAccess-ConsoleAnalyzer-<uuid>.
  5. Zone of trust = the boundary within which resource sharing is acceptable: Current organization (o-jqbqypd27k) or Current account (which defeats the purpose here). ▶ #136 01:51

With the organization as zone of trust: ▶ #136 02:01

  1. Resources shared between accounts in the organization are trusted.
  2. Findings are generated only for resources accessible from outside the organization. E.g. an S3 bucket configured for public access is flagged.

Behind the scenes: ▶ #136 03:21

  1. A trust relationship is created between AWS Organizations and IAM Access Analyzer.
  2. A service-linked role is created in every account in the organization. ▶ #136 03:41
  3. That role lets Access Analyzer interact with resources on your behalf; it then continuously monitors resources and their policies for access from outside the org.

After Create analyzer: success, “Last scan: –”, zone of trust shown; findings take a few minutes.

External access findings: archive or resolve

Demo with an earlier analyzer: 6 findings. ▶ #136 04:51 Columns:

  • Finding ID, Resource (e.g. aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/AWSReservedSSO_… IAM roles), Resource owner account
  • External principal (here Federated User: the IAM Identity Center SAML provider)
  • Condition, Shared through (blank here), Access level (Write, Tagging…)
  • Resource control policy (RCP) restriction (Not applicable), Last updated, Status

Actions: Export, Archive, or remediate by modifying the resource policy, using an RCP, or setting up automated remediation or notifications. ▶ #136 05:52

Finding details: external principal arn:aws:iam::488075507604:saml-provider/AWSSSO_…_DO_NOT_DELETE, resource …:role/aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_…. Access level expanded: Write → sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML, Tagging → sts:TagSession. ▶ #136 06:31

Decision Action Resulting status
Intended access Archive, or an archive rule for similar findings Archived
Not intended Modify/remove the granting policy → Rescan Resolved

The demo archives the SSO roles (intended), so the list drops to 5 under the default Active filter. Filter Archived / Resolved / All to see others; you can also unarchive and rescan. ▶ #136 06:31

Console demo: org-wide external access analyzer ([▶ #136](https://youtu.be/6o8qnLFo7go))
  1. Management account → IAM → Access Analyzer → Analyzer settings → Delegated administrator = Security Tooling account ID.
  2. Sign in to the Security Tooling account → Access Analyzer → Create analyzer.
  3. Findings type External access analysis; Region us-east-1; default name; Zone of trust: Current organization → Create analyzer.
  4. Wait for the scan → External access → review findings → open one → Archive (intended SSO role trust).
  5. Switch Region to us-east-2 → no analyzer → deploy per Region via StackSets.
  6. EventBridge rules on Access Analyzer findings → SNS / Lambda / CloudWatch Logs / Security Hub.

Regions and notifications

Analyzer Region scope
External access Regional: one in us-east-1 only sees resources in us-east-1; us-east-2 shows no analyzer ▶ #136 07:42
Unused access Created in one Region, analyzes IAM users and roles globally ▶ #135 02:00
  • For full coverage, create external analyzers in every Region where you have resources, ideally with CloudFormation StackSets. Unused access analyzers can be deployed multi-account the same way. ▶ #136 07:42
  • IAM roles are global, so role-trust findings appear in every Region’s external analyzer. Use archive rules to cut the duplicates.
  • Access Analyzer sends an event to EventBridge for each finding by default. Rules route to SNS (email/SMS), Lambda (automated remediation or enrichment), CloudWatch Logs and Security Hub (centralized findings). ▶ #136 09:01

Policy validation, generation and custom checks

  • Policy validation: 100+ checks (errors, security warnings, suggestions), in the console policy editor and the API.
  • Policy generation: builds a least-privilege policy from CloudTrail activity of a role or user.
  • Custom policy checks for CI/CD: CheckNoNewAccess (does the new policy grant more than the reference?), CheckAccessNotGranted (does it grant these sensitive actions?), CheckNoPublicAccess.
  • Preview access shows findings for a policy before you apply it (S3, KMS, IAM role, SQS, Secrets Manager…).
  • Access Analyzer for S3 in the S3 console uses the same analyzer and can block all public access from a finding (▶ #55, S3 notes).
aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --analyzer-name org-external --type ORGANIZATION
aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --analyzer-name org-unused --type ORGANIZATION_UNUSED_ACCESS \
  --configuration '{"unusedAccess":{"unusedAccessAge":90}}'
aws accessanalyzer validate-policy --policy-type IDENTITY_POLICY --policy-document file://p.json
aws accessanalyzer check-no-new-access --policy-type IDENTITY_POLICY \
  --existing-policy-document file://old.json --new-policy-document file://new.json
aws accessanalyzer check-access-not-granted --policy-type IDENTITY_POLICY \
  --policy-document file://new.json --access '[{"actions":["iam:PassRole","s3:DeleteBucket"]}]'
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Default tracking period is 90 days, configurable. ▶ #135 01:10
  • Unused access analysis isn’t Region-specific; it covers all Regions. ▶ #135 02:00
  • A service-linked role is required, and with an org analyzer it is created in all org accounts. ▶ #136 03:41
  • Delete if not needed; archive if expected to be unused. Archive rules auto-handle similar findings, e.g. excluding an account. ▶ #135 05:42
  • Unused access analysis costs money; deleting the analyzer loses its findings. ▶ #135 07:30
  • Delegate to the Security Tooling account per the SRA, from the management account. ▶ #136 00:10
  • Zone of trust = organization → only access from outside the org is flagged. ▶ #136 02:01
  • External access analyzers are Regional: one per Region, use StackSets. ▶ #136 07:42
  • Findings go to EventBridge by default. ▶ #136 09:12

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Find any S3 bucket or KMS key shared with external accounts across the org Org-level external access analyzer (delegated admin, every Region)
Block sharing outside the org RCPs / SCPs with aws:PrincipalOrgID / aws:ResourceOrgID (Access Analyzer only detects)
Fail the pipeline if a policy change grants new permissions check-no-new-access in CI
Least-privilege policy from what the role actually used Policy generation from CloudTrail
Find roles not used in 90 days / IAM roles unused for 60 days across all accounts, minimal effort Org-level unused access analyzer with that tracking period
S3 bucket public access review in the S3 console Access Analyzer for S3
Remediated finding Resolved (intended access = Archived)
Analyzer shows nothing for resources in another Region External analyzers are Regional: create one there
Updates since the videos
  • Region scope corrected after ▶ #135/#136: external access analyzers are Regional, while the unused access analyzer is created in one Region but analyzes IAM users and roles globally.
  • The unused access tracking period range is 1–365 days.
  • Preview access lets you see findings for a policy before applying it.

Real-world practice

  • Expect unused findings on break-glass and OrganizationAccountAccessRole-type roles. Create archive rules for those by name/path rather than deleting them.
  • Cost scales with identities: $0.20 × (users + roles) × accounts per month. Large orgs with many service roles should budget or scope. External access is free, so always enable it.
  • Don’t auto-delete roles: tag-and-disable first (remove trust or attach a deny), wait a grace period, then delete. Some roles are used rarely (DR, yearly jobs). Lambda automation can disable unused keys after N days.
  • Feed unused-permission recommendations into IaC PRs so least privilege sticks.
  • Deploy analyzers with a service-managed StackSet targeting the delegated admin account in all enabled Regions, and use a Config rule or Security Hub control to detect Regions without an analyzer.
  • Create org-wide archive rules for expected cross-account principals (e.g. the Identity Center SAML provider, known partner accounts) to keep the Active list meaningful.
  • Pipe findings through Security Hub and route by account owner tags. S3 public access and KMS cross-account findings should page someone.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create an account-level external access analyzer.
  2. Add a bucket policy that allows another account, and watch the finding appear.
  3. Add a check-no-new-access step to a local script and run it against an old/new policy pair.
  4. Cleanup: delete the bucket and the analyzer.

Part 2 – Detection & Logging

Which detection service? (most-tested comparison)

At a glance

The exam’s favourite question shape: several detection services sound alike, and the keyword in the question decides the answer. This page compares them side by side and shows the delegated-administrator pattern they all share.

  • Exam skills: aggregate security events (1.1.3) · metrics, alerts & dashboards (1.1.4) · automated assessments (1.1.5) · validate findings, assess scope (2.2.3) · root cause analysis (2.2.5) · scan compute for vulnerabilities (3.2.3) · delegated admin (6.1.4)
  • Videos: none in the course (knowledge-based; facts cross-checked against ▶ #36, ▶ #43, ▶ #46, ▶ #48, ▶ #49)
  • Memory hook: GuardDuty = threats, Inspector = vulnerabilities, Macie = S3 data, Detective = root cause, Security Hub = single pane + compliance standards, Config = configuration state/history, Trusted Advisor = account best-practice checklist.

Side-by-side comparison

Service Answers the question Data it looks at Output Agent?
GuardDuty “Is something malicious happening right now?” (threat detection) Foundational: CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 DNS logs (its own independent streams). Optional plans: S3 (data events), EKS audit, Runtime, Malware (EC2/S3), RDS logins, Lambda network Threat findings (Recon:, UnauthorizedAccess:, CryptoCurrency: …) No (only Runtime Monitoring uses an agent)
Inspector “Which workloads have known CVEs / exposed ports?” (vulnerability management) EC2 packages, ECR images, Lambda dependencies, your own Lambda code (code scanning), network reachability Vulnerability findings, Inspector score, SBOM SSM agent for EC2 (or agentless snapshot scan)
Macie “Where is sensitive data in S3, and is the bucket exposed?” S3 objects + bucket policies/ACLs Sensitive-data findings + policy findings No
Detective “What is the root cause / blast radius of this finding?” (investigation) Behavior graph of CloudTrail, Flow Logs, GuardDuty findings, EKS audit logs + Security Hub findings Visualizations, finding groups, investigations No (needs GuardDuty on ≥ 48 h)
Security Hub CSPM “What is my overall security posture?” (aggregation + compliance checks) Findings from the services above + its own control checks (via Config) Normalized findings (ASFF), security score No (needs Config)
Config “What did this resource look like, and is it compliant?” Resource configuration items Config history, rule compliance, remediation No
Trusted Advisor “Am I following basic AWS best practices in this account?” ▶ #36 Account configuration across 6 categories Check status (red / yellow / green), weekly email No

Keyword map from the videos

If the question says… Answer

Two “Security Hubs”

Security Hub CSPM AWS Security Hub (unified, GA late 2025)
What The original service: standards, controls, findings Sits on top of GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM and Macie
Output ASFF findings, security score Correlated exposures / attack paths in OCSF

See ▶ #49.

Delegated administrator pattern

Applies to GuardDuty, Security Hub, Detective, Inspector, Macie, Config, Security Lake, Access Analyzer, Firewall Manager, CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs centralization.

Done from Step
Management account Register a security/audit account as delegated admin (Organizations trusted access, EnableOrganizationAdminAccount) ▶ #47
Delegated admin Enable member accounts and turn on auto-enable for new accounts ▶ #47
  • Most of these services are Regional: delegate and enable in every Region you use (or use Security Hub central configuration).
  • Don’t run security tooling from the management account (SRA best practice).
  • The course uses one Security Tooling account as delegated admin for every security service. The Detective console even recommends the account that is already GuardDuty/Security Hub admin. ▶ #47
  • The Log Archive account only stores data. ▶ #40 Exception: CloudWatch Logs centralization makes Log Archive both delegated admin and destination. ▶ #106
  • Manage membership through Organizations, not invitations. Org members can’t disable or leave the service themselves, which stops an attacker in a member account from turning detection off. ▶ #44

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer

Single pane of glass, CIS / FSBP compliance score Security Hub CSPM (needs Config)
Configuration history, “was this compliant last week?” Config
New accounts must get the service automatically Delegated admin + auto-enable

AWS CloudTrail

At a glance

Records API activity (who, what, when, from where) across an account or a whole organization. It is the audit log behind every incident-response and authentication-troubleshooting question, and one of the first places to look in any investigation.

  • Exam skills: log sources & storage (1.2.1) · analyze logs (1.2.4) · troubleshoot logging config & permissions (1.3.1) · fix missing logs (1.3.2) · logs as forensic artifacts (2.2.1) · search & correlate logs (2.2.2) · delegated admin (6.1.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #37 About CloudTrail · ▶ #38 Management, data and Insights events · ▶ #39 3 ways of recording data · ▶ #40 Organization trail · ▶ #41 CloudTrail Lake for IR · (▶ #114 Athena with CloudTrail → see Amazon Athena + AWS Glue)
  • Defaults of a new account: management events only, 90-day Event history, no trails, no data events, no Insights events.

What CloudTrail records

  • View, search, download, archive, analyze and respond to account activity across a single Region, multiple Regions or multiple accounts. ▶ #37 00:00
  • It records AWS API calls made from the console, SDKs, CLI and AWS services, plus non-API events such as console sign-in: practically every action in your AWS infrastructure. ▶ #37 00:11
  • Use it to audit accounts and to monitor simple or large, complex environments for suspicious or dangerous actions. If something weird happens (security or operational), CloudTrail should be one of the first, if not the first, places you investigate. ▶ #37 00:50

Questions it answers: who took this action and when? What resources did they access or modify? What events happened in a given time frame? Changing an EC2 instance in the console still calls the AWS API, so it is logged. Each record holds the caller identity, time, source IP address, request parameters and response elements. ▶ #37 01:21

Defaults are limited (“a very important topic to understand”): a new account logs management events only, keeps them 90 days in Event history, and has no trails, no data events and no Insights events. To keep data longer you create a trail. ▶ #37 01:50

High-value events to track: ▶ #37 02:30

Event Why
Console sign-ins (success and failure) Spot brute-force attempts and after-hours logins, confirm every login uses MFA. “Your console is your most critical asset.” ▶ #37 02:40
Root logins Root should almost never be used. Alert on any root login. ▶ #37 03:01
Security group changes Even an accidental change can open a hole. Route changes through change management. ▶ #37 03:20
NACL and route table changes Unauthorized changes can be indicators of compromise; even intentional ones can weaken your posture. ▶ #37 03:41

The slide labels the root sign-in “API: RootAccountLogin”. The real event is ConsoleLogin (event source signin.amazonaws.com) with userIdentity.type = "Root", additionalEventData.MFAUsed, and responseElements.ConsoleLogin = Success/Failure.

Event types: management, data, Insights, network activity

Management events are on by default and many people think they log more than they do. Without data events an incident can leave you completely blind, and enabling logging afterwards only shows now and the future: you can’t see back in time. ▶ #38 00:10

Management events Data events Insights events Network activity events
Plane Control plane: create, read, update, delete, list resources ▶ #38 01:01 Data plane: operations on or within a resource, high volume ▶ #38 03:21 Anomalies in API call volume / error rate ▶ #38 05:30 API calls passing through VPC endpoints, including calls denied by the endpoint policy
Default On Off ▶ #38 03:01 Off ▶ #38 06:41 Off
Cost First copy per Region free (pay S3 storage); extra copies charged Charged Charged Charged

Management events examples: IAM AttachRolePolicy (configuring security), EC2 CreateDefaultVpc (registering devices), EC2 CreateSubnet (routing rules), CloudTrail CreateTrail (setting up logging), plus CreateUser, PutBucketPolicy, ConsoleLogin. ▶ #38 01:40 They can be logged as Read, Write or both. Exclude AWS KMS events / exclude RDS Data API events cut noise (KMS Decrypt/GenerateDataKey are high-volume management events).

Non-API events are also management events: ▶ #38 02:10

  • AWS service events: created by an AWS service, not by your request to a public API. eventType = AwsServiceEvent, e.g. KMS automatically rotating a customer managed key (RotateKey, invokedBy: "AWS Internal"). ▶ #38 02:21
  • Console sign-in events: successful or failed sign-in as IAM user or root, root changing its password or MFA settings, etc. ▶ #38 02:31

{
  "eventVersion": "1.05",
  "userIdentity": { "accountId": "123456789012", "invokedBy": "AWS Internal" },
  "eventTime": "2019-06-02T00:06:08Z",
  "eventSource": "kms.amazonaws.com",
  "eventName": "RotateKey",
  "awsRegion": "us-east-2",
  "sourceIPAddress": "AWS Internal",
  "userAgent": "AWS Internal",
  "requestParameters": null,
  "responseElements": null,
  "eventID": "234f004b-EXAMPLE",
  …
}

Sign-in via the global endpoint or as root records ConsoleLogin in us-east-1; sign-in via a Regional endpoint records it in that Region. Other global services (IAM, STS, CloudFront) are also logged as global service events in us-east-1.

Data events are ignored entirely unless configured, because AWS charges more for them. ▶ #38 03:01 AWS can change the list; check the docs. Examples: ▶ #38 03:40

  • DynamoDB: PutItem, DeleteItem, UpdateItem
  • Lambda: function execution via Invoke
  • S3: GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject
  • CloudTrail: PutAuditEvents on a CloudTrail Lake channel

Selectors: trails can use basic or advanced event selectors for S3, Lambda and DynamoDB; every other data event type needs advanced event selectors. Event data stores use only advanced selectors. Use advanced selectors to filter, e.g. only one bucket or only writes.

The S3 split (know which level is which): ▶ #38 04:21

Level Event type Actions
Account Management DeleteAccountPublicAccessBlock, GetAccountPublicAccessBlock, PutAccountPublicAccessBlock
Bucket Management (logged by default) CreateBucket, DeleteBucket, PutBucketPolicy, PutBucketPublicAccessBlock, PutBucketVersioning, PutBucketReplication, PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration, … (the OPTIONS object CORS preflight also counts as bucket-level)
Object Data (must be enabled) CopyObject, DeleteObject, GetObject, ListObjects, PutObject, …

Scenario: exfiltrated sensitive S3 data with only management events logged means you could completely miss it and have nothing to investigate. The trade-off is cost, an organizational decision. ▶ #38 05:00

Insights events continuously analyze management events, build a baseline of normal patterns, and fire when call volume or error rate leaves it. ▶ #38 05:41

  • Two types: ApiCallRateInsight (on write management events) and ApiErrorRateInsight (on management events, read and write). A baseline period (up to ~36 hours) is needed first.
  • Example: normally 1–2 AccessDenied errors on IAM CreateUser per 7 days, then suddenly ~15 per minute. CloudTrail writes one Insights event at the start of the unusual activity and one at the end. ▶ #38 05:50
  • Each gives the associated API, error code, incident time and statistics. ▶ #38 06:30
  • Delivered to the trail’s S3 bucket only when unusual activity is detected (management and data events are continuous). ▶ #38 06:50
  • View them in the console, send them to CloudWatch Logs, or match them with an EventBridge rule for email/SMS. ▶ #38 07:02

Network activity events let the VPC owner see who uses its VPC endpoints, including denied calls.

Three ways to record: Event history, trails, CloudTrail Lake

Event history ▶ #39 00:11 Trails ▶ #39 00:51 CloudTrail Lake ▶ #39 02:20
Setup On by default, none needed You create it You create an event data store (EDS)
Content Management events only, per Region Management, data and Insights events Management and data events, Config configuration items, Audit Manager evidence, non-AWS events (integrations: on-prem VMs, containers, SaaS)
Retention 90 days, can’t be extended As long as you keep the S3 objects Up to ~10 years
Tamper-proof Immutable Use integrity validation Immutable
Access Console search/download, LookupEvents API S3, optionally CloudWatch Logs and EventBridge ▶ #39 01:50 SQL queries, Lake dashboards (widgets backed by SQL queries)
Cost Free First copy of management events free (pay S3 storage); data events charged ▶ #39 02:01 Ingestion + storage + data scanned; “gets expensive with a lot of data” ▶ #39 03:52
  • Create a trail to keep management events beyond 90 days and to capture data and Insights events, which Event history never records. ▶ #39 01:10
  • Lake can import existing CloudTrail logs from S3 into an EDS. Event selectors control exactly which data is stored, and queries can filter on many more fields than Event history’s simple lookup.
  • Free tier: Event history (management events, last 90 days, console or lookup-events API). Lake: a 30-day trial with up to 5 GB ingested, 5 GB scanned, storage free during the trial. ▶ #39 03:57

SELECT eventTime, useridentity.arn, awsRegion
FROM event_data_store_ID
WHERE awsRegion IN ('us-east-1', 'us-west-2')
  AND eventName = 'ConsoleLogin'

This lists who logged into the console, and when, in two Regions.

Not real-time. CloudTrail typically delivers events within an average of about 5 minutes of the API call, and this is not guaranteed (see the CloudTrail SLA). There is always a delay between an attacker’s API call and your alert. ▶ #39 05:00 For near-real-time reaction use EventBridge (detail-type: "AWS API Call via CloudTrail"). Read-only Get/List/Describe calls are not delivered to EventBridge by default.

Trail settings that matter

  • Multi-Region trail is the default and the recommended choice. A trail created in the console is always multi-Region. Event history is per Region, so activity in an unused Region needs a multi-Region trail.
  • Log file integrity validation: hourly digest files (SHA-256 hash chain, RSA-signed) in a CloudTrail-Digest/ folder next to CloudTrail/. Verify with aws cloudtrail validate-logs. This proves logs weren’t modified or deleted, so they hold up as forensic evidence. “Definitely important.” ▶ #40 09:02
  • Encryption: SSE-S3 by default. Use SSE-KMS for separation of duties (the console enables it by default for new trails). The key policy must allow cloudtrail.amazonaws.com to kms:GenerateDataKey* (condition on aws:SourceArn / kms:EncryptionContext:aws:cloudtrail:arn), and readers need kms:Decrypt.
  • CloudTrail → CloudWatch Logs: needs an IAM role that CloudTrail assumes (logs:CreateLogStream, logs:PutLogEvents). This enables metric filters and alarms (see Amazon CloudWatch).

Organization trail

One org-wide trail sends every account’s logs to one central S3 bucket in the Log Archive account, per the AWS Security Reference Architecture (SRA). ▶ #40 00:10 In the course build this is step 3, after enabling Organizations and creating the member accounts. ▶ #40 00:35 In production use infrastructure as code or AWS Control Tower; the click-through is for learning. ▶ #40 00:51

  • Created from the management account or a delegated admin. It logs every member account. Members can see it but cannot modify or delete it. S3 prefix: AWSLogs/<org-id>/<account-id>/….
  • Delegated admin = Security Tooling (you administer CloudTrail there), data = Log Archive. Don’t make Log Archive the delegated admin. ▶ #40 02:21
  • The trail is owned by the management account even when the delegated admin creates it, so the bucket policy’s aws:SourceArn uses the management account ID, not the Security Tooling ID. ▶ #40 05:12
  • CloudWatch Logs delivery can’t be configured for an org trail in the console (as delegated admin). Use the API/CLI. ▶ #40 09:02

The log bucket (Log Archive): general purpose, Object Ownership: ACLs disabled (bucket owner enforced, the default), Block all public access on. Recommended for production but skipped in the demo: versioning, SSE-KMS default encryption and Object Lock. ▶ #40 03:40

Bucket policy: three statements, all for principal cloudtrail.amazonaws.com, each with aws:SourceArn = the trail ARN arn:aws:cloudtrail:us-east-1:<MANAGEMENT-account-id>:trail/<trail-name>: ▶ #40 04:10

Sid Action Resource
AWSCloudTrailAclCheck s3:GetBucketAcl The bucket ARN (bucket-level)
AWSCloudTrailWrite s3:PutObject + s3:x-amz-acl = bucket-owner-full-control arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/AWSLogs/<management-account-id>/* (object-level, so /…/*)
AWSCloudTrailOrganizationWrite s3:PutObject + same ACL condition arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/AWSLogs/<org-id>/*: this is where the organization ID goes

The trail name in the ARN (demo: org-management-events, meaning management events only) is a placeholder for a trail that doesn’t exist yet; it must match the name you give the trail later. The aws:SourceArn condition prevents confused-deputy use of the bucket by other trails. Bucket-owner-enforced (ACLs disabled) makes the ACL condition harmless.

Org trail bucket policy as shown in the demo (bucket org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs)

Management account 299551924423, org o-jqbqypd27k.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AWSCloudTrailAclCheck",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "s3:GetBucketAcl",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudtrail:us-east-1:299551924423:trail/org-management-events"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "AWSCloudTrailWrite",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs/AWSLogs/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudtrail:us-east-1:299551924423:trail/org-management-events",
          "s3:x-amz-acl": "bucket-owner-full-control"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "AWSCloudTrailOrganizationWrite",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs/AWSLogs/o-jqbqypd27k/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudtrail:us-east-1:299551924423:trail/org-management-events",
          "s3:x-amz-acl": "bucket-owner-full-control"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Create-trail options: Enable for all accounts in my organization is only available because the account is the delegated admin (or the management account). Storage: Use existing S3 bucket. An optional prefix goes in front of the AWSLogs/ directory. Log file SSE-KMS encryption needs a KMS key/alias (not enabled in the demo). ▶ #40 07:40 The demo trail org-management-events is multi-Region, enabled for all accounts, management events only (KMS and RDS Data API events not excluded), no data or Insights events.

Resulting layout: AWSLogs/<management-account-id>/ and AWSLogs/<org-id>/<each-account-id>/. Each account has CloudTrail/ (compressed .json.gz log files) and CloudTrail-Digest/ (for log file validation), both split by Region / year / month / day. ▶ #40 09:50 No more logging into 10–20 accounts: feed this one bucket to a SIEM or to CloudTrail Lake.

Console demo: deploy an organization trail ([▶ #40](https://youtu.be/xZHPVtLSpLQ))
  1. Access portal → copy the Security Tooling account ID (851725223689). ▶ #40 01:22
  2. Management account → CloudTrail → Settings → Delegated administrator → Register administrator → paste the Security Tooling ID.
  3. Organizations console → copy the org ID (o-xxxxxxxxxx). ▶ #40 02:38
  4. Log Archive → S3 → Create bucket (general purpose, e.g. org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs in us-east-1, ACLs disabled, block all public access). ▶ #40 03:00
  5. Bucket → Permissions → Bucket policy → paste the 3-statement policy, replacing bucket name, management account ID, trail name and org ID. ▶ #40 04:10
  6. Security Tooling → CloudTrail → Create trail → enable for all accounts → use existing bucket → (optional prefix, SSE-KMS) → log file validation on → management events → create. ▶ #40 07:40
  7. Log Archive with the ReadOnly permission set → S3 → confirm AWSLogs/<org-id>/<account-id>/CloudTrail/<region>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/*.json.gz. ▶ #40 09:50

If the AWSLogs/... folders don’t appear, the trail or the bucket policy is wrong: check the source ARN (management account ID + exact trail name) and the bucket ARN / resource paths. Any mistake means CloudTrail can’t write. ▶ #40 11:40

CloudTrail Lake for incident response

Use Lake for org-wide IR searches with SQL, without building an Athena pipeline: query 3, 100 or 1,000 accounts at once instead of chasing logs across 50 accounts during a time-sensitive incident. ▶ #41 11:10 It can be federated to the Glue Data Catalog for Athena (Lake query federation). Homework from the instructor: do the same centrally with Athena; it is mostly about getting permissions right. ▶ #41 11:50

Lake workflow (“How it works” panel): create event data stores → run SQL queries (results kept 7 days) → optionally add integrations (partner apps, containers, VMs, databases) → optionally copy trail events into Lake. ▶ #41 00:31

Pricing option Recommended when Retention
One-year extendable < 25 TB ingested per month First year included, extendable to max 10 years
Seven-year > 25 TB per month 7 years included, can’t go past 7

You can’t switch an existing store between them. Billing is on uncompressed data ingested. ▶ #41 00:51

Creating an organization event data store (from Security Tooling with AdministratorAccess; ReadOnly can’t create resources): ▶ #41 00:21

  • Choose events: CloudTrail events, management events (data events optional). ▶ #41 01:10
  • Enable for all accounts in my organization makes it org-wide. The copy-trail-events option becomes greyed out when you select it. ▶ #41 01:20
  • Ingest events: keep ingesting new events beyond the copy. For IR, leave it on if the attack is ongoing; otherwise typically just import past events. ▶ #41 01:40
  • All Regions (single Region is an option for cost); management events Read and Write. ▶ #41 02:01
  • Deleting a store takes days (pending deletion, 7-day window), so the demo store is named IncidentResponse2. Termination protection is on by default. ▶ #41 00:31

The EDS ARN (arn:aws:cloudtrail:us-east-1:299551924423:eventdatastore/107d0eb7-…) is in the management account even though the delegated admin created it. Retention 366 days, no customer managed KMS key, Lake query federation off.

Gotcha 1: copying trail events into an org EDS must be done from the management account. The delegated admin can’t do it (an AWS limitation at recording time; the instructor suspects it may be lifted). ▶ #41 03:01

  • Management account → event data store → Event copy status → Copy trail events. ▶ #41 03:31
  • The org trail’s default path covers only that account’s logs, so choose Enter S3 URI and trim it to the org ID level: s3://org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs/AWSLogs/o-jqbqypd27k/. ▶ #41 03:50
  • Time range (e.g. last 6 months) depends on how much data you need and want to pay for. ▶ #41 04:20 Only events within the EDS retention period are copied (90-day retention → nothing older than 90 days).
  • Create a new role (recommended), named with prefix CloudTrailLake-us-east-1- (CloudTrailLake-us-east-1-incidentresponse). ▶ #41 04:41

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "Service": "cloudtrail.amazonaws.com" },
      "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole"],
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "299551924423" },
        "ArnLike": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:cloudtrail:*:299551924423:eventdatastore/*" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Note the confused-deputy protections aws:SourceAccount and aws:SourceArn.

Gotcha 2: the tight Log Archive bucket policy blocks the role. The copy retries for a minute or two and fails with InvalidImportSourceException: Access denied. Verify that the IAM role policy, S3 bucket policy, and KMS key policy have adequate permissions. ▶ #41 05:10 Check exactly those three, as the error says.

Fix: ▶ #41 06:01

  1. IAM → Roles → copy the new role’s ARN. ▶ #41 06:12
  2. Log Archive (AdministratorAccess) → S3 → bucket → Permissions → Edit bucket policy. Above the existing CloudTrail statements, allow the role s3:ListBucket, s3:GetBucketAcl, s3:GetObject on the bucket and its objects. ▶ #41 06:32
  3. Save. Back in the management account, redo Copy trail events with Use existing role → “Successfully created import request”. ▶ #41 07:32

{
  "Sid": "AllowCloudTrailLakeImport",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::299551924423:role/CloudTrailLake-us-east-1-incidentresponse" },
  "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketAcl", "s3:GetObject"],
  "Resource": [
    "arn:aws:s3:::org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs",
    "arn:aws:s3:::org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs/*"
  ]
}

(Reconstructed from the narration; the template was not fully on screen.)

The import ended 1057/1065 prefixes copied (59 failures), status Failed, with “UNKNOWN FAILURE” on some prefixes. The instructor attributes it to other changes he was making; most data was copied. “Things don’t always go smoothly.” ▶ #41 08:31

Querying the whole organization: from Security Tooling (queries need more than ReadOnly; ideally a least-privilege query-only role) → Lake → Query → select the store. ▶ #41 09:10 The AI query generator (Preview) writes SQL from a prompt such as “I want to see the latest accessdenied error messages, and what the eventName was as well as which accountId it occurred in”. Then adjust the time filter and LIMIT. ▶ #41 09:41

SELECT eventname,
       useridentity.accountid,
       errormessage
FROM 107d0eb7-0ad3-4f69-afbb-6f1dc70312fa
WHERE errorcode = 'AccessDenied'
  AND eventtime >= '2024-06-29 20:00:00'
ORDER BY eventtime DESC
LIMIT 30;

The FROM target is the event data store ID.

The 30 rows come from multiple accounts: e.g. PutBucketPolicy Access Denied in Log Archive; ListRoots/DeleteLogGroup/CreateFunctionUrlConfig denied for OrganizationAccountAccessRole in Demo; GetCostAndUsage “IAM user access not activated”. ▶ #41 10:30

Console demo: org event data store + cross-account IR query ([▶ #41](https://youtu.be/EZjeMn4p_KY))
  1. Access portal → Security Tooling → AdministratorAccess → CloudTrail → Lake → Event data stores → Create event data store. ▶ #41 00:21
  2. Name IncidentResponse2, one-year extendable pricing, defaults, no Lake query federation → Next. ▶ #41 00:51
  3. CloudTrail events → management events → Enable for all accounts in my organization → (optional) ingest events → Read + Write → Next → Create. ▶ #41 01:10
  4. No copy option → switch to the management account → same store → Copy trail events. ▶ #41 03:21
  5. Source Enter S3 URI up to AWSLogs/<org-id>/, last 6 months, delivery = the store, Create a new role → Copy events → confirm the pricing warning. ▶ #41 03:50
  6. AccessDenied → copy the role ARN → in Log Archive add the bucket policy statement for the role. ▶ #41 06:01
  7. Management account → copy again with the existing role → monitor copy status. ▶ #41 07:32
  8. Security Tooling → Lake → Query → select the store → query generator → Generate → adjust → Run → review cross-account results. ▶ #41 09:10

Missing logs: troubleshooting

CloudTrail logs missing? Check these
  1. Trail IsLogging = false (someone called StopLogging). Check with get-trail-status.
  2. The S3 bucket policy doesn’t allow cloudtrail.amazonaws.com s3:PutObject (with aws:SourceArn), or the prefix is wrong. For an org trail the usual mistake is the source ARN (must use the management account ID + exact trail name) or the bucket ARN / resource paths. ▶ #40 11:40
  3. The KMS key policy doesn’t allow CloudTrail, or readers lack kms:Decrypt (logs exist but can’t be read).
  4. The trail is single-Region and the activity happened elsewhere.
  5. Data events were never enabled, or an advanced event selector filters them out.
  6. The CloudWatch Logs delivery role is missing or broken.
  7. An SCP or bucket policy denies the write.
  8. Lake copy/import fails (InvalidImportSourceException) → IAM role policy, S3 bucket policy, KMS key policy. ▶ #41 05:10
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • CloudTrail should be among the first places you investigate suspicious activity. ▶ #37 00:50
  • Defaults: management events only, 90-day Event history, no trails. ▶ #37 01:50
  • Management events ≠ everything; turning on data events after an incident won’t show the past. ▶ #38 00:30
  • S3 exfiltration with only management events → nothing to investigate. ▶ #38 05:00
  • Event history is free, default, immutable, 90 days, management events only. ▶ #39 00:11
  • “CloudTrail is not considered to be real-time logging”: about 5 minutes on average, not guaranteed. ▶ #39 05:00
  • Delegated admin = Security Tooling, data = Log Archive. ▶ #40 02:21
  • Bucket policy source ARN uses the management account ID. ▶ #40 05:12
  • Enable log file validation; org-trail CloudWatch Logs can’t be set in the console. ▶ #40 09:02
  • Copying trail events into an org event data store requires the management account. ▶ #41 03:01
  • Tight Log Archive bucket policies block the Lake import role; add an explicit statement for it. ▶ #41 05:10
  • Use admin or a dedicated query role; ReadOnly can’t create stores or run queries in this setup. ▶ #41 09:10

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Prove logs were not tampered with Log file integrity validation (+ S3 Object Lock / MFA delete on the bucket)
Who downloaded this S3 object? Data events for S3. If neither data events nor S3 server access logs were on, you can’t look back: enable them now (GuardDuty S3 Protection findings may give partial evidence)
Who changed the bucket policy / disabled Block Public Access? Management events, in Event history for 90 days even with no trail
Lambda invocations, DynamoDB item reads, S3 object reads Data events. CreateFunction, CreateTable, PutBucketPolicy → management events
Spike in TerminateInstances or AccessDenied errors CloudTrail Insights
Member-account admins must not stop logging Organization trail + SCP denying cloudtrail:StopLogging / DeleteTrail
Query a year of org API activity with SQL, minimal setup CloudTrail Lake
Cheapest for occasional queries over S3 logs Athena
Near-real-time on log groups, short term CloudWatch Logs Insights
