Keep logs 7 years for compliance Trail to S3 + lifecycle to Glacier (+ Object Lock), or a Lake EDS with long retention
Real-time alert when root logs in EventBridge rule on ConsoleLogin with userIdentity.type = Root (or metric filter + alarm on a trail sent to CW Logs)
Detect within seconds/minutes EventBridge on CloudTrail events, or GuardDuty, not querying S3 logs (~5 min delivery)
Attacker acted in an unused Region, nothing in Event history Event history is per Region → multi-Region trail
Which principals used our VPC endpoint, including denied calls Network activity events
Copy trail events to an org EDS, option greyed out Do it from the management account
Updates since the videos
  • There is no API called RootAccountLogin (as the #37 slide suggests). The event is ConsoleLogin (source signin.amazonaws.com) with userIdentity.type = "Root" and responseElements.ConsoleLogin = Success/Failure.
  • At ▶ #38 04:51 the instructor says you’d “create a trail and then create an event data store” to log data events. You need either a trail (data event selectors → S3) or a CloudTrail Lake event data store, not both.
  • Insights types, corrected: ApiCallRateInsight works on write management events; ApiErrorRateInsight on read and write management events.
  • AWS’s own org-trail bucket policy template scopes the AWSCloudTrailWrite statement to AWSLogs/<management-account-id>/*; the demo uses the broader AWSLogs/*.
  • The “copy trail events only from the management account” restriction was an AWS limitation at recording time and may change.

Real-world practice

CLI: KMS-encrypted org trail, S3 write data events on one bucket, integrity check 
# Org trail, multi-Region, KMS-encrypted, integrity validation on
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name org-trail --s3-bucket-name org-ct-logs-<acct> \
  --is-organization-trail --is-multi-region-trail --enable-log-file-validation \
  --kms-key-id arn:aws:kms:ap-southeast-1:<acct>:key/<id>
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name org-trail

# S3 data events only for write calls on one sensitive bucket
aws cloudtrail put-event-selectors --trail-name org-trail --advanced-event-selectors '[
 {"Name":"S3 writes on pii bucket","FieldSelectors":[
  {"Field":"eventCategory","Equals":["Data"]},
  {"Field":"resources.type","Equals":["AWS::S3::Object"]},
  {"Field":"readOnly","Equals":["false"]},
  {"Field":"resources.ARN","StartsWith":["arn:aws:s3:::pii-bucket/"]}]}]'

# Verify integrity for a time window
aws cloudtrail validate-logs --trail-arn <trail-arn> --start-time 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z

CloudTrail Lake query, “everything a compromised access key did”:

SELECT eventTime, eventSource, eventName, awsRegion, sourceIPAddress, errorCode
FROM <event-data-store-id>
WHERE userIdentity.accessKeyId = 'AKIAEXAMPLE'
  AND eventTime > '2026-11-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY eventTime;
  • Production layout: org trail → central Log Archive bucket (Object Lock, deny delete, KMS key owned by Log Archive). The Security/Audit account gets read-only access. An SCP blocks StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail and PutEventSelectors.
  • Harden the log bucket: SSE-KMS with a dedicated key, versioning + Object Lock (compliance mode) or at least MFA delete, lifecycle to Glacier, deny s3:DeleteObject and policy changes except from a break-glass role, and log access to the bucket itself. ▶ #40 03:40
  • Control Tower already creates an org trail into the Log Archive bucket. Don’t build a second one without reason; duplicate management-event copies are billed.
  • Data-event baseline: S3 data events on sensitive buckets (or all writes + reads on sensitive prefixes) and Lambda data events on critical functions, filtered with advanced selectors to control cost. Make sure Security Lake / SIEM ingest includes data events if detections rely on them.
  • Insights is cheap relative to data events and catches credential-stuffing-like spikes of AccessDenied from compromised keys.
  • Org-trail CloudWatch Logs delivery is usually configured once (CLI/IaC) in the management account, so the log group lives there, not in Log Archive. Many teams stream from S3 into a SIEM instead.
  • Pre-build the org event data store (or Athena tables) before an incident. Creating and importing during one costs time, and imports can partially fail (59 failed prefixes in the demo). ▶ #41 08:31
  • Give IR a dedicated query role with only cloudtrail:StartQuery, GetQueryResults, DescribeQuery, ListEventDataStores (a permission set in Security Tooling). Save common IR queries: root activity, ConsoleLogin failures, CreateAccessKey, PutBucketPolicy, StopLogging, activity by access key ID.
  • GuardDuty consumes CloudTrail management events (and S3 data events with S3 Protection) without you needing a trail. Still keep your own trail for evidence.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create a single-account, multi-Region trail with integrity validation, and send it to CloudWatch Logs.
  2. Upload an object to a bucket with S3 data events enabled, then find the PutObject event in S3 after ~5 minutes.
  3. Run validate-logs.
  4. (Org, ▶ #40, ▶ #41) Register Security Tooling as CloudTrail delegated admin, create the Log Archive bucket + 3-statement policy, create the org trail, then build an org event data store and run a cross-account AccessDenied query.
  5. Cleanup: delete-trail, then empty and delete the bucket and log group, and the event data store (disable termination protection, then delete).

Amazon CloudWatch (Metrics, Alarms, Logs, Logs Insights, Agent)

At a glance

AWS’s monitoring and observability service: metrics, alarms, dashboards, log storage and analytics for AWS services, EC2 (via the agent) and on-premises servers. It is the alerting backbone and the usual first log destination.

  • Exam skills: metrics, alerts & dashboards for anomalies (1.1.4) · configure service/app logging (1.2.2) · analyze logs (1.2.4) · fix missing logs / agent config (1.3.2) · search & correlate logs (2.2.2) · instance profiles & roles (3.2.2) · lifecycle & retention (5.2.3) · delegated admin (6.1.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #42 About CloudWatch · ▶ #106 Centralized CloudWatch logging · ▶ #107 Unified CloudWatch agent · (▶ #108 Logs data protection → file 04)
  • Cost trap: log groups never expire by default. Set retention.

CloudWatch vs CloudTrail

CloudWatch tracks applications and infrastructure through logs and performance metrics, across cloud and on-premises. ▶ #42 00:02 Collected data is stored historically and used for events and alarms, querying and anomaly detection. ▶ #42 00:22

CloudWatch CloudTrail
Purpose Performance & operational monitoring API activity logging & audit trails
Questions Is my app healthy? Is my code erroring or slow? Why did my Lambda crash? Who deleted my S3 bucket? Who accessed S3 objects? What changed in my security group, when, by whom?
Focus Metrics, logs, operational data User activity, compliance & governance logging

Know this distinction for the exam. ▶ #42 00:50

Core features and integrations

Service integrations (depth varies): ▶ #42 02:01

  • Lambda: execution logs, metrics, timeouts.
  • ECS/EKS: Container Insights, cluster metrics.
  • RDS: detailed database performance metrics.
  • API Gateway: access/execution logs, latency metrics.
  • Systems Manager: Session Manager session logs, Automation execution visibility.
  • Network Firewall: firewall metrics and logs. ▶ #42 02:10
  • EC2 sends only basic metrics by default. For OS-level metrics and logs install the CloudWatch agent, which uploads logs automatically. Then you can run Insights queries, export to S3, feed your SIEM. ▶ #42 03:00

Core functionality: ▶ #42 03:51

Feature What it gives you
Metrics Time-series data points: CPU utilization, memory usage, request counts, network throughput; custom metrics for gaps ▶ #42 03:51
Logs Application, AWS service and custom logs in log groups, queried with Logs Insights (SQL-like, pattern matching, statistics) ▶ #42 04:20
Traces (X-Ray) Technically separate, now deeply integrated: end-to-end request tracing, e.g. API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB, to find bottlenecks (or a developing attack) ▶ #42 04:51
Application Signals Automatic insights: Lambda cold starts, API latency spikes, DB connection issues (“something weird is going on, check this out”) ▶ #42 05:51
Network monitoring Unusual traffic patterns, connectivity debugging, network performance ▶ #42 06:11
Alarms (“super important”) Watch metrics, act when thresholds are crossed ▶ #42 06:20
Insights Container Insights (ECS/EKS), Lambda Insights, Database Insights, Application Insights, EC2 resource health ▶ #42 07:30

The X-Ray timeline shows exactly where time is spent: Init 696 ms, the function 707 ms, an S3 ListBuckets call 685 ms.

Operational scenario: a slow-API alarm fires → Application Insights identifies the slowdown → X-Ray traces it to one microservice → Container Insights checks if the ECS cluster is resource-constrained → CloudWatch Logs gives the service’s detailed logs. The cause could just as well be security-related. ▶ #42 08:10

Alarms, metric filters and security detections

  • Alarm use cases: CPU > 80% for 5 minutes; a spike in failed API requests (possible attack); billing visibility. Actions: SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2 actions, service-specific actions; integrate with EventBridge to route/transform, SQS, etc. ▶ #42 06:20
  • A metric filter turns a log pattern into a custom metric; an alarm on that metric notifies SNS (or triggers EC2/Auto Scaling/SSM actions).
  • Classic CIS pattern: CloudTrail → CW Logs → metric filter → alarm → SNS for root login, unauthorized API calls, console login without MFA, IAM policy changes, CloudTrail config changes, SG/NACL changes, and so on. EventBridge rules are the alternative for near-real-time single events.
  • Logs Insights is an ad-hoc query language over log groups (fields | filter | stats | sort) and can query several log groups at once. It is not an alerting tool.
  • Anomaly detection bands on metrics, or log anomaly detection on log groups, when there’s no known baseline.

Security use cases: ▶ #42 08:51

  • Alarms on suspicious API calls: repeated failed logins (especially root/admin), many unauthorized API requests. ▶ #42 09:01
  • VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch to detect unusual traffic patterns. ▶ #42 09:10
  • Dashboards for security metrics: failed root authentications, encryption errors. ▶ #42 09:22
  • Logs Insights to investigate incidents, e.g. tracking an attacker across services. ▶ #42 09:30

Data exfiltration detection: ▶ #42 09:41

  1. Send VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs.
  2. Create a metric filter for unusual outbound data transfer.
  3. Alarm when the metric spikes.
  4. Alarm → SNS → security team.

Log groups: retention, encryption, data protection

  • Retention: the default is Never expire. Set it per log group (1 day to 10 years). Many compliance frameworks need ~1 year; no need to keep logs forever unless required. The instructor calls this both a cost tip and an exam tip: CloudWatch “can get expensive fast”. ▶ #42 10:11 Archive cheaply to S3 (export task or Firehose). Enforce retention org-wide with the Config rule cw-loggroup-retention-period-check or automation.
  • Encryption: logs are always encrypted. Use a customer KMS key with associate-kms-key; the key policy must allow logs.<region>.amazonaws.com, with a kms:EncryptionContext:aws:logs:arn condition.
  • Data protection policies mask sensitive data (PII, credentials) in log events; unmasking needs logs:Unmask (skill 5.3.4, ▶ #108 in file 04).

Streaming and cross-account access

  • Subscription filters: real-time stream of log events to Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose, Lambda or OpenSearch. Max 2 subscription filters per log group; fan out via Kinesis if you need more.
  • Cross-account streaming uses a destination (wrapping a Kinesis stream or Firehose) in the central account, with a destination access policy allowing the source accounts or the org.
  • Cross-account observability: a monitoring account plus source accounts linked via Observability Access Manager (OAM) sinks and links. One account can view metrics, logs and traces of many accounts without copying them.
Need Use
Copy logs from all accounts, least overhead Centralization rules (below)
Analysts only view/query other accounts’ telemetry OAM cross-account observability
Stream in near real time to a custom pipeline (S3, OpenSearch, SIEM) Subscription filter → cross-account destination → Kinesis/Firehose

Org-wide log centralization

Native centralization rules copy log groups from source accounts and Regions into one destination account, the same idea as an org CloudTrail trail delivered to Log Archive, but for CloudWatch Logs. ▶ #106 00:00 It works with AWS Organizations to collect logs into one repository. ▶ #106 00:10

“CloudWatch only copies raw log data to your destination. Source account configurations and policies are not applied to centralized logs.” Set retention, data protection, etc. directly in the destination account.

Step 1: management account, trusted access + delegated admin ▶ #106 00:21

  1. CloudWatch → Setup → Settings → Organization tab. ▶ #106 00:30
  2. You can’t register a delegated admin until trusted access is on. ▶ #106 00:41
  3. Turn on trusted access: lets Organizations grant other AWS services permission to read information about the org and its accounts. It creates the service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForObservabilityAdmin. Only the management account can do this. ▶ #106 00:50
  4. Register delegated administrator → the Log Archive account, which is both delegated admin and destination. ▶ #106 01:11 Delegated admins can deploy CloudWatch features to all accounts or specific OUs; the management account cannot limit them to specific OUs.
  5. Result: status On, delegated administrators 1 of 1.

Step 2: delegated admin (Log Archive), create a rule. Sign in via the IAM Identity Center access portal → CloudWatch → Setup → Settings → Organization → Configure rule. ▶ #106 01:41 Without the delegated-admin registration this page errors. ▶ #106 01:50

Rule step Options
1. Source ▶ #106 02:01 Rule name (e.g. workload-accounts). Source accounts in Builder or Editor mode, filtered by account ID, OU ID, org ID, email, name. Filters are dynamic: “This rule updates automatically as changes occur in your AWS Organization”. Source Regions: one or more (demo us-east-1) ▶ #106 03:30
2. Destination ▶ #106 03:41 Destination account (Log Archive) and Region (us-east-1). Usually match source and destination Region to cut latency and cost ▶ #106 03:50; choose the Region with most log volume to avoid throttling against the centralization quota. Backup Region (optional): a synchronized copy in another Region of the destination account for Regional outages, at extra cost ▶ #106 04:01
3. Telemetry ▶ #106 04:20 All log groups (auto-updates as log groups come and go) or filter by name, prefix, keyword. “Log groups with identical names will be merged” in the destination
4. Review A service-linked role is created automatically in the destination account to read Organizations information

The instructor collected OU IDs (Infrastructure, Security, Workloads; Sandbox optional) from the management account, e.g. filter OrganizationalUnitId = 'ou-limh-8jwz2ox0', and complained the picker shows OU IDs without names. ▶ #106 02:21

KMS-encrypted source log groups (“very confusing”; docs and console didn’t match at recording time): ▶ #106 04:41

Option Result
1. Centralize with AWS KMS key Source log groups using a customer managed key are centralized and encrypted with a destination CMK whose ARN you supply. Its key policy must allow CloudWatch Logs, or centralization fails ▶ #106 05:13
2. Centralize without AWS KMS key Centralized, but the destination uses CloudWatch’s default server-side encryption (AES-GCM). Data is always encrypted either way ▶ #106 05:40
3. Do not centralize Those log groups are filtered out ▶ #106 06:10

KMS is best practice; the demo picks option 2 to skip key setup. ▶ #106 06:21

Rule health: status Healthy or Unhealthy in the console and API. Unhealthy means it hit an error; troubleshoot the configuration. ▶ #106 06:52

CloudTrail events for auditing and troubleshooting (be aware, don’t memorize): ▶ #106 07:02

  • CreateCentralizationRuleForOrganization: new rule
  • UpdateCentralizationRuleForOrganization: rule modified
  • DeleteCentralizationRuleForOrganization: rule deleted
  • GetCentralizationRuleForOrganization: rule details retrieved
  • ListCentralizationRulesForOrganization: rules listed

Use them to audit configuration changes and correlate with performance issues or replication failures.

Validation: more rules were created for the other OUs. In a member account (Containers) the CLI writes a test event to /cybr/demo-centralization. ▶ #106 07:30 In Log Archive → Logs → Log Management, the same log group and stream appear after a refresh, with log class Standard, retention Never expire, no KMS key, deletion protection Off. ▶ #106 08:10 Rules can cover the whole org, specific OUs or single accounts, e.g. exclude noisy dev accounts. ▶ #106 08:40

Console demo: centralize logs into Log Archive ([▶ #106](https://youtu.be/OIxIuyyg8-k))
  1. Management account → CloudWatch → Setup → Settings → Organization → Turn on trusted access. ▶ #106 00:50
  2. Register delegated administrator → Log Archive account. ▶ #106 01:11
  3. Access portal → Log Archive → CloudWatch → Settings → Organization → Configure rule. ▶ #106 01:41
  4. Rule workload-accounts; source OrganizationalUnitId = '<workloads OU>'; source Region us-east-1.
  5. Destination: Log Archive, us-east-1; no backup Region.
  6. Telemetry: all log groups; KMS option 2 (centralize without KMS in destination).
  7. Review → Create → status Healthy. Repeat for the Infrastructure and Security OUs. ▶ #106 06:42
  8. In a member account, write a test event:
REGION=us-east-1
LOG_GROUP="/cybr/demo-centralization"
LOG_STREAM="demo-$(date +%s)"
TS_MS=$(python - <<'PY'
import time
print(int(time.time()*1000))
PY
)

aws logs create-log-group --log-group-name "$LOG_GROUP" --region "$REGION" 2>/dev/null || true
aws logs create-log-stream --log-group-name "$LOG_GROUP" --log-stream-name "$LOG_STREAM" --region "$REGION"
aws logs put-log-events \
  --log-group-name "$LOG_GROUP" \
  --log-stream-name "$LOG_STREAM" \
  --log-events timestamp=$TS_MS,message="CYBR_CW_CENTRALIZATION_TEST success account=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text) region=$REGION" \
  --region "$REGION"
# returns {"nextSequenceToken": "…"}
  1. Log Archive → Logs → Log Management → refresh → /cybr/demo-centralization with the same stream is there. ▶ #106 08:10

Unified CloudWatch agent

Why it’s needed: out of the box EC2 ships no application logs, OS logs or detailed system metrics. Default metrics are only CPU utilization and CPU credit usage, high-level disk read/write operations, basic networking, status checks and a few more. ▶ #107 00:11 That’s too limited for production: when something breaks inside the instance you must log in and investigate by hand. ▶ #107 00:40

What the agent provides: ▶ #107 00:52

  • Collects application and system log files, and OS metrics like memory, disk and swap usage. ▶ #107 01:00
  • Sends everything to CloudWatch Logs and Metrics, so alarms, Logs Insights, etc. work on it.
  • One JSON config format for Linux, Windows and macOS, reusable across the fleet. ▶ #107 01:22 No need to log into the instance once configured.
  • Works on EC2, on-premises servers and containers, collecting metrics, logs and traces. ▶ #107 01:40
  • The old CloudWatch Logs agent (awslogs) is deprecated; exam answers use the unified agent.

Architecture: ▶ #107 01:52

  1. The agent runs on the instance.
  2. It reads a local JSON config file or fetches it from SSM Parameter Store (AmazonCloudWatch-*). ▶ #107 02:00
  3. It assumes the IAM role of the instance profile. ▶ #107 02:12
  4. It pushes logs and metrics to CloudWatch.

Installation options: ▶ #107 02:31

  • Manually on the server. The demo uses Amazon Linux 2023, whose repos already contain the package. ▶ #107 03:01
  • AWS Systems Manager: Run Command / Distributor package AmazonCloudWatchAgent (AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage).
  • CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on or Helm chart.
  • On-premises servers, new instances via CloudFormation, Workload Detection in the CloudWatch console.
  • Fleets: SSM Run Command / State Manager with AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage (install) and AmazonCloudWatch-ManageAgent (apply config from Parameter Store). Storing config in Parameter Store is best practice for fleets.
  • On-premises: -m onPremise with IAM user credentials, or better SSM hybrid activation / IAM Roles Anywhere for temporary credentials.

IAM: the instance role carries the AWS managed policy CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy (“Permissions required to use AmazonCloudWatchAgent on servers”), which lets the agent push logs and metrics. ▶ #107 03:20 It also allows ssm:GetParameter on AmazonCloudWatch-*, so configs in Parameter Store must use that prefix. Writing configs to Parameter Store from the wizard needs CloudWatchAgentAdminPolicy instead.

Install: connect with EC2 Instance Connect as ec2-user (not root) ▶ #107 03:40, then sudo yum install amazon-cloudwatch-agent (package amazon-cloudwatch-agent-1.300060.1-1.amzn2023.x86_64, 79 MB). Install creates the group and user cwagent, which the agent runs as. ▶ #107 04:10

Configuration wizard (sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-config-wizard) generates the JSON telling the agent what to collect, where, and as which user. The choices are not critical for the exam. ▶ #107 04:50

Question Demo answer
OS / host / user linux (also windows, darwin) / EC2 (not on-premises) / cwagent ▶ #107 05:00
StatsD daemon No. StatsD is a lightweight daemon on a local UDP/TCP port that receives custom application metrics ▶ #107 05:11
collectd · host metrics · per-core CPU · EC2 dimensions · aggregate EC2 dimensions No · yes · no · yes · yes
Collection interval 60 seconds (default) ▶ #107 05:33
Metric set Basic (memory and disk usage) · Standard (chosen: adds CPU, more memory/disk, swap) · Advanced (adds detailed CPU, disk and network statistics) ▶ #107 05:40
Import old CloudWatch Logs agent config None to import ▶ #107 06:20
Monitor log files Yes: path /var/log/myapp.log, log group ec2-app-logs, log group class Standard (CloudWatch Logs classes, not S3 storage classes), stream {instance_id}/myapp (default is the instance ID), retention option 2 = 1 day ▶ #107 06:31
X-Ray traces No ▶ #107 07:21
Store config in SSM Parameter Store No in the demo, but best practice when the template is reused across many instances ▶ #107 07:31

The wizard shows the generated JSON (what you could have written by hand) ▶ #107 06:00 and saves it to /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/config.json (“Edit it manually if needed”). ▶ #107 07:50

Start the agent: ▶ #107 08:00

sudo touch /var/log/myapp.log
sudo chmod 644 /var/log/myapp.log

sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \
  -a fetch-config \
  -m ec2 \
  -s \
  -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/config.json
Flag Meaning
-a fetch-config Load a configuration ▶ #107 08:31
-m ec2 Mode EC2 (vs onPremise) ▶ #107 08:40
-s (Re)start the agent after loading; used with fetch-config, append-config, remove-config ▶ #107 08:51
-c file:<path> Config source; for Parameter Store -c ssm:<parameter-name>
-l Log level (INFO, DEBUG, WARN, ERROR, OFF) for set-log-level

The browser terminal mangled the backslash continuations, so the instructor typed it on one line. ▶ #107 09:00 Output: config validation first/second phase succeeded, “Trying to detect region from ec2”, writes /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.toml, and creates the systemd symlink for amazon-cloudwatch-agent.service.

Verify: ▶ #107 09:41

sudo systemctl status amazon-cloudwatch-agent
# ● amazon-cloudwatch-agent.service - Amazon CloudWatch Agent
#    Loaded: … enabled …
#    Active: active (running) since …

echo "$(date) - Test message from CloudWatch agent lab" | sudo tee -a /var/log/myapp.log

CloudWatch → Logs → Log Management → filter ec2 → ec2-app-logs → stream i-…/myapp shows the test message (can take a minute, usually fast). ▶ #107 10:41 You now see OS and app logs without logging into the instance (no Instance Connect, Session Manager or SSH). ▶ #107 11:10

Console demo: install and configure the agent on EC2 ([▶ #107](https://youtu.be/2hk64gZWcnE))
  1. EC2 instance CloudWatch-Agent-Lab-Instance (t2.micro, Amazon Linux) with an instance role carrying CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy. ▶ #107 03:10
  2. Connect → EC2 Instance Connect → user ec2-user. ▶ #107 03:40
  3. sudo yum install amazon-cloudwatch-agent → creates the cwagent user/group. ▶ #107 04:10
  4. Run the wizard with the answers above. ▶ #107 04:21
  5. Create /var/log/myapp.log (chmod 644 so cwagent can read it). ▶ #107 08:00
  6. Start with amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:…/config.json.
  7. systemctl status → active (running). ▶ #107 09:41
  8. Append a test line; find it in CloudWatch Logs under ec2-app-logs / i-…/myapp. ▶ #107 10:41
CloudWatch agent not sending data? Check these
Symptom Cause
No logs/metrics at all Instance profile missing CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy, or the agent isn’t running (amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a status, systemctl status amazon-cloudwatch-agent)
Works in a public subnet, not a private one No route to the CloudWatch endpoints → add VPC interface endpoints logs and monitoring (or NAT)
Some files missing Wrong file_path in the config, or cwagent can’t read the file (e.g. chmod 644)
Config changes ignored Config not re-fetched: -a fetch-config -c ssm:<param> or -c file:<path>, with -s to restart
Need error details /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Know CloudWatch vs CloudTrail: performance/operations vs API audit. ▶ #42 00:40
  • EC2 gives basic metrics only; install the CloudWatch agent for logs, memory, disk. ▶ #42 03:00
  • Alarms are “super important”. ▶ #42 06:20
  • Logs never expire by default → set retention policies: a cost tip and an exam tip. ▶ #42 10:11
  • Trusted access must be on before you can register a delegated admin; it creates AWSServiceRoleForObservabilityAdmin. ▶ #106 00:41
  • Make Log Archive the delegated admin and destination. ▶ #106 01:21
  • Match source and destination Region for latency/cost; a backup Region adds cost. ▶ #106 03:50
  • With a destination CMK, its key policy must allow CloudWatch Logs or centralization fails. ▶ #106 05:13
  • Watch rule health and the centralization CloudTrail events; no need to memorize the names. ▶ #106 07:02
  • Memory, disk space, swap and log files need the agent. ▶ #107 01:00
  • Config in Parameter Store is best practice for fleets; the agent uses the instance profile role. ▶ #107 07:31
  • The agent also works on-premises, hybrid and in containers, on Linux/Windows/macOS. ▶ #107 11:30

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Memory / disk utilization for EC2 CloudWatch agent (not a built-in metric)
Stream logs from 50 accounts into one place in near real time Subscription filter → cross-account destination → Kinesis/Firehose → S3/OpenSearch
Least operational overhead to collect/copy CW logs from all accounts Org-level centralization rule with a delegated admin
Analysts only need to view/query other accounts’ logs OAM cross-account observability
Third subscription filter on a log group fails 2-filter limit; fan out via Kinesis
Alert when a specific error string appears in logs Metric filter + alarm (Logs Insights is ad-hoc)
Dedicated logging account (1.2.2) Central Log Archive account receiving CloudTrail, Config, Flow Logs and centralized CW logs
Can’t register a CloudWatch delegated admin Trusted access isn’t on yet (management account only)
Centralized log groups keep logs forever / PII not masked centrally Retention and data protection policies aren’t copied; set them in the destination
Centralization fails for KMS-encrypted log groups Destination CMK key policy doesn’t allow CloudWatch Logs
Unknown baseline for a metric / log volume Anomaly detection on metrics or log anomaly detection on log groups
Root login alarm via CloudWatch CloudTrail → CW Logs → metric filter → alarm → SNS
Detect exfiltration from flow logs Flow logs → CW Logs → metric filter on outbound bytes → alarm → SNS
Updates since the videos
  • The KMS options for centralization were “very confusing” at recording time because the docs and the console didn’t match. Check the current console wording; the three behaviours (with destination CMK, without KMS, don’t centralize) are what matter.
  • X-Ray is now presented inside CloudWatch, though it is technically a separate service.

Real-world practice

CLI: CIS root-usage metric filter, alarm and retention 
# CIS: alarm on root account usage (trail already sends to log group CloudTrail/org)
aws logs put-metric-filter --log-group-name CloudTrail/org --filter-name RootUsage \
  --filter-pattern '{ $.userIdentity.type = "Root" && $.userIdentity.invokedBy NOT EXISTS && $.eventType != "AwsServiceEvent" }' \
  --metric-transformations metricName=RootUsage,metricNamespace=CISBenchmark,metricValue=1
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name RootUsage --namespace CISBenchmark --metric-name RootUsage \
  --statistic Sum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 --threshold 1 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:...:security-alerts

aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name CloudTrail/org --retention-in-days 365

Logs Insights, “top AccessDenied callers in the last 24h” (CloudTrail log group):

fields @timestamp, userIdentity.arn, eventSource, eventName, errorCode
| filter errorCode like /AccessDenied|UnauthorizedOperation/
| stats count(*) as denials by userIdentity.arn, eventName
| sort denials desc
| limit 20

VPC Flow Logs in CW Logs, “rejected traffic by source”:

filter action = "REJECT" | stats count(*) as hits by srcAddr, dstPort | sort hits desc | limit 20
  • Biggest cost drivers are ingestion (per GB) and unbounded retention. Use the Infrequent Access log class for rarely queried logs and export/archive to S3 for the long term. ▶ #42 10:22
  • Centralize security-relevant logs (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 Resolver logs, WAF logs) in the Log Archive account / Security Lake rather than leaving them per account.
  • Alarm fatigue: route alarms through EventBridge → incident tooling with dedupe, and use composite alarms.
  • Centralization copies data, so you pay ingestion/storage twice (plus any backup Region). Shorten retention in source accounts. ▶ #106 04:01
  • Protect centralized log groups with SCPs denying logs:DeleteLogGroup and logs:PutRetentionPolicy except for a break-glass role. Alert on DeleteCentralizationRuleForOrganization (an attacker disabling collection).
  • Merged log groups from many accounts are hard to attribute. Name log streams by account or embed the account ID, and use the Logs Insights @log field.
  • Bake the agent and a baseline config into the golden AMI (Image Builder) and pull role-specific config from Parameter Store at boot. ▶ #107 07:31
  • Private subnets: interface endpoints for logs, monitoring and ssm avoid NAT costs and internet egress.
  • Collect security-relevant OS logs (/var/log/secure, /var/log/audit/audit.log, the Windows Security event log), not just app logs, and forward them to the central log account.
Hands-on lab
  1. Send the trail to CW Logs and create the RootUsage filter and alarm.
  2. Log in as root, confirm the alarm fires and the SNS email arrives.
  3. Install the agent on an EC2 instance (manually as in ▶ #107, or through SSM), ship /var/log/myapp.log, then remove the IAM policy and watch the agent log errors.
  4. (Org, ▶ #106) Turn on trusted access, register a delegated admin, create a centralization rule for one OU, write a test event in a member account and find it in the destination.
  5. Cleanup: delete the alarm, filter, log groups, centralization rule and instance.

Amazon EventBridge

At a glance

Serverless event router. AWS services (GuardDuty, Security Hub, Config, CloudTrail API calls, Health…) emit events to the default event bus, rules match patterns and send the events to targets. Not a security service itself, but the glue of every automated detection → response flow: event-driven security. ▶ #45 00:20

  • Exam skills: aggregate security events (1.1.3) · metrics, alerts & dashboards (1.1.4) · normalize & correlate logs (1.2.5) · response runbooks (2.1.1) · automated remediation (2.1.4) · mask sensitive data (5.3.4) · IaC & noncompliance detection (6.2.1, 6.3.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #45 Amazon EventBridge · ▶ #87 Monitoring Config with EventBridge · ▶ #88 Customizing and monitoring rules · ▶ #89 Transforming events
  • Limits: 5 targets per rule (console) · input transformer up to 100 variables · retry defaults 24 h / 185 attempts

Building blocks: buses, pipes, rules

EventBridge is a serverless service for building event-driven applications: one thing emits an event, something else responds to it. ▶ #45 00:20 GuardDuty (and other services) integrate with it to either act on an issue or send a notification. ▶ #45 00:00

Five main features: event buses, pipes, rules, schedules (Scheduler), schema registries. ▶ #45 00:41

Block What it does
Event bus Router that receives events and delivers them to targets. Many sources in, zero to many targets out, can transform on delivery. ▶ #45 00:53
Pipe Point-to-point: one single source → one single target, optional processing. A pipe can send to a bus, which fans out. ▶ #45 01:21
Rule What action to take when an event matches the rule’s event pattern; routes the event to the target. ▶ #45 01:50 Type = event pattern (reacts to events) or schedule (cron-like). ▶ #45 03:51
  • Every account has a default event bus, created by AWS with the account. AWS service events go directly there. ▶ #45 01:12
  • You can add custom buses and partner buses for SaaS sources. ▶ #45 03:30

“GuardDuty Detections Response” (event-driven security):

  1. Event producer (GuardDuty) detects a threat and emits an event (the finding).
  2. The event lands on the EventBridge event bus (the default bus for AWS service events).
  3. A rule with a matching event pattern picks it up.
  4. The rule’s targets act: a clean-up action (e.g. Lambda / SSM Automation remediation) and/or Amazon SNS.
  5. SNS delivers an email to the subscriber.

Rule wizard step 1: name (max 64 chars: numbers, letters, ., -, _), optional description, Event bus (default / custom / partner), Enable the rule on the selected event bus, and Rule type. The banner recommends IAM roles for cross-account event bus targets and SCPs to bound who can send/receive events in the organization.

Event patterns and common sources

Patterns match on source, detail-type and detail.*, with prefix, anything-but, exists, numeric ranges and wildcards.

Source detail-type Notes
aws.guardduty GuardDuty Finding
aws.securityhub Security Hub Findings - Imported / Security Hub Findings - Custom Action
aws.config Config Rules Compliance Change Filter newEvaluationResult.complianceType: NON_COMPLIANT
aws.config Config Configuration Item Change messageType: ConfigurationItemChangeNotification, filter on configurationItem.resourceType (e.g. AWS::S3::Bucket)
(service) AWS API Call via CloudTrail Needs a trail with logging on. Read-only API events need rule state ENABLED_WITH_ALL_CLOUDTRAIL_MANAGEMENT_EVENTS
aws.signin AWS Console Sign In via CloudTrail
  • Event source options: AWS events or EventBridge partner events · Other (custom events, partner sources, more than one source) · All events, which captures everything and can get expensive. ▶ #87 02:10
  • For S3 configuration changes detected by Config, the source is Config, not S3 (pick Config, not AppConfig). ▶ #87 03:52
  • Pattern creation methods: Use schema / Use pattern form / Custom pattern (JSON editor). ▶ #87 03:31
  • Config change events reach EventBridge only if the Config recorder records that resource type, in that Region.
  • Service events such as GuardDuty’s are Regional: you need a rule per Region, or aggregate first (GuardDuty delegated admin per Region, Security Hub cross-Region aggregation).

Always test the pattern against a sample event before creating the rule. ▶ #87 06:20 AWS provides samples (for Config: “Config Rules Compliance Change”, “Config Rules Re-evaluation Status”), or use Enter my own. ▶ #87 02:43 The course’s sample is in the Cybr GitHub repo Cybr-Inc/aws-security-specialty → EventBridge/sample-event-s3-bucket.json. Required fields: id, account, source, time, region, resources, detail-type. The sample shows source: aws.config, resources: [bucket ARN], detail.messageType and detail.configurationItemDiff.changedProperties (e.g. encryption config CREATE, versioning status UPDATE). Test pattern gives green success; a non-S3 sample fails (red). ▶ #87 06:01

Pattern form for the S3 rule: AWS services → Config → Config Configuration Item Change → specific message type ConfigurationItemChangeNotification (fires when a resource Config evaluates changes) ▶ #87 04:20 → specific resource type AWS::S3::Bucket (could be AWS::EC2::Instance, etc.; see “Supported Resource Types for AWS Config”, updated monthly) ▶ #87 04:40 → Any resource ID (all buckets). ▶ #87 05:12 The generated JSON is the filter; in production deploy it as infrastructure as code. ▶ #87 05:40

{
  "source": ["aws.config"],
  "detail-type": ["Config Configuration Item Change"],
  "detail": {
    "messageType": ["ConfigurationItemChangeNotification"],
    "configurationItem": {
      "resourceType": ["AWS::S3::Bucket"]
    }
  }
}
Narrowing the pattern to cut alert fatigue

The original pattern matches anything about S3 buckets from Config. That floods the security team, “which means that they will end up ignoring them.” ▶ #88 00:40 Fix: add a second block under detail, configurationItemDiff → changeType: ["UPDATE"]. ▶ #88 01:01

Find the field to filter on by reading a sample event: it contains detail.configurationItemDiff.changeType (UPDATE) and detail.configurationItem.resourceType (AWS::S3::Bucket). ▶ #88 01:24 Each changed property has its own changeType; the top-level one is what the new pattern filters on. Fields in different blocks are ANDed, so the rule now fires only for updates to S3 bucket configuration items. ▶ #88 01:55

{
  "source": ["aws.config"],
  "detail-type": ["Config Configuration Item Change"],
  "detail": {
    "messageType": ["ConfigurationItemChangeNotification"],
    "configurationItem": {
      "resourceType": ["AWS::S3::Bucket"]
    },
    "configurationItemDiff": {
      "changeType": ["UPDATE"]
    }
  }
}

The same filtered pattern is what the input-transformer lesson starts from. ▶ #89 01:35

Severity filter example (only High GuardDuty findings): "detail": {"severity": [{"numeric": [">=", 7]}]}.

Console demo: narrow the rule to UPDATE changes ([▶ #88](https://youtu.be/71gd8gzk0WU))
  1. EventBridge → Rules → detect-s3-events → Edit.
  2. Switch to the JSON editor and add the configurationItemDiff block above. ▶ #88 01:01
  3. Next → Skip to review and update → Update rule. ▶ #88 02:00

Targets and permissions

  • Target types: EventBridge event bus (another account’s/Region’s bus), EventBridge API destination (SaaS / HTTP endpoint), or AWS service. ▶ #87 06:31
  • AWS service targets: Lambda, SNS, SQS, Step Functions, SSM Automation / Run Command, Kinesis, ECS task, API destinations (3rd-party HTTP, e.g. a SIEM or chat), and another event bus (cross-account / cross-Region).
  • The console shows a limit of 5 targets per rule. ▶ #87 06:31 A bus allows multiple targets, so you can add more later. ▶ #45 05:00
Target How EventBridge gets permission
Lambda, SNS, SQS Resource-based policy on the function/topic/queue allowing events.amazonaws.com (ideally with aws:SourceArn = rule ARN)
Step Functions, Kinesis, SSM Automation, ECS tasks, API destinations, cross-account buses An IAM role (RoleArn) that EventBridge assumes
  • The console configures target permissions for you; with CLI/SDK/CloudFormation you must do it yourself.
  • In the console prefer Use execution role (recommended) → Create a new role for this specific resource (Amazon_EventBridge_Invoke_Sns_<id>) over one shared role, even if you end up with many roles. ▶ #87 07:10
  • Encrypted SNS topic with a customer managed KMS key: the key policy must allow events.amazonaws.com kms:GenerateDataKey / kms:Decrypt. The most common reason notifications to an encrypted topic silently fail.
  • An SNS email subscription must be confirmed or nothing arrives. ▶ #45 03:00

The Targets tab of the finished rule: SNS topic SecurityTeam receives the matched event, the console attached Amazon_EventBridge_Invoke_Sns_…, and no dead-letter queue is configured.

Input transformer: readable, safe payloads

Raw events are complex and verbose, hard to understand quickly in a notification. ▶ #89 00:00 What you actually want in an alert: source/account (multi-account), time, Region, resource name and what happened (changeType: UPDATE). Details can be checked in logs later. ▶ #89 00:52

Configure target input options (on the target, under Additional settings): ▶ #89 02:00

  • Matched events (whole event, the default; that’s why the full JSON dump arrives) ▶ #89 01:31
  • Part of the matched event (a JSON path)
  • Constant (JSON text)
  • Input transformer → Configure input transformer

The transformer: ▶ #89 02:10

  • Input path (InputPathsMap): key-value pairs defining variables via JSON path, up to 100 variables.
  • Template (InputTemplate): string or JSON passed to the target, with <variable> placeholders that must match the variable names.
  • Sample event (optional) → Enter my own, then Generate output previews the result. ▶ #89 03:50
  • Reserved variables: <aws.events.rule-arn>, <aws.events.rule-name>, <aws.events.event.ingestion-time>, <aws.events.event>.
  • Configured per target, not per rule, so each target can get a different payload. ▶ #89 05:30

The course’s EventBridge/InputTransformer.json plucks 5 fields (bucket name, change type, capture time, Region, account) and injects them into a sentence: ▶ #89 03:13

{
  "bucketName": "$.detail.configurationItem.resourceName",
  "changeType": "$.detail.configurationItemDiff.changeType",
  "captureTime": "$.detail.configurationItem.configurationItemCaptureTime",
  "awsRegion": "$.region",
  "awsAccount": "$.account"
}

"S3 Bucket Security Alert: Bucket <bucketName> had a <changeType> change at <captureTime> in account <awsAccount> region <awsRegion>. Please investigate this change."

Result: "S3 Bucket Security Alert: Bucket cybr-eventbridge-config-event-demo-4 had a UPDATE change at 2025-04-29T18:22:39.314Z in account 851725223689 region us-east-1. Please investigate this change." ▶ #89 04:50 Compared with the raw email (e.g. a versioning Enabled → Suspended dump) it is “much more actionable” and cuts alert noise and alert fatigue. ▶ #89 05:00

When to use input transformation: ▶ #89 05:50

  1. Human-readable notifications (SNS email to the security team).
  2. Target payload requirements: normalize inputs from different source events into the format a target expects.
  3. Filter out sensitive or unnecessary information before it reaches certain targets: “a really important use case, be sure to remember this one”. ▶ #89 06:11 Other PII/PHI options: CloudWatch Logs data protection, SNS message data protection, Macie.
  4. Combine information from multiple parts of the event into a more logical structure. ▶ #89 06:41

In CloudFormation the transformer sits on the target (Targets[].InputTransformer.InputPathsMap / InputTemplate), in the repo file S3BucketConfigChangeMonitorInputTransformer.yml. ▶ #89 05:10 Shape (reconstructed; the YAML was not shown in detail):

Targets:
  - Arn: !Ref SecurityTeamTopic
    Id: SecurityTeamSNS
    InputTransformer:
      InputPathsMap:
        bucketName: $.detail.configurationItem.resourceName
        changeType: $.detail.configurationItemDiff.changeType
        captureTime: $.detail.configurationItem.configurationItemCaptureTime
        awsRegion: $.region
        awsAccount: $.account
      InputTemplate: '"S3 Bucket Security Alert: Bucket <bucketName> had a <changeType> change at <captureTime> in account <awsAccount> region <awsRegion>. Please investigate this change."'
Console demo: add an input transformer to the S3 rule ([▶ #89](https://youtu.be/R-EJ31AEEi0))
  1. EventBridge → Rules → detect-s3-events → Targets → Edit → Next to Select target(s). No new rule needed. ▶ #89 01:31
  2. SNS target SecurityTeam (existing execution role) → Additional settings → Configure target input: Input transformer → Configure input transformer. ▶ #89 02:00
  3. Sample event: Enter my own → paste the sample S3 Config event.
  4. Paste the input path and template from InputTransformer.json → Generate output → Confirm. ▶ #89 03:50
  5. Skip to Review and update → Update rule. ▶ #89 04:10
  6. Because the rule filters UPDATE only, modify an existing bucket: S3 → cybr-eventbridge-config-event-demo-4 → Permissions → Block public access → Edit → enable → confirm. About 1 minute later the readable email arrives.

Reliability and monitoring

  • Retry policy per target: defaults maximum age of event 24 hours and 185 retry attempts.
  • Dead-letter queue: none / SQS queue in this account / SQS queue in another account (standard SQS only).

  • The rule page’s Monitoring tab embeds the rule’s CloudWatch metrics for free. ▶ #88 02:11
  • Metrics: MatchedEvents, Invocations, TriggeredRules, FailedInvocations, plus latency, throttling and retry attempts. ▶ #88 02:24
  • View metrics in CloudWatch: customize graphs, query with SQL (Metrics Insights) and create alarms, e.g. when matched events spike. ▶ #88 02:53
  • The CloudFormation Template button (top right of the rule page) exports a rule as a template.
  • Archive & Replay re-processes past events, useful after fixing a broken rule.
Rule not delivering? Check these
  • MatchedEvents = 0 → the pattern is wrong (or a typo). Test it with the console’s Test pattern or the TestEventPattern API.
  • FailedInvocations > 0 → target permissions: the SNS topic / SQS queue policy or Lambda resource policy must allow events.amazonaws.com, or the RoleArn for role-based targets.
  • KMS-encrypted SNS topic → the key policy must allow events.amazonaws.com to use the key.
  • SNS email subscription still Pending confirmation. ▶ #45 08:10
  • Config events missing → the Config recorder isn’t recording that resource type in that Region.
  • Check the DLQ. Malformed input templates (bad quoting) also show up as failed invocations.

Cross-account, cross-Region and IaC

  • Cross-account: the source account’s rule targets the central account’s bus ARN. The central bus resource policy allows events:PutEvents from the source accounts (or aws:PrincipalOrgID). AWS recommends IAM roles for cross-account bus targets and SCPs to bound who can send/receive events.
  • EventBridge gives near-real-time reactions to Config events, including cross-account events. ▶ #87 00:00 Config aggregators give views only; they don’t emit events.
  • Deploy rules as IaC so the same detection exists in every account. ▶ #88 03:32

The course template S3BucketConfigChangeMonitor.yml (repo Cybr-Inc/aws-security-specialty/EventBridge) creates an AWS::Events::Rule (the UPDATE-filtered pattern) targeting the SecurityTeam SNS topic (a parameter with a default ARN), and an IAM role that events.amazonaws.com can assume with sns:Publish on the topic. ▶ #88 03:50 Deploying it gives the same pattern and target with a different rule name. To reuse it, change the default parameter to your account ID and topic name. Config must already be enabled. ▶ #88 04:46

CloudFormation: rule for S3 bucket UPDATE changes → SNS 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: 'CloudFormation template to create EventBridge Rule that monitors S3 bucket updates via AWS Config and sends notifications to an existing SNS topic'
Parameters:
  SecurityTeamTopicArn:
    Type: String
    Description: ARN of the existing SecurityTeam SNS Topic
    Default: arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:<account-id>:SecurityTeam
Resources:
  S3BucketUpdateRule:
    Type: AWS::Events::Rule
    Properties:
      Name: S3BucketUpdateNotificationRule
      Description: Rule to detect S3 bucket updates from AWS Config notifications
      State: ENABLED
      EventPattern:            # lines 17–30 scrolled past on screen; same pattern as the JSON above
        source: [aws.config]
        detail-type: [Config Configuration Item Change]
        detail:
          messageType: [ConfigurationItemChangeNotification]
          configurationItem:
            resourceType: [AWS::S3::Bucket]
          configurationItemDiff:
            changeType: [UPDATE]
      Targets:
        - Arn: !Ref SecurityTeamTopicArn
          Id: S3UpdateNotificationSNSTarget
  SNSPublishPolicy:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal:
              Service: events.amazonaws.com
            Action: 'sts:AssumeRole'
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: SNSPublishPermission
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: 'sns:Publish'
                Resource: !Ref SecurityTeamTopicArn
Outputs:
  RuleArn:
    Description: ARN of the EventBridge Rule
    Value: !GetAtt S3BucketUpdateRule.Arn

Demo: GuardDuty finding → SNS email

Goal: email every time GuardDuty finds a potential threat. ▶ #45 02:11

The email contains just five formatted fields plus a URL straight to the finding: “You have a severity 5 GuardDuty finding type Backdoor:EC2/Spambot in the us-east-1 region. Finding Description: …”. ▶ #45 08:22

Console demo: GuardDuty → EventBridge → SNS ([▶ #45](https://youtu.be/_0ZHsClx9wc))

SNS topic and subscription

  1. SNS → Topics → Create topic: name GuardDuty, type Standard, rest default → Create. ▶ #45 02:32
  2. Create subscription → Protocol Email → your address. ▶ #45 02:51
  3. Status is Pending confirmation: click the confirmation link in the AWS email before anything arrives. ▶ #45 03:00

EventBridge rule

  1. EventBridge → Rules → Create rule: name guardduty-threats (description recommended). ▶ #45 03:11
  2. Event bus default, keep “Enable the rule on the selected event bus”, rule type Rule with an event pattern. ▶ #45 03:30
  3. Event source AWS events or EventBridge partner events. ▶ #45 04:01
  4. Sample event (optional): search “GuardDuty Finding”. Creation method Use pattern form. ▶ #45 04:20
  5. Event source AWS services → GuardDuty → GuardDuty Finding, generating {"source": ["aws.guardduty"], "detail-type": ["GuardDuty Finding"]}.
  6. Targets: AWS service → SNS topic → GuardDuty. ▶ #45 05:00
  7. Additional settings → Configure target input: Matched events → Input transformer → Configure input transformer, to make the JSON readable. ▶ #45 05:20
  8. Paste an input path extracting severity, finding ID, finding type, region, finding description and a template; Generate output previews it → Confirm. ▶ #45 05:51 The exact text wasn’t legible on screen; a typical version: 
    {
  "severity": "$.detail.severity",
  "Finding_ID": "$.detail.id",
  "Finding_Type": "$.detail.type",
  "region": "$.region",
  "Finding_description": "$.detail.description"
}

    "You have a severity <severity> GuardDuty finding type <Finding_Type> in the <region> region."
"Finding Description:"
"<Finding_description>."
"For more details open the GuardDuty console at https://console.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/home?region=<region>#/findings?search=id%3D<Finding_ID>"
  9. Leave retry (24 h / 185) and no DLQ, skip tags → Create rule. guardduty-threats shows Enabled. ▶ #45 06:26

Test

  1. Generate one sample finding, not the console’s “Generate sample findings” (100+ findings would flood your inbox). GuardDuty must be enabled in that Region. ▶ #45 06:41
  2. Open CloudShell in the same Region as GuardDuty: ▶ #45 07:00 
    aws guardduty list-detectors
aws guardduty create-sample-findings \
  --detector-id <detector-id> \
  --finding-types Backdoor:EC2/Spambot
  3. The finding appears in GuardDuty; the email arrives within seconds to a minute. If not, check the SNS subscription was confirmed. ▶ #45 07:50

Demo: Config detects S3 bucket changes → SNS

Scenario: S3 buckets hold sensitive customer data and changes should be rare, so any bucket configuration change must email the security team’s monitored mailbox. Built in the security tooling account. ▶ #87 00:30 EventBridge receives the event and invokes a target action: send notifications, capture event info, take corrective action, initiate other events. ▶ #87 00:50

  • CREATE email: "changeType":"CREATE", configurationItemStatus":"ResourceDiscovered", full bucket configuration. ▶ #87 08:50

  • UPDATE email: changedProperties per field with previousValue / updatedValue and changeType: UPDATE, e.g. SupplementaryConfiguration.PublicAccessBlockConfiguration.BlockPublicAcls. ▶ #87 09:10 The UPDATE email shown comes from an earlier test bucket (…-demo-3) where values went false → true (BPA enabled, versioning Off → Enabled).
  • Emails (“AWS Notification Message” from no-reply@sns.amazonaws.com) are the unfiltered raw event; filtering, metrics and IaC come next (#88, #89). ▶ #87 09:30
Console demo: Config S3 change rule ([▶ #87](https://youtu.be/ZwozjgkFsEk))
  1. EventBridge → Rules → Create rule: name detect-s3-events, description “Detect S3 events that require further investigation from the security team”. ▶ #87 01:20
  2. Event bus default (normally you’d separate buses), keep the rule enabled, Rule type: Rule with an event pattern. ▶ #87 01:50
  3. Event source AWS events; sample event → Enter my own → paste the repo sample. ▶ #87 02:43
  4. Pattern form: AWS services / Config / Config Configuration Item Change / ConfigurationItemChangeNotification / AWS::S3::Bucket / Any resource ID → Test pattern (success). ▶ #87 06:01
  5. Target: AWS service → SNS topic SecurityTeam (this account; create it if needed and refresh), create a new execution role → leave input (Matched events), retry and DLQ default → skip tags → Create. ▶ #87 06:31
  6. Confirm the email subscription if the topic is new. ▶ #87 07:41
  7. S3: create bucket cybr-eventbridge-config-event-demo-4 (SSE-S3, Bucket Key on) → CREATE event. ▶ #87 07:51
  8. Permissions → Block public access → uncheck Block all public access → Save → type confirm (“this is a stupid idea”) → UPDATE event. Notifications can take a minute or two. ▶ #87 08:21
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • EventBridge is how GuardDuty and other services get automation: act on the issue or send a notification. ▶ #45 00:00
  • Every account has a default event bus; AWS service events go there directly. ▶ #45 01:12
  • Pipes for single source → single target; buses for many sources → many targets. ▶ #45 01:21
  • Confirm the SNS email subscription, a classic reason notifications don’t arrive. ▶ #45 03:00
  • Create a single sample finding via CLI, not the console bulk generator (100+ emails); CloudShell in the same Region as GuardDuty. ▶ #45 06:41
  • “All events” as the source can get expensive. ▶ #87 02:30
  • The source for S3 configuration changes is Config, not S3. ▶ #87 03:52
  • Build in the console to learn, deploy patterns via IaC in production. ▶ #87 05:50
  • Always test the pattern with a sample event. ▶ #87 06:20
  • Prefer a dedicated execution role per target over a shared one. ▶ #87 07:10
  • Broad patterns cause alert fatigue; filter to what matters (e.g. only UPDATE). ▶ #88 00:40
  • Every rule gets CloudWatch metrics for free; alarm on spikes or failures. ▶ #88 03:11
  • Input transformer turns busy events into clear, actionable messages and reduces alert noise. ▶ #89 00:11 It is per target. ▶ #89 05:30
  • Remember the sensitive-data filtering use case. ▶ #89 06:21 EventBridge + reshaping/filtering event content → input transformation. ▶ #89 06:52

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Auto-remediate when GuardDuty finds X EventBridge rule → Lambda / SSM Automation / Step Functions
Notify the security team when GuardDuty / Security Hub / Inspector / Macie / Config finds X EventBridge rule on the default bus → SNS
Only alert on High severity Filter in the pattern: "severity": [{"numeric": [">=", 7]}]
Rule matches, but Lambda never runs Missing Lambda resource policy for events.amazonaws.com, or a pattern typo. Check FailedInvocations and the DLQ
SNS target receives nothing Topic policy for events.amazonaws.com, KMS key policy if encrypted, confirmed email subscription
Rule never triggers MatchedEvents = 0 → fix the pattern (Test pattern / TestEventPattern)
Centralize findings from all accounts in near real time Cross-account event bus (or Security Hub aggregation). Config aggregators don’t emit events
Readable email instead of JSON Input transformer
Only alert on UPDATE changes Event pattern (filters which events)
Remove fields / strip PII / readable message before the target Input transformer (reshapes content); also CloudWatch Logs / SNS message data protection, Macie
Near-real-time alert when a resource becomes noncompliant Config Rules Compliance Change with newEvaluationResult.complianceType: NON_COMPLIANT. Config’s SNS delivery channel sends everything (noisy)
Alert on S3 bucket changes, with caller identity, fastest CloudTrail management events (aws.s3, PutBucketPublicAccessBlock, DeleteBucketPolicy). Config events give the state diff but take minutes
Delayed repeat notifications for the same GuardDuty finding GuardDuty finding publishing frequency (6 h default; 15 min / 1 h)
Updates since the videos
  • The course’s S3BucketConfigChangeMonitor.yml role is never attached to the target (no RoleArn), so it is unused. For SNS, SQS and Lambda targets EventBridge uses no role: the topic’s resource-based policy must allow events.amazonaws.com to sns:Publish, ideally with aws:SourceArn = the rule ARN. Roles are for Kinesis, Step Functions, ECS tasks, SSM Automation, API destinations and cross-account buses. If deliveries from this template fail, check the topic policy and look for a FailedInvocations spike.
  • The GuardDuty input transformer text in #45 wasn’t legible on screen; the JSON shown above is a typical reconstruction. The #89 CloudFormation target shape is also reconstructed.

Real-world practice

  • Use AWS User Notifications or Amazon Q Developer in chat apps (AWS Chatbot) for Slack/Teams instead of raw email in production.
  • Manage rules with IaC (CloudFormation StackSets / Terraform) across all accounts and Regions; console rules drift. Or send events from every account to a central security event bus (cross-account bus + bus policy) and keep the rules there.
  • Deduplicate: GuardDuty re-emits updated findings (count increments), so ticketing should key on the finding ID.
  • Pricing: AWS service events on the default bus are free to deliver; custom/partner events and cross-account delivery are charged per million events.
  • Configure a DLQ and alarm on FailedInvocations > 0 for every security rule. A silently broken notification path is worse than a noisy one.
  • Config event latency is minutes, not seconds. For sensitive buckets use preventive controls (account-level S3 Block Public Access + SCP/RCP) and keep EventBridge alerting as the detective backup. Combine with Config managed rules (e.g. s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited) to get compliance state as well as change notifications.
  • Useful alert fields: account alias, console deep link, who made the change (from CloudTrail-based rules). Several targets per rule can each have their own transformer: a terse SNS email plus the full event to Lambda or an S3 archive.
{
  "source": ["aws.guardduty"],
  "detail-type": ["GuardDuty Finding"],
  "detail": { "severity": [{ "numeric": [">=", 7] }] }
}

aws events put-rule --name gd-high --event-pattern file://gd-high.json
aws events put-targets --rule gd-high --targets '[{"Id":"sns","Arn":"arn:aws:sns:...:security-alerts",
 "InputTransformer":{"InputPathsMap":{"type":"$.detail.type","acct":"$.account","sev":"$.detail.severity"},
 "InputTemplate":"\"GuardDuty <type> severity <sev> in account <acct>\""}}]'
# Central bus accepts events from the whole org
aws events put-permission --event-bus-name central-sec --action events:PutEvents \
  --principal "*" --statement-id org --condition Type=StringEquals,Key=aws:PrincipalOrgID,Value=o-xxxx
Hands-on lab
  1. Create the gd-high rule above, then generate one sample finding from CloudShell in the GuardDuty Region (aws guardduty create-sample-findings --detector-id <id> --finding-types Backdoor:EC2/Spambot) and receive the transformed email. Don’t use the console bulk generator (100+ findings).
  2. Create a detect-s3-events rule on Config Configuration Item Change for AWS::S3::Bucket → SNS, toggle Block Public Access on a bucket, then add an input transformer and compare the emails.
  3. Cleanup: remove the targets, delete the rules, the SNS topic and the execution roles.

Amazon GuardDuty

At a glance

Managed, Regional threat detection. It continuously monitors for compromised accounts, anomalous behavior and malware using ML anomaly detection, malware scanning and threat intelligence over AWS log sources, and prioritizes the findings so you act on them in the console, through EventBridge workflows, or with Lambda auto-remediation. ▶ #43 00:00

  • Exam skills: aggregate security events (1.1.3) · alerts for anomalies (1.1.4) · automated remediation (2.1.4) · validate findings & scope (2.2.3) · scan compute for vulnerabilities (3.2.3) · Organizations & delegated admin (6.1.1, 6.1.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #43 About GuardDuty · ▶ #44 Delegating and centralizing GuardDuty
  • 30-day free trial · findings kept 90 days (export for longer)

Data sources: foundational vs protection plans

GuardDuty can ingest, aggregate and analyze information from many AWS data sources. ▶ #43 00:10 Because CloudTrail tracks all API calls, it has visibility into just about everything happening in the account. ▶ #43 00:20 Detection methods: ML anomaly detection, malware scanning, threat intelligence. ▶ #43 00:52 It helps you identify and prioritize threats instead of drowning in random data. ▶ #43 01:00

Foundational sources (always on, no setup): CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 DNS logs.

  • GuardDuty reads independent copies, so you don’t need to enable trails or Flow Logs yourself, and disabling them doesn’t affect GuardDuty. Enabling GuardDuty also doesn’t create those logs for you to query.
  • DNS findings only work if instances use the Amazon-provided resolver.

Protection plans (opt-in), shown as “features” on the slide (EKS audit logs, RDS login activity, S3 logs, EBS volumes, Runtime monitoring, Lambda network activity logs): ▶ #43 00:30

Plan What it analyzes
S3 Protection CloudTrail S3 data events: exfiltration, anomalous access, disabled block public access
EKS Protection (Audit Log Monitoring) Kubernetes audit logs (control-plane activity), consumed directly from the EKS control plane via an independent, duplicative stream. No setup, no effect on your own EKS logging config. ▶ #43 02:20
Runtime Monitoring A GuardDuty security agent (managed via SSM / EKS add-on / ECS Fargate sidecar) for OS-level events (file access, process execution, network connections) on EKS, ECS (incl. Fargate) and EC2. 30+ runtime finding types
Malware Protection for EC2 Agentless: takes EBS snapshots and scans them when a suspicious finding fires (also on demand)
Malware Protection for S3 Scans newly uploaded objects in chosen buckets. Usable without enabling GuardDuty fully
RDS Protection Anomalous login activity on Aurora / RDS
Lambda Protection Network activity of Lambda functions (crypto mining, C2)

Extended Threat Detection correlates multiple signals into attack-sequence findings (critical severity).

Runtime Monitoring enablement is two steps: enable the feature for the account, then deploy the GuardDuty security agent (EKS add-on) to all or selected clusters, automatically or per cluster with inclusion/exclusion tags. Then check coverage status (“healthy”). ▶ #43 02:20 The doc page also explains the 30-day free trial behavior.

What it detects: findings

Example detections: ▶ #43 01:30

  • Compromised credentials from unusual API activity. ▶ #43 01:30
  • S3 data exfiltration: unusual geolocation, or S3 security controls disabled. ▶ #43 01:42
  • Access from known malicious IP addresses (threat intel). ▶ #43 01:51
  • Lambda threats like unauthorized crypto mining or traffic to known threat-actor servers (C2). ▶ #43 02:00
  • Malware on EBS volumes attached to EC2 or container workloads. ▶ #43 02:11
  • EKS control-plane and runtime threats. ▶ #43 02:20

Finding type format: ThreatPurpose:ResourceType/ThreatFamily.Mechanism!Artifact

Finding type Meaning
UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce SSH brute force
CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS Crypto mining (seen in DNS)
Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort Port probe on an open port
UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS Instance role creds used outside AWS
Policy:IAMUser/RootCredentialUsage Root used
Policy:S3/BucketBlockPublicAccessDisabled S3 BPA turned off
Stealth:IAMUser/CloudTrailLoggingDisabled Trail logging stopped
Discovery:S3/…, Exfiltration:S3/…, Impact:…, Backdoor:EC2/C&CActivity.B, Backdoor:EC2/Spambot, Trojan:… Other families
  • Severity: Low / Medium / High (plus Critical for attack sequences).

Tuning: IP lists and suppression rules

Control Effect Limit
Trusted IP list No findings for these IPs 1 per account per Region
Threat IP list Generate findings when these IPs are seen Up to 6
Suppression rule Auto-archive findings matching filter criteria (expected noise, e.g. a vulnerability scanner hitting port probes). Findings still exist but don’t alert
  • In an org, only the administrator account manages IP lists, and they apply to members.

Acting on findings

Detailed findings in the console, integration into event management / workflow systems, and AWS Lambda to automatically remediate or prevent. ▶ #43 01:10

  • Findings are automatically published to EventBridge: new findings within ~5 minutes. Also sent to Security Hub and Detective.
  • Optional export to an S3 bucket (KMS-encrypted; the bucket policy and key policy must allow guardduty.amazonaws.com).
  • Updated findings frequency: 15 min / 1 h / 6 h (default), editable on the Settings page. ▶ #44 00:30
  • GuardDuty keeps findings only 90 days; export for longer retention.
  • GuardDuty detects; it doesn’t investigate. Root cause → Amazon Detective. Single view across Regions → Security Hub cross-Region aggregation.
  • Suspend keeps findings and config. Disable deletes all findings.

Typical response: GuardDuty finding → EventBridge → Step Functions: isolate the instance (forensic SG), snapshot EBS, tag it, notify (see Amazon EventBridge, this part, and the remediation sections in Part 5).

Multi-account: delegated admin and auto-enable

Delegated admin + auto-enable is set per Region. Use the same delegated admin account in every Region.

1. Delegate from the management account. GuardDuty → Settings → Delegated Administrator → enter the 12-digit Security Tooling account ID → Delegate. If you don’t see the option, you’re in the wrong account. ▶ #44 00:10

  • Screen text: “This account will be assigned the two GuardDuty roles required to administer GuardDuty policy in your organization.” Banner: “You have authorized an account to supervise GuardDuty in your organization on your behalf. You can revoke or change this designation at any time.”
  • Toggle “Allow delegated administrator to attach relevant permissions to enable Malware Protection for member accounts”: an org decision, enabled in the demo. ▶ #44 00:30
  • The same page shows Findings export options: EventBridge automatically, optional S3, new findings within 5 minutes, updated findings every 6 hours by default.

2. Manage from the delegated admin. In Security Tooling → GuardDuty (same Region) → confirm it’s enabled; Settings no longer offers delegation. ▶ #44 01:01 The Accounts page lists all org accounts (prod, Shared Services, cybr_demo_management, Log Archive, Demo, Example, network, dev, Containers) with Type Via Organizations and Status Not a member, under the banner “Enable GuardDuty for your organization in this region”. ▶ #44 01:11

  • Add accounts by invitation exists, but there’s no real use case: manage membership through AWS Organizations. ▶ #44 01:20
  • Edit Protection Plans: choose plans for selected accounts (auto-enable all / disable all per plan). ▶ #44 01:31
  • Actions: invite, resend invitations, suspend, re-enable, disassociate, delete accounts; mostly ignore and manage via Organizations. ▶ #44 01:40

3. Auto-enable. Options: ALL (new + existing), NEW, NONE, plus which protection plans to auto-enable. Choosing plans: maybe no RDS, maybe no runtime monitoring yet; likely S3 Protection; EKS if you run EKS; Malware Protection for EC2; Lambda network activity monitoring. The demo enables S3 Protection and Lambda Protection. ▶ #44 02:10

Banner: “If you chose the ’enable for all accounts’ preference option, it may take up to 24 hours to update the configuration for all the member accounts.” ▶ #44 02:52

After ~24 hours: Via Organizations (Active/All) 9/9, Invitation 0/0; every account Enabled with Protection Plans 2/6; EKS Audit Log Monitoring and Runtime Monitoring Not enabled, Lambda network activity monitoring and S3 Protection enabled; a per-account breakdown shows whether it’s managed via Organizations. ▶ #44 03:00

Rules of the org setup:

  • Use Organizations, not invitations. The management account must also be enabled as a member.
  • Members managed by the delegated admin cannot disable/suspend GuardDuty or change protection plans.
Console demo: delegate and auto-enable GuardDuty org-wide ([▶ #44](https://youtu.be/G605o4HNdpw))
  1. Management account → GuardDuty → Settings → Delegated Administrator → Security Tooling account ID → Delegate. ▶ #44 00:10
  2. Toggle “Allow delegated administrator to attach relevant permissions to enable Malware Protection for member accounts”. ▶ #44 00:41
  3. Security Tooling → GuardDuty (same Region) → Accounts. ▶ #44 01:01
  4. Auto-enable → Edit → Enable for all accounts → select S3 Protection + Lambda Protection → Save changes. ▶ #44 02:10
  5. Wait (up to 24 h) → refresh → verify Status Enabled and Protection Plans 2/6 per account. ▶ #44 02:52
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • GuardDuty = threat detection from CloudTrail, DNS and VPC Flow Logs + optional features. ▶ #43 00:10
  • It uses ML, malware scanning and threat intel, and prioritizes findings. ▶ #43 00:52
  • Response options: console, workflow integration, Lambda auto-remediation. ▶ #43 01:10
  • Delegate from the management account; if the option is missing you’re in the wrong account. ▶ #44 00:20
  • The Malware Protection permission toggle for the delegated admin is an org decision. ▶ #44 00:41
  • Don’t use invitation-based membership; use Organizations. ▶ #44 01:20
  • Auto-enable can take ~24 hours to reach all accounts. ▶ #44 02:52

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Detect crypto mining / C2 / compromised instance credentials, least overhead GuardDuty
Network threat detection without enabling VPC Flow Logs GuardDuty (independent stream)
Scan EC2 for malware without an agent Malware Protection for EC2
Scan uploaded files in S3 Malware Protection for S3
Container runtime threats (reverse shell, privilege escalation) Runtime Monitoring
Pentest / scanner generating noise Suppression rule (or trusted IP list)
GuardDuty not detecting in eu-west-1 It’s Regional: enable it there too
No DNS-based findings Instances use a non-AWS resolver; GuardDuty only sees Route 53 Resolver DNS logs
New accounts must automatically have GuardDuty Delegated admin + auto-enable (per Region)
Stop an attacker in a member account turning GuardDuty off Org-managed membership + SCP denying guardduty:Delete*, Disassociate*, UpdateDetector, etc.
Investigate the finding / root cause Detective
Single view across Regions Security Hub cross-Region aggregation
Updates since the videos
  • The #43 slide lists “CloudTrail management and data events” as foundational. S3 data events are only analyzed with S3 Protection, an opt-in plan.
  • The #43 doc snapshot said EKS Runtime Monitoring supported EKS on EC2 only, not Fargate. Today ECS on Fargate is supported; EKS on Fargate still is not.
  • In #44 the narration says “head over to Security Hub”, but the screen shows GuardDuty → Settings. Delegation is done in GuardDuty; Security Hub has its own, separate delegation.

Real-world practice

  • Enable org-wide in all Regions, even unused ones (attackers like unused Regions). Keep cost down by choosing protection plans per OU / account type (e.g. Runtime Monitoring only for prod EKS/ECS).
  • Automate delegation + auto-enable across all Regions with CloudFormation StackSets or Control Tower / Landing Zone tooling.
  • Export findings to S3 (KMS-encrypted) for long-term retention.
  • IR runbook by severity: High → page; Medium → ticket; Low → weekly review.
  • Route findings: EventBridge in the Security Tooling account → SNS/Slack/ticketing; Security Hub for central triage.
# From management account
aws guardduty enable-organization-admin-account --admin-account-id <security-acct>
# From delegated admin, each Region
aws guardduty update-organization-configuration --detector-id <id> --auto-enable-organization-members ALL \
  --features '[{"Name":"S3_DATA_EVENTS","AutoEnable":"ALL"},{"Name":"RUNTIME_MONITORING","AutoEnable":"ALL"}]'
aws guardduty create-filter --detector-id <id> --name scanner-noise --action ARCHIVE \
  --finding-criteria '{"Criterion":{"type":{"Eq":["Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort"]},
   "resource.instanceDetails.tags.value":{"Eq":["vuln-scanner"]}}}'
Hands-on lab
  1. Enable GuardDuty (30-day free trial) and run create-sample-findings with a single finding type (e.g. Backdoor:EC2/Spambot) to avoid 100+ samples.
  2. Read the finding JSON (resource, service.action), create a suppression rule, then wire it to EventBridge.
  3. Org: delegate to the Security Tooling account, set auto-enable for all accounts with S3 + Lambda Protection, and check the Accounts page the next day.
  4. Cleanup: disable the detector (this deletes findings).

AWS Security Hub CSPM

At a glance

Cloud security posture management. Three jobs: run automated best-practice control checks against standards, aggregate and prioritize findings from AWS and third-party tools in one normalized view (ASFF), and enable automated remediation. ▶ #49 00:51 “Not a SIEM replacement, but a sort of mini SIEM.” ▶ #49 02:21

  • Exam skills: aggregate security events (1.1.3) · alerts & dashboards (1.1.4) · automated regular assessments (1.1.5) · analyze logs (1.2.4) · automated remediation (2.1.4) · validate findings (2.2.3) · Organizations & delegated admin (6.1.1, 6.1.4) · detect & remediate noncompliance (6.3.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #49 About Security Hub CSPM · ▶ #50 Delegating and centralizing Security Hub CSPM
  • Requires AWS Config recording · 30-day free trial · findings kept ~90 days

Security Hub CSPM vs the new Security Hub

AWS launched a new Security Hub a couple of months before recording. The original is now called Security Hub CSPM, which is what the course uses. ▶ #49 00:00 The new one was in early preview at recording, so the instructor waited before covering it. ▶ #49 00:30

Security Hub CSPM (classic) Security Hub (new, unified)
Console tagline “Automated security checks across your AWS environment” “Detect, prioritize, and respond to critical cloud security issues faster”
Does Standards, controls, insights, automation rules, cross-Region aggregation Sits on top of GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM and Macie; correlates signals into exposures and attack paths
Finding format ASFF OCSF (like Security Lake)

What it does and how it works

Problem it solves: everything so far was decentralized and hard to manage at scale. ▶ #49 01:10

  1. Automated security checks across your environment: FSBP plus industry benchmarks like CIS and PCI. ▶ #49 01:40
  2. Consolidated, prioritized findings from GuardDuty, Config, Systems Manager, Inspector, Firewall Manager, IAM Access Analyzer, AWS Health, Macie and integrated partner solutions. ▶ #49 01:20
  3. Take action: custom actions, send findings to ticketing, chat, email or automated remediation via EventBridge. With a SOAR it can enrich findings and send them to a ticketing system to start SOAR workflows; same with a SIEM. ▶ #49 01:50

Pricing (per account, per Region, per month; 2023 figures on the slide):

  • Security checks: first 100,000 $0.0010/check, 100,001–500,000 $0.0008, 500,001+ $0.0005.
  • Finding ingestion: first 10,000 free, then $0.00003/finding. Updates to Security Hub’s own check findings are free.
  • AWS Config is billed separately and is often the hidden cost driver.

Enabling: AWS Config and standards

AWS Config must be enabled (resource recording) for standards and controls, otherwise you may have issues. ▶ #49 02:40

  • Recording must be on in all accounts and all Regions where you use standards. Config is billed separately; you can Download a CloudFormation template to deploy it as a StackSet.
  • Config must also record global resources (IAM) in one Region.
  • Enabling standards grants Security Hub service-linked roles (CloudWatch, SNS, Config, CloudTrail). Enabling AWS integrations grants permission to import findings from enabled AWS services.

Standards (defaults when enabling in the console: FSBP v1.0.0 + CIS v1.2.0):

Standard Default on?
AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (FSBP) v1.0.0 Yes
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.2.0 Yes
CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.4.0 No
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 No
PCI DSS v3.2.1 No
AWS Resource Tagging standard No
  • The security score is calculated over time and depends entirely on the standards you select; research each one. ▶ #49 03:11
  • Results take up to 2 hours after enabling; until then controls show “No data”. ▶ #49 03:31
  • Settings → General: turn on Consolidated control findings (one finding per control instead of one per standard) and Auto-enable new controls in enabled standards.

Each control is backed by a Config rule. Example: [IAM.1] IAM policies should not allow full “*” administrative privileges: related requirements PCI DSS 7.2.1, CIS 1.2.0/1.22, CIS 1.4.0/1.16, NIST 800-53 AC-2, AC-3, AC-5, AC-6…; category Protect > Secure access management; severity High; resource type AWS::IAM::Policy; Config rule iam-policy-no-statements-with-admin-access; schedule type: Change triggered; parameter excludePermissionBoundaryPolicy: true.

Console tour

Section What’s there
Summary Enabled standards with passed/failed checks and % score; resources with the most failed checks; findings by Region (Critical/High/Medium/Low); findings from integrations (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie…). ▶ #49 03:41
Controls Details of failed controls. ▶ #49 04:11
Security standards Enabled standards and others available. ▶ #49 04:21
Insights Pre-created managed insights grouping important findings; create custom insights. ▶ #49 04:30
Findings Filter, select and set a workflow status to track investigation. ▶ #49 04:41
Integrations Which services/third parties send findings in, or receive findings out. ▶ #49 05:00
