Automations Automation rules that update findings. ▶ #49 05:30
Settings Multiple accounts (Organizations), Region aggregation, custom actions to EventBridge, usage (monthly cost), general settings, and where you disable Security Hub. ▶ #49 06:01

Right after enabling the score is “–” and standards show 0 passed / 0 failed. The Summary prompts “View findings across multiple Regions – use finding aggregation to replicate findings from linked Regions to a single aggregation Region” (Configure finding aggregation), with insight charts of new findings over time by provider and by severity.

Integrations

Every integration has a direction: it sends findings in, receives findings out, or both. AWS integrations are enabled automatically when the service is on. Third-party findings come in via the BatchImportFindings API.

Direction Examples
Sends findings to Security Hub AWS Config (CSPM/CMDB, “Accepting findings / Stop accepting findings”), Firewall Manager, GuardDuty, AWS Health, IAM Access Analyzer, Inspector, Macie, SSM Patch Manager
Receives findings Audit Manager (GRC), AWS Chatbot (→ Amazon Chime, Microsoft Teams, Slack), Detective (network forensics, investigations), Security Lake, Trusted Advisor
Receives and updates SSM OpsCenter and Explorer (SOAR), Jira Service Management

Atlassian Jira Service Management (and Cloud): “Security Hub findings will automatically create issues in Jira Service Management, and JSM updates those findings in Security Hub if they are updated within the issue.” Activation: purchase a subscription and follow the configuration instructions. ▶ #49 05:20 Partners shown include 3CORESec, Alert Logic, Aqua Security.

Findings, workflow and insights

  • Format: ASFF (AWS Security Finding Format).
  • Workflow status: NEW / NOTIFIED / RESOLVED / SUPPRESSED. The finding’s History tab records who changed it and when: an audit trail. ▶ #49 08:21
  • Record state (ACTIVE / ARCHIVED) and compliance status (PASSED / FAILED) are separate fields.
  • Insights: managed insights group important findings; you can create custom ones.
  • Findings are kept ~90 days: export via EventBridge / Security Lake for long-term storage.

Example finding: “Ensure IAM password policy requires minimum password length of 14 or greater”. MEDIUM; “Password policies are, in part, used to enforce password complexity requirements… recommended that the password policy require a minimum password length 14”; related requirements CIS v1.2.0/1.9, CIS v1.4.0/1.8; Workflow status: New; Record state: ACTIVE; Compliance status: FAILED; product Security Hub, company AWS; resource type AwsAccount; an Investigate in Amazon Detective link and a Remediation link to the controls documentation. Other findings in the list: SNS topics should be encrypted at rest using KMS, S3 buckets should have event notifications enabled, S3 server access logging enabled, Athena workgroups encrypted at rest.

Console demo: enable Security Hub CSPM and remediate a failed control ([▶ #49](https://youtu.be/RDG39tDq9QQ))
  1. Security Hub landing → Go to Security Hub (30-day trial). ▶ #49 02:32
  2. Enable page: ensure AWS Config is on; keep default standards (FSBP v1.0.0, CIS v1.2.0) → Enable Security Hub. ▶ #49 02:40
  3. Tour Summary, Controls, Security standards, Insights, Findings, Integrations (search “ji” → Jira integrations), Automations, Settings. ▶ #49 03:41
  4. After time passes, the Summary shows a calculated security score. ▶ #49 06:30
  5. Findings → sort by severity, most critical first → open “Ensure IAM password policy requires minimum password length of 14 or greater”. Side panel: details and History tabs; finding ID, account, severity label, affected resources, Detective link, remediation link. ▶ #49 06:50
  6. Remediation doc: CIS recommends a minimum length of 14; a complexity policy increases resiliency against brute-force logins. ▶ #49 07:30
  7. IAM → Account settings → Password policy → Edit → Custom → set minimum length (the instructor used 20) → Save changes. IAM’s default: minimum length 8, at least three of uppercase/lowercase/numbers/non-alphanumeric, never expires, not identical to account name/email. ▶ #49 07:50
  8. Back in Security Hub → finding → Workflow status → Resolved. The History tab shows when it was detected, the workflow changes, who changed it and when. ▶ #49 08:12

Automation rules, custom actions and EventBridge

Mechanism What it does Trigger
Automation rules Modify findings at ingest: change severity, set workflow to SUPPRESSED, add notes, user-defined fields. No Lambda needed. Run before EventBridge and don’t remediate resources Automatic, on criteria
Custom actions Console button that sends selected findings/insights to EventBridge as Security Hub Findings - Custom Action Analyst, on demand
Security Hub Findings - Imported Every finding goes to EventBridge: the standard hook for automated remediation (AWS “Automated Security Response on AWS” solution) Automatic, every finding

Why automation rules: the same finding may be low for a sandbox but critical for a business-critical workload, so you suppress, re-score or annotate based on business context. ▶ #49 05:30

Cross-Region aggregation and multi-account

  • Cross-Region aggregation: choose an aggregation (home) Region; findings, insights and control status from linked Regions replicate there.
  • Multi-account is different: a delegated admin via Organizations.
  • Central configuration: configuration policies define which standards/controls are enabled across accounts, OUs and Regions from one place. It replaces the older local configuration (auto-enable for new accounts only).

The management account’s Summary shows the banner “Central configuration is now available – use configuration policies to configure Security Hub across multiple Regions, accounts, and OUs.” Security score 85% (294 of 344 controls passed); CIS v1.2.0: 10 passed / 27 failed / 24%. Left nav: Summary / Controls / Security standards; Insights / Findings / Integrations; Management (Automations, Custom actions); Settings (General, Regions, Configuration – New, Usage). Widget “Assets with the most findings” by resources / accounts / applications.

Step 1: delegate from the management account. Settings → General → Delegated Administrator → paste the 12-digit Security Tooling account ID → Delegate. It can be removed at any time. ▶ #50 00:12

  • The delegated account gets Security Hub enabled and a service-linked role required to administer Security Hub for the organization.
  • The same General page shows Controls settings (Auto-enable new controls in enabled standards: On, Consolidated control findings: On), plus Service permissions and Resource policies.

Step 2: start central configuration in the delegated admin. Switch to Security Tooling (IAM Identity Center access portal, admin access) → Security Hub → Settings → Configuration. ▶ #50 00:30

The overview shows Local configuration: “limited access to security settings for your organization, for new accounts only” (Security Hub: disable in new accounts; default standards: enable in new accounts). “When you switch, configuration policies replace the limited configuration settings for new organization accounts.” → Start central configuration. ▶ #50 00:51

  • Home Region: us-east-1 (N. Virginia). ▶ #50 00:51
  • Linked Regions: option to link all available Regions (31 at the time); not done in the demo, but probably a good idea depending on where you operate. ▶ #50 01:01
  • Checkbox to automatically link future Regions as AWS launches them; unchecked in the demo. ▶ #50 01:11
  • Central configuration also turns on cross-Region aggregation, with the home Region as the aggregation Region.

Step 3: configure the organization. ▶ #50 01:31

Wizard: 1 Designate delegated administrator → 2 Centralize organization → 3 Configure organization → 4 Review and apply. “How central configuration works”: Centralize (home Region + linked Regions where policies apply), Configure (policies for the whole org or specific accounts/OUs), Manage (create/edit policies as the org evolves).

Configuration type Result
Use the AWS recommended configuration across my entire organization (chosen in the demo) Enable FSBP v1, all new and existing controls in it, all org accounts use the same configuration ▶ #50 01:51
Customize my Security Hub configuration Choose standards, controls, control parameters, target accounts/OUs
I’m not ready to configure yet Only the delegated admin has Security Hub on; no standards or controls; create a policy later

Heads-up shown: AWS Config resource recording must be enabled, since Security Hub uses Config heavily behind the scenes. ▶ #50 02:10 Central configuration does not enable Config: deploy it separately (StackSets / Control Tower).

Step 4: review and apply. Review: 1 Region, no linked Regions, Security Hub enabled with FSBP and all controls → tick I’ve reviewed this policy overview → Create policy and apply. ▶ #50 02:30 Result: configuration policy 01, viewable and editable, applied from the delegated admin in the home Region to the entire organization. ▶ #50 02:41

  • The overview shows counters for Policies and Failed policies, and tabs Organization (structure → policy → status → last updated, Re-apply policy), Policies, Invitation accounts.
  • With the custom option you can target specific accounts or OUs, create more policies and change coverage over time. ▶ #50 03:00
  • Policies are inherited down the OU tree. An account/OU can be self-managed or get a different policy. Invited (non-org) accounts can’t be centrally configured.
  • Allow ~24 hours for data to gather. ▶ #50 03:31
Console demo: delegate and centrally configure Security Hub CSPM ([▶ #50](https://youtu.be/GJ9_b1wpB_8))
  1. Management account → Security Hub → Settings → General → enter the Security Tooling account ID → Delegate → “Successfully delegated admin”. ▶ #50 00:12
  2. Access portal → Security Tooling (AdministratorAccess) → Security Hub. ▶ #50 00:30
  3. Settings → Configuration → Start central configuration. ▶ #50 00:41
  4. Home Region us-east-1; don’t link all Regions; uncheck auto-link future Regions → Confirm. ▶ #50 00:51
  5. Configuration type AWS recommended (FSBP, all controls, all org accounts) → Next. ▶ #50 01:41
  6. Review → acknowledge → Create policy and apply → configuration policy 01 created. ▶ #50 02:30
Controls show no data or a policy failed? Check these
  • Config not enabled, or not recording that resource type, in that account/Region.
  • Config not recording global resources (IAM) in one Region.
  • Less than 2 hours since enabling (24 hours for an org rollout).
  • Configuration policy Failed: SCPs blocking securityhub:*, a Region denied by SCP, or Config missing.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Use Security Hub CSPM (the original); the new “Security Hub” is a different service. ▶ #49 00:12
  • Security Hub is not a SIEM replacement but a “mini SIEM” / CSPM. ▶ #49 02:21
  • AWS Config is required for standards and controls. ▶ #49 02:40
  • The security score depends entirely on the standards you select. ▶ #49 03:11
  • Up to 2 hours before check results appear. ▶ #49 03:31
  • Automation rules suppress, re-score severity or add notes based on business context. ▶ #49 05:30
  • Workflow status changes are recorded in History (who/when): an audit trail. ▶ #49 08:21
  • Delegate from the management account; manage from the security tooling delegated admin. ▶ #50 00:12
  • Central configuration makes it easier to deploy everywhere; local configuration is limited. ▶ #50 00:51
  • Consider linking all Regions you operate in, plus future Regions. ▶ #50 01:01
  • Policies can target the whole org, specific OUs or specific accounts. ▶ #50 03:00

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Single dashboard of GuardDuty + Inspector + Macie findings across all accounts and Regions Security Hub delegated admin + cross-Region aggregation
Controls show no data / failed to evaluate Config not enabled (or not recording that type) in that account/Region; record global resources (IAM) in one Region
Lower the severity of a known-accepted finding automatically Automation rule
Analyst clicks a button to quarantine Custom action → EventBridge → Lambda / Step Functions
Automatic response for every finding EventBridge on Security Hub Findings - Imported
Continuous CIS compliance checking Security Hub CIS standard (Config conformance packs are the alternative)
Every existing and new account in all Regions has Security Hub with FSBP Central configuration policy at the root, linked Regions + auto-link new Regions
Configuration policy shows Failed SCPs blocking securityhub:*, a Region denied by SCP, or Config missing
Control requires CloudTrail in each account but you use an org trail Disable that control (or rely on consolidated findings) to keep the score meaningful
Finding format Security Hub CSPM = ASFF; Security Lake and the new Security Hub = OCSF
Updates since the videos
  • The new AWS Security Hub went GA in late 2025. It sits on top of GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM and Macie and correlates their signals into exposures and attack paths (OCSF). Security Hub CSPM keeps the standards, controls and ASFF findings. Expect exam questions on CSPM features; C03 may also reference the unified Security Hub.
  • Pricing on the #49 slide is from 2023; check current rates.

Real-world practice

  • Delegate to the security tooling account (same account as the GuardDuty / Detective / Inspector admin), use central configuration, aggregate into your home Region, and pipe findings to the SIEM / ticketing via EventBridge.
  • Separate policies per OU: e.g. prod gets FSBP + CIS + PCI, sandbox gets FSBP only with noisy controls disabled. Write automation rules to downgrade known-accepted risks instead of disabling controls org-wide.
  • Config recording is the hidden cost driver. Consider periodic recording or excluding high-churn resource types in non-prod.
  • Linked Regions should mirror your SCP-allowed Regions. Disable global-resource controls (IAM, CloudFront) in non-home Regions or rely on consolidated control findings to avoid duplicates.
  • Track MTTR via workflow status (NEW → NOTIFIED → RESOLVED / SUPPRESSED). Auditors like the History trail.
  • Password-policy controls only matter if you still have IAM users; prefer Identity Center and no IAM users.
aws securityhub enable-organization-admin-account --admin-account-id <security-acct>
aws securityhub create-finding-aggregator --region-linking-mode ALL_REGIONS   # in home Region
aws securityhub create-automation-rule --rule-name suppress-dev-s3-logging --rule-order 1 \
  --criteria '{"ProductName":[{"Value":"Security Hub","Comparison":"EQUALS"}],
   "ComplianceSecurityControlId":[{"Value":"S3.9","Comparison":"EQUALS"}],
   "ResourceTags":[{"Key":"env","Value":"dev","Comparison":"EQUALS"}]}' \
  --actions '[{"Type":"FINDING_FIELDS_UPDATE","FindingFieldsUpdate":{"Workflow":{"Status":"SUPPRESSED"},
   "Note":{"Text":"Accepted risk for dev","UpdatedBy":"secops"}}}]'
Hands-on lab
  1. Enable Security Hub CSPM with FSBP (Config must be on) and wait for scores.
  2. Open the failed CIS control “IAM password policy minimum length 14”, fix it in IAM → Account settings, set the finding to Resolved and read the History tab.
  3. Make a bucket public, watch the S3 control fail, then fix it and watch it pass.
  4. Org: delegate to the Security Tooling account and create the AWS-recommended central configuration policy.
  5. Cleanup: disable Security Hub and the Config recorder.

Amazon Detective

At a glance

Investigation and root cause analysis. Detective builds a behavior graph linking entities (IAM users/roles, IPs, EC2, EKS, S3) and their activity over time. In AWS’s words it provides “security investigation visualization, which helps you triage security findings, investigate incidents, and track down threats”. ▶ #46 03:10

  • Exam skills: aggregate security events (1.1.3) · search & correlate logs (2.2.2) · validate findings, assess scope (2.2.3) · root cause analysis (2.2.5) · Organizations (6.1.1) · delegated admin (6.1.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #46 Amazon Detective · ▶ #47 Delegating and centralizing Detective
  • Prerequisite: GuardDuty enabled for ≥ 48 hours. Retention: up to 1 year. Trial: 30 days.

What Detective does

Detective consolidates findings so you investigate the whole security event, not isolated findings. ▶ #46 02:21

  • Simplifies log collection and data extraction, and reduces the steps needed to investigate and spot anomalies.
  • Builds behavior graphs made of nodes and edges from all sources. ▶ #46 02:40
  • Calculates baselines and visualizes them against the scope time, to flag anomalies such as an abnormal increase in failed API calls. During an incident that tells you what’s going on, what’s affected and where to focus. ▶ #46 02:51
  • Finding groups correlate related findings into one investigation. Investigations for IAM entities summarize indicators of compromise (TTPs mapped to MITRE ATT&CK).
  • It does not generate threat findings itself (GuardDuty does) and does not remediate.
  • Further reading: re:Inforce talk “Using Amazon Detective to improve security investigations” (youtube.com/watch?v=vd_VHg6-xWc). ▶ #46 03:10

Data sources

Once enabled, Detective collects everything automatically, with no action on your part. ▶ #46 01:20

Source package Contents
Detective core (can’t be disabled) GuardDuty findings, VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail logs
EKS audit logs (optional) Amazon EKS audit logs
AWS security findings (via Security Hub) Security Hub, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer, Firewall Manager, SSM Patch Manager, IoT Device Defender, Macie, AWS Health ▶ #46 01:31

Optional integration with Security Lake gives access to raw logs. Like GuardDuty, Detective reads an independent, duplicate stream of flow logs and CloudTrail directly from AWS, so you don’t need to enable those logs yourself. ▶ #46 01:50

Cost angle: because Detective pulls flow log data itself, the instructor suggests you might even disable your own VPC flow log collection to offset cost, unless you need to store the logs differently or longer than Detective keeps them (he believes one year). Many organizations don’t enable flow logs because of cost and data volume, and Detective helps them. ▶ #46 02:01 See the warning box below: this is usually a bad idea.

Enabling Detective: prerequisite, trial and pricing

GuardDuty must be enabled for at least 48 hours before you can enable Detective. If you can’t enable it, that’s probably why. ▶ #46 00:31

The enable page lists Required permissions for administrator accounts: full access to all Detective actions, via the managed policy AmazonDetectiveFullAccess. The key fact is the red error: “GuardDuty is a prerequisite of Amazon Detective. After you enable GuardDuty on this account, wait at least 48 hours before you try again.” Give analysts AmazonDetectiveInvestigatorAccess instead of full access.

  • 30-day free trial; be aware of pricing if you leave it on. ▶ #46 00:20
  • Data population: up to 24 hours for initial extraction. In practice some data appears in ~10 minutes, but not all, and a quiet demo account shows little. ▶ #46 00:51

Pricing: per behavior graph ID, per month, per Region, by ingested log volume: ▶ #46 00:20

Monthly ingestion Price per GB
First 0–1,000 GB $2.00
Next 4,000 GB (to 5,000 GB) $1.00
Next 5,000 GB (to 10,000 GB) $0.50
Over 10,000 GB $0.25

After enabling: “We are now ingesting your data… invite member accounts to your behavior graph.” The banner shows the 30-day trial covers the three source packages. Two ways to add members: Option 1: AWS Organizations (Recommended), where the management account delegates a Detective administrator that enables members with one click, and Option 2: By invitation. ▶ #46 00:40

Console demo: from a GuardDuty finding to Detective ([▶ #46](https://youtu.be/IYshiyYDBWg))
  1. GuardDuty → Findings → open a finding (demo: [SAMPLE] Backdoor:EC2/Spambot, Medium, instance i-99999999). Hover Investigate with Detective for a high-level summary and links; clicking opens Detective, which only shows data if Detective is already enabled. ▶ #46 00:00
  2. Detective landing page → Get started. Review admin permissions (AmazonDetectiveFullAccess) → Enable. If GuardDuty is < 48 h old you get the prerequisite error. ▶ #46 00:31
  3. The Account management page appears (add members via Organizations or invitation); skipped → Summary. ▶ #46 00:40
  4. Summary is mostly empty / loading at first (“Loading finding groups. This may take a few minutes.”). ▶ #46 00:51
  5. Settings menu: Account management, General, Preferences, Usage. Left nav: Summary, Finding groups, Search.

Investigating: summary, finding groups, entity profiles

Summary panel Shows
Finding groups Entities and findings from the same underlying activity: severity, title, observed tactics, accounts, entities, findings
Roles and users with the most API call volume Principal, account, 7-day trend, success/failure counts
EC2 instances with the most traffic volume Top talkers

All panels are bounded by a scope time window. Pivot straight from GuardDuty / Security Hub findings with the Investigate with Detective link.

Example flow: GuardDuty UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS → open in Detective → role profile → “API calls by IP” and “newly observed geolocations” → scope which resources were touched → decide containment (revoke sessions; see the incident response notes).

Multi-account: delegated admin and auto-enable

Delegate from the management account. When you enable Detective there, the console detects your security tooling account and recommends delegating to it; you can accept or enter another account number. ▶ #47 00:00 AWS recommends Detective admin = GuardDuty admin.

  • The page shows the required permissions (AmazonDetectiveFullAccess, or copy the policy ARN) and Delegated Administrator: “The delegated administrator is granted all of the permissions required to administer Detective for your organization and Detective will be enabled for that account.” ▶ #47 00:20
  • Option selected: Security Tooling (851725223689) – Recommended; Delegated administrator: GuardDuty, SecurityHub → Delegate. A collapsible Enable Detective for this account section sits below.
  • If you enabled Detective in one account without delegating, delegate later from Settings, as with GuardDuty. ▶ #47 00:31
  • The delegated admin must be the same account in every Region.

In the Security Tooling account: “As the delegated administrator for your organization, you can add any organization account as a member of your behavior graph.” ▶ #47 00:57 The newer console adds Investigations (with Run investigation) and Integrations in the left nav, a radial layout for finding groups, and generative-AI finding group summaries.

Account management columns: Account ID, Account name, Type (By organization), Date updated, Daily ingested volume, Status. Only Security Tooling (Administrator account) is Enabled; prod, Shared Services, management, Log Archive, Demo, Example… are Not a member. Options: ▶ #47 01:08

  • Select accounts → Enable accounts.
  • Actions → invite non-org accounts (max 1,200 members per behavior graph; org accounts join with no acceptance).
  • Enable all accounts (banner or list button).
  • Toggle Enable new organization accounts as member accounts (auto-enable). ▶ #47 01:30

“Successfully turned on auto-enable. Newly added organization accounts are automatically enabled as member accounts.” All nine accounts move to Verification in progress, then Enabled, and ingestion begins. ▶ #47 01:41 Note the management account is enrolled as a member too. Each member adds ingestion cost, and every new member gets its own 30-day trial. ▶ #47 01:50 End state: Detective across the whole organization for present and future accounts. ▶ #47 02:01

Console demo: delegate and enable org-wide ([▶ #47](https://youtu.be/PC28KoEQ288))
  1. Management account → Detective → Enable Amazon Detective → Delegated Administrator: select Security Tooling (Recommended) → Delegate. ▶ #47 00:00
  2. Sign in to Security Tooling → Detective → Summary shows the delegated-admin banner → Go to account management. ▶ #47 00:50
  3. Account management → Enable all accounts. ▶ #47 01:20
  4. Toggle Enable new organization accounts as member accounts on. ▶ #47 01:30
  5. Members show Verification in progress, then Enabled; ingestion begins. ▶ #47 01:41

CLI equivalent:

aws detective enable-organization-admin-account --account-id <security-acct>
aws detective update-organization-configuration --graph-arn <graph-arn> --auto-enable
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • “You have to have Amazon GuardDuty enabled for at least 48 hours before you can enable Detective.” ▶ #46 00:31
  • Initial extraction can take up to 24 hours. ▶ #46 00:51
  • Detective = security investigation visualization for triage, investigation and threat tracking. ▶ #46 03:10
  • Watch pricing after the 30-day trial. ▶ #46 00:20
  • Keep all security services in the same tooling account; the console recommends the GuardDuty/Security Hub admin. ▶ #47 00:00
  • Turn on auto-enable so new org accounts are enrolled automatically. ▶ #47 01:30

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Root cause / who else did this IP talk to / what did this role do before and after the finding Detective
Visualize relationships between IPs, roles, instances / scope of compromise Detective
Investigate / triage a GuardDuty finding Detective
Raw log search with SQL CloudTrail Lake / Athena (visual entity investigation → Detective)
Can’t enable Detective GuardDuty not enabled for 48 h in that account/Region
Investigate findings across all accounts from one place Delegated admin + auto-enable, not per-account enablement
Generate threat findings / remediate Not Detective: GuardDuty / automation
Updates since the videos
  • Disabling your own VPC Flow Logs because Detective collects them (▶ #46 02:01) is usually a bad idea. Detective’s data is for investigation in its own UI, not a log archive: you can’t export raw flow logs from it for compliance, Athena queries or third-party SIEMs. Detective retains up to 1 year of history in the behavior graph.
  • The newer console adds generative-AI finding group summaries, a radial layout, Investigations and Integrations (▶ #47).

Real-world practice

  • Enable GuardDuty org-wide first, then Detective from the same delegated admin with auto-enable for new accounts. Automate with the APIs or a Control Tower customization.
  • Cost scales with CloudTrail/flow-log volume. Watch the Usage page and the per-member daily ingested volume during the trial. Exclude sandbox accounts if cost matters, but document the gap.
  • In an IR runbook, Detective is the “scope and impact” step before containment.
  • Keep your own CloudTrail org trail and flow logs in the Log Archive account. Detective complements them, it doesn’t replace them.
Hands-on lab
  1. With GuardDuty on for 48 h, enable Detective and open a sample finding.
  2. Explore the entity profile panels.
  3. In an org: delegate to the Security Tooling account, enable all accounts and turn on auto-enable (▶ #47).
  4. Cleanup: disable Detective (aws detective delete-graph).

Amazon Inspector

At a glance

Automated, continuous vulnerability management for EC2, container images in ECR and Lambda. It looks for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure, and rescans automatically on change.

  • Exam skills: metrics, alerts & dashboards (1.1.4) · automated assessments (1.1.5) · scan compute for vulnerabilities (3.2.3) · patch compute (3.2.4) · pipeline vulnerability scanning (3.2.6) · unnecessary network access (3.3.5) · delegated admin (6.1.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #48 Amazon Inspector · related: ▶ #102 hardening, ▶ #138 Patch Manager, ▶ #147 code vulnerability tools
  • Trial: 15 days. Cost is per instance / image / function per month.

What Inspector does

  • Automatically discovers and scans running EC2 instances, container images in ECR and Lambda functions. ▶ #48 00:12
  • Looks for known software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. ▶ #48 00:12
  • Each finding describes the vulnerability, the affected resource, the severity and remediation guidance. ▶ #48 00:20
  • No manual scheduling: it responds to changes by rescanning, e.g. when you install a new package or patch on EC2, or a new relevant CVE is published. ▶ #48 00:32
  • In DevSecOps it sits on top of SAST scans in the build pipeline, on the operate and monitor side of the lifecycle. ▶ #48 01:02

What gets scanned, and how

Resource Mode Notes
EC2 Agent-based via the SSM Agent Instance must be SSM-managed: agent + instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore + connectivity to SSM endpoints
EC2 Agentless via EBS snapshots “Hybrid” mode scans instances without SSM
EC2 Network reachability Which ports are reachable from the internet / outside the VPC through IGW, SG, NACL and ELB paths. No agent needed
EC2 CIS benchmark scans OS configuration, on-demand or scheduled, SSM-managed instances
ECR Enhanced scanning (Inspector) Continuous rescans when new CVEs appear; OS + language packages; configurable rescan duration (e.g. lifetime, 30/180 days)
ECR Basic scanning ECR’s own on-push-only scan
Lambda Standard scanning Package dependencies only. Does not scan your function code ▶ #48 04:50
Lambda Code scanning Your own code (injection, hard-coded secrets…). Activated separately in Account management ▶ #48 05:10
CI/CD Pipeline image scans Jenkins/TeamCity plugins, inspector-sbomgen + ScanSbom API

Console tour and scoring

Get started → 15-day free trial → Activate Inspector. Activation creates a service-linked role and activates this account only. With no resources the dashboard is empty. ▶ #48 01:11

Console area What it’s for
Findings All findings ranked by severity, or by vulnerability, instance, container image, container repository, Lambda function ▶ #48 01:41
Export SBOMs Software bill of materials (third-party libraries, dependencies) in CycloneDX or SPDX to S3, KMS-encrypted ▶ #48 01:50
Suppression rules Hide accepted findings, reducing noise and false positives ▶ #48 02:10
Account management “Really important”: what is activated per account, and activate more ▶ #48 02:30
Vulnerability database search Check whether Inspector covers a CVE ID (CVE-<year>-<id>) ▶ #48 02:51
General settings / Usage EC2 and ECR scanning settings; cost usage

The 2023 banners announce deep inspection of EC2, Lambda code scanning GA, and enhanced vulnerability intelligence (malware kits, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, CISA KEV date, EPSS score, public exploit evidence).

Inspector risk score = CVSS adjusted with environment context (network exposure, exploitability).

Searching CVE-2023-5586 (NULL pointer dereference in gpac) shows severity (NVD), CVSS v2/v3, detection platforms, CWE-476, EPSS score 0.00043, vendor dates, and Vulnerability intelligence (Amazon: targets, last known public exploit; CISA: remediation action, date added to catalog). View findings jumps to findings for that CVE. You can copy a newly published CVE from a list like Tenable’s “Newest CVEs” and paste it. ▶ #48 02:51

Lambda: standard vs code scanning

The key gotcha: standard scanning checks the application package dependencies of your function, not your function code, so it would not find a hard-coded credential. ▶ #48 04:50 Code scanning scans your own code using Amazon CodeGuru detectors (Python detector library: e.g. Hardcoded credentials, Hardcoded IP address). ▶ #48 03:50

Account management tabs: Accounts / Instances / Container repositories / Container images / Lambda functions. The demo account shows EC2 scanning Activated, ECR scanning Activated, Lambda scanning: Activated standard scan (Deactivated code scan). The Activate dropdown turns on code scanning. A banner links a GitHub CLI script to enable Inspector across all accounts and Regions. ▶ #48 02:30

The finding panel: runtime PYTHON_3_11, version $LATEST, package type ZIP, finding summary 1 Critical; CWE-798 – Hardcoded credentials; finding ARN arn:aws:inspector2:us-east-1:…:finding/…; description (credentials in source can leak even after removal because version control retains old versions); Severity Critical; Type Code Vulnerability; detector Hardcoded credentials; Rule ID; tags #secrets #security #owasp-top10; Fix available: Yes; file path lambda_function.py; exact code location; suggested remediation. ▶ #48 05:41

Suggested remediation: use environment variables or AWS profiles, delete and rotate the secret key, and monitor CloudWatch for unexpected activity. Lambda should get permissions from its execution role, never access keys. ▶ #48 06:22

Console demo: catch a hard-coded secret in Lambda ([▶ #48](https://youtu.be/XFlL_PnayiE))
  1. Inspector → Get started → Activate Inspector (15-day trial). ▶ #48 01:11
  2. Account management → Activate → enable Lambda standard scanning + Lambda code scanning. ▶ #48 02:30
  3. Vulnerability database search → paste CVE-2023-5586 → details shown. ▶ #48 02:51
  4. Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch → name vulnLambda → runtime Python 3.11 → defaults → Create. ▶ #48 03:11
  5. Replace the code in Code source with the vulnerable code, then Deploy: ▶ #48 03:40 
    import boto3

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    # Noncompliant: uses hardcoded secret access key.
    sample_key = "AjWnyxxxxx45xxxxZxxxX7ZQxxxxYxxx1xYxxxxx"
    boto3.session.Session(aws_secret_access_key=sample_key)

    return {
        'statusCode': 200,
        'body': sample_key
    }
  6. Back on the dashboard: Lambda functions 100% (1/1) coverage. Clicking 100% opens Settings → Account management → Lambda functions, where the function appears under standard scanning and, below, code scanning (actively monitored). ▶ #48 04:31
  7. Data can take hours (up to 24 h) to show up. ▶ #48 05:20
  8. Click the function → overview → Critical finding CWE-798 Hardcoded credentials with code location and remediation. ▶ #48 05:41

Acting on findings

  • Inspector publishes each finding to Amazon EventBridge for near-real-time automation (as with GuardDuty), and to AWS Security Hub. ▶ #48 06:52
  • Suppression rules hide accepted findings.
  • Inspector finds vulnerabilities; SSM Patch Manager fixes them (▶ #138).
aws inspector2 enable --resource-types EC2 ECR LAMBDA LAMBDA_CODE --account-ids <acct>
aws inspector2 list-findings --filter-criteria '{"severity":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"CRITICAL"}],
  "findingStatus":[{"comparison":"EQUALS","value":"ACTIVE"}]}' --query 'findings[].title'
aws inspector2 create-sbom-export --report-format CYCLONEDX_1_4 \
  --s3-destination bucketName=sbom-bucket,keyPrefix=sbom,kmsKeyArn=<key>

Multi-account

  • Delegated admin + auto-enable, per Region. Max 10,000 member accounts per delegated admin.
  • Activating in the console activates this account only. ▶ #48 01:11
  • Inspector Classic (assessment templates, rules packages, Inspector agent) is legacy. v2 (inspector2) is current, so answers mentioning “assessment templates” are old-style.
EC2 missing from Inspector coverage? Check these
  • Is it an SSM managed instance? SSM Agent installed and running.
  • Instance profile includes AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  • Network route to the SSM endpoints (VPC interface endpoints or NAT).
  • Otherwise turn on agentless (snapshot-based) scanning.
  • Just activated? Findings and coverage can take up to 24 h.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Inspector scans EC2, ECR images, Lambda automatically and rescans on change (new package/patch, new CVE). ▶ #48 00:40
  • Lambda standard scanning does not scan your function code, only dependencies. Enable code scanning for code-level issues like hard-coded credentials. ▶ #48 04:50
  • Account management is “really important”: check what’s activated. ▶ #48 02:30
  • Never hard-code credentials; Lambda gets permissions from its execution role. ▶ #48 06:42
  • Findings → EventBridge (near-real-time automation) and Security Hub. ▶ #48 06:52
  • Findings can take up to 24 h to fully render. ▶ #48 05:41

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Continuously find CVEs on EC2/ECR/Lambda, least overhead Inspector (not GuardDuty)
Malicious activity / sensitive data in S3 GuardDuty / Macie
EC2 not showing in Inspector coverage Not an SSM managed instance (no agent, missing role, no route to SSM), or turn on agentless scanning
Which instances have SSH open to the internet, without an agent Network reachability findings
Produce an SBOM for audit Inspector SBOM export (CycloneDX / SPDX)
Fix the vulnerabilities SSM Patch Manager (Inspector only finds them)
Inspector didn’t flag a hard-coded secret in Lambda Only standard scanning is on; activate Lambda code scanning
Findings / coverage not visible yet Data can take up to 24 h
Question mentions “assessment templates” / “rules packages” Inspector Classic (legacy)
Updates since the videos
  • Lambda code scanning was originally powered by Amazon CodeGuru detectors (▶ #48). AWS has since wound down CodeGuru Security and launched Inspector code security (repo scanning for SAST, SCA and IaC via GitHub/GitLab integrations). Check current console naming; the code-level vs dependency-level split is unchanged.

Real-world practice

  • Use suppression rules sparingly and document why (e.g. vulnerable package not in the runtime path). Auditors ask.
  • Route Critical/High findings through EventBridge → ticketing (Jira/ServiceNow) and auto-trigger Patch Manager for EC2. For ECR findings, rebuild images rather than patching running containers.
  • Cost is per instance/image/function per month. Dev accounts with many short-lived images get pricey, so tune the ECR rescan duration.
  • Secrets in code: pair Inspector with pre-commit scanning (gitleaks) and Secrets Manager. Rotate any key that reached a repo, even if deleted.
  • Hardening and code-scanning tooling are covered in the hardening (▶ #102) and code vulnerability tools (▶ #147) notes.
Hands-on lab
  1. Launch an old AMI (e.g. outdated Amazon Linux) as an SSM-managed instance, enable Inspector and review the CVEs.
  2. Activate Lambda standard + code scanning, deploy a function with a hard-coded secret key, and find the CWE-798 finding (▶ #48).
  3. Run Patch Manager AWS-RunPatchBaseline, then watch the findings close.
  4. Cleanup: terminate the instance, delete the function and disable Inspector.

AWS Trusted Advisor

At a glance

Account-level best-practice checking, enabled in every account by default: part is free, a paid support plan unlocks many more checks. ▶ #36 00:00 It is not threat detection: threats → GuardDuty; continuous compliance with custom rules → AWS Config; aggregated security posture → Security Hub.

  • Exam skills: metrics, alerts & dashboards (1.1.4) · automated assessments (1.1.5) · detect & remediate noncompliance (6.3.1) · best practices / Well-Architected (6.3.3)
  • Videos: ▶ #36 AWS Trusted Advisor

Six check categories

Trusted Advisor scans your account and gives recommendations across six categories. The instructor says to memorize these six: they may appear on this exam and certainly on other AWS exams. ▶ #36 00:20

  1. Cost optimization
  2. Performance
  3. Security
  4. Fault tolerance
  5. Service limits (quotas)
  6. Operational excellence

Free vs paid support plans

Support plan What you get
Basic / Developer Core security checks + service quotas: S3 bucket permissions, security groups with unrestricted (specific) ports, IAM use, MFA on root, public EBS / RDS snapshots
Business / Enterprise On-Ramp / Enterprise All checks in all categories, the Trusted Advisor API (via the AWS Support API), EventBridge integration, and the organizational view (management account, trusted access in Organizations) ▶ #36 02:12

Trusted Advisor Priority (Enterprise) surfaces prioritized recommendations from your TAM.

Recommendations dashboard

  • Checks summary at the top: Action recommended (red), Investigation recommended (yellow), Checks with excluded items, with counts per category. Buttons Refresh all checks and Download all checks. ▶ #36 00:51
  • Left nav: the six categories plus Preferences (Manage Trusted Advisor, Notifications).
  • Demo: 0 action recommended, 1 investigation recommended (Security).
  • Checks refresh automatically, or you refresh them manually.

Example check: Security Groups – Specific Ports Unrestricted. “Checks security groups for rules that allow unrestricted access (0.0.0.0/0) to specific ports”; “1 of 31 security group rules allow unrestricted access to a specific port”; last updated 14 hours ago. ▶ #36 01:00

Expanding a check shows Alert criteria, Recommended action, Additional resources and the affected resources: Region us-east-1, SG launch-wizard-1 (sg-0dcaa608ac68e2ed5), tcp, from port 435. ▶ #36 01:11 Recommended fixes:

  • restrict the CIDR;
  • manage SGs at scale with Firewall Manager;
  • use Systems Manager Session Manager instead of opening SSH 22 / RDP 3389.

If an item is acceptable, Exclude & Refresh it; otherwise fix the resource. ▶ #36 01:30

Security category and Security Hub

Free security checks shown in the demo: ▶ #36 01:40

  • Security Groups – Specific Ports Unrestricted
  • Amazon EBS Public Snapshots
  • Amazon RDS Public Snapshots
  • Amazon S3 Bucket Permissions
  • MFA on Root Account (“MFA is enabled on the root account”)

Many more checks are greyed out (e.g. “Amazon VPC Peering Connections With DNS Resolution Disabled”) on the free plan. ▶ #36 02:01 The upgrade banner lists technical support, the AWS Support API, IAM users can create cases, and all Trusted Advisor checks.

The banner “Trusted Advisor checks sourced from AWS Security Hub”: enable Security Hub to see its findings as Trusted Advisor check recommendations.

Exposed access keys: Trusted Advisor detects access keys found on public code repositories, with an EventBridge alert. AWS also attaches the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine policy to the user.

Console demo: review checks and set notifications ([▶ #36](https://youtu.be/6S7gfI9JnhQ))
  1. Console → Trusted Advisor → Recommendations. ▶ #36 00:40
  2. Expand Security Groups – Specific Ports Unrestricted → read alert criteria / recommended action / flagged resources → optionally Exclude & Refresh. ▶ #36 01:00
  3. Left nav → Security → list of free checks, greyed-out paid checks. ▶ #36 01:30
  4. Preferences → Notifications → select the security contact → Save preferences (weekly email). ▶ #36 02:31

Notifications and EventBridge automation

Weekly email: Preferences → Notifications → choose recipients from the account’s alternate contacts: billing, operations, security (the demo has only a security contact) → Save preferences. ▶ #36 02:41 You then get an email with recommendations once per week after Trusted Advisor refreshes (or after a manual refresh on the free tier). ▶ #36 02:50

EventBridge detects check status changes (e.g. green → red) and invokes targets. ▶ #36 03:01 Trusted Advisor events are delivered in us-east-1.

Docs examples: ▶ #36 03:22

  • Lambda function → notification to a Slack channel
  • push check data to a Kinesis stream for real-time monitoring
  • SNS topic → email
  • CloudWatch alarm action

More examples: “Trusted Advisor tools” on GitHub. The instructor says a paid support plan is needed for EventBridge rules on Trusted Advisor. ▶ #36 03:41

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Memorize the six categories. ▶ #36 00:31
  • Free tier = limited checks (SG ports unrestricted, EBS/RDS public snapshots, S3 bucket permissions, MFA on root). Paid support plans unlock all checks + API. ▶ #36 01:52
  • Weekly email notifications to billing/operations/security contacts. ▶ #36 02:41
  • EventBridge integration for automated responses, needing a paid plan. ▶ #36 03:41

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Check for open SG ports / public snapshots / root without MFA, no extra cost, account-level Trusted Advisor (deeper, continuous, org-wide → Security Hub / Config)
Alert when an access key is exposed on GitHub Trusted Advisor exposed-keys check (+ AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine) → EventBridge → rotate the key
Avoid outages from hitting quotas Service limits category, with Service Quotas + CloudWatch alarms
Trusted Advisor report across all member accounts Organizational view (Business+ support)
All checks / API access / EventBridge automation Upgrade to a paid support plan
Centralized security findings across accounts Security Hub, not Trusted Advisor
Updates since the videos
  • AWS is folding security checks into Security Hub (the console already shows checks “sourced from AWS Security Hub”). For centralized security findings, Security Hub is the better answer.

Real-world practice

  • Exclusions are per check per resource. Document why (e.g. a public web SG on 443) to avoid alert fatigue.
  • Set alternate contacts (security / operations / billing) in every account via Organizations, so Trusted Advisor notifications and AWS security emails reach a monitored mailbox.
  • For “SG specific ports unrestricted”: restrict the CIDR, manage SGs at scale with Firewall Manager, and use Session Manager instead of opening SSH 22 / RDP 3389.
Hands-on lab
  1. Open Trusted Advisor → Recommendations, review the free security checks, and set the security contact for weekly notifications.
  2. Open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 on a test SG, refresh checks, and watch “Security Groups – Specific Ports Unrestricted” turn yellow/red.
  3. Cleanup: remove the rule (or delete the SG).

Amazon Macie

At a glance

A data security service that discovers sensitive data in S3 with machine learning and pattern matching, and evaluates S3 bucket security posture (public, unencrypted, shared outside the org).

  • Exam skills: sensitive data classification · mask sensitive data (5.3.4) · alerts & dashboards for anomalies (1.1.4) · log sources & storage (1.2.1) · automated remediation (2.1.4) · delegated admin (6.1.4) · tagging (6.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #93 About Amazon Macie · ▶ #94 Deploying Amazon Macie
  • Scope: S3 only. Regional: enable it per Region.

What Macie finds, and where

Finding sensitive data across terabytes in S3 by hand is very hard. Macie automates it. ▶ #93 00:00

Level What Macie does
Bucket On first enablement, inventories all S3 buckets in the account and flags risks: unencrypted, publicly accessible, shared outside your organization. ▶ #93 00:21
Object Analyzes individual objects for PII (names, credit card numbers, social security numbers…) and for sensitive data types you define. ▶ #93 00:40 ▶ #93 01:00
  • S3 only. Sensitive data in CloudWatch Logs → Logs data protection policies. In SNS → message data protection (see file 04). PII in DynamoDB/RDS → not Macie.
  • SSE-KMS objects: the key policy must allow Macie’s service-linked role to kms:Decrypt, or the objects are skipped.
  • Macie can’t read client-side-encrypted data or objects encrypted with SSE-C.

Detection building blocks

Building block What it is
Managed data identifiers Built-in detectors: PII (names, addresses, passports, national IDs), financial (credit cards), credentials (AWS secret keys, private keys)
Custom data identifiers Regex plus optional keywords, ignore words and match distance (e.g. employee IDs)
Allow lists Text or regex Macie should ignore. Reduces false positives (e.g. test SSNs) ▶ #94 03:30

Discovery modes: automated discovery vs jobs

Automated sensitive data discovery Sensitive data discovery jobs
How Continuous daily sampling across the estate One-time or scheduled, targeted full scans
Output A sensitivity score per bucket, at low cost Findings for the scoped objects
Scope Whole estate Bucket list, bucket criteria, tags, prefix, object criteria
Default On by default for new accounts You create them
  • “Automatically detect PII in all buckets across accounts at low cost” → automated discovery from the delegated admin, not one-time jobs.
  • Job bucket scope: Select specific buckets (a fixed list) or Specify bucket criteria (filter rules, e.g. Account ID eq …, re-evaluated on each run as the inventory changes). ▶ #94 02:01
  • Scheduled vs one-time: in real life use scheduled jobs so scans run regularly “and not just when someone is thinking about doing it”. One-time is for the demo. ▶ #94 02:20
  • Sampling depth trades coverage against cost: 100% is fine for tiny data but can be cost-prohibitive on terabytes. ▶ #94 02:41
  • Object include/exclude criteria save time and money on large data. ▶ #94 02:50

The left nav shows Findings (by bucket/type/job), S3 buckets, Jobs, Discovery results, Allow lists, Custom data identifiers, Accounts, Automated discovery and Reveal samples. The bucket-criteria example is Include Account ID eq 272281913033.

Findings and discovery results

Finding type Examples
Policy findings (bucket posture) Policy:IAMUser/S3BucketPublic, S3BucketSharedExternally, S3BucketEncryptionDisabled, S3BlockPublicAccessDisabled, S3BucketReplicatedExternally
Sensitive data findings SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal, /Financial, /Credentials, /CustomIdentifier, /Multiple
  • Findings are kept ~90 days and published to EventBridge and Security Hub. ▶ #94 04:10
  • Discovery results (detailed records for every object scanned) must go to an S3 bucket encrypted with a KMS key you configure, for long-term retention. The key is a symmetric customer managed key whose key policy allows Macie. ▶ #94 04:20
  • For longer retention of findings or a SIEM feed → EventBridge → Firehose/S3, or the Security Hub integration.
  • Reveal samples shows the actual sensitive values from a finding (needs the KMS key configured). Restrict it with IAM, because it exposes the data itself.

Multi-account setup and automation

  • Feed Macie data from every account into one central administrator account for an overall posture view. ▶ #93 01:10
  • Delegate Macie administration to the security tooling account, and auto-enable new members (per Region). ▶ #93 01:21
  • Store findings in a central S3 bucket in the log archive account, encrypted with a KMS key. ▶ #93 01:31
  • Send findings to EventBridge and Security Hub to start automated remediation where it makes sense: ▶ #93 01:41
    • EventBridge → Jira, Slack, email. Destinations can be outside AWS. ▶ #93 02:00
    • Lambda tags buckets that contain sensitive data, and the tags drive permission policies (ABAC), cost analysis, etc. ▶ #93 02:12
    • QuickSight visualizes findings for the team and management. ▶ #93 02:32
    • Step Functions for other workflows. ▶ #93 02:40

Deploying Macie and running a job (single account)

The demo creates a bucket with two files of fake sensitive data, enables Macie and runs one discovery job. ▶ #94 00:00

  • customers.txt holds customer names + credit card numbers; ssn.csv holds names + US social security numbers. ▶ #94 00:21

Enabling Macie starts a 30-day free trial and creates a service-linked role that gathers S3 information, evaluates and monitors buckets for security and access control, and finds and reports sensitive data. ▶ #94 00:51

Pricing item Free allowance
Bucket inventory / monitoring First 30 days
Automated sensitive data discovery Up to 150 GB in the first 30 days
Discovery jobs Not in the trial. First 1 GB analyzed per month per account is free ▶ #94 01:32

Charges are based on buckets evaluated, objects monitored for automated discovery, and data inspected.

Console demo: one-time discovery job ([▶ #94](https://youtu.be/kn7aCqA_Nvc))
  1. S3 → Create bucket cybr-test-macie (us-east-1, defaults) → upload customers.txt and ssn.csv. ▶ #94 00:00
  2. Macie console → Get started → Enable Macie. The Summary dashboard’s initial scan takes 1–2 minutes and finds all buckets in the account (all accounts if enabled org-wide). ▶ #94 01:01
  3. Get started recommends analyzing buckets for sensitive data and analyzing public buckets → Create job under analyze buckets. ▶ #94 01:20
  4. Step 1: Select specific buckets → the test bucket. Step 2: review → Next. ▶ #94 02:01
  5. Step 3: One-time job, sampling depth 100%, no object criteria. ▶ #94 02:20
  6. Step 4: managed data identifiers Recommended. Step 5: no custom identifiers. Step 6: no allow lists. ▶ #94 03:10
  7. Step 7: name cybr-macie-test (optional description/tags). Step 8: review the cost estimate. It should be $0; if not, check bucket selection and data volume. Submit. ▶ #94 03:52
  8. A banner warns that no repository for sensitive data discovery results is configured. ▶ #94 04:10
  9. Refresh until the status is no longer “Active (Running)”. It took ~15 minutes. ▶ #94 04:30
  10. Show findings → two High-severity findings, one per file, with exact file and location, how much sensitive data, and what type (credit card vs SSN). ▶ #94 05:00
  11. If a job fails → Show CloudWatch logs. ▶ #94 04:52

Next steps after the demo: configure the long-term results bucket, then automate (EventBridge → Jira/Slack/email, tag sensitive buckets with Step Functions or Lambda, visualize with QuickSight). ▶ #94 05:21

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Macie is the answer for discovering sensitive data (PII) in S3 at scale. ▶ #93 00:00
  • Delegate Macie admin to the security tooling account. Findings bucket in log archive, KMS-encrypted. ▶ #93 01:21
  • Findings → EventBridge / Security Hub for automated remediation, including non-AWS tools. ▶ #93 01:41
  • Prefer scheduled jobs in real environments. ▶ #94 02:20
  • Sampling depth trades coverage vs cost. Use include/exclude criteria on large data. ▶ #94 02:41
  • Check the job’s cost estimate before submitting. ▶ #94 03:52
  • Configure a discovery results repository in S3: Macie only keeps data 90 days. ▶ #94 04:20
  • Failed jobs → CloudWatch logs. ▶ #94 04:52

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Find PII / credit card numbers in S3 across 200 accounts Macie delegated admin + automated discovery
Macie skipped objects KMS key policy doesn’t allow Macie, or objects are client-side encrypted / SSE-C / unsupported formats
Company-specific ID format Custom data identifier
Keep classification evidence > 90 days Configure the discovery results repository (S3 + KMS)
Discovery results aren’t written KMS key policy or bucket policy doesn’t allow Macie
PII in CloudWatch Logs CloudWatch Logs data protection policies
PII in SNS messages SNS message data protection
A Macie job failed Check the job’s CloudWatch logs (Show CloudWatch logs)
Updates since the videos
  • The #94 demo is from 2023 (older console, single account). Current best practice: enable Macie through the Organizations delegated admin, use automated discovery by default, and keep jobs for targeted or scheduled deep scans.
  • Automated sensitive data discovery is now on by default for new accounts.

Real-world practice

  • Enable Macie via the Organizations delegated administrator and turn on auto-enable for new member accounts. It is Regional, so enable it in every Region you use.
  • Cost has several dimensions (bucket inventory per bucket, objects monitored, GB inspected) and scales with bytes inspected. Use automated discovery for coverage and targeted jobs for high-risk buckets. Use include/exclude criteria and sampling on big data lakes, and exclude log/archive buckets that don’t need scanning.
  • Macie findings in Security Hub land in ASFF/OCSF format, so one pipeline (EventBridge → Step Functions/Lambda) handles Macie and the other detectors.
  • Route SensitiveData:* findings via EventBridge to a ticket queue.
  • Remediation workflow: tag the bucket data-classification=sensitive (or confidential) to drive ABAC and SCP guardrails, check encryption / public access / Object Lock, notify the data owner. Avoid auto-deleting data.
aws macie2 enable-organization-admin-account --admin-account-id <security-acct>
aws macie2 create-custom-data-identifier --name employee-id --regex 'EMP-[0-9]{6}' \
  --keywords employee staff --maximum-match-distance 50
aws macie2 create-classification-job --job-type ONE_TIME --name pii-scan \
  --s3-job-definition '{"bucketDefinitions":[{"accountId":"<acct>","buckets":["customer-data"]}]}'
Hands-on lab
  1. Upload a CSV with fake credit card numbers and a fake AWS key, then run a one-time job.
  2. Review the SensitiveData:S3Object/Multiple finding.
  3. Cleanup: delete (cancel) the job, delete the bucket, and disable Macie.

Amazon Security Lake

At a glance

A managed service that centralizes, normalizes and stores security data in an S3 data lake in your own account, across accounts and Regions. Logs are converted to OCSF (Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework) in Apache Parquet, managed through Lake Formation + Glue. It has no analytics of its own: subscribers analyze the data.

  • Exam skills: aggregate security events (1.1.3) · log data lakes & 3rd-party integration (1.2.3) · normalize, parse & correlate logs (1.2.5) · OCSF / 3rd-party integrations (3.1.4) · search & correlate logs (2.2.2) · lifecycle & retention (5.2.3) · delegated admin / RAM sharing (6.1.4, 6.2.4)
  • Videos: ▶ #116 Amazon Security Lake · ▶ #117 Enable Security Lake · ▶ #118 Querying with Athena
  • Data ownership: the data stays in your S3 buckets (unlike CloudTrail Lake, which is AWS-managed storage)

What it is and what it collects

Security Lake centralizes security data across your AWS environment, and also accepts data from outside AWS: on-premises, SaaS providers, other clouds and third-party sources. ▶ #116 00:00 ▶ #116 00:11

  1. Inputs: Amazon VPC, CloudTrail, Route 53, AWS WAF, S3, Lambda, EKS. Below them, Security Hub findings (GuardDuty, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer, 50+ partner solutions), and AppFabric / SaaS / partner / cloud / customer data converted to OCSF.
  2. Centralize and normalize your security data and findings to OCSF.
  3. Store in Amazon S3: data lake storage in your account.
  4. Take action: analyze with your choice of tools (Athena, OpenSearch Service, SageMaker) or AWS Partner Network security, automation and analytics solutions.

Native AWS sources (collected out of the box): ▶ #116 00:22

Source Notes
CloudTrail management events Collected by Security Lake itself, no trail required
CloudTrail data events (S3, Lambda) S3 data events are high-volume
VPC Flow Logs Collection managed by Security Lake
Route 53 Resolver (VPC Resolver) query logs Collection managed by Security Lake
AWS WAFv2 logs High-volume
EKS audit logs Kubernetes API activity
Security Hub findings Carry GuardDuty, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer and partner findings ▶ #116 00:53. Security Hub must be enabled to get them

Plus AWS AppFabric, SaaS apps, partner solutions, cloud providers and customer data. ▶ #116 01:05

Custom sources (3rd-party / on-prem) must already be in OCSF Parquet before they are added to the lake. A Glue crawler/role is used for custom sources. ▶ #116 01:45

Normalization: Parquet + OCSF

  • On ingest, Security Lake partitions the data and converts it to Apache Parquet (open-source, column-oriented, efficient compression/encoding) and OCSF, an open-source, vendor-agnostic schema (a Linux Foundation project since Nov 2024). ▶ #116 01:15
  • Result: more storage- and query-efficient, compatible with other tools, stored in S3. ▶ #116 01:35
  • OCSF is the answer whenever a question says “normalize logs from many sources into a common schema” or “ingest third-party data in a standard format” (3.1.4).

Common OCSF fields for queries:

OCSF field CloudTrail equivalent
api.operation eventName
api.service.name eventSource
actor.user.uid / actor.user.name userIdentity
src_endpoint.ip sourceIPAddress
cloud.account.uid account ID
api.response.error errorCode
time_dt event time (timestamp)

Table naming: amazon_security_lake_table_<region>_<source>_<version>, e.g. ..._cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0, ..._vpc_flow_2_0, ..._route53_2_0, ..._sh_findings_2_0, ..._eks_audit_2_0, ..._lambda_execution_2_0, ..._s3_data_2_0. Filter on partition columns (accountid, region, eventday) to cut data scanned.

Security Lake as an orchestrator

One place to configure instead of jumping between services. When enabled it creates and uses these on your behalf, which matters for IAM permissions and cost: ▶ #116 02:00 ▶ #116 02:19

Service Role in Security Lake
Amazon S3 Stores the data: the data lake itself (one bucket per Region)
AWS Lake Formation Maps, governs and shares the data
AWS Glue Data Catalog: schemas and table definitions
Amazon EventBridge + SNS Event routing; notifies subscribers when objects are written
AWS Lambda ETL, especially for third-party sources
Amazon SQS Event-driven processing / notifications

Subscribers: data access vs query access

Security Lake has no analysis tools. Analyze with Athena (SQL), OpenSearch (search and visualization), SageMaker, or partner query engines. ▶ #116 03:27 ▶ #116 03:35 Subscribers consume the data in one of two ways: ▶ #116 03:52

Data access (S3) Query access (Lake Formation)
How Notified when new objects land in S3, via an HTTPS endpoint or by polling an SQS queue; reads S3 objects directly ▶ #116 04:00 Queries Lake Formation tables directly, shared cross-account ▶ #116 04:20
Typical consumer A SIEM such as Splunk Analysts using Athena, Redshift or OpenSearch
Extra setup None Accept a RAM share, create a resource link, grant Lake Formation permissions
  • Subscriber access is granted per source: ingesting a source doesn’t decide who can consume it. ▶ #117 05:00
  • A subscriber is created with the consumer account ID + external ID. The external ID is appended to the RAM share name and protects the subscriber role against the confused deputy problem. ▶ #117 06:51

Multi-account, Regions and retention

  • Delegated admin: set from the Organizations management account. The course delegates to the Log Archive account. Enable for all accounts and auto-enable new ones. ▶ #117 00:00
  • Rollup Regions: Security Lake is Regional. Contributing Regions replicate into a rollup Region for central querying or data residency (your choice). You can’t pick a rollup Region unless two or more Regions are enabled. ▶ #116 05:05 ▶ #117 03:11
  • Retention and storage tiering are set per Region at setup: transition to cheaper S3 storage classes over time, or expire after a set period. That controls cost while keeping enough for compliance and investigations. It is S3 lifecycle under the hood. ▶ #116 04:35

Security Lake is enabled org-wide by the management account or the delegated administrator, not from a member account.

Enabling Security Lake for the organization

At recording time there was a 15-day free trial per account (from first ingestion). Check current pricing. ▶ #117 00:10

Wizard step 1: define the collection objective. Data is encrypted with S3 managed keys. Choose Ingest the AWS default sources (Recommended) or Ingest specific AWS sources. All sources are version 2.0. ▶ #117 01:00

Source Default? Note
CloudTrail – Management events Recommended Management operations
CloudTrail – Lambda data events Recommended Lambda API incl. console/code calls
EKS Audit Logs Recommended Kubernetes API activity
Route 53 Recommended DNS queries from VPC resources
Security Hub Recommended Security findings
VPC Flow Logs Recommended IP traffic to/from ENIs
CloudTrail – S3 data events No High volume data → higher cost ▶ #117 01:30
AWS WAF No High volume data

Wizard step 2: define the target objective. Optional rollup Regions (disabled in the demo: “Cannot select rollup Regions without enabling two or more Regions”) and optional storage classes: default S3 Standard, with transitions such as Standard-IA after N days. ▶ #117 03:00 ▶ #117 03:31

Console demo: enable Security Lake org-wide ([▶ #117](https://youtu.be/hZQG0naBmZQ))
  1. Management account → Security Lake → Get started → “Delegate administration to your Log Archive account” → enter the 12-digit account ID (from the access portal) → Delegate. Banner: “<id> is now the delegated administrator of Security Lake”. ▶ #117 00:21
  2. Log Archive account → Security Lake → Get started → Ingest specific AWS sources: demo picks CloudTrail management events, Security Hub, VPC Flow Logs (Lambda and EKS deselected). ▶ #117 01:41
  3. Regions: all supported (recommended) or specific. Demo: US East (N. Virginia) only. ▶ #117 02:01
  4. Accounts: all accounts in the org / specific accounts / this account. Demo: all accounts + automatically enable for new accounts. ▶ #117 02:22
  5. Service access: let the wizard create and use a new service role unless you have one. Add tags in production. ▶ #117 02:42
  6. No rollup Regions, no storage transitions → Review and create. “Turning on Security Lake” takes a minute or two per Region. ▶ #117 03:51
  7. Summary page → orange banner “Register Security Lake managed buckets with Lake Formation for improved permission management” (all Regions) → Register buckets → “Successfully registered buckets”. ▶ #117 04:22
  8. Sources page shows Enabled/Disabled per source: CloudTrail mgmt Enabled, Lambda Disabled, EKS Disabled, Route 53 Disabled, Security Hub Enabled… ▶ #117 04:40

The Summary page has Get started cards: Run queries (Lake Formation databases/tables, third-party subscribers), Integrate partners (source partners sending logs in OCSF; subscriber partners for threat detection, investigation, IR) and Visualize data (OpenSearch, SIEM, QuickSight via Athena). Overview: Regions 1, Rollup Regions 0, Issues (last 14 days) none. Left nav: Summary, Sources, Subscribers, Regions, Custom sources, Issues, Accounts; Settings: General, Rollup Regions, Usage. ▶ #117 04:11

Creating a query-access subscriber

Sources → CloudTrail – Management events → Configure shows Enable/Disable, Version v2.0 (Latest), “Disable all other source versions” and Regions. The banner “Update subscriber settings” reminds you that ingestion doesn’t decide who can consume the data. Grant per source, or repeat for all sources to the same subscriber. ▶ #117 04:52 ▶ #117 05:12

Console demo: create the Security Tooling subscriber ([▶ #117](https://youtu.be/hZQG0naBmZQ))

  3. Data access method: S3 (data access: notified as new objects land, via HTTPS endpoint or SQS polling, reads objects directly) or Lake Formation (query access: queries tables, usually with Athena). Choose Lake Formation. ▶ #117 05:54 ▶ #117 06:11
