Gap in the automated setup: RAM shares were created, but at recording time the setup didn’t grant permissions on the database itself, so queries would fail. Possibly fixed since. Fix it in the Log Archive account. ▶ #117 07:52

Console demo: grant database Describe in Lake Formation ([▶ #117](https://youtu.be/hZQG0naBmZQ))
  1. Log Archive account → AWS Lake Formation → Data permissions (12 permissions already exist) → Grant. ▶ #117 08:20
  2. Principal type: Principals (not “Principals by attributes”).
  3. Principals: External accounts → paste the Security Tooling account ID and press Enter. Clicking doesn’t add it (UI quirk). ▶ #117 08:50
  4. Resources: Named Data Catalog resources (not LF-Tags) → catalog = this account → Database = the Security Lake database. No tables/views needed (already configured). ▶ #117 09:11
  5. Permissions: Describe only → Grant → “Granting catalog permissions to ARNs: <security tooling account>”. ▶ #117 09:21
  6. Security Tooling account → RAM → Shared with me → Resource shares: two shares, one with tables/views (from subscriber creation) and one for the database. ▶ #117 09:50
  7. Normally you must Accept them (select → Accept resource share). Here they were already Active (auto-accepted, unexpected). ▶ #117 10:01

Querying cross-account with Athena: resource links

Even with the database shared via RAM, Athena cannot query databases/tables across accounts by default. You need a resource link: a pointer in your local Data Catalog to a database (or table) owned by another account. Create one per table, or one for the database. ▶ #118 00:31 ▶ #118 00:41 ▶ #118 00:51 ▶ #118 01:01

  1. Producer account: Lake Formation Data Catalog (database/table) with data permissions “Account Consumer | Table A | Select, Describe”.
  2. Resource Access Manager carries a resource share to the consumer account, where the shared catalog object appears (greyed).
  3. The consumer creates a Resource Link pointing to it.
  4. The consumer grants its local datalake-user Select, Describe on Table A and Select, Describe on Resource Link A. Two grants: on the target and on the link.
  5. datalake-user queries through Athena → resource link → shared table → producer data.

Cross-account query access checklist:

  1. Producer grants the consumer account Describe on the database and Select/Describe on tables (add the database Describe grant in Lake Formation → Data permissions if missing).
  2. Consumer accepts the RAM share.
  3. Consumer Lake Formation admin creates a resource link.
  4. Consumer grants its IAM principals Describe on the resource link and Select on the target table.
  5. Athena workgroup with a query result location.

The two shares are LakeFormation-V4-EN2T8B3XCL and LakeFormation-V4-PP8QQOJX7A-5f3a9c2d8b1e4c0. The external ID appended to the name is how the subscriber identifies the right share. ▶ #118 00:00

The Lake Formation console’s resource-link flow was buggy (selecting the shared database required Enter, which acted as Cancel), so the link is created with the Glue CLI, run with the Security Tooling profile: ▶ #118 01:21 ▶ #118 02:10

aws glue create-database --database-input '{
    "Name": "security_lake_link",
    "TargetDatabase": {
      "CatalogId": "<log-archive-account-id>",
      "DatabaseName": "amazon_security_lake_glue_db_us_east_1"
    }
  }' --profile "demo_Security-Tooling…"

Console demo: query Security Lake from Security Tooling ([▶ #118](https://youtu.be/KE5_arRKu2A))
  1. Be in the Security Tooling account and the right Region. RAM → Shared with me → confirm both Lake Formation shares are Active. ▶ #118 00:00
  2. Lake Formation is a separate service from Security Lake. First visit: “Welcome to Lake Formation” → initial administrative users and roles → Add myself → Get started. In production be more selective. Result: Data lake administrators (1/1) = the AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_… role, access Full; catalog creators IAMAllowedPrincipals. ▶ #118 00:10 ▶ #118 00:21
  3. Data Catalog → Databases (2): the shared amazon_security_lake_glue_db_us_east_1 with Catalog ID = Log Archive account (3397…), Lake Formation permissions “All users”, plus the local default. If the shared one isn’t visible yet, just use the Log Archive account ID as the catalog ID. ▶ #118 01:40
  4. Run the aws glue create-database command above → refresh → security_lake_link with shared resource owner = Log Archive. Allow ~30 s to propagate. ▶ #118 02:32 ▶ #118 02:50
  5. Athena: a first visit may offer SageMaker Unified Studio; choose Athena → Get started. ▶ #118 03:01
  6. Data source AwsDataCatalog, database security_lake_link → Tables (1): amazon_security_lake_table_us_east_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0. Only CloudTrail because the subscriber was scoped to that source; more sources would add more tables. ▶ #118 03:21 ▶ #118 03:30
  7. Query settings must have a result location (s3://aws-athena-query-results-<account>-us-east-1/ from the Athena lesson). They also show Execution controls: data scanned limit, min/max DPU per query. ▶ #118 04:00
  8. Run SELECT * FROM "security_lake_link"."amazon_security_lake_table_us_east_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0" LIMIT 10; → Completed in 1.951 s, 14.62 KB scanned, 10 OCSF rows such as {product={version=1.11, name=CloudTrail, vendor_name=AWS, feature={name=Management}}, event_code=AwsApiCall, …}. ▶ #118 04:31 ▶ #118 04:51

The table’s OCSF columns include metadata (product version/name/vendor/feature, event_code, uid, profiles, version), time (bigint), time_dt (timestamp), cloud (region, provider), api (response error/message/data, operation, version, service name, request data/uid), dst_endpoint (svc_name) and actor (user type/name/uid/uid_alt/ account uid/credential_uid, session created_time_dt/is_mfa/issuer, invoked_by, idp name). ▶ #118 03:21

Why it matters: multi-account CloudTrail → Security Lake in Log Archive → shared with Security Tooling → queried with Athena. The security team never needs access to the Log Archive account, and gets continuous access for operational and security troubleshooting and incident response, for CloudTrail, Security Hub, VPC Flow Logs, EKS, Route 53 and more. ▶ #118 05:02 ▶ #118 05:31 ▶ #118 05:41

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • “If you have a question on the exam that’s related to running Security Lake across your Regions, remember that you can do this with rollup Regions.” ▶ #116 05:23
  • Typical themes: centralizing security data across accounts, Regions and sources (incl. on-prem); normalizing to OCSF stored as Parquet in S3; consuming via Athena, OpenSearch or subscribers. ▶ #116 05:31
  • “A service that aggregates, normalizes, and stores security data at scale across an organization” → Security Lake. ▶ #116 06:02
  • Security Lake creates other services for you, which affects IAM permissions and cost. ▶ #116 02:20
  • Delegate admin to the Log Archive account from the management account. ▶ #117 00:10
  • CloudTrail S3 data events and WAF logs are high-volume and raise cost. ▶ #117 01:30
  • Enable for all accounts and auto-enable new accounts to avoid gaps. ▶ #117 02:31
  • Subscriber access is per source: ingestion ≠ consumption permission. ▶ #117 05:00
  • Query access = Lake Formation (Athena); data access = S3 objects + SQS/HTTPS notifications. ▶ #117 06:01
  • Lake Formation subscribers must accept a RAM share; the console may miss the database Describe grant. ▶ #117 07:52
  • RAM sharing alone isn’t enough: Athena needs a resource link for cross-account databases. ▶ #118 00:41
  • The Lake Formation console was buggy; the Glue CLI works. Athena still needs a query result location. ▶ #118 01:30 ▶ #118 04:00

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Centralize and normalize security logs from all accounts + 3rd-party into a standard schema, keep data ownership Security Lake
Normalize logs into a common schema / 3rd-party data in a standard format OCSF
Give a SIEM vendor access to raw files; least overhead to feed a SIEM in another account Data access subscriber (SQS notifications)
Analyst account runs SQL from another account Query access subscriber (Lake Formation) + RAM + Athena resource links
Shared via RAM but Athena can’t see/query the database Create a Lake Formation resource link in the consumer account
Athena error “Insufficient Lake Formation permission(s)” Grant in Lake Formation, not the S3 bucket policy
Run across Regions / consolidate to one Region / data residency Rollup Regions
Storage/normalization of logs vs findings/posture Security Lake vs Security Hub
Investigate relationships between entities Detective
Updates since the videos
  • Security Lake doesn’t always enable the underlying services: it collects CloudTrail events itself (no trail needed) and manages VPC Flow Logs / Route 53 collection, but Security Hub must be enabled to get findings.
  • The missing database-level Describe grant seen in #117 may be fixed in newer consoles. Verify it in Lake Formation → Data permissions anyway.
  • The 15-day free trial and the SageMaker Unified Studio prompt in Athena reflect the console at recording time. Check current pricing.

Real-world practice

  • Cost drivers: per-GB ingestion/normalization (VPC Flow Logs, S3/Lambda data events and WAF can be very large), S3 storage, Athena scans. Start with a narrow set of sources and Regions. Use rollup Regions and lifecycle/expiration to control storage cost.
  • Typical layout: Log Archive = Security Lake delegated admin; Security Tooling = query subscriber (Athena) and/or SIEM subscriber (data access via SQS).
  • Lake Formation permissions are the usual pain point for teams used to IAM/S3 policies. Check database Describe, table Select, RAM share acceptance and resource links in the subscriber account.
  • Automate resource links and grants with CloudFormation (AWS::Glue::Database with TargetDatabase, AWS::LakeFormation::PrincipalPermissions) so every new source/table is queryable without console work.
  • Enforce a data scanned limit in the analysts’ Athena workgroup.
  • If the subscriber is a SIEM rather than humans, prefer the S3 + SQS data access subscriber. Resource links are for SQL/Athena consumers.
  • Lock down the Security Lake S3 buckets and the Lake Formation admin role with SCPs so workload accounts, and even admins, can’t tamper with the lake.
-- Query subscriber: who called DeleteBucket in the last 7 days (OCSF CloudTrail table)
SELECT time_dt, actor.user.uid, api.operation, src_endpoint.ip, cloud.account.uid
FROM amazon_security_lake_glue_db_ap_southeast_1.amazon_security_lake_table_ap_southeast_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0
WHERE api.operation = 'DeleteBucket'
  AND time_dt > current_timestamp - interval '7' day;

-- AccessDenied calls in the last day, through the resource link from #118
SELECT time_dt, actor.user.name, api.operation, src_endpoint.ip
FROM "security_lake_link"."amazon_security_lake_table_us_east_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0"
WHERE api.response.error = 'AccessDenied'
  AND time_dt > current_timestamp - INTERVAL '1' DAY
LIMIT 100;
Hands-on lab
  1. Enable Security Lake in one Region with CloudTrail + VPC Flow Logs.
  2. Run the queries above in Athena (create a resource link if you query from another account).
  3. Cleanup: disable Security Lake, then delete the S3 bucket and Glue database it created (check retention first).

Amazon Athena + AWS Glue

At a glance

Athena is serverless SQL over data where it already lives (mainly S3), priced per data scanned. The Glue Data Catalog stores table definitions (schema + location + format) and Glue crawlers infer schemas. Together they are the standard “query logs in S3” answer: Athena = query engine, Glue Data Catalog = metastore, S3 = storage.

  • Exam skills: analyze logs (1.2.4) · normalize, parse & correlate logs (1.2.5) · search & correlate logs for IR (2.2.2) · log data lakes (1.2.3) · troubleshoot logging permissions (1.3.1) · cross-account resource policies (4.2.1) · IaC (6.2.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #113 About Athena · ▶ #114 Athena with CloudTrail logs · ▶ #115 About AWS Glue (▶ #118 Querying Security Lake with Athena is under Amazon Security Lake)
  • Cost: $5 per TB scanned (at recording time)

What Athena is

  • Serverless, marketed as petabyte scale. ▶ #113 00:00
  • Data can be on-premises, in a data lake, or in cloud storage. Athena queries across many sources through Federated Query connectors. ▶ #113 00:21
  • Integrates with ML frameworks and visualization tools such as QuickSight. ▶ #113 00:40
  • Query language is SQL, like CloudTrail Lake’s. ▶ #113 00:51
  • Three steps: point to your data source → run SQL queries → analyze the results. ▶ #113 01:00

Athena reads from operational databases, data warehouses, big data, ERP, other cloud services and the S3 data lake/data mesh (“on premises or in the cloud”), and returns results to ML tools (forecast revenue, predict churn) and BI apps.

Connectors include Azure Data Lake Storage, Azure Synapse, Cloudera Hive/Impala, CloudWatch, CloudWatch metrics, CMDB, Db2, DocumentDB, DynamoDB, Google BigQuery, Google Cloud Storage, HBase, Hortonworks, Kafka, MSK, MySQL, Neptune, OpenSearch… ▶ #113 00:30

CloudTrail Lake vs Athena

The process is very similar, but pricing differs: Athena is $5 per TB scanned, while CloudTrail Lake can be a lot more expensive if you’re not careful. ▶ #113 01:10 ▶ #113 01:21 ▶ #113 01:30

CloudTrail Lake Athena
Focus CloudTrail data; other sources supported but less mature ▶ #113 01:40 Any source; more mature ▶ #113 01:51
Cross-source queries Limited Yes: e.g. VPC flow logs + CloudTrail, even on-premises data ▶ #113 02:01
Storage Its own event data store; doesn’t read the trail’s S3 data ▶ #113 02:20 No new data store; reads the trail data in S3 ▶ #113 02:31
Cost model Ingestion + retention + query (can be high) $5/TB scanned + S3 storage
Good for Simpler setups, simplicity and focus ▶ #113 02:41 Large orgs with many sources, or when Lake is cost-prohibitive ▶ #113 02:50

Since Nov 26, 2023, CloudTrail Lake data is available for zero-ETL analysis in Athena: enable data federation on the event data store, CloudTrail creates Glue Data Catalog resources and registers the data with Lake Formation, where you choose which users/roles can query it. Queries are charged at Athena pricing, data at CloudTrail Lake pricing. You can correlate Lake activity logs with app/traffic logs in S3 and visualize with QuickSight and Amazon Managed Grafana, so you can use both if budget allows. ▶ #113 02:50

Creating an Athena table for CloudTrail

CloudTrail → Event history has two buttons: Create Athena table and Query in Lake. Create Athena table generates the CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE DDL for a trail bucket. The table definition lands in the Glue Data Catalog (database default, classification cloudtrail). ▶ #114 00:10 The VPC Flow Logs console also offers an Athena integration (CloudFormation).

  • Storage location: the S3 bucket with CloudTrail logs. The demo picks the organization trail bucket org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs that all accounts feed into. ▶ #114 00:32
  • Selecting the bucket regenerates the SQL for an external table, named cloudtrail_logs_orgcybrdemocloudtraillogs (can be renamed in Athena). ▶ #114 01:01
  • The DDL maps CloudTrail fields into columns: eventVersion, userIdentity STRUCT<type, principalId, arn, accountId, invokedBy, accessKeyId, userName, sessionContext STRUCT<attributes STRUCT<mfaAuthenticated, creationDate>, sessionIssuer STRUCT<…>>>, plus eventSource, eventName, awsRegion, sourceIpAddress, etc. ▶ #114 01:20 ▶ #114 01:31
  • At the bottom: a COMMENT, ROW FORMAT (CloudTrail SerDe), Hadoop OUTPUT FORMAT and LOCATION = the bucket path. Not exam-relevant detail. ▶ #114 01:42
  • Create table → “Successfully created Athena table … open the Amazon Athena console. Athena charges for running queries.” ▶ #114 02:11
Shape of the generated DDL (abridged) 
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE cloudtrail_logs_orgcybrdemocloudtraillogs (
    eventVersion STRING,
    userIdentity STRUCT<
        type: STRING,
        principalId: STRING,
        arn: STRING,
        accountId: STRING,
        invokedBy: STRING,
        accessKeyId: STRING,
        userName: STRING,
        sessionContext: STRUCT<
            attributes: STRUCT<mfaAuthenticated: STRING, creationDate: STRING>,
            sessionIssuer: STRUCT<type: STRING, principalId: STRING, arn: STRING, accountId: STRING, userName: STRING>,
            ec2RoleDelivery: STRING,
            webIdFederationData: STRUCT<federatedProvider: STRING, attributes: MAP<STRING,STRING>>>>,
    eventTime STRING,
    eventSource STRING,
    eventName STRING,
    awsRegion STRING,
    sourceIpAddress STRING,
    userAgent STRING,
    errorCode STRING,
    errorMessage STRING,
    requestParameters STRING,
    responseElements STRING,
    …
)
COMMENT 'CloudTrail table for <bucket> bucket'
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.apache.hive.hcatalog.data.JsonSerDe'   -- older versions: com.amazon.emr.hive.serde.CloudTrailSerde
STORED AS INPUTFORMAT 'com.amazon.emr.cloudtrail.CloudTrailInputFormat'
OUTPUTFORMAT 'org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.io.HiveIgnoreKeyTextOutputFormat'
LOCATION 's3://<bucket>/AWSLogs/<account-id>/CloudTrail/'
TBLPROPERTIES ('classification'='cloudtrail');

Query result location and the query editor

Before the first query Athena needs an S3 query result location: it reads from S3 and stores query results in S3. ▶ #114 02:31 ▶ #114 02:41

Edit settings → Manage settings → Query result location and encryption: ▶ #114 02:52

Setting Value / meaning
Location of query result aws-athena-query-results-<account-id>-us-east-1, auto-created by Athena when the table was created ▶ #114 03:00
Expected bucket owner Optional ▶ #114 03:20
Assign bucket owner full control For result buckets owned by another account
Encrypt query results Optional: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS or CSE-KMS (client-side with KMS) ▶ #114 03:30

The editor has tabs Editor, Recent queries, Saved queries, Settings, and workgroup primary. The data panel shows data source AwsDataCatalog, database default, and the CloudTrail table. The table menu offers Preview table, Generate table DDL (data definition language), insert into editor, delete table and view properties. ▶ #114 04:00 ▶ #114 04:12 Preview table generates: ▶ #114 04:32

SELECT * FROM "default"."cloudtrail_logs_orgcybrdemocloudtraillogs" limit 10;

Recent queries keeps the history (including failed runs); Saved queries holds queries you rerun often. ▶ #114 07:10 ▶ #114 07:30

Troubleshooting cross-account queries

Problem 1: AccessDenied on s3:ListBucket. The query runs in the Security Tooling account but the bucket is in the Log Archive account: ▶ #114 04:40 ▶ #114 04:50

com.amazonaws.services.s3.model.AmazonS3Exception: User: arn:aws:sts::<security-tooling-acct>:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_…/christophe
is not authorized to perform: s3:ListBucket on resource: "arn:aws:s3:::org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs"
because no resource-based policy allows the s3:ListBucket action (Service: Amazon S3; Status Code: 403; Error Code: AccessDenied …)

Cross-account → the bucket policy must grant access (here s3:ListBucket). The fix was applied off-camera. ▶ #114 05:02 Athena uses the caller’s credentials, so the bucket policy must allow that principal/account (s3:ListBucket on the bucket, s3:GetObject on objects), and with SSE-KMS the key policy must allow kms:Decrypt for that role.

Problem 2: the table covers only one account. The org trail layout is org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs/AWSLogs/o-jqbqypd27k/<account-id>/…, one folder per member account (10 accounts). The generated table pointed at a single account’s path. ▶ #114 05:31 ▶ #114 05:40

Point it at the org prefix: ▶ #114 06:00

ALTER TABLE cloudtrail_logs_orgcybrdemocloudtraillogs
  SET LOCATION 's3://org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs/AWSLogs/o-jqbqypd27k/'

Re-running the preview: Completed, queue 110 ms, run time 15.685 s, 51.12 KB scanned, 10 results. ▶ #114 06:20 Columns include eventversion, useridentity, eventtime, eventsource, eventname, awsregion, sourceipaddress. Sample rows: sts.amazonaws.com AssumeRole, kinesis.amazonaws.com ListStreams, s3.amazonaws.com GetBucketAcl, ec2.amazonaws.com DescribeNetworkInsightsAccessScopes, mostly from config.amazonaws.com / securityhub.amazonaws.com. ▶ #114 06:31

Select only the columns you need instead of *: ▶ #114 06:50

SELECT eventtime, eventsource, eventname, awsregion
FROM "default"."cloudtrail_logs_orgcybrdemocloudtraillogs"
LIMIT 10;
Console demo: Athena over the org CloudTrail bucket ([▶ #114](https://youtu.be/IReDwvrjHXw))
  1. CloudTrail (Security Tooling account) → Event history → Create Athena table → bucket org.cybrdemo.cloudtrail.logs → Create table.
  2. Open Athena → Edit settings → result location aws-athena-query-results-… → Save.
  3. Editor → table menu → Preview table → AccessDenied (s3:ListBucket, cross-account).
  4. Update the Log Archive bucket policy to allow the Security Tooling principal.
  5. ALTER TABLE … SET LOCATION 's3://…/AWSLogs/<org-id>/'.
  6. Re-run the preview → 10 results.
  7. Review Recent queries / Saved queries.
Athena AccessDenied or empty results? Check these
  • IAM on the caller: athena:* query actions and glue:GetTable / GetDatabase / GetPartitions (or Lake Formation grants).
  • S3 ListBucket / GetObject on the log bucket. Cross-account → bucket policy.
  • KMS Decrypt on the trail’s key. Cross-account → key policy.
  • S3 PutObject on the query results bucket.
  • “Table not found” or zero rows → the Glue table’s location/partitions (an org trail table may cover one account only).

AWS Glue: the catalog behind Athena

Glue is a serverless data integration service that gives three things: ▶ #115 00:21 ▶ #115 00:36

  1. Discover and organize data (Data Catalog, crawlers).
  2. Transform, prepare and clean data for analysis (ETL jobs: Visual ETL, notebooks).
  3. Build and monitor data pipelines (workflows/orchestration, job run monitoring).

Security use case: take data from many sources, infer a schema, then query it with Athena. ▶ #115 00:55 The console landing page has tiles Prepare your account for AWS Glue (default IAM role), Catalog and search for datasets (Data Catalog, Crawlers) and Move and transform data (Zero-ETL integrations, ETL jobs). Left nav: ETL jobs, Data Catalog tables, Data connections, Workflows, Zero-ETL integrations, Data Catalog → Databases / Tables / Stream schema registries / Connections / Crawlers / Classifiers / Catalog settings. ▶ #115 00:04

The CloudTrail “Create Athena table” button silently used Glue: the table definition lives in Glue → Data Catalog → Tables (database default, location s3://org.cybrdemo..., classification cloudtrail). ▶ #115 01:20 “Glue told Athena where the logs were, how they were formatted, and what fields existed.” ▶ #115 01:30

  • The table page shows Schema (24 columns), Partitions, Indexes, Column statistics and Data quality. Actions → edit the table, Edit schema or Edit schema as JSON. ▶ #115 01:48
  • View data warns “You will be taken to Athena to preview data, and you will be charged separately for Athena queries.” ▶ #115 02:01
  • Glue jobs transform/normalize logs (ETL). Crawlers keep the catalog in sync and add partitions for new prefixes.
  • The Data Catalog can be encrypted (metadata encryption with KMS), and connection passwords too. Lake Formation adds fine-grained (column/row) permissions.

When you touch Glue directly (console one-click setups usually hide it): ▶ #115 02:05

Situation Why
Infrastructure as code You must define the Glue database and tables in templates for Athena to work ▶ #115 02:21
Multiple data sources Managing how they are cataloged ▶ #115 02:35
Manual schema management Something broke or the schema must change after the fact ▶ #115 02:45
Console demo: find the CloudTrail table in Glue ([▶ #115](https://youtu.be/koQo_VfoXvY))
  1. Recap: CloudTrail → Event history → Create Athena table → pick the log bucket → Create table. ▶ #115 01:11
  2. AWS Glue → Data Catalog tables → the CloudTrail table is under database default. ▶ #115 01:23
  3. Click the table → details/schema; Actions offers edit table / edit schema. ▶ #115 01:48
  4. View data → dialog → Proceed opens Athena (charged per query). ▶ #115 02:01

Performance, cost and security

  • Partition projection: Athena computes partitions (Region / year / month / day) from table properties. No MSCK REPAIR TABLE or crawler runs, and queries are faster and cheaper on huge log buckets.
  • Cost/perf: filter on partition columns, select only needed columns, use columnar formats (Parquet/ORC with compression; Security Lake already uses Parquet), and set workgroup data-scanned limits.
  • Workgroups enforce the query result location, result encryption (SSE-KMS) and per-query data-scanned limits.
  • The caller needs S3 read on the log bucket, kms:Decrypt on the log key, and Glue catalog permissions (or Lake Formation grants).
  • Common security queries: errorcode IN ('AccessDenied','UnauthorizedOperation'), useridentity.type = 'Root', eventname = 'ConsoleLogin' AND responseelements LIKE '%Failure%', eventname IN ('StopLogging','DeleteTrail','PutBucketPolicy','DisableKey'), activity of one useridentity.accesskeyid.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Athena costs $5 per TB scanned; CloudTrail Lake can be much more expensive. ▶ #113 01:21
  • Lake = CloudTrail-focused, own data store, simpler. Athena = any source, reads trail data in S3 in place, more mature. ▶ #113 01:40
  • Simple setup → Lake; many sources or cost-sensitive → Athena; both possible since late 2023. ▶ #113 02:41
  • Use Create Athena table in CloudTrail Event history to get the DDL automatically. ▶ #114 00:10
  • The DDL internals (SerDe, Hadoop formats) are not exam-relevant. ▶ #114 01:42
  • Athena needs an S3 query results location; results can be encrypted with SSE-S3/SSE-KMS/CSE-KMS. ▶ #114 02:41
  • Cross-account queries need the bucket policy to grant access. ▶ #114 05:02
  • For an org trail, point the table at AWSLogs/<org-id>/ to include all accounts. ▶ #114 06:00
  • “This exam is not very heavy on data analysis at all”, beyond troubleshooting and IR investigations: keep Glue high-level. Glue is “the behind-the-scenes service” for Athena over S3 logs. ▶ #115 02:55 ▶ #115 03:00

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Ad-hoc SQL over months of CloudTrail/ALB/Flow logs in S3, cheapest, serverless Athena
Queries scan too much / new days missing from the table Partition projection
Athena Access Denied on encrypted CloudTrail logs Missing kms:Decrypt on the trail’s KMS key
Athena in Security Tooling gets AccessDenied s3:ListBucket on the Log Archive bucket Cross-account bucket policy grant
Athena returns “table not found” or zero rows Check the Glue table location/partitions (org trail location covers one account)
Infer a schema automatically / add partitions for new prefixes Glue crawler (prefer partition projection for CloudTrail/ALB/Flow Logs)
Near-real-time dashboards / full-text search OpenSearch
SQL over large historical logs Athena
Normalized OCSF security data lake Security Lake (queried via Athena/Lake Formation)

Real-world practice

  • Pattern: Log Archive owns the bucket; Security Tooling runs Athena with read-only cross-account access (bucket policy scoped with aws:PrincipalArn / aws:PrincipalOrgID), and the KMS key policy grants decrypt to the same principals. Never grant write/delete.
  • Keep a security “hunting” workgroup with enforced result encryption, a bytes-scanned limit, and saved queries for CloudTrail (AccessDenied spikes, root activity, ConsoleLogin failures), VPC flow logs (REJECTs, egress to rare IPs) and S3 access logs.
  • Without partitions, one query over years of org-wide CloudTrail can scan many TB. Partition projection is the usual fix. For heavy use, convert CloudTrail JSON to Parquet (Glue job / CTAS) or use Security Lake (OCSF Parquet).
  • Define the Glue database/table (with partition projection) in CloudFormation/Terraform (AWS::Glue::Database, AWS::Glue::Table), not via the console button.
  • Schema drift: CloudTrail adds fields over time (e.g. tlsDetails). Update the Glue schema or use the AWS-published DDL.
  • For an organization trail, the generated table covers one account: ALTER TABLE … SET LOCATION to AWSLogs/<org-id>/.
CloudTrail table with partition projection + hunting queries 
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE cloudtrail_logs (
  eventversion STRING,
  useridentity STRUCT<type:STRING, principalid:STRING, arn:STRING, accountid:STRING, accesskeyid:STRING>,
  eventtime STRING, eventsource STRING, eventname STRING, awsregion STRING,
  sourceipaddress STRING, useragent STRING, errorcode STRING, errormessage STRING,
  requestparameters STRING, responseelements STRING
)
PARTITIONED BY (region STRING, dt STRING)
ROW FORMAT SERDE 'org.apache.hive.hcatalog.data.JsonSerDe'
STORED AS INPUTFORMAT 'com.amazon.emr.cloudtrail.CloudTrailInputFormat'
OUTPUTFORMAT 'org.apache.hadoop.hive.ql.io.HiveIgnoreKeyTextOutputFormat'
LOCATION 's3://org-ct-logs/AWSLogs/o-xxxx/111122223333/CloudTrail/'
TBLPROPERTIES (
  'projection.enabled'='true',
  'projection.region.type'='enum',
  'projection.region.values'='us-east-1,ap-southeast-1',
  'projection.dt.type'='date',
  'projection.dt.format'='yyyy/MM/dd',
  'projection.dt.range'='2025/01/01,NOW',
  'projection.dt.interval'='1', 'projection.dt.interval.unit'='DAYS',
  'storage.location.template'='s3://org-ct-logs/AWSLogs/o-xxxx/111122223333/CloudTrail/${region}/${dt}'
);

-- Console logins without MFA
SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, sourceipaddress
FROM cloudtrail_logs
WHERE eventname = 'ConsoleLogin'
  AND json_extract_scalar(additionaleventdata, '$.MFAUsed') = 'No'   -- add additionaleventdata STRING column
  AND dt >= '2026/11/01';

-- VPC Flow Logs (S3, default format): top talkers to port 22
SELECT srcaddr, count(*) AS flows FROM vpc_flow_logs
WHERE dstport = 22 AND action = 'ACCEPT' AND day >= '2026/11/10'
GROUP BY srcaddr ORDER BY flows DESC LIMIT 20;
Hands-on lab
  1. Create the projected CloudTrail table above, then run the queries.
  2. Cleanup: drop the table, the workgroup and the results bucket.

Amazon OpenSearch Service

At a glance

Managed OpenSearch (open-source, Apache-2.0, GitHub opensearch-project) for fast, near-real-time search, correlation and dashboards over large volumes of logs: a SIEM-like use case. AWS runs the clusters so you focus on indexing and querying. Includes a Security Analytics plugin with detection rules.

  • Exam skills: analyze logs (1.2.4) · normalize, parse & correlate logs (1.2.5) · metrics, alerts & dashboards for anomalies (1.1.4) · search & correlate logs for IR (2.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #119 Amazon OpenSearch
  • Uses: log analytics, security analytics, application search, near-real-time dashboards over constantly changing data

What it is and how it works

  • A search and analytics engine for fast querying over large volumes of data. ▶ #119 00:00
  • OpenSearch is open-source; Amazon OpenSearch Service is AWS-managed and paid. ▶ #119 00:12
  • Common uses: log analytics, security analytics, application search, near-real-time dashboards, especially search/filter over constantly changing data like security data. ▶ #119 00:20

  1. Input: documents/lists, messages, metrics, log files, config info (“capture, process, and load data”). Sources include Security Lake, CloudWatch, nginx, Apache and many more. ▶ #119 00:41
  2. OpenSearch Service: search, visualize and analyze up to petabytes of text and unstructured data, giving it “just enough structure”. ▶ #119 01:12
  3. Output: application monitoring, feeding SIEMs, in-app search, infrastructure monitoring. OpenSearch does much of the heavy lifting. ▶ #119 01:20 ▶ #119 01:40

Deployment options

The console Get started offers the Observability use case (creates an optimized workspace in OpenSearch UI), Create an OpenSearch UI without a use case, and three Quick create tiles. Pricing differs by option. ▶ #119 01:51 ▶ #119 02:10

Managed cluster (“domain”) Serverless collection
Tagline “Deploy a fully-managed, secure OpenSearch cluster in minutes” “Eliminate infrastructure management with on-demand Serverless collections” ▶ #119 02:01
You manage Version, VPC, IAM roles, node types/sizes (price, availability) and storage ▶ #119 03:00 No node sizes ▶ #119 03:40
Network VPC access (recommended) / dual stack Public or private, but you don’t pick the VPC ▶ #119 04:11
Security Domain access policy, fine-grained access control, KMS, node-to-node encryption, HTTPS Encryption, network and data access policies

Ingestion pipelines (“Ingest, transform, and route data to domains or Serverless collections at scale”) feed both, e.g. create a serverless collection, then a pipeline into it. ▶ #119 02:10 ▶ #119 02:22

Managed cluster = “domain”

AWS uses domain to mean a managed cluster deployment. Create domain configures node types and storage. Creation method: Easy create (Multi-AZ with standby, change later) or Standard create (all options). ▶ #119 02:30 ▶ #119 02:50

Easy create setting Value
Engine OpenSearch 3.3 (latest)
Availability 3-AZ with standby
Data nodes r8g.large.search ×3 (Active 2, Standby 1)
Storage EBS gp3 300 GiB
Dedicated master m7g.large.search ×3
Network VPC access (recommended) / dual stack
Access Fine-grained access control
Encryption “HTTPS for all traffic to the domain”

AWS manages the complexity, but you still control node sizes and placement. ▶ #119 03:21

Serverless collection

Collection type Use
Time series Large volumes of semi-structured machine-generated data/events in near real time → typical for security logs ▶ #119 03:50
Search Full-text search powering applications
Vector search Embeddings, semantic/similarity search
  • Deployment type: Enable redundancy (active replicas) is the default for production; disable it to cut cost at the expense of availability. ▶ #119 04:01
  • Encryption with an AWS owned key or a customer managed key. ▶ #119 04:01
  • Serverless = higher-level configuration, less management. ▶ #119 04:20
  • Console Serverless → Security: Authentication, Data access policies, Encryption policies, Network policies; plus Data lifecycle policies and VPC endpoints.

Domain security

  • VPC access (no public endpoint).
  • Fine-grained access control: index-, document- and field-level roles.
  • Resource-based domain access policy.
  • Dashboards authentication via Cognito or SAML / IAM Identity Center.
  • Encryption at rest (KMS), node-to-node encryption, HTTPS required (TLS policy).

Getting data in: ingestion options

Path Notes
CloudWatch Logs subscription filter To OpenSearch directly, or via Lambda/Firehose
Firehose → OpenSearch Managed delivery, optional S3 backup
OpenSearch Ingestion pipelines Data Prepper based, from S3/SQS, Kinesis, Kafka, HTTP/OTel
Direct query (zero-ETL) Query Security Lake / S3 / CloudWatch data in place instead of ingesting it

Ingestion pipelines copy data into indexes for faster search; direct query avoids the copy.

Creating a pipeline: drawer → Ingestion → Pipelines → Create pipeline → Visual pipeline (guided wizard) or Configuration editor (code). ▶ #119 08:00 ▶ #119 08:10 There are 47 blueprints, grouped by use case (contextual search, custom processing, DLQ replay, GeoIP, log analytics, migration, observability, security analytics, streaming, zero-ETL) and by service. ▶ #119 08:21

Blueprint examples: ALB access logs, Apache logs, CloudTrail logs (enriches CloudTrail logs pulled from an SQS queue), Lambda custom enrichment, ELB access logs, GeoIP enrichment for VPC Flow Logs / WAF access logs, log aggregation with conditional routing, logs to metrics, Kinesis Data Streams, MSK/Kafka, RDS/Aurora CDC, OpenTelemetry logs/metrics/traces, S3 logs (SQS notifications), S3 scan, Security Lake S3 Parquet OCSF, Transit Gateway Flow Logs, VPC Flow Logs, WAF logs. ▶ #119 08:40 Then query, visualize and build alerts. ▶ #119 08:52

Dashboards, UI and analytics plugins

OpenSearch Dashboards OpenSearch UI
Deployment Bundled with each domain or serverless collection ▶ #119 04:33 Separate, cloud-hosted, created independently ▶ #119 04:51
Scope That single deployment Multiple data sources: several domains, serverless collections, CloudWatch, Security Lake, S3 ▶ #119 05:00
  • Security analysts use them for incident response, threat hunting and general security/ops queries. ▶ #119 05:10
  • Query languages: DQL, Lucene, PPL, SQL.
  • Security Analytics plugin = Sigma-rule detections and correlation. Alerting plugin sends notifications (SNS, Slack, webhooks) on query monitors.

AWS reference flow: CloudTrail logs, VPC flow logs, DNS logs → Security Lake → S3 → OpenSearch Service → OpenSearch Dashboards ← queries and investigations by security analysts.

Connecting Security Lake (zero-ETL)

Prerequisites: ▶ #119 05:41

  1. Enable Security Lake in the same Regions as the OpenSearch resource.
  2. Set up permissions (accept the service-linked role).
  3. Set up query access: if OpenSearch runs in a different account from the Security Lake delegated admin, you need a Security Lake query subscriber for that account (see Amazon Security Lake, #117).

Overview: Start exploring logs (Discover → Explore logs), Create dashboard, and prebuilt templates: VPC flow logs (flows over time, top talkers, MB/packets; VPC v2), WAF logs (total requests, by terminating action, top countries), CloudTrail logs (events over time, by account ID, event APIs). Connection details: type Amazon Securitylake, IAM role DSRoleOS-…; OpenSearch resource: a collection (AWS owned key). ▶ #119 06:22
  5. Explore logs → the URL switches to application-opensearchui-…: this is OpenSearch UI. Discover: select data, query with DQL/Lucene/PPL/SQL. Menu: Overview, Discover, Dashboards, Visualizations; Manage workspace: details, collaborators, data sources, index patterns, assets, sample data. ▶ #119 06:40 ▶ #119 07:00
