At a glance

Managed API front door (REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, plus private REST APIs reachable only from a VPC) with its own authentication, authorization, throttling and logging. Preferred over exposing Lambda directly: a public function URL has no rate limiting and an exposed endpoint. ▶ #142 00:00

  • Exam skills: edge strategy (3.1.1) · edge protection (3.1.2) · edge rules: rate limiting (3.1.3) · authentication strategies (4.1) · authorization controls, resource policies (4.2.1) · configure/troubleshoot logging (1.2.2, 1.3.1) · encryption in transit & private access (5.1.1, 5.1.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #142 API Gateway security
  • Default account throttle: burst 5,000 / rate 10,000 rps, shared by all APIs in the Region

Why not call Lambda directly

  • Direct invocation (console, CLI, or a public Function URL like https://abc123.lambda-url.us-east-1.on.aws/) is fine for testing and internal automation, but makes it hard to add security layers: no rate limiting, exposed function URL. ▶ #142 00:00
  • API Gateway gives clients a stable, well-defined API without knowing the backend, and much more security control. ▶ #142 00:12 The course diagram’s “Via API Gateway” toggle inserts API Gateway between client and Lambda.

API types

Type Backends Notes
HTTP API Lambda, HTTP OIDC, OAuth 2.0, native CORS; simple and standard
WebSocket API Lambda, HTTP, AWS services Real-time apps: chat, live dashboards
REST API Lambda, HTTP, AWS services Full-featured REST
REST API Private Lambda, HTTP, AWS services Only accessible from within a VPC

▶ #142 01:12 The demo uses an HTTP API.

  • Routes are “an HTTP method and a resource path” (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, HEAD, OPTIONS, DELETE, or ANY). You can route different methods/paths to different functions, giving a single responsibility per Lambda. ▶ #142 02:21
  • Stages (optional): dev/test/prod. The demo uses $default with auto-deploy.
  • Private API: only reachable through an interface VPC endpoint (execute-api). Combine it with a resource policy that limits the VPC endpoint.
Console demo: build an HTTP API in front of Lambda ([▶ #142](https://youtu.be/2Kk5wYRn1Vw))
  1. API Gateway → Create API → HTTP API → Build. Name cybr-example-api, IP address type IPv4. ▶ #142 02:21
  2. Integration: Lambda (others like HTTP; some types are greyed out and only configurable after creation). Pick the pre-deployed hello-world Lambda, payload version 2.0 (recommended for new functions).
  3. Add route GET /hello → Lambda target. Stages: $default with auto-deploy. Review and create.
  4. Result: API ID rrrg24lgri, protocol HTTP, default endpoint https://rrrg24lgri.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.
  5. Authorization: inspect the IAM (built-in), JWT and Lambda authorizer options; leave the route unauthenticated. ▶ #142 04:31
  6. Review CORS, route metrics and throttling defaults. ▶ #142 06:01
  7. Call https://rrrg24lgri.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/hello → {"message": "Hello, World!"}. Without logging there’s no visibility into who requested what. ▶ #142 08:42
  8. Create log group cybr-example-api, enable access logging with the JSON template (minus source IP), call the API, view the log stream. ▶ #142 09:22

Authentication and authorization

Develop → Authorization → Attach authorizers to routes / Manage authorizers. ▶ #142 04:31

Authorizer Use for Details
IAM (SigV4) Internal automation / service-to-service Built in with every account. AWS principals; cross-account through a resource policy ▶ #142 04:51
Cognito user pool (REST) / JWT (HTTP) Public consumers (web, mobile apps) JWT authorizer accepts any OIDC issuer. Settings: Name, Identity source $request.header.Authorization, Issuer URL (from the IdP’s well-known metadata), Audience (client IDs / aud claim) ▶ #142 05:12
Lambda authorizer Custom access control that needs compute Token or request based, returns an IAM policy; result can be cached (TTL) ▶ #142 05:42
  • IAM is chosen separately as the built-in authorizer; the create dialog offers JWT vs Lambda.
  • The demo leaves the public /hello route without authorization. A real public API would use JWT.
  • API keys are not authentication. They are for usage plans.
  • Resource policies (REST only): allow or deny by source IP, VPC (aws:SourceVpc), VPC endpoint (aws:SourceVpce) or account, e.g. restrict to a corporate CIDR. They are required for private APIs.
  • mTLS on custom domain names, with a trust store in S3 (B2B client-certificate auth). Disable the default execute-api endpoint so clients can’t bypass the custom domain/mTLS (or CloudFront/WAF).
  • CORS is configurable natively on HTTP APIs: which other origins browsers may load resources from, same concept as with S3 and CloudFront. ▶ #142 06:01
Resource policy: allow invoke only through one VPC endpoint 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "execute-api:Invoke", "Resource": "execute-api:/*" },
    { "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "execute-api:Invoke", "Resource": "execute-api:/*",
      "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:SourceVpce": "vpce-0a1b2c3d4e5f" } } }
  ]
}

Throttling and usage plans

“One of the best ways of reducing your costs and preventing abuse”: bots, threat actors driving up costs, or accidental runaway clients. ▶ #142 07:21

Level Scope
Account throttling “Applies to the account and is shared by all APIs in this Region”: Burst 5000, Rate 10000
Default route throttling Each route in the stage. Not configured by default
Selected route throttling Overrides the default for one route
Route settings on stage Custom per route via CLI/SDK
Usage plans + API keys (REST) Per client
  • Set default route limits lower than the account limit when you run several APIs. Limit increases can be requested but raise cost/abuse risk. ▶ #142 08:21
  • Throttled requests get 429 Too Many Requests. 403 = auth / WAF / resource-policy denial.

Logging and monitoring

  • Metrics (Monitor → Metrics): select stage; route settings on stage, selected route metrics, default route metrics. Detailed route metrics incur CloudWatch fees. ▶ #142 06:32
  • Access logs: “Access logs are written for every API request. The format can be customized before it gets written to CloudWatch Logs.” Extra cost, but you want visibility into who is accessing what. ▶ #142 07:00 Without it you can’t tell who’s making requests. ▶ #142 09:00
  • Execution logs (REST) can contain full request/response bodies (sensitive data). Use access logs for audit and mask data.
  • REST APIs need an account-level IAM role for CloudWatch (the apigateway service role ARN in settings). X-Ray tracing is optional.

Enabling access logging: ▶ #142 09:22

  1. Logging → Edit → toggle Access logging.
  2. Create CloudWatch log group cybr-example-api (retention 1 day for the demo, log class Standard). The instructor notes he “should have followed standard naming” (a prefix like /aws/apigateway/…); it works anyway.
  3. Paste the log group ARN as Log destination (remove the trailing :*).
  4. Log format templates: CLF, JSON, XML, CSV, using $context variables. He chose JSON and removed $context.identity.sourceIp to hide his IP.
  5. Call the API a few times. Within about a minute a log stream appears with requestId, requestTime, httpMethod, routeKey, status, protocol, responseLength.

Logs can then be shipped to a SIEM or other tools for security visibility.

JSON access-log template (approximately as the console provides it):

{ "requestId":"$context.requestId", "ip": "$context.identity.sourceIp",
  "requestTime":"$context.requestTime", "httpMethod":"$context.httpMethod",
  "routeKey":"$context.routeKey", "status":"$context.status",
  "protocol":"$context.protocol", "responseLength":"$context.responseLength" }

Private backends: VPC links

Problem: an API in front of private resources (ALB, ECS containers) inside a VPC. How do you route traffic there? ▶ #142 12:10

  1. Client → HTTPS → API Gateway (HTTP API).
  2. API Gateway → VPC link → the private VPC.
  3. VPC link → ALB or ECS tasks (Fargate or EC2 launch types). Backends stay private. ▶ #142 12:41
  • “Old way”: a REST API using a VPC endpoint / NLB to bridge. With HTTP APIs the VPC link needs no VPC endpoint or NLB. “Be aware that they exist.”
  • Alternatively, API Gateway can present a client certificate to the backend.

Edge security: CloudFront + WAF

  • Put CloudFront in front of API Gateway: global edge locations, DDoS protection (Shield Standard, or Advanced if upgraded), HTTPS/TLS offloading, caching, geo-restriction. ▶ #142 13:21
  • Add AWS WAF for more advanced protections than API Gateway alone, e.g. rate-based rules beyond normal throttling.
  • WAF attaches to REST API stages only, not HTTP or WebSocket APIs. For an HTTP API, put CloudFront + WAF in front.
  • Layering: client → CloudFront/WAF → API Gateway controls (authorizers, throttling) → Lambda. By the time traffic reaches Lambda it has been filtered end to end.
  • To prevent bypassing CloudFront: disable the default endpoint, use a custom-header secret checked by WAF/authorizer, or a private origin.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Avoid exposing Lambda directly; API Gateway adds security control. ▶ #142 00:12
  • IAM authorizer → internal/service-to-service; JWT → public web/mobile clients; Lambda authorizer → custom logic needing compute. ▶ #142 04:51
  • Enable access logging for visibility. ▶ #142 07:00
  • Throttling reduces cost and abuse; default account limits burst 5,000 / rate 10,000 shared by all APIs; set route defaults lower. ▶ #142 07:21
  • VPC links reach a private ALB/ECS without a VPC endpoint or NLB. ▶ #142 12:41
  • CloudFront + WAF in front of API Gateway adds edge DDoS protection, TLS offload, caching, geo-restriction and WAF rate-based rules. ▶ #142 13:21

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
API reachable only from inside the VPC Private REST API + VPC endpoint + resource policy
Validate JWT from a third-party IdP cheaply HTTP API JWT authorizer
Custom logic or non-JWT tokens Lambda authorizer
Service-to-service / internal automation calls IAM authorizer (SigV4)
API keys used for security Wrong. Use IAM/Cognito/Lambda authorizers; API keys are for usage plans
No logs in CloudWatch for a REST API Set the CloudWatch role ARN in API Gateway account settings and enable stage logging
SQLi protection on the API AWS WAF on the REST API stage; on an HTTP API → CloudFront + WAF in front
Public Lambda function URL abused, no rate limiting Put API Gateway (throttling, authorizers) in front
Expose private ALB / ECS tasks through an API without making them public VPC link
Clients bypass the mTLS custom domain Disable the default execute-api endpoint
Sensitive data showing up in API logs Access logs (selected $context fields) rather than full execution logging
429 errors Throttled (account/stage/route/usage-plan limit)
Updates since the videos
  • VPC link history: REST API VPC links (v1) required an NLB; HTTP API VPC links (v2) target ALB, NLB or Cloud Map (so ECS on Fargate/EC2 via ALB or Cloud Map). AWS has since added VPC link v2 support for REST APIs too. Don’t confuse this with a private REST API, which is reached from a VPC via an execute-api interface endpoint.

Real-world practice

  • Front-door pattern: Route 53 → CloudFront (WAF, Shield Advanced) → API Gateway (authorizer, throttling) → Lambda with a least-privilege execution role.
  • Ship access logs to a central logging account via subscription filter → Firehose → S3/OpenSearch/Security Lake. Name log groups with a standard prefix (e.g. /aws/apigateway/…).
  • Use per-stage throttling and per-client usage plans to contain noisy tenants. Alarm on 4XX/5XX and Count metrics.
  • Lambda authorizer result caching (TTL) trades latency against revocation speed.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create a REST API with a Cognito authorizer. Test with and without a token.
  2. Enable access logs (JSON format).
  3. Optionally build the ▶ #142 HTTP API (GET /hello → Lambda) with access logging and a lowered default route throttle.
  4. Cleanup: delete the APIs, the user pool and the log groups.

Part 4 – Data Protection

Encryption decision table (keyword → answer)

At a glance

A one-page map from the wording of an exam question to the encryption or data-protection service it points at. Domain 5 (18%) is the core of data protection. Some services also appear in D1 (monitoring keys), D2 (backups and recovery) and D3 (TLS at the edge).

  • Exam skills: encryption at rest (5.2.1) · key management & custom key stores (5.3.2) · secrets & rotation (5.3.1) · encryption in transit (5.1.1) · backup protection (5.2.4)
  • Videos: none in the course (see the service pages that follow)

Where the key lives and who controls it

If the question says… Answer
“Least operational overhead”, no key-control requirement SSE-S3 / AWS-owned or AWS managed key
“Audit who used the key”, “control key policy”, “cross-account”, “disable key on demand” KMS customer managed key
“Single-tenant HSM”, “FIPS 140-3 Level 3 under customer control”, “AWS must not have access”, PKCS#11 / JCE / Oracle TDE / SSL offload CloudHSM (direct)
KMS integration with S3/EBS and key material inside your own HSM cluster; “customer-managed HSM”, “dedicated cryptographic hardware on AWS” KMS CloudHSM custom key store
“Keys must stay outside AWS”, “hold your own key (HYOK)”, regulator demands on-prem key manager, “revoke AWS access from outside” KMS external key store (XKS). If the question says on-prem, think XKS, not CloudHSM
“Generate key material ourselves”, “must be able to delete key material immediately”, “set an expiry” KMS key with imported key material (BYOK)
“Same key usable in several Regions”, DR, global tables, client-side encrypt in one Region and decrypt in another KMS multi-Region keys
“Rotate keys without changing application code” (manual rotation) Re-point a KMS alias to the new key

S3 and client-side options

If the question says… Answer
“Two independent layers of encryption” on S3 DSSE-KMS
“Customer supplies the key on every request, AWS must not store it” SSE-C (HTTPS required)
“Data encrypted before it leaves the client”, “AWS never sees plaintext” Client-side encryption (AWS Encryption SDK / S3 Encryption Client)
“Reduce KMS request cost / throttling on S3” S3 Bucket Keys

Secrets, certificates and guardrails

If the question says… Answer
“Rotate DB password automatically” Secrets Manager rotation
“Rotate with no downtime” Secrets Manager alternating-users rotation
“Store config / non-rotating string cheaply”, hierarchy Parameter Store (SecureString for secrets)
“Prevent any external account from reading our secrets even if a resource policy is misconfigured” RCP with aws:PrincipalOrgID
“Internal services, mTLS, private PKI” AWS Private CA

Immutability, backups and PII

If the question says… Answer
“Write-once-read-many (WORM)”, “even root cannot delete” S3 Object Lock compliance mode / Backup Vault Lock compliance
“Protect backups from ransomware / compromised account” AWS Backup Vault Lock + cross-account copy / logically air-gapped vault
“Hide PII in logs / messages” CloudWatch Logs data protection policy / SNS message data protection

AWS KMS

At a glance

The core managed, Regional key service, backed by FIPS-validated HSMs (AWS-managed, multi-tenant, keys logically isolated per customer). KMS keys never leave KMS unencrypted. Services use envelope encryption: KMS encrypts a data key, and the data key encrypts the data.

  • Exam skills: encryption at rest, KMS vs CloudHSM (5.2.1) · imported material & external key stores (5.3.2, 5.3.3) · keys across Regions (5.3.5) · key policies & cross-account (4.2.1) · least privilege, ABAC (4.2.3, 4.2.2) · key alerts & logging (1.1.4, 1.2.2) · detect/remediate noncompliance (6.3.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #61 AWS KMS · ▶ #62 Key lifecycle · ▶ #63 Cross-account & multi-Region keys · ▶ #64 Aliases · ▶ #65 Creating a symmetric key · ▶ #66 Imported key material · ▶ #67 Monitoring keys · ▶ #68 EBS volume encryption
  • Cost: $1/month per customer managed key (prorated hourly) + ~$0.03 per 10,000 requests; 20,000 free requests/month

What KMS is and the three key types

  • KMS is the core key management service in AWS for controlling and managing encryption keys. ▶ #61 00:00
  • It uses hardware security modules (HSMs) behind the scenes to store and protect keys. ▶ #61 00:10
  • You could run your own key management (on-prem or a third-party cloud), but KMS is usually the fastest and simplest. ▶ #61 00:10
  • KMS stores and manages logical keys called AWS KMS keys. ▶ #61 00:42

Cryptographic operations KMS offers:

  • Encrypt/decrypt data.
  • Sign and verify (asymmetric keys).
  • Generate and export data keys (envelope encryption).
  • Generate and verify MACs (HMAC keys).

Keys never leave the HSMs in plaintext.

Key types by owner ▶ #61 00:52

AWS owned AWS managed (aws/s3, aws/ebs…) Customer managed
Created by AWS AWS on your behalf You
Visible in your account No Yes Yes
Usage AWS internal only One specific AWS service only Controlled by you (key policy / IAM)
Key policy editable No visibility No (managed by AWS) Yes
Delete n/a Cannot be deleted Can delete (scheduled)
Rotation AWS decides Automatic every year, mandatory Optional automatic + on-demand
Cross-account n/a No Yes
Cost Free No monthly fee Monthly fee + requests
  • AWS owned keys are created and used only by AWS for internal encryption. You see no key policy or usage. Not relevant to the course. ▶ #61 01:41
  • AWS managed keys can’t be deleted, edited, rotated manually, or have your own aliases attached.

Control vs overhead: customer managed keys give the highest degree of control over lifecycle and permissions, but more management overhead. AWS managed keys remove the burden of managing keys, but you give up some control over something very sensitive. ▶ #61 02:01 Choose based on operational needs and the sensitivity of the data. ▶ #61 02:31

HSM tenancy: by default the HSMs are managed by AWS and shared among customers. Other customers’ keys may be in the same HSM but are logically isolated. ▶ #61 06:20 For higher requirements, AWS CloudHSM gives you your own dedicated HSM cluster, and you are responsible for generating, storing, importing, exporting and managing keys. ▶ #61 06:31 Or integrate your own key management solution with AWS. ▶ #61 06:50 (See AWS CloudHSM, Part 4.)

Creating a key: specs, origins, Regionality and cost

Properties fixed at creation (key spec, key usage, origin, Regionality can’t be changed later): ▶ #62 01:51

Property Options
Key spec Symmetric SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT (AES-256-GCM, the default and the only spec most AWS services accept; SM4 in China Regions) · asymmetric RSA / ECC (encrypt/decrypt or sign/verify; the public key can be downloaded) · HMAC
Key usage ENCRYPT_DECRYPT, SIGN_VERIFY, or GENERATE_VERIFY_MAC ▶ #62 02:10
Origin AWS_KMS (default, AWS generates material) · EXTERNAL (imported) · AWS_CLOUDHSM (CloudHSM key store) ▶ #62 02:41 · EXTERNAL_KEY_STORE (XKS)
Key policy Every key has one. Custom is recommended, otherwise a default key policy is attached ▶ #62 03:00

For a customer managed key, KMS generates the key material inside an HSM, via the CreateKey API or the console. ▶ #62 01:32

  • RSA keys: encrypt/decrypt or sign/verify. ECC_NIST_P256/P384/P521 and ECC_SECG_P256K1: sign/verify (the last one for cryptocurrency). SM2: China Regions only.
  • The key spec can’t be changed after creation. The condition key kms:KeySpec restricts which specs principals can create.
  • The old name was “customer master key spec”: CustomerMasterKeySpec is deprecated in favour of KeySpec.

SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT = AES-256-GCM: AES in Galois/Counter Mode with 256-bit keys, an industry standard. ▶ #65 07:01 Ciphertext supports additional authenticated data (AAD) such as an encryption context, and GCM adds an integrity check. AES-256-GCM is considered quantum resistant (effective security drops to 128 bits, still infeasible to brute-force). Symmetric keys can have imported key material and can live in custom key stores.

The create-key wizard ▶ #65 00:51

  • Region first: a single-Region key lives in the Region selected in the console, and that “can’t be changed once it’s created”. Check the Region selector (demo: N. Virginia, us-east-1). ▶ #65 00:32
  • Key type: Symmetric (one key encrypts and decrypts, or generates/verifies HMAC) vs Asymmetric (public/private pair for encrypt/decrypt or sign/verify). Many AWS services that integrate with KMS require symmetric encryption keys. ▶ #65 00:51
  • Key usage: Encrypt and decrypt (default) or Generate and verify MAC (HMAC only). ▶ #65 01:10
  • Key material origin (Advanced options): ▶ #65 01:31
Origin Who creates/holds the key material
KMS (recommended, default) AWS KMS creates and manages it
External (Import key material) You generate it yourself (e.g. on your own computer) and import it
AWS CloudHSM key store KMS creates it inside your CloudHSM cluster (extra CloudHSM cost)
External key store It stays in an external key manager outside AWS. It is not imported: KMS calls out to it
  • Regionality: single-Region vs multi-Region. Multi-Region costs $1/month per key per Region (N Regions = N dollars a month, which adds up with hundreds of keys), and copies in several Regions make compliance, access control and auditing harder. The demo keeps single-Region. ▶ #65 02:40
  • Labels: alias = display name (demo cybr-key-example). Fill in description and tags for real keys. ▶ #65 03:20
  • Key administrative permissions (“very important”): who can administer the key through the KMS API and console. Demo: user Kristoff, with Allow key administrators to delete this key left checked. ▶ #65 03:40
  • Key usage permissions: who may use the key in cryptographic operations. A user can need usage rights without admin rights. Demo: user Julia. ▶ #65 04:00
  • Other AWS accounts: add an account ID. That account’s administrators can then grant their own users/roles use of the key. ▶ #65 04:21

The generated key policy ▶ #65 04:38

  1. The account root principal gets kms:* on *: full access, which delegates to IAM. ▶ #65 04:48
  2. Key administrator Kristoff gets the admin actions (Create*, Describe*, Enable*, List*, Put*, Update*, Revoke*, Disable*, Get*, Delete*, TagResource, UntagResource, ScheduleKeyDeletion, CancelKeyDeletion…).
  3. Key user Julia gets kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt, kms:ReEncrypt*, kms:GenerateDataKey*, kms:DescribeKey: all usage actions. ▶ #65 05:01
  4. Julia also gets kms:CreateGrant, kms:ListGrants, kms:RevokeGrant for attaching persistent resources, with "Bool": {"kms:GrantIsForAWSResource": "true"}. ▶ #65 05:22 That condition lets integrated AWS services (e.g. EBS) create grants on Julia’s behalf, but stops Julia from creating arbitrary grants directly. ▶ #65 05:40
Default console key policy (admins vs users, reconstructed) 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Id": "key-consolepolicy-3",
  "Statement": [
    { "Sid": "Enable IAM User Permissions", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root" },
      "Action": "kms:*", "Resource": "*" },
    { "Sid": "Allow access for Key Administrators", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/Kristoff" },
      "Action": ["kms:Create*","kms:Describe*","kms:Enable*","kms:List*","kms:Put*","kms:Update*",
                 "kms:Revoke*","kms:Disable*","kms:Get*","kms:Delete*","kms:TagResource","kms:UntagResource",
                 "kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion","kms:CancelKeyDeletion"],
      "Resource": "*" },
    { "Sid": "Allow use of the key", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/Julia" },
      "Action": ["kms:Encrypt","kms:Decrypt","kms:ReEncrypt*","kms:GenerateDataKey*","kms:DescribeKey"],
      "Resource": "*" },
    { "Sid": "Allow attachment of persistent resources", "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/Julia" },
      "Action": ["kms:CreateGrant","kms:ListGrants","kms:RevokeGrant"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "Bool": { "kms:GrantIsForAWSResource": "true" } } }
  ]
}

After creation: the left menu has Customer managed keys and AWS managed keys. The key page shows the ARN (arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:<account>:key/<key-id>), status Enabled, Regionality Single Region, and tabs Key policy, Cryptographic configuration, Tags, Key rotation, Aliases. ▶ #65 06:10 Cryptographic configuration: Key Type Symmetric, Origin AWS KMS, Key Spec SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT, Key Usage Encrypt and decrypt. ▶ #65 06:40 The (i) link opens the docs page Selecting the key spec. ▶ #65 06:52

Console demo: create a symmetric key and schedule its deletion ([▶ #65](https://youtu.be/oCNjhVd7-nw))
  1. Check the Region selector (us-east-1) → KMS console → Create a key.
  2. Key type Symmetric, key usage Encrypt and decrypt, Advanced options: origin KMS, Single-Region key → Next.
  3. Alias cybr-key-example (no description/tags) → Next.
  4. Key administrators: Kristoff. Keep Allow key administrators to delete this key checked → Next.
  5. Key users: Julia. Optionally add other AWS accounts → Next.
  6. Review the key policy → Finish.
  7. Open the key → check the ARN, Cryptographic configuration (SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT) and the Key rotation tab (yearly automatic rotation toggle). ▶ #65 07:21
  8. Key actions → Schedule key deletion → waiting period 7 days → confirm → status Pending deletion. ▶ #65 08:20

Pricing ▶ #65 00:00

  • $1/month per customer managed key, prorated hourly. Create and quickly delete a key and you pay cents (the instructor estimates about 23 cents, matching ~7 days at $1/month).
  • The same $1/month applies to symmetric, asymmetric, HMAC, multi-Region (each primary and each replica), imported-material keys, and keys in CloudHSM or external key stores (XKS).
  • Rotation charge: the pricing page in the video says each newly generated backing key adds $1/month (prorated), to cover keeping old material for decrypting older ciphertext. See the update box below for current pricing.
  • Free: AWS managed and AWS owned keys, customer managed keys pending deletion (if you cancel, it is billed as if never scheduled), and data keys / data key pairs beyond the API call.
  • Free tier: 20,000 KMS requests per month. Then ~$0.03 per 10,000 requests.

Quotas: request rate quotas are per account and Region, shared by symmetric cryptographic operations (roughly 5,500–100,000 req/s depending on Region and operation). ThrottlingException on S3 → enable S3 Bucket Keys, use data key caching, or request a quota increase.

Controlling access: key policies, IAM policies and grants

Three mechanisms control access to a key: key policies, IAM policies and grants. ▶ #61 02:50

Key policy IAM policy Grant
Kind Resource-based, attached to one key Identity-based Programmatic delegation on one key
Scope Exactly one key policy per key ▶ #61 03:12 Many keys at once, and operations not tied to a key ▶ #61 04:01 One key per grant ▶ #61 04:30
Typical use Who can administer/use this key kms:CreateKey, broad role permissions Temporary access, AWS services (EBS, RDS)
Can deny Yes Yes No ▶ #61 04:30

Key policies ▶ #61 02:50

  • Resource-based policies define who can access a resource and how. Identity-based policies define what a user can access. ▶ #61 03:01
  • IAM policies grant access to a key only if the key policy lets the account delegate: "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::<acct>:root"} with kms:*. Remove that statement and IAM policies stop working for that key, even for admins. Unlike most resources, the key policy is always required.
  • Key policy lockout: if no statement grants anyone admin access, only AWS Support can recover the key.

IAM policies ▶ #61 03:20

  • Can control any KMS operation, including ones not tied to a key. kms:CreateKey can only be controlled by IAM, because the key doesn’t exist yet. ▶ #61 03:31
  • Can cover multiple keys at once and grant permissions for operations of several related services. ▶ #61 04:01

Grants ▶ #61 04:10

  • Let AWS principals use keys in cryptographic operations. Flexible, often for temporary permissions, and mostly used by AWS services (EBS, RDS). ▶ #61 04:10
  • Create a grant, use it and delete it without changing key or IAM policies. ▶ #61 04:30 API: CreateGrant, RetireGrant, RevokeGrant.
  • Grants never expire on their own: retire or revoke them, and set a timeline or conditions for retirement whenever you create one. ▶ #61 04:40
  • Grants are eventually consistent, so use a grant token to use a grant immediately. A grant can name a principal in another account.

Best practices ▶ #61 05:10

  1. Least privilege: only the permissions needed. ▶ #61 05:10
  2. Use key policies for permissions that affect only one key. ▶ #61 05:20
  3. Be careful who can create keys, and regularly verify who has that permission. ▶ #61 05:31
  4. In IAM policies, name the key ARNs. If that’s hard, limit scope by other values such as account or Region. ▶ #61 05:41

Useful condition keys

Condition key Use
kms:ViaService Key usable only through a given service, e.g. s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
kms:CallerAccount Restrict the calling account
kms:EncryptionContext:<key> Require a specific encryption context
kms:GrantIsForAWSResource Let integrated services (EBS/RDS) create grants on a user’s behalf while blocking ad-hoc grants
kms:RequestAlias / kms:ResourceAliases Control access by alias (see Aliases)
kms:KeySpec Restrict which key specs can be created
aws:PrincipalOrgID Share a key org-wide safely

Encryption context: a non-secret key/value pair used as additional authenticated data (AAD). It must match exactly on decrypt and is logged in plaintext in CloudTrail, so never put secrets in it. Use it to bind ciphertext to a resource and to scope policies. It becomes the “for what purpose” audit field.

Envelope encryption: Encrypt handles at most 4 KB of plaintext. For bigger data:

  1. Call GenerateDataKey. It returns a plaintext data key + the same key encrypted under the KMS key.
  2. Encrypt the data locally with the plaintext key.
  3. Discard the plaintext key and store the encrypted one with the data.

GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext is for components that only store keys.

Key lifecycle: states, rotation and deletion

A poorly managed key can make data inaccessible. ▶ #62 00:12 The lifecycle from the AWS docs diagram: ▶ #62 00:22

# State Meaning
1 Creation Key created, initial material generated ▶ #62 00:32
2 Enabled Usable for cryptographic operations ▶ #62 00:40
3 Rotation New material generated, backward compatible ▶ #62 00:40
4 Disabled Unusable but re-enable any time, not deleted ▶ #62 00:50
5 Pending deletion Scheduled, waiting period min 7 days, default 30 ▶ #62 01:01
6 Deleted Permanent: cannot be recovered, not even by contacting AWS, and nor can the data encrypted with it ▶ #62 01:10

Disabled ▶ #62 04:11

  • Temporarily prevents use without deleting. Useful before deletion to make sure nobody depends on the key.
  • Any use fails with an error. Set a CloudWatch alarm on attempted uses to see who still uses it.
  • Re-enable any time: immediately available, no waiting period. ▶ #62 04:41
  • Disabling a key used by EBS/RDS: running resources may continue until restart/reattach and then fail. Find consumers first (CloudTrail Decrypt calls with that key ID).
Rotation

Rotation limits how much data is encrypted under one version of key material, reducing the impact of a compromise. ▶ #62 04:51 Three types: automatic, on-demand, manual. ▶ #62 05:10

Automatic On-demand Manual
For Customer managed symmetric keys with AWS-generated material ▶ #62 05:20 Same keys (and since 2025 single-Region imported-material keys) Everything else
Schedule Yearly by default, configurable 90–2,560 days Immediately (RotateKeyOnDemand), up to 25 per key ▶ #62 06:40 When you choose
Key ID / ARN / alias Same ▶ #62 05:31 Same New key, re-point the alias
Effect on automatic schedule n/a Doesn’t disable or interfere with it ▶ #62 06:40 n/a
  • KMS keeps all previous material versions indefinitely inside the same key, so existing ciphertext needn’t be re-encrypted. On decrypt, KMS picks the right version automatically. Transparent to applications. ▶ #62 05:52 That is why rotation never breaks encrypted data. ▶ #62 08:20
  • Rotation does not re-encrypt existing data and does not rotate data keys already generated. To limit the blast radius of a leaked data key, re-encrypt the data.
  • AWS managed keys rotate automatically every year. This can’t be disabled or changed. ▶ #62 06:20
  • On-demand is for a security event or a compliance need. ▶ #62 06:51
  • GetKeyRotationStatus / ListKeyRotations show config and history. CloudTrail shows RotateKey (AWS-initiated) / RotateKeyOnDemand.

Manual rotation ▶ #62 07:21

  1. Create a new KMS key.
  2. Update apps to encrypt with it, ideally by re-pointing an alias (UpdateAlias) so code doesn’t change.
  3. Keep the old key enabled to decrypt old data.
  4. Once old data is migrated or no longer needed, schedule the old key for deletion.

Required for asymmetric keys, HMAC keys, keys in custom key stores, and keys with imported material (including multi-Region imported keys). ▶ #62 08:01 Since 2025 KMS also supports on-demand rotation of symmetric keys with imported material (single-Region only when #66 was recorded, and you supply new material every time), but the alias-swap answer is still valid.

Deletion
  • Deleting a key makes all data encrypted with it permanently inaccessible: the same as deleting that data. ▶ #62 08:52
  • So there is a mandatory waiting period of 7–30 days (default 30) during which you can reverse it. ▶ #62 09:10 AWS doesn’t let you delete a key immediately “for fear that customers would accidentally delete a key”. ▶ #65 00:12
  • In pending deletion the key can’t decrypt, can’t be enabled, can’t be rotated, but you can cancel any time (CancelKeyDeletion, then re-enable). ▶ #62 09:31
  • After the period KMS deletes the key: permanent and irreversible. ▶ #62 09:51
  • Prefer disabling (DisableKey, reversible) first and alarm on attempted use.
  • Crypto-shred quickly: 7-day deletion, or for imported material delete the material (immediate).
  • Multi-Region keys: a primary can’t be deleted until its replicas are. Each replica has its own waiting period.

Monitoring the lifecycle: state changes are logged in CloudTrail. Use it as the data source → CloudWatch metrics and alarms → SNS for keys entering pending deletion, keys disabled, failed attempts to use a disabled or deleted key, and rotation events. ▶ #62 10:11 In practice: a CloudTrail trail → CloudWatch Logs metric filter { $.eventSource = kms.amazonaws.com && ($.eventName = DisableKey || $.eventName = ScheduleKeyDeletion) } → alarm → SNS, or an EventBridge rule on aws.kms events (KMS CMK Rotation, KMS CMK Deletion, KMS Imported Key Material Expiration) and CloudTrail API calls.

Likely exam scenarios ▶ #62 10:51

  • “Temporarily stop encrypting new data but still decrypt existing data” → a disabled key can’t decrypt either. Don’t disable: deny kms:Encrypt/GenerateDataKey* in the key policy while allowing kms:Decrypt, or point apps at a new key.
  • Minimum waiting period before deletion → 7 days.
  • Data encrypted with an old version after rotation → still decryptable; KMS uses the stored older material.

Aliases

Key IDs (UUIDs) aren’t user-friendly. An alias is a friendly name like alias/database-key or alias/app-encryption-key that points to one key. ▶ #64 00:11

Why use them

  • Simpler code: reference the alias instead of hard-coding a key ID that might change or that nobody recognizes. ▶ #64 00:32
  • Re-point an alias to a different key to change the key apps use, without redeploying code (manual rotation). ▶ #64 00:40
  • Multi-Region architectures: create the same alias name in each Region, each pointing to a Region-specific key, for Region-independent code. ▶ #64 01:00

How they work ▶ #64 01:21

  • Aliases are independent AWS resources with their own ARNs, not properties of keys. Actions on an alias don’t affect the key.
  • An alias is a pointer: create, update (re-point) or delete it without touching the key. ▶ #64 01:42
  • One alias → exactly one key at a time, in the same account and Region. ▶ #64 01:50 One key → many aliases. ▶ #64 02:10
  • Names must start with alias/ and can’t start with alias/aws/. Alias changes are eventually consistent (up to ~5 min).
  • Aliases are not replicated with multi-Region keys. Create them in each Region.

AWS managed key aliases ▶ #64 02:20

  • AWS creates aliases for the AWS managed keys of services you’ve used, always aws/<service>, a reserved namespace: aws/s3, aws/dynamodb, aws/rds, aws/sns, aws/ebs…
  • You can’t create, update or delete AWS managed keys or their aliases, and you can’t attach your own aliases to AWS managed keys. ▶ #64 02:50

Using aliases in operations ▶ #64 03:12

# key ID
aws kms encrypt --key-id 1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab --plaintext fileb://data.txt
# alias
aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/app-encryption-key --plaintext fileb://data.txt
  • Not accepted by every operation. Many management operations need the key ID or ARN: EnableKey, DisableKey, ScheduleKeyDeletion. ▶ #64 03:21
  • Alias names don’t work for a key in another account. ▶ #64 03:50 The alias ARN (arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111111111111:alias/app-key) does work for cryptographic operations.
  • UpdateAlias needs permissions on the alias and both the old and new keys. Re-pointing doesn’t re-encrypt: ciphertext embeds the key ID, so keep the old key enabled.

Aliases and IAM authorization ▶ #64 03:50

  • You can’t use alias names or alias ARNs as the Resource in an IAM policy to grant access to a key. That policy applies to the alias resource itself (e.g. kms:CreateAlias/UpdateAlias), not the key.
  • To control key access by alias, use condition keys: ▶ #64 04:21
Condition key Matches on Operator
kms:RequestAlias The alias used in the request (only if the caller actually passed it) Single-valued: StringEquals
kms:ResourceAliases All aliases associated with the key, even if not in the request Multi-valued: ForAnyValue: 
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["kms:Decrypt", "kms:GenerateDataKey"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:*:111111111111:key/*",
  "Condition": {
    "ForAnyValue:StringEquals": {
      "kms:ResourceAliases": "alias/finance-key"
    }
  }
}
  • Alias-based ABAC: lock down who can CreateAlias/UpdateAlias, otherwise someone can grant themselves access by adding an alias. Tag-based alternative: aws:ResourceTag/....

Likely exam scenarios ▶ #64 05:00: rotate keys without updating application code → re-point the alias. Region-independent encryption logic → same alias name in each Region. ▶ #64 05:10

Cross-account access and multi-Region keys

Cross-account access

Scenario: resources in one account must encrypt/decrypt with a key in another account. ▶ #63 00:12 Both are required, otherwise AccessDenied: ▶ #63 00:20

  1. A key policy in the owner account granting the external account or specific principals in it.
  2. An IAM policy in the external account allowing its users/roles to use the key (kms:Decrypt etc. on the key ARN).

Both accounts explicitly agree to the access. ▶ #63 00:51 Example: Account A owns the key, Account B needs it. The key policy in A grants B, and IAM in B grants specific users/roles. ▶ #63 01:02

  • Only customer managed keys work cross-account.
  • The caller must use the full key ARN (or alias ARN).
  • Granting arn:aws:iam::222222222222:root in the key policy delegates to Account B’s admins, who decide via IAM which principals get it. In a key policy "Resource": "*" means “this key”.
Cross-account key policy (Account A) and IAM policy (Account B), reconstructed

Key policy statement in Account A (111111111111):

{
  "Sid": "AllowAccountBUseOfTheKey",
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::222222222222:root"},
  "Action": [
    "kms:Encrypt",
    "kms:Decrypt",
    "kms:ReEncrypt*",
    "kms:GenerateDataKey*",
    "kms:DescribeKey"
  ],
  "Resource": "*"
}

IAM policy attached to a role in Account B (222222222222):

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": [
      "kms:Encrypt",
      "kms:Decrypt",
      "kms:ReEncrypt*",
      "kms:GenerateDataKey*",
      "kms:DescribeKey"
    ],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111111111111:key/1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab"
  }]
}
Multi-Region keys
  • Purpose: encrypt in one Region, decrypt in another. A normal key is Region-specific: data encrypted with a us-east-1 key must be decrypted in us-east-1. ▶ #63 01:31
  • Functionally identical keys in multiple Regions. Main use case: disaster recovery and continuity. If us-east-1 is down and your only key is there, you can’t decrypt. ▶ #63 01:52
  • Structure: a primary key in one Region, then replica keys (mrk- prefix) in others. ▶ #63 02:12
Shared by primary and replicas Independent per key
Same key ID, so apps use one ID in any Region ▶ #63 02:22 Key policy, grants, aliases, tags ▶ #63 02:40
Same key material, which makes cross-Region decrypt possible ▶ #63 02:31 Enable / disable / delete state ▶ #63 03:01
Rotation (set on the primary, syncs) ARN (differs by Region)
  • Per-key settings give fine-grained per-Region control, but more management and auditing complexity. ▶ #63 02:40
  • Disable, enable or delete replicas independently. Deleting a replica doesn’t affect the primary or other replicas. Promote a replica to primary (UpdatePrimaryRegion); only one primary at a time. ▶ #63 03:01
  • They are not a “global” key: they are separate resources that replicate the key only, not data. ▶ #63 03:31
  • Multi-Region is chosen at creation: a single-Region key can’t be converted. Still not exportable.
  • Use cases: DynamoDB global tables / S3 CRR with client-side encryption, active-active apps, signing in several Regions. For S3 Replication with SSE-KMS you don’t need them: S3 re-encrypts with a destination-Region key you specify.
  • Cost: each replica is billed as a separate key ($1/month).

Imported key material and custom key stores

In Create key → Advanced options → Key material origin there are four origins: KMS – recommended, External (Import key material), AWS CloudHSM key store, External key store (XKS). ▶ #66 00:21 KMS is by far the easiest and the recommended option. ▶ #66 00:52 Know the other three for the exam “even if you never plan on using the others on the job”. ▶ #66 01:00

The 2026 console wizard also has optional steps for admin permissions, usage permissions and Edit key policy before Review, and the asymmetric option now mentions “deriving shared secrets” (key agreement).

Imported key material (BYOK)

KMS creates the key object (metadata, key ID, ARN, policies…) but doesn’t generate the cryptographic bits: you import them. ▶ #66 01:11

  1. KMS creates the key with origin EXTERNAL in a disabled state, more precisely Pending import, because it has no material. ▶ #66 01:40
  2. You download a public wrapping key and an import token (valid 24 hours), which protect the material during import. ▶ #66 01:50
  3. You generate the 256-bit material locally and wrap it with the public wrapping key. ▶ #66 02:00
  4. You upload the wrapped material with the import token. ▶ #66 02:10
  5. You choose whether the material is permanent or expires at a set time. ▶ #66 02:10

CLI: create-key --origin EXTERNAL → get-parameters-for-import (e.g. RSA_AES_KEY_WRAP_SHA_256, RSA_4096) → wrap with OpenSSL → import-key-material --expiration-model KEY_MATERIAL_DOES_NOT_EXPIRE|KEY_MATERIAL_EXPIRES.

  • At expiry, or after DeleteImportedKeyMaterial (immediate, no waiting period), the key becomes unusable at once (PendingImport). Restore it by re-importing the same material. ▶ #66 02:20
  • Pro tip: CloudWatch alarms before expiration ▶ #66 02:33: metric SecondsUntilKeyMaterialExpiration (namespace AWS/KMS) and the EventBridge event “KMS Imported Key Material Expiration”.
  • You own durability (keep a copy). Imported material can’t be extracted. Different material can never be imported into the same key, except via the 2025 rotation feature.
  • Use cases: compliance requires generating keys in your own infrastructure, or identical keys in AWS and on-premises. ▶ #62 03:31
  • Imported material doesn’t support automatic rotation. ▶ #62 03:42 It supports on-demand rotation (same key ID and ARN), at recording time only for single-Region keys, and you must supply new material for every rotation. ▶ #66 02:40
  • On-demand ≠ manual rotation: on-demand keeps the same key ID; manual = a completely new key (new ID), usually by re-pointing an alias. ▶ #66 03:10
Imported material AWS-generated material
Generation You AWS KMS
Expiry You can set one None
Immediate deletion Yes (DeleteImportedKeyMaterial) No (7–30 day wait)
Durability You AWS
Automatic rotation No Yes
AWS CloudHSM key store

  • KMS still generates the material, but creates and stores it inside your CloudHSM cluster in your VPC. Crypto operations run in your HSMs. ▶ #66 03:31
  • Requires ≥2 active HSMs in different AZs. Symmetric encryption keys only, no automatic rotation.
  • Benefit: hardware-isolated control (single-tenant HSMs). ▶ #66 03:50
  • Downsides: much higher cost (~$1.45+/HSM-hour × 2) and operational complexity: you set up the cluster, scaling, backups, and run the HSMs. ▶ #66 04:01
  • Exam keywords: “customer-managed HSM”, “dedicated cryptographic hardware on AWS”. ▶ #66 04:11 If the question says on-prem, think XKS, not CloudHSM. ▶ #66 04:31
External key store (XKS, HYOK)
  • Goes further: the key material never leaves your environment. Keys are generated and stored in your own HSM / external key manager outside AWS, reached through an XKS proxy that you provide. ▶ #66 05:02
  • The proxy can run on-prem, or in a VPC behind a Network Load Balancer, linked to the external key manager over Direct Connect (or the internet). ▶ #66 05:10
  • Flow: the key is generated in the external manager → KMS sends requests (encrypt, decrypt…) over a secure channel → the external manager enforces its own policies, logging and controls. ▶ #66 05:31 Called Hold Your Own Key (HYOK). ▶ #66 05:52
  • KMS still uses double encryption (KMS HSM material + external key). Symmetric only. The external manager can revoke access at any time (kill switch).
  • Availability risk: losing connectivity to the external manager means AWS can’t encrypt or decrypt, which probably means an outage. ▶ #66 06:02 You own availability, latency (KMS timeout ~250 ms per XKS call) and durability.
  • Very complex. Only for strict regulatory or sovereignty requirements. ▶ #66 06:21 Usually not the answer unless the question says the key can’t be stored in the cloud or must be kept on-prem. ▶ #66 06:41

  1. AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, EC2, Lambda…) call AWS KMS. The KMS key lives in an external key store.
  2. KMS sends requests over HTTPS to a Network Load Balancer in your VPC.
  3. The NLB spreads them across XKS proxy instances in two AZs (subnets 1 and 2, for HA).
  4. The proxies reach the external key manager outside AWS over Direct Connect or the internet.
  5. The external key manager holds the keys and performs the cryptographic operation.

Every hop is a potential failure point, which is the availability risk. (Source: AWS blog “Announcing AWS KMS External Key Store (XKS)”.)

Choosing a key material origin

▶ #66 07:01

Option Who generates material Where it lives Rotation Pick it when…
KMS (default) AWS KMS KMS HSMs Automatic (and on-demand) Default for almost everything, least operational overhead
Import (BYOK) You KMS (copy) + your source On-demand (you supply material; single-Region) or manual You must generate the material yourself, control its expiry, or delete it instantly
CloudHSM key store AWS KMS, inside your cluster Your CloudHSM cluster in a VPC Manual only “Customer-managed / dedicated HSM in AWS”, single-tenant hardware
External key store (XKS) Your external key manager Outside AWS In the external manager Key must never be stored in AWS / must stay on-prem (sovereignty)

Monitoring keys and encryption

The exam asks how to track key usage, detect suspicious activity and ensure compliance: who used the key, when, and for what purpose. ▶ #67 00:00 “The challenge is knowing which tool to use for which scenario.” ▶ #67 00:20 Main tools: CloudTrail, CloudWatch Logs, CloudWatch alarms, EventBridge, plus AWS Config. ▶ #67 00:30

Scenario Tool
Who used key X, when, from where, with what encryption context; failed decrypt attempts CloudTrail (Event history / trail → Athena / CloudTrail Lake)
Usage trends, spikes, most-used keys CloudWatch metrics (+ anomaly detection)
Notify when a pending-deletion key is used CloudTrail → CloudWatch Logs metric filter → alarm → SNS
React automatically to rotation / expiry / deletion EventBridge → Lambda / SNS / SSM
Prove resources are encrypted (EBS, RDS, S3, DynamoDB, CloudTrail) and auto-fix AWS Config managed rules + SSM Automation

▶ #67 05:02

CloudTrail
  • CloudTrail logs every KMS API call automatically, as management events (including Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey). There’s no separate data-event configuration: everything is captured unless you explicitly exclude it. ▶ #67 01:01
  • You can’t cherry-pick KMS events: all or nothing. ▶ #67 01:12 The only filters are excluding all KMS events from a trail (a cost lever and an audit gap) or read-only/write-only.
You can see ▶ #67 01:20 You cannot see ▶ #67 01:40
Who made the call (IAM principal) The plaintext being encrypted/decrypted
Which key was used Key material and ciphertext
The encryption context, if provided Key policy contents from GetKeyPolicy responses
Success or failure
Source IP and time

The docs page Examples of AWS KMS log entries notes that KMS writes entries when you call an operation, when an AWS service calls one on your behalf, and when KMS calls one itself, e.g. the final DeleteKey after the waiting period. ▶ #67 02:01

Forensic clues: errorCode: AccessDenied and KMSInvalidStateException (disabled or pending-deletion key) on Decrypt show which app broke after a key was disabled.

CloudWatch metrics and alarms
  • CloudTrail = audit trail of who did what and when. CloudWatch metrics = operational trends and usage patterns. ▶ #67 02:01
  • KMS publishes metrics for key usage and health. ▶ #67 02:10 The instructor’s example is a “successful request” metric counting successful cryptographic operations per key, to find the most-used keys. ▶ #67 02:20
  • Anomaly example: a key that normally does ~100 operations/hour spikes to 10,000/hour, which could mean data exfiltration or ransomware. ▶ #67 02:41 Use anomaly detection alarms. ▶ #67 02:51
  • Alarm when someone uses a key pending deletion: CloudTrail → CloudWatch Logs (metric filter) → CloudWatch alarm → SNS. ▶ #67 03:01 If it fires, something still depends on the key: investigate and probably cancel the deletion. ▶ #67 03:20
  • Also alert on DisableKey, ScheduleKeyDeletion, PutKeyPolicy, CreateGrant and DeleteImportedKeyMaterial.
EventBridge
  • Triggers automated responses in near real time, from events sent by CloudTrail and Security Hub CSPM. ▶ #67 03:40
  • KMS events: key material rotated (automatic or on-demand), imported material expired, a key scheduled for deletion actually deleted. ▶ #67 03:50 Detail-types: “KMS CMK Rotation”, “KMS Imported Key Material Expiration”, “KMS CMK Deletion”, plus “AWS API Call via CloudTrail”.
  • Targets include AWS Lambda. ▶ #67 04:00
AWS Config and other compliance tools

  • encrypted-volumes (identifier ENCRYPTED_VOLUMES) checks that attached EBS volumes are encrypted, optionally with a specified KMS key. NON_COMPLIANT if unencrypted or encrypted with another key. Resource type AWS::EC2::Volume, trigger Configuration changes. ▶ #67 04:20
  • AWS managed rules already cover RDS snapshot, CloudTrail, S3 bucket and DynamoDB table encryption ▶ #67 04:31: cmk-backing-key-rotation-enabled, kms-cmk-not-scheduled-for-deletion, s3-default-encryption-kms, rds-storage-encrypted, cloud-trail-encryption-enabled, dynamodb-table-encrypted-kms. Custom rules are possible too.
  • Non-compliant resources can be auto-remediated with SSM Automation. Config and SSM Automation “are often hand-in-hand”. ▶ #67 04:50
  • Security Hub CSPM controls KMS.1–KMS.4 (KMS.3 = no unintended deletion, KMS.4 = rotation enabled).
  • IAM Access Analyzer finds keys shared outside your zone of trust.

EBS volume encryption with KMS

A scenario “the exam absolutely loves to ask about”. ▶ #68 00:00 (See also Amazon EBS encryption, Part 4.)

What gets encrypted (“this is important to remember”): ▶ #68 00:41

  1. Data at rest in the volume.
  2. All data moving between the volume and the instance.
  3. All snapshots created from the volume.
  4. All volumes created from those snapshots.

It’s transparent, done at the storage layer with AES-256-XTS, so apps need no changes. ▶ #68 01:10 No performance penalty on Nitro.

Which key and how EBS gets permission ▶ #68 01:21

  • The AWS managed key aws/ebs or a symmetric customer managed key.
  • EBS gets access through the key policy and a grant, which lets it generate and use data keys on your behalf. ▶ #68 01:40

The aws/ebs key page says: “you cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys, rotate them, change their key policies, or schedule them for deletion”. Its description is “Default key that protects my EBS volumes when no other key is defined”. ▶ #68 01:43

EBS encryption by default
  • An account-level, Regional setting. New EBS volumes and snapshot copies are encrypted automatically with your default KMS key for EBS in that Region. ▶ #68 02:11
  • Enable it in each Region and in every account. ▶ #68 02:22
  • Not retroactive: existing volumes and snapshots must still be encrypted separately. ▶ #68 02:30
  • Changing the default key re-encrypts nothing.

Console: EC2 → Settings → Data protection and security → EBS encryption → Manage → toggle Always encrypt new EBS volumes, set the Default encryption key (default alias/aws/ebs, or paste a CMK ARN) → Update EBS encryption. The banner warns that settings apply only to the current Region, and that once account-level encryption is on you can only launch instance types that support EBS encryption.

Encrypting existing unencrypted volumes

“You can’t directly encrypt an existing unencrypted volume.” ▶ #68 02:50 Make an encrypted copy:

  1. Snapshot the volume. Stopping the instance isn’t required but is recommended for consistency. ▶ #68 03:01
  2. Copy the snapshot with encryption, specifying the KMS key. This is the step that encrypts. ▶ #68 03:10
  3. Create a new volume from the encrypted snapshot (encrypted automatically). ▶ #68 03:20
  4. Detach the old volume and attach the new one. ▶ #68 03:30
  • A root volume can be swapped without technically stopping the instance, but needs a reboot: seconds to minutes of downtime. ▶ #68 03:41
  • With encryption by default on, snapshot copies are encrypted automatically. ▶ #68 03:41
  • Shortcut: create an encrypted volume directly from an unencrypted snapshot, or launch from an AMI with encryption in the block device mapping.
  • Root volume swap without detaching: the Replace Root Volume task (reboots, keeps IPs/ENIs).

Hundreds of volumes: AWS Prescriptive Guidance pattern Automatically encrypt existing and new Amazon EBS volumes. ▶ #68 04:12

  1. AWS Config detects unencrypted volumes. ▶ #68 04:30
  2. An administrator manually triggers the remediation, sent to Systems Manager, because the instance may need stopping. Fully removing humans is possible but probably not advisable. ▶ #68 04:51
  3. SSM Automation snapshots the unencrypted volume. ▶ #68 05:11
  4. It uses KMS to create an encrypted copy of the snapshot. ▶ #68 05:20
  5. It stops the instance if running, attaches the new encrypted volume, and starts the instance again. ▶ #68 05:31
Sharing and copying encrypted snapshots
  • Snapshots can be public, but never snapshots of encrypted volumes. Encrypted snapshots can only be shared with specific accounts. ▶ #68 05:51
  • You can’t share snapshots encrypted with aws/ebs, because you can’t modify that key’s policy. ▶ #68 06:01
  • To share: use a customer managed key and share the key via cross-account permissions in the key policy. ▶ #68 06:11
  • Use cases: migrations, DR, data retention and auditing, expansion. Plan for the limits up front. ▶ #68 06:42
  • Cross-account checklist: CMK (not aws/ebs) → key policy allows the target account kms:DescribeKey, kms:CreateGrant, kms:Decrypt, kms:ReEncrypt*, kms:GenerateDataKey* → snapshot permissions add the account → the target’s IAM allows the same KMS actions → the target copies the snapshot with its own key.
  • Cross-Region: attaching an encrypted volume in another Region fails. Copy the snapshot to that Region first ▶ #68 07:42; the copy re-encrypts with a key in the destination Region (or a multi-Region replica).

Console: Snapshots → select → Actions → Modify permissions. For an unencrypted snapshot: “When you share an unencrypted snapshot, you give the specified accounts permission to copy the snapshot and to create volumes from it.” Options Public / Private, then Shared accounts → Add account (ID without hyphens). Public access shows “Not blocked” because the account-level block public access for snapshots setting is off. ▶ #68 05:51

Unauthorized errors with encrypted EBS? Check these
  • The user lacks the required KMS permissions. ▶ #68 07:11
  • The KMS key grant doesn’t allow EC2 to use the key.
  • The snapshot is encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/ebs and you’re trying to share it.
  • The CMK is disabled or pending deletion: the instance can’t start or attach the volume (Client.InvalidKMSKey.InvalidState).
  • Attaching in another Region: copy the snapshot to that Region first. ▶ #68 07:42

Enforce and detect: an SCP denying ec2:CreateVolume / ec2:RunInstances when ec2:Encrypted is false; Config encrypted-volumes / ec2-ebs-encryption-by-default; Security Hub EC2.7. “Block public access for EBS snapshots” can be enforced with a declarative policy.

Console demo: EBS default encryption and snapshot sharing ([▶ #68](https://youtu.be/fKKzYvK2gfM))
  1. EC2 → Volumes (empty, us-east-1) → KMS console → AWS managed keys → open aws/ebs to show it’s AWS-managed and non-editable.
  2. EC2 Dashboard → Settings (Data protection and security) → EBS encryption shows Disabled with default key alias/aws/ebs.
  3. Manage → tick Always encrypt new EBS volumes, keep or choose the default key → Update EBS encryption.
  4. EC2 → Snapshots: two 5 GiB snapshots, encrypted-with-aws/ebs and unencrypted.
  5. Select unencrypted → Actions → Modify permissions → Public/Private options → Add account (ID without hyphens) → Modify permissions. The aws/ebs-encrypted snapshot can’t be shared.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Know the three key types and how they differ: deletion, rotation, scope, policy ownership. ▶ #61 00:52
  • CreateKey can only be governed by IAM policies, not key policies. ▶ #61 03:41
  • Grants can’t deny, apply to one key, and never expire on their own: retire or revoke them. ▶ #61 04:30
  • In IAM policies, scope to specific key ARNs, or at least account/Region. ▶ #61 05:41
  • Deleted keys are gone forever, and so is the data. AWS can’t recover them. ▶ #62 01:10
  • Disable first and alarm on usage before scheduling deletion. ▶ #62 04:21
  • Waiting period 7 (min) – 30 (default/max) days, cancelable while pending deletion. ▶ #62 09:10
  • Asymmetric, HMAC, custom key store and multi-Region imported keys need manual rotation. ▶ #62 08:01
  • Cross-account AccessDenied → check both sides: key policy (owner) and IAM (consumer). ▶ #63 00:51
  • Multi-Region keys replicate the key only, not your data, and each replica has its own key policy. ▶ #63 03:31
  • Expect scenarios on sharing encrypted data across accounts and keeping encryption across Regions for DR while keeping costs low. ▶ #63 03:40
  • aws/ is reserved for AWS managed keys. Aliases aren’t accepted by all operations or cross-account, and aren’t an IAM Resource: use kms:RequestAlias / kms:ResourceAliases. ▶ #64 03:50
  • Many AWS services that integrate with KMS require symmetric keys. ▶ #65 00:51
  • Multi-Region keys cost more (per Region) and bring compliance, access control and auditing considerations. ▶ #65 02:40
  • “Understanding how to use and manage imported key material is important for the exam, especially… how to rotate imported key material, as well as how to manage and configure external key stores.” ▶ #66 00:00
  • “Remember that on-demand rotation and manual rotation are two separate things.” ▶ #66 03:10
  • “If they mention on-prem, I don’t want you to think CloudHSM, I want you to think XKS.” ▶ #66 04:31
  • XKS: connectivity loss = outage. Not the answer unless compliance requires keys outside the cloud. ▶ #66 06:41
  • CloudTrail captures KMS by default, all or nothing, and never shows plaintext or GetKeyPolicy contents. ▶ #67 01:12
  • Spike from 100 to 10,000 ops/hour = possible exfiltration or ransomware. ▶ #67 02:41
  • Encrypted snapshots: never public; aws/ebs snapshots can’t be shared; share via a CMK. ▶ #68 06:01
  • “Make sure you’re quite familiar with that process because you might see some questions related to that process on your exam.” ▶ #68 08:00

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Admin has kms:* in IAM but gets AccessDenied The key policy doesn’t delegate to the account, or an explicit deny exists
Cross-account AccessDenied Check both the key policy (owner) and IAM (consumer)
Share encrypted EBS/RDS snapshot or AMI with another account Must use a customer managed key, and share that key. The AWS managed key can’t be shared
Shared AMI fails to launch / “You are unauthorized to perform this operation” Missing KMS permissions, the grant doesn’t allow EC2, or the snapshot uses aws/ebs
Attach encrypted volume in another Region Copy the snapshot to that Region first
Encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume No in-place encryption: snapshot → encrypted copy → new volume → swap
Ensure every new volume is encrypted in all accounts EBS encryption by default in each Region of each account + SCP on ec2:Encrypted
Rotate key yearly with no app change Enable automatic rotation (same ARN), not a new key
Rotate keys without updating application code (asymmetric/imported/custom store) New key + re-point the alias
Region-independent encryption code Same alias name in each Region
Re-encrypt old data with new key material Rotation doesn’t do this. Use ReEncrypt or re-copy the data
Data encrypted with an old key version after rotation Still decryptable; KMS keeps old material
Immediately make data unreadable, then possibly restore Imported material: DeleteImportedKeyMaterial, then re-import. AWS-generated: DisableKey
Stop encrypting new data but keep decrypting existing data Don’t disable. Deny kms:Encrypt/GenerateDataKey* while allowing kms:Decrypt, or point apps at a new key
Minimum waiting period before deletion 7 days (default 30)
Key accidentally scheduled for deletion CancelKeyDeletion within the window, then re-enable
Imported key suddenly unusable Material expired: re-import the same material
Restrict a key so only S3 in this Region can use it kms:ViaService
Same ciphertext must decrypt in the DR Region Multi-Region key (one key replicated, no re-encryption, low cost)
Who can create keys? Only IAM controls kms:CreateKey
Alias used as IAM Resource doesn’t grant key access Use kms:RequestAlias / kms:ResourceAliases
Keys must never leave on-prem / sovereign control XKS
Dedicated / customer-managed HSM with KMS integration CloudHSM key store
Generate material ourselves / set expiry / delete immediately Imported material
Least operational overhead KMS-generated material
Need automatic rotation with imported, CloudHSM or XKS keys Not available
Alarm when someone uses a key pending deletion CloudTrail → CloudWatch Logs metric filter → alarm → SNS
React automatically to rotation / expiry / deletion EventBridge
Prove resources are encrypted and auto-fix Config + SSM Automation
Which keys are accessible from other accounts IAM Access Analyzer
ThrottlingException from KMS on S3 S3 Bucket Keys, data key caching, or a quota increase
Updates since the videos
  • ▶ #61 01:52 says AWS managed keys rotate every 3 years. Since 2022 they rotate every year (as ▶ #62 06:20 says), and this can’t be disabled or changed.
  • Since 2024 the automatic rotation period for customer managed keys is configurable from 90 to 2,560 days (default 365); the videos mention only the yearly default. On-demand rotation (RotateKeyOnDemand, up to 25 per key) is supported for symmetric keys. Only symmetric keys with AWS-generated material support automatic rotation.
  • In a key policy, the arn:aws:iam::<acct>:root principal means the account, not only the root user. IAM policies grant nothing on a key unless the key policy delegates to the account this way.
  • ▶ #64 03:50 says aliases can’t be used for keys in another account. That’s true of the alias name; cryptographic operations do accept the alias ARN cross-account.
  • ▶ #67 02:20 describes a per-key “successful request” KMS metric. It could not be confirmed in the docs. Documented KMS metrics include SecondsUntilKeyMaterialExpiration and XKS metrics (XksProxyErrors, XksProxyHsmLatency, XksProxyCertificateDaysToExpire). Request rates are in AWS/Usage (CallCount). Per-key usage counts usually come from CloudTrail (metric filters, Athena, CloudTrail Lake).
  • Rotation pricing: rotation now adds $1/month only for the first and second rotations (later ones are free). The older pricing page in ▶ #65 00:00 says $1/month per rotated backing key.
  • Since 2025 symmetric keys with imported material support on-demand rotation (single-Region only when ▶ #66 02:40 was recorded).

Real-world practice

  • One CMK per data classification and app, not one for everything. Separate key administrators (manage, no use) from key users (use, no manage). Use customer managed keys for anything regulated or shared cross-account, AWS managed keys for low-sensitivity convenience.
  • Create keys per workload account with IaC (CloudFormation/Terraform): key admins = platform/security role, key users = application roles.
  • SCP: keys can’t be deleted, disabled or have their policy changed outside a security / break-glass role (kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion, kms:DisableKey, kms:PutKeyPolicy), and alarm on any attempt. Ransomware actors sometimes schedule key deletion or re-encrypt data with their own external keys.
  • Monitor CloudTrail for ScheduleKeyDeletion, DisableKey, PutKeyPolicy, CreateGrant, UpdateAlias. An attacker re-pointing an alias to a key they control silently redirects new encryptions. SCP idea: deny kms:UpdateAlias/kms:DeleteAlias on production aliases except from the pipeline role.
  • Audit open grants periodically (ListGrants) and retire stale ones.
  • Retiring a key: query CloudTrail (Lake/Athena, last 90 days) for principals calling Decrypt/GenerateDataKey on it, disable first, watch for failures, then schedule deletion. Use 30-day waiting periods in production, 7 days only in sandboxes.
  • Aliases: name them alias/<env>/<app>/<purpose>, manage them in IaC, reference aliases for encrypt and rely on embedded key IDs for decrypt.
  • Shared keys in Organizations: keep them in a central security/data account, grant via aws:PrincipalOrgID + specific role paths, review with IAM Access Analyzer.
  • Multi-Region keys: replicate only to SCP-allowed Regions, keep replica key policies in IaC, verify in DR tests that apps decrypt with the local replica (CloudTrail Decrypt in the DR Region), and document the UpdatePrimaryRegion runbook.
  • Imported material: track expiry with an alarm or calendar (expired-material outages are common), and keep the material in an HSM or escrow: you own durability.
  • XKS in production: proxies in several AZs/sites, redundant Direct Connect links, failover tests. Vendors (Thales, Fortanix, Entrust, HashiCorp) provide XKS proxies.
  • Logging: an organization trail including KMS events, delivered to the Log Archive account and encrypted with its own KMS key. KMS calls are high-volume management events: the first copy is free, extra trails pay per event.
  • Deploy encryption Config rules org-wide as conformance packs from the delegated admin, with SSM Automation documents (e.g. AWS-EnableEbsEncryptionByDefault) for remediation.
  • EBS: turn on encryption by default in every account and Region (Control Tower / StackSets / account vending) with a per-account CMK rather than aws/ebs, so snapshots and AWS Backup copies can go to backup/DR accounts. Bulk swaps change volume IDs: update backup selections, monitoring and tags, and test runbooks on non-prod.
  • Cost levers: S3 Bucket Keys and data key caching for high-volume workloads.
Key policy: separated admins, app use only through S3 in one Region, cross-account reader 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "EnableIAMPolicies",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root"},
      "Action": "kms:*",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "KeyAdmins",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/KeyAdmin"},
      "Action": [
        "kms:Create*", "kms:Describe*", "kms:Enable*", "kms:List*", "kms:Put*",
        "kms:Update*", "kms:Revoke*", "kms:Disable*", "kms:Get*", "kms:Delete*",
        "kms:TagResource", "kms:UntagResource",
        "kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion", "kms:CancelKeyDeletion", "kms:RotateKeyOnDemand"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "AppUseViaS3Only",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/app-role"},
      "Action": ["kms:Encrypt", "kms:Decrypt", "kms:ReEncrypt*", "kms:GenerateDataKey*", "kms:DescribeKey"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:ViaService": "s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com",
          "kms:CallerAccount": "111122223333"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "AllowCrossAccountDecrypt",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/reader"},
      "Action": ["kms:Decrypt", "kms:DescribeKey"],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

The cross-account reader also needs an IAM policy in 444455556666 allowing kms:Decrypt on this key’s ARN.

Hands-on lab
  1. Create a symmetric CMK with alias alias/lab-scs. Enable rotation and set the period to 180 days.
  2. aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/lab-scs --plaintext fileb://<(echo hi) --encryption-context app=lab, then decrypt without the context and watch it fail.
  3. Find the Encrypt / Decrypt events in CloudTrail Event history and look at encryptionContext.
  4. Cleanup: aws kms schedule-key-deletion --key-id alias/lab-scs --pending-window-in-days 7 and delete the alias.

AWS CloudHSM

At a glance

Dedicated, single-tenant HSMs in your VPC. You hold the crypto users and keys. AWS manages the hardware but cannot access your keys.

  • Exam skills: encryption at rest, choose KMS vs CloudHSM (5.2.1) · custom key stores (5.3.2)
  • Videos: none dedicated in the course. CloudHSM is discussed inside ▶ #61 and ▶ #66 (see AWS KMS, Part 4)
  • Cost: roughly $1.45+ per HSM-hour × 2 HSMs minimum, about $2k+/month before KMS charges

What it is and who does what

  • KMS’s default HSMs are AWS-managed and shared. If you need more, CloudHSM gives you your own dedicated HSM cluster, and you are responsible for generating, storing, importing, exporting and managing the keys. ▶ #61 06:31
  • Users: the crypto officer (CO) manages users. The crypto user (CU) owns and uses keys. If you lose the credentials, AWS cannot recover the keys.
  • High availability = a cluster with ≥2 HSMs in different AZs. Keys sync across the cluster. Backups go to S3 automatically (encrypted).

FIPS level is no longer the differentiator

CloudHSM KMS
Validation Current HSM type hsm2m.medium is FIPS 140-3 Level 3 (older hsm1 was FIPS 140-2 Level 3) KMS’s own HSMs are also FIPS 140-3 Level 3
Tenancy Single-tenant, exclusive control Multi-tenant, keys logically isolated
AWS service integration None directly (only through a KMS key store) Native
Cost / ops High: you run the cluster Low

So “FIPS L3” alone is no longer a reason to pick CloudHSM. Single tenancy / exclusive control is.

APIs and use cases

  • Standard APIs: PKCS#11, JCE, OpenSSL Dynamic Engine, Microsoft CNG/KSP.
  • Use cases: TLS offload on web servers, Oracle TDE, Microsoft SQL Server TDE / AD CS, document signing, custom asymmetric crypto that KMS doesn’t support.

Using CloudHSM from AWS services: the KMS CloudHSM key store

CloudHSM is not integrated with AWS services directly. Integration happens via a KMS CloudHSM key store:

  • KMS still generates the key material, but creates and stores it inside your CloudHSM cluster, and crypto runs in your HSMs. ▶ #66 03:31
  • Requirements and limits: symmetric keys only, ≥2 active HSMs in different AZs, no automatic rotation.
  • Benefit: hardware-isolated control. Downsides: much higher cost and operational complexity. ▶ #66 03:50
Question keywords Answer
“Single-tenant”, “exclusive control”, “AWS can’t access”, “PKCS#11/JCE/CNG”, “SSL offload”, “Oracle TDE” CloudHSM directly
“Customer-managed HSM”, “dedicated cryptographic hardware on AWS” + S3/EBS integration CloudHSM key store ▶ #66 04:11
“On-prem” XKS, not CloudHSM ▶ #66 04:31
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Need dedicated HSMs → CloudHSM. ▶ #61 06:31
  • “If they mention on-prem, I don’t want you to think CloudHSM, I want you to think XKS.” ▶ #66 04:31

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
AWS services (S3/EBS) must use keys in a single-tenant HSM KMS custom key store on CloudHSM, not CloudHSM directly
Need automatic key rotation Not available for custom key store keys
Lowest cost / least ops KMS, not CloudHSM
Keys must stay on-premises KMS external key store (XKS), not CloudHSM

Real-world practice

  • Use it only when a regulator or a contract requires exclusive HSM control, or for PKCS#11 workloads.
  • Run ≥2 HSMs, keep CO/CU credentials in a break-glass process, and send HSM audit logs to CloudWatch Logs.
  • Budget roughly $1.45+ per HSM-hour × 2 minimum, about $2k+/month before KMS charges.
Hands-on lab

Skip it, or keep it short: it costs roughly an hour of HSM time. Read the “Getting started” flow instead:

  1. Create a cluster.
  2. Initialize it.
  3. Activate it.
  4. Create a crypto user (CU).
  5. Cleanup: delete the HSMs and the cluster.

AWS Secrets Manager

At a glance

Stores, encrypts (with KMS), rotates and audits secrets: DB credentials, API keys, OAuth tokens. Apps fetch them at runtime instead of hard-coding them, so a change is made in one place and nothing leaks into Git.

  • Exam skills: manage & rotate secrets (5.3.1) · encryption at rest (5.2.1) · multi-Region keys & replication (5.3.5, 5.2.4) · cross-account resource policies (4.2.1) · SCP/RCP guardrails (6.1.3) · Access Analyzer (4.2.5)
  • Videos: ▶ #69 Secrets Manager · ▶ #70 Rotating secrets · ▶ #71 Replication · ▶ #72 Cross-account access
  • Cost: $0.40 per secret per month (each replica too) + $0.05 per 10,000 API calls

Why it exists: instead of hard-coding credentials in code or config files, apps retrieve them at runtime. When a credential changes you update one central place instead of hunting every copy, and nobody accidentally pushes credentials to Git. ▶ #69 00:12

Secret types: managed vs “other”

The console’s Store a new secret wizard offers five types: Credentials for Amazon RDS database, …DocumentDB database, …Redshift data warehouse, Credentials for other database, and Other type of secret (API key, OAuth token, other). ▶ #69 01:02

Managed secret Other type of secret
Who creates it The owning service (RDS, Aurora, DocumentDB, Redshift, App Runner, CodeBuild, DataSync…) You
Examples RDS master user password (--manage-master-user-password, name prefix rds!) API keys (Stripe, SendGrid, Twilio), OAuth/refresh tokens, service-account creds, SSH private keys, app encryption keys
Rotation Some get managed rotation automatically You set up rotation (Lambda)
Extras Service enforces dependencies, so you can’t delete a secret still in use Key/value or plaintext JSON
  • Secrets Manager knows the credential structure of managed secrets and can configure rotation automatically for some of them. The owning service manages the lifecycle. ▶ #69 02:00
  • “Other” secrets are stored as Key/value pairs or Plaintext (a free string or JSON). Switching from JSON plaintext back to key/value auto-fills the pairs. ▶ #69 03:11
  • Managed secrets can only be created by the service that manages them. That’s why the console’s RDS type won’t continue until you select a database. ▶ #69 05:12
  • Names can be hierarchical with / (prod/AppBeta/MySql). That helps with thousands of secrets and lets IAM scope by path. ▶ #69 06:12
  • Tags are “extremely important”: environment, owner, cost-center, compliance. They drive ABAC (aws:ResourceTag/owner = ${aws:PrincipalTag/team}). Also restrict aws:RequestTag on CreateSecret/TagResource so nobody can re-tag a secret to gain access. ▶ #69 06:41

Encryption and the two permissions every consumer needs

  1. Secrets Manager encrypts the secret with KMS: aws/secretsmanager by default, or a customer managed key (CMK). It uses envelope encryption with encryption context SecretARN.
  2. The encrypted secret is stored.
  3. On GetSecretValue it decrypts with KMS and returns plaintext. ▶ #69 09:51

So the caller needs both secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and permission to use the KMS key. ▶ #69 10:21 With a CMK, your roles and Secrets Manager itself need key permissions. ▶ #69 04:51

  • On AWS compute (EC2, ECS, Lambda) the SDK picks up temporary credentials from the attached IAM role. Outside AWS, use IAM Roles Anywhere. ▶ #69 10:42
  • Resource-based policies attach directly to the secret, like S3 bucket or KMS key policies, and grant actions such as secretsmanager:GetSecretValue / DescribeSecret. ▶ #69 08:00 Use them for:
    • least privilege,
    • sharing across accounts without making the secret public,
    • letting a service role read it (ECS task role, Lambda),
    • delegating management to another team or a client. ▶ #69 08:10
  • Private access: interface VPC endpoint com.amazonaws.<region>.secretsmanager + endpoint policy, and aws:SourceVpce in the secret policy.
  • Clients should cache secrets (caching libraries, Lambda Parameters & Secrets extension, Secrets Manager Agent, ECS/EKS injection), but refresh on auth failure. Never cache forever.
Console demo: store a new secret ([▶ #69](https://youtu.be/yoOZVaTS6I8))
  1. Secrets Manager → Store a new secret.
  2. Type Other type of secret → Key/value tab → switch to Plaintext and enter my-api-key-12345, or paste JSON {"username": "admin", "password": "…"}. Switching back to Key/value fills in the pairs.
  3. Encryption key: the default aws/secretsmanager, or a CMK (or Add new key, then refresh).
  4. Switch the type to Credentials for Amazon RDS database → enter credentials → Next stays blocked until you select a database. Switch back to Other.
  5. Next → Secret name (e.g. prod/AppBeta/MySql), description, Tags (environment, owner, cost-center, compliance).
  6. Resource permissions → Edit permissions: a resource policy, e.g. grant GetSecretValue / DescribeSecret to another account or role.
  7. Replicate secret → Region eu-north-1 → error: the SSO role is “not authorized to perform kms:ListAliases … with an explicit deny in a service control policy” (Region-restriction SCP).
  8. Rotation and review continue in ▶ #70.

Rotation
