Two mechanisms, and the difference matters: ▶ #70 00:11

Managed rotation Rotation by Lambda function
Applies to Only some managed secrets: Aurora, ECS, RDS, Redshift ▶ #70 00:50 Any secret
Where the logic runs Not in your account (fully managed, invisible) A Lambda in your account: an AWS template from the Serverless Application Repository, or your own code
You maintain Nothing The function, its network path and its permissions

Schedule: rate() in hours/days (as often as every 4 hours) or cron() via the schedule builder, plus an optional window. ▶ #70 01:21 “Rotate immediately” is on by default when you enable rotation. That can break apps that hard-coded the initial password.

The 4 Lambda steps (know the labels): ▶ #70 02:41

Step What it does Version label
createSecret Generate a new value new version = AWSPENDING
setSecret Apply it to the target system (change the DB password)
testSecret Verify the new credentials work
finishSecret Promote it new → AWSCURRENT, old → AWSPREVIOUS

Strategies:

  • Single user: change the same user’s password. Simple, but connections can fail briefly.
  • Alternating users: a clone user (user_clone) takes turns with the original, giving no downtime. It needs a superuser secret to run setSecret.

Manual rotation (RotateSecret from the console, CLI or API) is for a suspected compromise. Regular rotation should always be automated. ▶ #70 03:23

Rotation failing? Check these
  • The Lambda needs a network path to both the database and the Secrets Manager endpoint (interface endpoint or NAT). A timeout almost always means this is missing.
  • The DB security group must allow the Lambda’s security group.
  • Execution role: secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, PutSecretValue, DescribeSecret, UpdateSecretVersionStage, GetRandomPassword + kms:Decrypt / GenerateDataKey on the CMK.
  • The function’s resource policy must allow Secrets Manager to call lambda:InvokeFunction.
  • Read the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs. CloudTrail shows RotationStarted / RotationSucceeded / RotationFailed.

Replication across Regions

Secrets are Regional. A replica is a read-only copy (same value and metadata) in another Region of the same account. It’s used for low latency and DR. ▶ #71 00:00

  • Each replica is encrypted with a KMS key in its own Region (aws/secretsmanager or a CMK there). ▶ #71 01:21
  • Rotation happens on the primary and propagates to every replica. ▶ #71 02:12
  • In a disaster, promote a replica to a standalone secret (StopReplicationToReplica). This is one-way: it stops receiving updates. ▶ #71 02:02
  • The replica ARN keeps the same name and suffix, with the replica’s Region. Resource policies and tags replicate but are managed on the primary. Each replica is billed as a secret.
  • You don’t need a replica just to read a secret from another Region. Call that Region’s endpoint, with IAM and the resource policy allowing it. ▶ #71 00:21

Console demo: replicate a secret ([▶ #71](https://youtu.be/H--RsFNrJ7Q))
  1. Open the secret (testing/Example/Secret) → Replication tab (status Disabled) → Replicate secret to other Regions. ▶ #71 00:52
  2. Choose a Region, e.g. eu-west-3 (Paris), and an encryption key in that Region: aws/secretsmanager or your own CMK there. ▶ #71 01:21
  3. Add Region for more replicas (e.g. eu-west-1) → Replicate secret. A status indicator per Region shows progress until complete. ▶ #71 01:51
  4. In the demo account both Regions fail with the SCP’s kms:ListAliases explicit deny.

The same can be done with the CLI, SDK or API (ReplicateSecretToRegions).

Replication AccessDenied: Secrets Manager must decrypt with the primary key and then re-encrypt in the replica Region:

  • missing kms:Decrypt on the primary key → error ▶ #71 02:31
  • with CMKs, also kms:GenerateDataKey + kms:Encrypt on the replica key ▶ #71 02:41
  • “explicit deny in a service control policy” → a Region-restriction SCP (aws:RequestedRegion), as in the demo above

Cross-account access

By default only principals in the secret’s own account can use it. ▶ #72 00:00 Cross-account access needs three things together, or you get AccessDenied: ▶ #72 01:21

  1. A resource policy on the secret (Account A) allowing B’s role.
  2. A KMS key policy (Account A) letting B’s role decrypt. The key must be a customer managed key: the aws/secretsmanager policy can’t be edited, so AWS managed keys can’t be used cross-account. ▶ #72 00:40
  3. An IAM policy in Account B allowing Secrets Manager and KMS actions on A’s resources.
The three policies (Account A 111111111111 → Account B 222222222222) 
// 1. Resource policy on the secret (Account A)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/AppRole" },
    "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}

// 2. Statement in the KMS key policy (Account A)
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/AppRole" },
  "Action": ["kms:Decrypt", "kms:DescribeKey"],
  "Resource": "*",
  "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": "secretsmanager.us-east-1.amazonaws.com" } }
}

// 3. IAM policy on AppRole (Account B)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:111111111111:secret:prod/app/db-??????" },
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "kms:Decrypt",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111111111111:key/<key-id>" }
  ]
}

The consumer must use the secret’s full ARN. The 6-character random suffix means IAM resource ARNs end with -??????. After switching an existing secret to a CMK, old versions stay on the old key until a new version is written: put a new value or rotate.

Use it for a central security/infrastructure account or for sharing with another organization, such as a client. ▶ #72 00:50

Guardrails against accidental exposure

“Never rely on that complexity as protection.” One "Principal": "*" is the worst case. ▶ #72 02:51

Guardrail Applies to What it does
BlockPublicPolicy One PutResourcePolicy call Rejects policies granting broad/wildcard access. Enforce it org-wide with an SCP on secretsmanager:BlockPublicPolicy = true. ▶ #72 03:40
SCP Your principals e.g. deny PutResourcePolicy except for a security role, stopping internal mistakes. ▶ #72 04:11
RCP Your resources Data perimeter: deny when aws:PrincipalOrgID ≠ your org, even if a resource policy is wrong. Not applied to the management account. ▶ #72 04:40
IAM Access Analyzer Detection Findings when a secret is accessible from outside your account, allows principals outside your organization, or a principal can reach a secret in another account you didn’t intend. Also policy validation and custom policy checks (CheckNoPublicAccess, CheckAccessNotGranted) for CI. “The main tool AWS recommends.” ▶ #72 05:10

Even without a wildcard, a policy can grant more than least privilege. Complexity breeds mistakes, so put guardrails in place instead of trusting each policy. ▶ #72 03:01

RCP: only principals in my org can touch secrets 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "EnforceOrgIdentities",
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "secretsmanager:*",
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": {
      "StringNotEqualsIfExists": { "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-exampleorgid" },
      "BoolIfExists": { "aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false" }
    }
  }]
}

Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store

Secrets Manager Parameter Store
Built-in rotation Yes (Lambda / managed) No (DIY with EventBridge + Lambda)
Cross-Region replication Yes No
Resource policy / cross-account Yes Advanced tier only, shared via RAM
Generate random password Yes (GetRandomPassword) No
Max size 64 KB 4 KB standard / 8 KB advanced
Cost Per secret + API calls Standard free, advanced paid
Best for DB creds, anything that rotates Config, feature flags, static secrets

Monitoring, deletion, compliance

  • CloudTrail: GetSecretValue, RotationStarted/Succeeded/Failed, PutResourcePolicy, DeleteResourcePolicy, ReplicateSecretToRegions, StopReplicationToReplica.
  • Config rules: secretsmanager-rotation-enabled-check, secretsmanager-scheduled-rotation-success-check, secretsmanager-secret-unused. Security Hub: SecretsManager.1–4.
  • Deletion: recovery window 7–30 days (default 30). --force-delete-without-recovery deletes immediately.
  • Secrets Manager keeps about 100 versions. Unlabelled versions are cleaned up over time.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Apps need two permissions: the Secrets Manager API and the KMS key. ▶ #69 10:21
  • Managed rotation = Aurora, ECS, RDS, Redshift only. Not every managed secret gets it. ▶ #70 00:50
  • Know the 4 Lambda steps and AWSPENDING → AWSCURRENT → AWSPREVIOUS. ▶ #70 02:41
  • “You can’t use AWS managed keys for cross-account secrets because you can’t change their policies.” ▶ #72 00:40
  • Access Analyzer is “the main tool AWS recommends to verify cross-account access”. ▶ #72 05:41

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Rotate DB credentials automatically, least effort Secrets Manager (not Parameter Store)
Rotation must cause no downtime Alternating-users strategy
Rotation Lambda times out No route to the Secrets Manager endpoint (add an interface endpoint/NAT), or DB SG blocks the Lambda
Other account gets AccessDenied reading the secret Secret uses aws/secretsmanager → switch to a CMK + key policy. Error names kms:Decrypt → key side; names GetSecretValue → resource/IAM policy
Replication fails with AccessDenied kms:Decrypt on the primary key (+ GenerateDataKey/Encrypt on a replica CMK). “Explicit deny” → SCP
Primary Region is down Promote the replica
No external account may read secrets, even if a policy is wrong RCP with aws:PrincipalOrgID
Block resource policies that make secrets public BlockPublicPolicy
Find secrets shared outside the org IAM Access Analyzer
Secret suspected compromised RotateSecret now, review CloudTrail GetSecretValue
Secret deleted by accident Restore within the 7–30 day window
On-prem app must read secrets IAM Roles Anywhere for credentials
Hard-coded password in code/AMI Move it to Secrets Manager, read it via the role
Updates since the videos
  • The console’s “Credentials for Amazon RDS database” type is not strictly a managed secret. True managed secrets are created by the service itself (rds!…), can only be changed through that service, and rotate without a Lambda in your account.
  • AWS-supplied Lambda rotation templates (deployed into your account) exist for RDS, Aurora, Redshift, DocumentDB and more. That is different from managed rotation, which uses no Lambda in your account and covers Aurora, ECS, RDS and Redshift only.
  • The 4-hour minimum rotation interval dates from 2023. Older material says once a day at most.

Real-world practice

  • One secret per app per environment, named by path (prod/payments/db), with path-based IAM ARNs (secret:prod/app1/*) or ABAC on secretsmanager:ResourceTag/app, and a CMK per environment.
  • Scope the CMK with kms:ViaService = secretsmanager.<region>.amazonaws.com and kms:EncryptionContext:SecretARN.
  • Turn on rotation from day one. Alert with EventBridge on RotationFailed and on GetSecretValue from unexpected principals.
  • After a compromise: rotate immediately, check CloudTrail for GetSecretValue by unexpected principals, tighten the resource policy. Replicas get the new value automatically.
  • DR runbook: test the promote-replica step and make apps Region-aware. If you have a Region-restriction SCP, allow the DR Regions or exempt Secrets Manager (aws:PrincipalIsAWSService / aws:CalledVia).
  • Prefer per-account secrets + replication over a central secrets account, to reduce blast radius. If you centralize, use ABAC and aws:PrincipalOrgID instead of ever-growing resource policies (20 KB limit).
  • Watch cost: hundreds of per-tenant secrets and replicas add up. Use one JSON secret per app where the rotation semantics allow it.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create an RDS MySQL instance with --manage-master-user-password. RDS creates and rotates the secret.
  2. Or create a generic secret, attach a resource policy for a second account, switch it to a CMK, and run aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <full-arn> from the other account.
  3. Try replicating it to another Region with a CMK there, then promote the replica.
  4. Cleanup: aws secretsmanager delete-secret --secret-id <arn> --force-delete-without-recovery (otherwise a 7–30 day window applies), and delete the DB.

AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store

At a glance

A managed, hierarchical key/value store for configuration values and secrets (feature flags, connection strings, API keys, environment variables), part of Systems Manager. Apps read values at runtime instead of hard-coding them: less risk of leaking values into Git, and a single source of truth for configuration. ▶ #73 00:51

  • Exam skills: manage credentials and secrets (5.3.1) · encryption at rest (5.2.1) · share resources with RAM (6.2.4) · instance profiles / service roles (3.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #73 AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
  • Key difference from Secrets Manager: no automatic rotation

What it stores and who reads it

  • Also called Parameter Store or SSM Parameter Store: a centralized, secure location for config and secrets. ▶ #73 00:00
  • Typical contents: app configuration, feature flags, DB connection strings, API keys, environment variables, any runtime parameter. ▶ #73 00:11
  • Native integrations: Amazon ECS, Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda, AWS CodeBuild, AWS CloudFormation. ▶ #73 00:31
  • It overlaps with Secrets Manager, so know the pros and cons of both for exam scenarios. ▶ #73 01:00

The console page has tabs My parameters, Public parameters and Settings, and a banner: “Introducing cross-account parameter sharing: You can now use AWS Resource Access Manager to share parameters with other accounts in your organization” (Share in RAM). ▶ #73 01:31

Names and hierarchies

  • Be descriptive and use / to build hierarchies, e.g. prod/database/…, staging/…. Demo: /myapp/production/db/password. ▶ #73 01:41
  • Read a whole branch with GetParametersByPath, and scope IAM by path (arn:aws:ssm:*:*:parameter/myapp/prod/*).
  • Description is optional. ▶ #73 02:10

Standard vs Advanced tier

Standard Advanced
Max parameters 10,000 100,000
Max value size 4 KB 8 KB
Parameter policies No Yes
Share with other AWS accounts No Yes (via RAM)
Cost No additional charge (KMS still charges if you use a key) Charged ($0.05 per parameter per month)

▶ #73 02:10. An Advanced parameter can’t be converted back to Standard without delete/recreate.

Parameter types

Type Use for Example
String Non-sensitive config: env vars, feature flags, Region names, file paths, URLs (data type text) ▶ #73 03:00 api.myservice.com
StringList Several comma-separated values: domains, IP ranges, allow/block lists, multiple ARNs or IDs ▶ #73 03:23 us-east-1,us-west-2,eu-central-1
SecureString Sensitive data encrypted with KMS keys from your account or another account: API keys, passwords, DB credentials ▶ #73 04:00 my-super-secret-db-password

SecureString encryption

  • The KMS key ID is prefilled with alias/aws/ssm (AWS managed key). You can pick a CMK instead. ▶ #73 04:22
  • The value is masked in the form. Click into it to see or edit it. ▶ #73 04:42
  • Reading needs ssm:GetParameter with WithDecryption and kms:Decrypt.
  • With the AWS managed key, by default every principal in this account and Region with Parameter Store permissions can decrypt. For tighter control use a customer managed key with a key policy. ▶ #73 05:31
  • Only the parameter value is encrypted. The name, description and other metadata are not, so never put secrets in names. ▶ #73 05:50

After creation the parameter has tabs Overview / History / Tags. Details: Name, ARN (arn:aws:ssm:us-east-1:<acct>:parameter/myapp/production/db/password), Tier Standard, Type SecureString, Data type text, Last modified user (the SSO role session), Version 1. The value stays encrypted until you toggle Show decrypted value, which requires decrypt access. ▶ #73 06:21

Console demo: create String, StringList and SecureString parameters ([▶ #73](https://youtu.be/mx6vAQDavVk))
  1. Systems Manager → Parameter Store → Create parameter.
  2. Name /myapp/production/db/password, no description, Tier Standard.
  3. Type: try String (data type text, api.myservice.com), StringList (us-east-1,us-west-2,eu-central-1), then SecureString.
  4. KMS key source: My current account, key ID alias/aws/ssm. Value: my-super-secret-db-password.
  5. Create parameter → open it → Overview shows Type SecureString and the Show decrypted value toggle.
  6. Create parameter /myapp/db/password with Advanced + SecureString → Parameter policies: Expiration (absolute/relative), ExpirationNotification, NoChangeNotification (not created).

Parameter policies (Advanced tier)

Easily misunderstood as a resource policy that controls access. It is not. ▶ #73 07:01 The demo uses a second parameter, /myapp/db/password, with Advanced tier + SecureString. ▶ #73 06:50

Policy What it does
Expiration No expiration, an absolute date/time, or a relative time (15 hours, 15 days…) ▶ #73 07:11
ExpirationNotification Notify before the expiration date
NoChangeNotification Notify if the parameter hasn’t changed for a period
  • Each policy has a value and a value type. You can add or remove several.
  • This partially mimics rotation but is nowhere near as advanced: nothing rotates, the parameter can only expire. ▶ #73 07:41
  • The console says notifications go through “CloudWatch Events”. That service was renamed EventBridge; the console text is outdated. ▶ #73 08:00

Events, versions and other features

  • Changes emit EventBridge events (“Parameter Store Change”, “Parameter Store Policy Action”). History keeps up to 100 versions, and labels can pin versions.
  • Throughput: default ~40 TPS shared. ThrottlingException → enable higher throughput (paid).
  • Public parameters (e.g. /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/…) give the latest AMI IDs, useful in hardened-AMI pipelines.
  • CloudFormation dynamic references: {{resolve:ssm:name}}, {{resolve:ssm-secure:name}} (limited resource support), {{resolve:secretsmanager:…}}.

Cross-account sharing

  • Advanced-tier parameters only, shared through AWS RAM within the organization.
  • Shared SecureStrings need a CMK shared with the consumer.
  • Consumers get read-only access and must use the full ARN.

Parameter Store vs Secrets Manager

SecureString is the closest equivalent to a Secrets Manager secret, but Parameter Store lacks lifecycle features. ▶ #73 04:53

Parameter Store (SecureString) Secrets Manager
KMS encryption Yes (AWS managed key or CMK) Yes
Automatic rotation No (expiration ≠ rotation) ▶ #73 08:20 Yes
Cross-account sharing Only Advanced tier via RAM Resource policy
Cross-Region replicas No Yes
Resource-based policies No Yes ▶ #73 05:02
Cost Standard tier free Per secret per month
  • If rotation is critical, use Secrets Manager. ▶ #73 08:40
  • If you already use Parameter Store, you can store the secret in Secrets Manager and reference it through Parameter Store (/aws/reference/secretsmanager/<name> with GetParameter --with-decryption), keeping one consistent way of reading values. Otherwise just call Secrets Manager directly. More a practical tip than an exam point. ▶ #73 08:52
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Understand both Parameter Store and Secrets Manager “so that if you’re presented with a scenario on the exam, you know which one to select.” ▶ #73 01:00
  • Standard = 10k / 4 KB / free / no policies / no sharing. Advanced = 100k / 8 KB / policies / sharing / paid. ▶ #73 02:10
  • Only the value of a SecureString is encrypted, not the name, description or metadata. ▶ #73 05:50
  • With aws/ssm, everyone in the account/Region with SSM access can decrypt. Use a CMK + key policy for control. ▶ #73 05:31
  • Parameter policies are not access-control policies. They handle expiration and notification. ▶ #73 07:01
  • “CloudWatch Events” in the console = EventBridge. ▶ #73 08:00
  • No automatic rotation in Parameter Store. Choose Secrets Manager when rotation matters. ▶ #73 08:20

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Need an expiry reminder on a parameter Advanced tier + parameter policy
Cheapest store for a non-rotating secret / config, feature flags, hierarchical config Parameter Store (SecureString for secrets)
Automatic rotation, “rotate RDS credentials every 30 days”, cross-Region replication, resource policy on the secret Secrets Manager
Parameter policy to restrict who reads the parameter Wrong: parameter policies only handle expiry/notification. Use IAM + KMS key policy
Share a parameter with another account Advanced tier + RAM (+ CMK for SecureString)
Secret visible in the parameter name Only the value is encrypted

Real-world practice

  • Put config in Parameter Store and rotating credentials in Secrets Manager. Many teams mix them through the /aws/reference/secretsmanager/ path so apps have one client.
  • Inject both into ECS/Lambda via native integrations, never through plaintext environment variables in IaC.
  • For ABAC, combine paths with tags (ssm:ResourceTag/…), and use SCPs denying ssm:GetParameter* on /prod/* for non-prod roles.
  • Use labels (LabelParameterVersion) to pin versions for deployments and roll back.
Hands-on lab
  1. aws ssm put-parameter --name /lab/db-pass --type SecureString --value 'x' --key-id alias/lab-scs
  2. aws ssm get-parameter --name /lab/db-pass --with-decryption
  3. Remove kms:Decrypt from your role and retry: the read fails.
  4. Cleanup: aws ssm delete-parameter --name /lab/db-pass

AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and AWS Private CA

At a glance

ACM provisions, manages, deploys and auto-renews public and private TLS certificates for integrated AWS services, and can import certificates obtained outside AWS. AWS Private CA runs your own private CA hierarchy (root and subordinate) without managing infrastructure, with HSM-backed CA keys.

  • Exam skills: require TLS to resources (5.1.1) · keys & certificates across Regions, Private CA (5.3.5) · edge protection (3.1.2) · network controls, TLS inspection (3.3.1) · Roles Anywhere trust anchors (4.2.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #143 Creating and managing certificates
  • Cost: ACM public certs are free with integrated services. Private CA: 30-day free trial for the first CA, then per CA per month (~$400 for general-purpose) plus per certificate.

What ACM does and where certificates can be used

  • Fully managed: ACM provisions, manages, deploys and renews SSL/TLS certificates. ▶ #143 00:10
  • Console options: Request a certificate (public from Amazon, or private from your org’s CA), Import a certificate (obtained outside AWS), Create a private CA. ▶ #143 00:00
  • Pricing (console): certificates provisioned through ACM are free with integrated AWS resources like CloudFront. You can also request and export certificates for use outside AWS for an additional fee. ▶ #143 00:00
  • Integrated services: CloudFront, Elastic Load Balancers, API Gateway, EKS, Cognito, Elastic Beanstalk, App Runner, OpenSearch, Network Firewall, and more. ▶ #143 03:21
  • Network Firewall TLS inspection requires an ACM certificate to decrypt and re-encrypt TLS traffic passing through the firewall. Clients must trust the inspection CA. ▶ #143 03:51
  • ACM public certs can’t be installed directly on EC2 the classic way (the private key isn’t exportable). Put ACM on an ELB/CloudFront in front of EC2, or use a Private CA certificate (exportable). ACM added a paid “exportable public certificate” option in 2025.

Regions

ACM certs are Regional:

Where the cert is used Region the cert must be in
ALB / NLB / API Gateway Regional endpoint The same Region as the resource
CloudFront, edge-optimized API Gateway us-east-1
One name in several Regions Request a cert in each Region

Requesting and validating a public certificate

  • Certificate type: request a public certificate. Private is disabled until a private CA exists. ▶ #143 00:40
  • Fully qualified domain name: a domain you own and can edit DNS for (demo 30daystolearncloud.com), plus more names (SANs) if needed. ▶ #143 00:40
  • Export: leave it not exportable.
  • Validation method: DNS validation (a CNAME record; Route 53 offers a Create records in Route 53 button) or email validation.
  • Key algorithm: RSA 2048 in the demo, or ECDSA P-256/P-384. Several exist because not every service supports every algorithm. ▶ #143 00:40
  • After the request the status is Pending validation, type Amazon Issued. The demo domain’s DNS is in Cloudflare, so the CNAME is added there by hand. Validation took a few minutes → Issued.

Renewal and expiry monitoring

Certificate Renewal
ACM-issued, DNS validation Automatic, as long as the validation CNAME stays in place
ACM-issued, email validation Needs manual action
Imported Never renewed by ACM. You re-import it
  • ACM sends EventBridge “ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration” events, starting 45 days before expiry by default.
  • CloudWatch metric DaysToExpiry, and the AWS Config managed rule acm-certificate-expiration-check.

Serving an API over HTTPS: API Gateway custom domain

Setting Options
Domain visibility Public (internet, REST/HTTP/WebSocket) or Private (only within a VPC, REST only) ▶ #143 04:21
Routing mode (new) API mappings only (REST/HTTP/WebSocket) · Routing rules only (recommended, header and base-path conditions, REST only) · Routing rules then API mappings (rules win, REST only)
Endpoint type Regional (recommended, REST/HTTP/WebSocket) or Edge-optimized (REST only, replicated with CloudFront)
IP address type IPv4 or Dualstack

  • Mutual TLS authentication: clients must present X.509 certificates. Supports REST and HTTP APIs. ▶ #143 04:21
  • Security policy (new): the demo chooses TLS 1.3, shown later as SecurityPolicy_TLS13_1_3_2025_09.

The last step is a DNS CNAME from the custom domain to the API Gateway domain name. The API is then served over valid TLS on a friendly name instead of the default execute-api hostname.

Console demo: public cert on an API Gateway custom domain ([▶ #143](https://youtu.be/ym9lYP_Vl7c))
  1. ACM → Request certificate → public → FQDN 30daystolearncloud.com → not exportable → DNS validation → RSA 2048 → Request.
  2. Copy the CNAME name/value into Cloudflare DNS → wait → Issued.
  3. API Gateway → Custom domain names → Add: public, routing rules only, Regional, IPv4, TLS 1.3 security policy, select the ACM cert → Add domain name → wait until Available.
  4. Add a routing rule: no conditions (“A rule with no conditions will match all requests”), target the REST API + stage production, optional Strip base path, priority 1 (several rules are evaluated by priority).
  5. Add DNS CNAME 30daystolearncloud.com → d-ocrzbuiiuh.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.
  6. Browse https://30daystolearncloud.com → {"message":"Hello, World!"}.
  7. Private CA console tour (no CA created).

Enforcing TLS versions and mTLS

  • TLS version policies: API Gateway custom-domain security policy (e.g. SecurityPolicy_TLS13_1_3_2025_09), ELB security policy (ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-…), CloudFront viewer security policy (TLSv1.2_2021).
  • mTLS: API Gateway custom domain (truststore in S3, REST and HTTP APIs), ALB mTLS (trust store), IoT Core device certs, IAM Roles Anywhere (Private CA or an external CA as the trust anchor, so on-prem workloads get temporary credentials).

AWS Private CA

Not a huge exam topic, but it appears in scenarios about issuing certificates for internal services, mutual TLS (mTLS) and managing a private PKI. “If you see PKI … managing your private PKI within your organization, they’re probably talking about this service.” ▶ #143 08:03

  • Mode: general-purpose vs short-lived certificate mode (≤7 days validity, cheaper, no revocation infrastructure needed).
  • CA type: Root (new hierarchy) or Subordinate (issuing/intermediate CA under an existing CA). The subject distinguished name can’t be changed after creation. ▶ #143 08:03
  • The IT team owns the CAs while developers get limited rights to issue and revoke certificates through IAM. ▶ #143 08:51
  • Manage a root + subordinate hierarchy without managing infrastructure.
  • Integrates with ACM: developers request certs in ACM, and your private CA issues them.
  • Use cases: internal TLS, Kubernetes (cert-manager AWS Private CA Issuer plugin), IoT and mobile device identity, IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchors, code-signing-like internal PKI, enterprises needing full control over issuance.
  • Share the CA across accounts with AWS RAM, and restrict issuance with IAM conditions and CA policies.
  • Keep the root CA offline-like with tight IAM, and issue from a subordinate CA.

Console features: AWS-managed CA (HA, patching, backups), lifecycle management via ACM (ELB, API Gateway), HSM-backed CA key storage, IAM integration, CRLs published to your S3 bucket and OCSP, cross-account sharing, standalone use without ACM, and audit reports.

ACM vs Private CA

ACM public AWS Private CA
Trust Internet-facing, publicly trusted Internal trust only
Cost Free (mostly) with integrated services Extra cost per CA and per certificate
Complexity Low Higher: you design the hierarchy
Typical keywords HTTPS for CloudFront/ALB/API Gateway “internal services”, “mTLS”, “private PKI”

This is the key exam distinction. ▶ #143 10:00

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • ACM provisions, manages, deploys and renews certificates. ▶ #143 00:10
  • Network Firewall TLS inspection requires an ACM certificate for decrypt/re-encrypt. ▶ #143 03:51
  • Private CA keywords: internal services, mTLS, private PKI. ▶ #143 08:12
  • Private CA lets IT own the CAs while developers get limited issue/revoke rights. ▶ #143 08:51
  • ACM = public certs, free or mostly free, internet-facing. Private CA = internal trust, extra cost and complexity. ▶ #143 10:00

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Certificate for CloudFront not showing in the list It was created outside us-east-1
Imported certificate expired and caused an outage Imported = no auto-renew. Alert with EventBridge/Config, or switch to an ACM-issued cert
ACM cert stopped renewing The DNS validation CNAME was deleted
Internal services need mTLS without a public CA, “private PKI” AWS Private CA
Install a TLS cert directly on EC2 Terminate at ALB/NLB/CloudFront, or use an exportable cert / Private CA
Network Firewall must inspect TLS traffic ACM certificate for decrypt/re-encrypt
Share a CA with other accounts Private CA + RAM
Updates since the videos
  • The instructor says certificates can be used “in a single Region or multiple Regions depending on the services”. ▶ #143 00:00 In practice ACM certs are Regional: Regional endpoints need the cert in the same Region, CloudFront and edge-optimized API Gateway need it in us-east-1, and one name in several Regions needs a cert requested in each.

Real-world practice

  • Use DNS validation via Route 53 so renewal is automatic, and keep the validation records permanently. Deleting them breaks renewal silently until expiry warnings fire.
  • Run a central Private CA in a security account: keep the root offline-ish, issue only subordinate CAs, and share subordinates to workload accounts via RAM.
  • Consolidate CAs and use short-lived mode where possible to control cost.
  • Add a Config rule on expiry and an EventBridge → SNS alert.
  • With Network Firewall TLS inspection, distribute the inspection CA to clients (MDM/GPO/AMIs).
Hands-on lab
  1. Request a DNS-validated cert in us-east-1 for a domain you own.
  2. Attach it to a CloudFront distribution.
  3. Cleanup: detach the cert, then delete it.

Encryption in transit (cross-service)

At a glance

How to require and achieve encryption in transit across AWS: TLS at load balancers and APIs, private access paths, and encryption between instances, nodes and containers.

  • Exam skills: require encryption in transit (5.1.1) · private access: PrivateLink, endpoints, Client VPN (5.1.2) · inter-node encryption: Nitro, EMR, EKS, SageMaker (5.1.3)
  • Videos: none dedicated here. Related: ▶ #104 ELB health checks & encryption and ▶ #151 VPC endpoints & PrivateLink (Part 3), ▶ #143 ACM and AWS Private CA, ▶ #68 EBS volume encryption (AWS KMS)

TLS at load balancers and APIs

  • ELB terminates TLS with security policies, e.g. ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 for TLS 1.2/1.3 only. FIPS policies exist.
  • End-to-end encryption: an HTTPS listener → an HTTPS target group (the ALB re-encrypts), or an NLB TCP passthrough so the instance terminates TLS. Details: see Elastic Load Balancing (Part 3).
  • API Gateway custom domains and CloudFront have their own TLS security policies (see ACM and AWS Private CA, Part 4).

Enforcing TLS in resource policies

Control Where
aws:SecureTransport = false → Deny S3, EFS, SNS, SQS resource policies
s3:TlsVersion Minimum TLS version for S3 requests

Private access paths

  • VPC interface endpoints (PrivateLink) and gateway endpoints (S3/DynamoDB), each with endpoint policies.
  • Restrict a bucket to an endpoint with aws:SourceVpce.
  • Also Client VPN and Verified Access: see Hybrid connectivity and Verified Access (Part 3).

Between instances, volumes and nodes

Where How it’s encrypted
EC2 ↔ EC2 (Nitro) Traffic between supported Nitro-based instance types in the same VPC (or peered VPCs) is encrypted automatically at the hardware level (AES-256), with no performance cost. The “no app change” answer
EBS ↔ instance Data moving between an encrypted volume and its instance is encrypted too ▶ #68 00:41
EMR A security configuration enables in-transit encryption (TLS certs from S3 PEM or a custom provider) plus at-rest encryption for EBS/local disks and EMRFS on S3
EKS Encrypt Kubernetes secrets with a KMS key (envelope encryption). Pod-to-pod encryption needs a service mesh with mTLS (e.g. Istio/Linkerd) or Nitro instance encryption
SageMaker AI Inter-container traffic encryption flag for distributed training jobs (slower), KMS keys for volumes, output and notebooks, plus network isolation and VPC-only mode
Exam tips

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Encrypt traffic between EC2 instances without changing the app Nitro instance types that support in-transit encryption, in the same VPC
Distributed training data between nodes must be encrypted SageMaker inter-container traffic encryption
S3 access must never traverse the internet Gateway endpoint + bucket policy aws:SourceVpce condition
Secrets Manager / KMS calls from a private subnet without NAT Interface VPC endpoints
Require HTTPS on a bucket/queue/topic Deny when aws:SecureTransport is false

Amazon S3 (data security)

At a glance

Object storage. Security comes from layered controls: Block Public Access, Object Ownership, bucket policy, IAM, access points, Access Grants, encryption and immutability (versioning, Object Lock).

  • Exam skills: require TLS & private access (5.1.1, 5.1.2) · encryption at rest (5.2.1) · integrity: Object Lock, versioning (5.2.2) · lifecycle & retention (5.2.3) · replication, backup, ransomware (5.2.4) · resource policies, cross-account & presigned URLs (4.2.1, 4.1.2) · find unintended access (4.2.4, 4.2.5)
  • Videos: ▶ #51 Managing access to S3 buckets · ▶ #52 Signed URLs · ▶ #53 Access Points · ▶ #54 Access Grants · ▶ #55 IAM Access Analyzer for S3 · ▶ #57 Object Versioning · ▶ #58 Object Lock · ▶ #59 Storage classes · ▶ #60 S3 Glacier
  • Other mapped skills: external IdP (4.1.1), ABAC/RBAC (4.2.2), least privilege (4.2.3), S3 CORS (3.1.2, see Part 3), network segmentation (3.3.4, 3.3.5), log storage (1.2.1), forensic artifacts and recovery (2.2.1, 2.2.4), org policies and noncompliance (6.1.3, 6.3.1).

Access control: policies, ACLs and Block Public Access

As with other AWS services there are two approaches: ▶ #51 00:00

  • Resource-based: bucket policies and bucket or object ACLs. ▶ #51 00:10
  • Identity-based: IAM policies on users, groups and roles, granting access to buckets and objects. ▶ #51 01:20

Evaluation: same account = union of allows. Cross-account = both sides must allow. An explicit deny always wins.

Bucket policies grant other AWS accounts or IAM users permissions on the bucket and its objects, and can supplement or replace ACL-based access. ▶ #51 00:50

Key bucket policy conditions

Condition key Use
aws:SecureTransport Deny HTTP (require TLS)
aws:SourceVpce / aws:SourceVpc Only via a VPC endpoint / VPC
aws:PrincipalOrgID Only principals in your organization
s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption(-aws-kms-key-id) Enforce SSE-KMS (and a specific key)
aws:SourceIp Restrict by IP
  • RCPs (resource control policies) enforce org-wide guardrails on S3 resources, e.g. deny access from principals outside the org.
  • “Serve S3 content publicly without making the bucket public” → CloudFront + Origin Access Control (OAC).
ACLs and Object Ownership

An ACL is a list of grants naming the grantee and the permission granted. Each bucket and object can have one. By default all ACLs are disabled and their use is discouraged unless you have to use them. Use case: basic read/write for other AWS accounts. They use an S3-specific XML schema. ▶ #51 00:20

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<AccessControlPolicy xmlns="http://s3.amazonaws.com/doc/2006-03-01/">
  <Owner>
    <ID>Owner-Canonical-User-ID</ID>
    <DisplayName>owner-display-name</DisplayName>
  </Owner>
  <AccessControlList>
    <Grant>
      <Grantee xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
               xsi:type="Canonical User">
        <ID>Owner-Canonical-User-ID</ID>
        <DisplayName>display-name</DisplayName>
      </Grantee>
      <Permission>FULL_CONTROL</Permission>
    </Grant>
  </AccessControlList>
</AccessControlPolicy>

Grantees are identified by canonical user ID (or predefined groups such as AllUsers/AuthenticatedUsers). Permissions: READ, WRITE, READ_ACP, WRITE_ACP, FULL_CONTROL.

  • Object Ownership = Bucket owner enforced (“ACLs disabled (recommended)”) disables ACLs entirely: “All objects in this bucket are owned by this account. Access … is specified using only policies.” It’s the default for new buckets since April 2023. The modern answer: use policies, not ACLs.
  • The alternative, ACLs enabled, lets objects be owned by other AWS accounts, with access set by ACLs.
  • With ACLs disabled the bucket owner owns every object, so the bucket policy applies to all objects regardless of uploader. The video’s “object permissions apply only to the objects that the bucket owner creates” was true with ACLs enabled (object writer owned the object). ▶ #51 01:01
  • Disabling ACLs fails while the bucket policy/ACL still relies on ACL grants: migrate the grants to the bucket policy first.
Block Public Access (BPA)

Enabled by default: new buckets and objects don’t allow public access. Even if users modify bucket policies or object permissions to allow it, BPA overrides them. Buckets accidentally left open to the public were one of the main causes of S3 breaches. ▶ #51 01:40

# Setting Effect
1 Block public access through new ACLs Rejects new public ACLs; existing ones unchanged
2 Block public access through any ACLs S3 ignores all public ACLs
3 Block new public bucket / access point policies Rejects new public policies
4 Block public and cross-account access through any public bucket / access point policy S3 ignores them: only AWS service principals and the owner account
  • Applies at account and bucket level. The account-level setting wins.
  • Org-wide pattern: set account-level BPA in every account (StackSets / Control Tower) plus an SCP denying s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock / s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock so members can’t turn it off (or a declarative policy).

Presigned URLs

A presigned (“signed”) URL shares an object with someone outside your AWS organization, or lets them upload one, without AWS credentials or IAM permissions for the recipient. After expiry the URL stops working. ▶ #52 00:00

The URL (https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/abc/sharedfile.txt?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Credential=AKIA3S…) carries the SigV4 algorithm, the signer’s access key ID, date, expiry and signature.

How it really works

  • A presigned URL carries no JSON policy of its own. It’s signed with the creating principal’s credentials (SigV4) and inherits that principal’s permissions at request time, limited to one operation (GET/PUT) on one object until X-Amz-Expires. The video describes “creating a JSON policy with a validity period”: that model belongs to CloudFront signed URLs/cookies (custom policy with DateLessThan, IpAddress). The JSON on the slide is a bucket policy restricting presigned requests. ▶ #52 00:10
  • Max validity: 7 days (SigV4 with IAM user keys).
  • Effective lifetime = the shorter of X-Amz-Expires and the signer’s credential lifetime (role session e.g. 1 h, instance-profile creds ~6 h). With a role or STS the URL dies when the session credentials expire, even if the expiry is set longer.
  • Console-generated URLs: up to 12 hours or until the console session expires (1–720 minutes). ▶ #57 01:50
  • Revoke by removing the signer’s permission or deactivating its key.
  • With SSE-KMS objects the signer also needs kms:Decrypt (GET) / kms:GenerateDataKey (PUT).

Risks: an easy way to share with third parties, but careful with sensitive data. A signed URL is literally just a link: it can be forwarded or leak accidentally, and you have no control over who uses it until it expires. ▶ #52 00:40

Upload use case: a new app user uploads an avatar picture; the app generates a presigned URL that the client uploads to. ▶ #52 01:00

Restrict presigned use centrally with bucket policy conditions: s3:signatureAge (milliseconds), s3:authType (REST-QUERY-STRING = presigned), aws:SourceIp, aws:SourceVpce, s3:signatureversion (AWS4-HMAC-SHA256). The slide’s policy denies requests whose signature is older than 10 minutes, even if the URL was generated with a 7-day expiry: ▶ #52 00:10

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "Deny a presigned URL request if the signature is more than 10 min old",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "444455556666"},
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::DOC-EXAMPLE-BUCKET/*",
      "Condition": {
        "NumericGreaterThan": {
          "s3:signatureAge": 600000
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

600000 ms = 10 minutes.

S3 Access Points

Named network endpoints attached to a bucket (not to be confused with VPC endpoints), each with its own access point policy, network origin (VPC-only or Internet), Block Public Access settings and ARN/alias. They give more control over who or what can reach buckets and objects. Console: S3 → Access management and security → Access Points; also available for Amazon FSx file systems (out of scope). ▶ #53 00:00

The Access Points page has tabs General purpose buckets / Directory buckets / Multi-Region / Object Lambda and columns name, data source type, data source ID and Access Point alias.

Use case: a bucket must only be accessed by apps inside specific VPCs → create one access point per VPC with network origin VPC only and the VPC ID. ▶ #53 00:30

Creating one: ▶ #53 00:50

  • Name: unique per account per Region.
  • Data source: a bucket in this account or in another account (cross-account access points). Can’t be edited later.
  • Network origin: VPC (no internet access; requests over AWS private networks from that VPC only) or Internet (non-VPC apps). ▶ #53 01:01
  • VPC ID (starts with vpc-).
  • Block Public Access for the access point: the same four settings, available in either network mode, not editable after creation. ▶ #53 01:30
  • Access point policy (optional): JSON like a bucket policy. The resource is the access point ARN, which you only know after creation, so you’d usually add it afterwards. ▶ #53 01:41

Note on the form: “The S3 console doesn’t support accessing bucket resources using a VPC access point. Use the AWS CLI, AWS SDK, or Amazon S3 REST API.”

The policy section warns: “Access Point policies don’t apply to objects owned by other accounts” and “Access Point aliases can’t be used in the Access Point policy.” The editor shows the ARN to use: arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:396212980357:accesspoint/accesspoint-vpc-1.

Bucket policy vs access point policy
  • You can have both, only a bucket policy, or only an access point policy. ▶ #53 02:20
  • The instructor’s version: AWS recommends only using access point policies when you create access points (e.g. a bucket used only by 5 VPC apps through 5 access points), or making both policies identical, “otherwise they will conflict”. ▶ #53 02:30
  • More precisely: a request through an access point must be allowed by the access point policy and the bucket policy (plus IAM). AWS’s recommended pattern is delegating access control to access points: the bucket policy allows * only when the request comes through an access point owned by your account ("Condition": {"StringEquals": {"s3:DataAccessPointAccount": "<account-id>"}}), and fine-grained rules live in each access point policy. You don’t delete or duplicate the bucket policy.
  • Other condition keys: s3:DataAccessPointArn, s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin.

Using it: after creation, Properties show the S3 URI (s3://arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:…:accesspoint/accesspoint-vpc-1), ARN and alias (accesspoint-vpc-1-…-s3alias, usable wherever a bucket name is expected). Hand these to the apps; they call S3 through the access point. ▶ #53 03:11 If clients hit the bucket directly, the access point and its policy aren’t evaluated, which defeats the purpose: restrict the bucket to access-point-only use. ▶ #53 03:40

Why not just bucket policies? ▶ #53 04:11

  1. Network origin enforcement: with VPC only, AWS automatically blocks connections not from the specified VPC, even if your policy is over-permissive. A fail-safe extra layer. ▶ #53 04:30 The VPC still needs an S3 gateway/interface endpoint whose endpoint policy allows the access point ARN. To force VPC-only access, deny requests where s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin ≠ VPC (SCP or bucket policy).
  2. A dedicated resource policy per access point. ▶ #53 04:50
  3. Many access points per bucket: each app/VPC gets an isolated access configuration. With Internet origin, e.g. on-prem or data engineering teams each governed by their own policy. ▶ #53 05:01
  4. Each app gets its own URL and ARN, so you can cut off access without editing policies: delete the access point and access stops immediately. ▶ #53 05:21
  5. Helps protect against accidental data exposure. ▶ #53 05:42

Limits: access points are for object operations (and limited bucket ops such as ListObjects), not bucket management like PutBucketPolicy. Each policy up to 20 KB; up to 10,000 access points per account per Region by default. Name, data source and BPA settings can’t be edited after creation. Multi-Region Access Points give a single global endpoint with failover; Object Lambda access points transform data on read.

Console demo: create a VPC-only access point ([▶ #53](https://youtu.be/JrT6FwPaCl0))
  1. S3 → Access Points → Create access point. ▶ #53 00:50
  2. Name accesspoint-vpc-1; data source: bucket in this account → cybr-s3-security-demo-bucket.
  3. Network origin VPC; VPC ID vpc-12345 (made up). ▶ #53 01:01
  4. Leave Block all public access on. ▶ #53 01:30
  5. Optional access point policy. The one on screen wasn’t captured; an example:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::396212980357:role/AppRole"},
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:396212980357:accesspoint/accesspoint-vpc-1/object/app1/*"
  }]
}
  1. Create → open it → Properties shows the S3 URI, ARN and alias to hand to applications. ▶ #53 03:11

S3 Access Grants

Gives users direct access to S3 using their identity from an external identity system. Instead of managing bucket policies or IAM roles per user, it maps identities to S3 permissions automatically. ▶ #54 00:00 Best for thousands of users with identities in Microsoft Entra ID or Okta, federated through IAM Identity Center. ▶ #54 00:20

Use case: data scientists, analysts and data engineering teams need different slices of data in the same buckets, often with end-to-end CloudTrail auditing. ▶ #54 00:32

The problem without it: corporate identities → shared roles → permissions. Since everyone uses the same roles, CloudTrail can’t easily tell which human did what, and you end up building custom solutions. ▶ #54 01:10

What it does: ▶ #54 01:30

  • Directory users/groups and IAM principals access S3 directly, without new roles/users.
  • Access is defined as a grant (READ / WRITE / READWRITE on a bucket, prefix or object) and grants vend just-in-time temporary credentials. ▶ #54 01:43
  • Per-end-user access history in CloudTrail, because users aren’t assuming shared roles. ▶ #54 01:52
  • An Access Grants instance gives you a unique domain and a grant manager handling identity → permission mapping. ▶ #54 02:40

Flow:

  1. The app calls GetDataAccess. Identity Center users first get an identity-enhanced session via trusted identity propagation.
  2. S3 matches a grant.
  3. Access Grants assumes the location’s IAM role and vends credentials scoped down to the grant.
  • Location role trust policy: principal access-grants.s3.amazonaws.com with sts:AssumeRole, sts:SetSourceIdentity, sts:SetContext. CloudTrail records the directory user (onBehalfOf / sourceIdentity), so per-user audit works.
  • One instance per Region per account, up to 100,000 grants, shareable cross-account via RAM. Grants are additive; explicit Denies in bucket policy, SCP or RCP still apply to the vended session.

The wizard: 1 Create instance → 2 Register buckets or prefixes as locations → 3 Create grant → 4 Review and finish. The Identity Center instance (arn:aws:sso:::instance/<instanceIdentifier>) must be in the same Region as the Access Grants instance.

Location scope formats: all buckets s3://, a bucket s3://<bucket>, a prefix s3://<bucket>/<prefix-with-path>. Can’t be edited after registering. The console lists the permissions the location role needs.

Grant scope = location + optional subprefix: bucket <bucket>/*, prefix <bucket>/<prefix-with-path>*, object <bucket>/<prefix-with-path>/<object> (tick “The grant scope is an object”). With the default s3:// location a subprefix is mandatory. Warning: “The S3 console can’t be used to access the data specified in the grant scope. … the grantee must do so through the AWS CLI, the application, or other AWS services.”

The instance page (arn:aws:s3:us-east-1:<acct>:access-grants/default) offers Share instance (RAM), Delete instance, Identity Center Deregister/Add, and tabs Grants (scope, grant ID, permission, grantee type/ID, location ID, application ARN) and Locations.

Console demo: Access Grants instance, location and grant ([▶ #54](https://youtu.be/pWdh0pisI9c))
  1. S3 → Access Grants → read “Getting started” → Create S3 Access Grants instance. ▶ #54 02:52
  2. Tick Add IAM Identity Center instance, paste the instance ARN copied from the Identity Center console → Next (the instance is created now). ▶ #54 03:02
  3. Register location: Browse S3 → cybr-s3-security-demo-bucket, no prefix filter. IAM role: existing pre-created role lab → Next. ▶ #54 03:40
  4. Create grant: path in bucket; permission Read and/or Write; grantee type = IAM principal (user or role) or directory identity from IAM Identity Center (user or group). Selected role lab. ▶ #54 04:10
  5. Forgot the permission → set Read. The subprefix had to be /* (shown as optional, but the wizard wouldn’t proceed without it) → Review → Finish. ▶ #54 04:51
  6. Instance page: share, delete, deregister Identity Center; Grants list; Locations tab. ▶ #54 05:11

IAM Access Analyzer for S3

Answers “who can access my S3 buckets?”, from outside your account or within your account and organization. ▶ #55 00:22 It is not enabled by default: the S3 console page “IAM Access Analyzer for S3” is empty until you create an analyzer in IAM (IAM → Access Analyzer → Create analyzer). ▶ #55 00:31

Analyzer type Finds Cost
Resource analysis – External access Access from outside the zone of trust (other accounts, public) Free
Resource analysis – Internal access Which principals inside the account/org can reach selected resources Paid; can be significant with many resources and roles
Principal analysis – Unused access Unused access of IAM users and roles Paid

▶ #55 00:52

  • Analyzers are Regional: “You should enable Access Analyzer in each Region where you use resources”. ▶ #55 01:41
  • Zone of trust = current account or organization (org analyzer in the management or delegated admin account).
  • A service-linked role gives Access Analyzer permission to read resources. Optional tags (up to 50). ▶ #55 01:51
  • Evaluates bucket policies, access point policies, bucket ACLs, Multi-Region Access Point configs and account-level BPA. ▶ #55 05:00
  • Timing: policy / access point policy / ACL changes → findings within 30 minutes. Account-level BPA or MRAP changes → up to 6 hours. ▶ #55 05:31
  • External-access resource types include S3 (and directory) buckets, IAM role trust policies, KMS keys, Lambda, SQS, SNS, Secrets Manager, EBS/RDS/DocumentDB snapshots, ECR, EFS, DynamoDB streams/tables.
  • Other features: policy validation, custom policy checks (CheckNoNewAccess, CheckAccessNotGranted, CheckNoPublicAccess in CI/CD), policy generation from CloudTrail, access preview for bucket policy changes. Findings go to EventBridge and Security Hub.
  • It reasons about policies (what could access), not traffic. For what did access, use CloudTrail data events.

Findings columns: finding ID, resource, external principal, condition, shared through (e.g. bucket policy), access level (read, write, both; also tagging), RCP restriction, last updated, status. ▶ #55 03:00 Role trust policies are resources too, so cross-account role trusts (StackSets execution role, Identity Center AWSReservedSSO_… roles as Federated user, OrganizationAccountAccessRole) show up as external access.

The S3 console view has two tables: Buckets with public access (0, good) and Buckets with access from other AWS accounts – including third-party accounts (the demo bucket, shared through the bucket policy, Read and Write). ▶ #55 03:51 Buckets with private access are not listed. Actions: View findings, Mark as active, Archive, Block all public access (one click), Download report (CSV).

  • Finding details show the exact actions, e.g. s3:GetObject (read) and s3:PutObject (write). ▶ #55 04:40
  • Intended access → Archive (status Archived) to reduce noise, or use archive rules. ▶ #55 04:20
  • Not intended → modify/remove the policy in the service console, then Rescan. If the access is gone, status → Resolved.

Internal access analyzer: create a separate analyzer, then Resources to analyze → Add resources by CSV upload, pasted ARNs (very selective), or by account with all supported types or specific ones (e.g. S3 Bucket). The picker also offers DynamoDB streams/tables, RDS DB (cluster) snapshots and S3 Express directory buckets. ▶ #55 05:50 “You are only charged for the resources you configure for analysis.” Scope it to control cost and alert floods. ▶ #55 06:32

After 2–3 minutes: 145 findings, many more than external as expected. Same columns, but principal instead of external principal (mostly the same IAM role). ▶ #55 07:01

Resource analysis (new at recording): all affected resources from your analyzers, active findings (hover for external vs internal split), resource type, owner account. A good high-level overview. ▶ #55 07:41

Console demo: external and internal analyzers ([▶ #55](https://youtu.be/0ySZgVGHxjA))
  1. S3 → IAM Access Analyzer: empty, not enabled. ▶ #55 00:22
  2. IAM → Access Analyzer → Create analyzer → External access → name default (ExternalAccess-ConsoleAnalyzer-<uuid>), zone of trust current account → Create. ▶ #55 01:31
  3. Refresh after ~2 minutes → 5 findings. ▶ #55 03:00 (02:10–02:59 of the video is a sponsor segment, not exam content.)
  4. S3 → IAM Access Analyzer for S3 → public (0) and cross-account (1) tables → View findings / Archive. ▶ #55 03:51
  5. Open the finding → actions s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject. ▶ #55 04:40
  6. Create analyzer → Internal access → Add resources → by account → specific type S3 Bucket → Add → Create (paid warning). ▶ #55 05:50
  7. After 2–3 minutes → 145 internal findings. ▶ #55 07:01
  8. Access Analyzer → Resource analysis overview. ▶ #55 07:41

Encryption

Option Key facts
SSE-S3 Default for all new objects since Jan 2023
SSE-KMS Audit trail in CloudTrail. Caller needs kms:GenerateDataKey (PUT) and kms:Decrypt (GET). Encryption context = bucket/object ARN
DSSE-KMS Two layers of encryption, for compliance requiring multi-layer encryption
SSE-C You send the key with every request, HTTPS only; S3 stores only an HMAC of it. Lose the key = lose the data
Client-side Encrypt before upload (S3 Encryption Client / AWS Encryption SDK)
  • S3 Bucket Keys: a bucket-level data key cuts KMS calls by up to 99%. The CloudTrail encryption context becomes the bucket ARN, not the object ARN.
  • Changing default encryption does not re-encrypt existing objects. Use S3 Batch Operations (copy in place).
  • Objects under aws/s3 can’t be shared cross-account: use a CMK and grant the other account decrypt.

Baseline bucket policy: deny non-TLS, deny old TLS, and force SSE-KMS with a specific key.

Bucket policy forcing TLS 1.2+ and SSE-KMS with one key 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::example-secure-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::example-secure-bucket/*"],
      "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:SecureTransport": "false"}}
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyOldTLS",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::example-secure-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::example-secure-bucket/*"],
      "Condition": {"NumericLessThan": {"s3:TlsVersion": "1.2"}}
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyWrongEncryptionHeader",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-secure-bucket/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "aws:kms"},
        "Null": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "false"}
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyWrongKmsKey",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-secure-bucket/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEqualsIfExists": {
          "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id": "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:111122223333:key/1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
  • Set default encryption = SSE-KMS with that key + Bucket Key, so clients that send no header still comply. The two encryption statements reject only requests that ask for a different algorithm or key.
  • The older pattern “deny if the header is missing” ("Null": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "true"}) still appears in exam answers. It works, but breaks clients that rely on default encryption.

Versioning and MFA Delete

Versioning keeps every version of every object, so overwrites and deletes are recoverable: a simple yet effective control against accidental loss, tampering and ransomware. ▶ #57 00:00

  • Enable: bucket → Properties → Bucket Versioning → Edit → Enable → Save. The other option, Suspend, “suspends the creation of object versions for all operations but preserves any existing object versions”. ▶ #57 00:20
  • Once enabled it can only be suspended, never removed. Suspended: existing versions stay, new writes get version ID null.
  • Allow about 15 minutes after enabling before relying on it. ▶ #57 01:00
  • After saving, the console suggests lifecycle rules “to transition, archive, or delete older object versions”.
  • A plain DELETE (no version ID) only adds a delete marker; remove the marker to “undelete”. Permanent deletion = DeleteObject with versionId (s3:DeleteObjectVersion).
  • Versioning is a prerequisite for replication and Object Lock.
  • Trade-off: more versions = more storage cost. ▶ #57 04:00 Control it with NoncurrentVersionExpiration / NoncurrentVersionTransition and expired-delete-marker cleanup.
  • Ransomware resilience: deny s3:DeleteObjectVersion and s3:PutBucketVersioning (bucket policy/SCP). GuardDuty S3 Protection flags mass deletes or disabling versioning.

MFA Delete requires MFA for changing the versioning state or permanently deleting object versions. ▶ #57 00:31 If an attacker could disable versioning and delete prior versions, they could erase traces of tampering; MFA makes that much harder. ▶ #57 00:41

  • Can’t be enabled from the console: use the CLI/API, and only the root user can enable it (with the root MFA device). ▶ #57 00:50
  • Per AWS docs it can’t be used together with S3 Lifecycle configurations. “Nobody may permanently delete versions” is more often answered with Object Lock compliance mode.
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket cybr-lab-example \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled \
  --mfa "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:mfa/root-account-mfa-device 123456"

Restoring a previous version — two approaches: ▶ #57 02:50

  1. Copy the previous version over the same key; it becomes current.
  2. Permanently delete the current version (by version ID); the prior version becomes current automatically. ▶ #57 03:00

The version-specific presigned URL includes versionId=… and X-Amz-Security-Token (temporary session credentials). “Anyone can access the object with this presigned URL until it expires, even if the bucket and object are private.” “Time intervals for presigned URLs can be restricted by your IAM policy.”

Console demo: versions, per-version presigned URLs, restore ([▶ #57](https://youtu.be/yn6earwT_9k))
  1. Bucket cybr-lab-example → Properties → Bucket Versioning → Edit → Enable → Save. Wait ~15 minutes. ▶ #57 00:20
  2. Upload test-object.txt (“Test”) → Versions tab: one version, marked Current version. ▶ #57 01:10
  3. Edit it to “Test version 2” and re-upload with the same key → two versions, told apart by size (14 B vs 4 B). Toggling Show versions in the bucket list shows the same. ▶ #57 01:20
  4. Object actions → Share with a presigned URL → 10 minutes → open → “Test version 2”. Repeat on the prior version ID → “Test”. Each version can be linked individually to compare without restoring. ▶ #57 01:50
  5. Versions tab → tick the current version → Delete → type permanently delete → Delete objects. ▶ #57 03:11
  6. One version remains; opening it shows “Test”. ▶ #57 03:31

Object Lock (WORM)

Object Lock stores objects as WORM (write once, read many): once a version is locked, no one can overwrite or delete it until the lock expires. Strictly, “not even root or admins” holds only in Compliance mode. ▶ #58 00:20

  • Bucket → Properties → Object Lock → Edit. Disabled by default and works only on versioned buckets. Can be enabled on existing buckets. ▶ #58 00:42
  • Enabling is irreversible: “After you enable Object Lock for a bucket, you can’t disable Object Lock or suspend Versioning for that bucket.” You must tick an acknowledgement.
  • Default retention (mode + period in days or years, e.g. 30 days, 1 or 2 years) applies only to new objects. ▶ #58 03:40 Existing objects need retention set via S3 Batch Operations. Setting retention needs s3:PutObjectRetention.

Governance mode Compliance mode Legal hold
Who can delete/overwrite Users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention (header x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true) Nobody, root included, until retention expires Anyone with permission to remove the hold
Change retention Privileged users Can be extended, never shortened (only way out early: close the account) No expiry date
Use for Protection against accidental deletion/ransomware; testing retention before Compliance ▶ #58 01:40 Regulatory requirements, immutable backups ▶ #58 01:11 Investigations, litigation, external audits: unknown end date ▶ #58 02:51

Legal hold details: ▶ #58 02:51

  • Placed on an object version, with no fixed duration: it stays until removed.
  • Toggled with s3:PutObjectLegalHold / the PutObjectLegalHold API. ▶ #58 03:40
  • A version can have a legal hold and a retention period at the same time; they’re independent. ▶ #58 03:10
  • Not supported on directory buckets or S3 on Outposts.

Behaviors to know

  • Locks apply to versions: a plain DELETE still “succeeds” by adding a delete marker; the locked version stays.
  • Lifecycle can’t delete locked versions early.
  • Replicating locked objects needs Object Lock on the destination too.

Scenarios from the instructor:

  1. Protect CloudTrail logs from deletion/tampering: a dedicated bucket in a dedicated (log archive) account + Object Lock in Compliance mode + retention (e.g. 6 months, 1 year). Attackers can’t cover their tracks even if they compromise the central account. ▶ #58 04:00
  2. Immutable backups against ransomware: same steps, Governance or Compliance depending on strictness. In Governance, an attacker with bypass permissions could still delete. ▶ #58 04:30
  3. Forensics / legal investigations: legal holds, because the end date is unknown. ▶ #58 05:01
Console demo: enable Object Lock with default retention ([▶ #58](https://youtu.be/_NKihZZyu5k))
  1. S3 → bucket cybr-s3-security-demo-bucket → Properties → Object Lock → Edit. ▶ #58 00:42
  2. Select Enable; tick “I acknowledge that enabling Object Lock will permanently allow objects in this bucket to be locked.”
  3. Default retention → Enable; mode → Governance or Compliance; period → number + Days/Years. ▶ #58 02:32
  4. Save. Newly uploaded objects inherit the default retention.
  5. Legal holds are applied per object version via PutObjectLegalHold (docs page shown). ▶ #58 03:40

Glacier Vault Lock (legacy vaults): a vault lock policy is initiated (in progress for 24 hours to test or abort), then completed → immutable. New archives use S3 Glacier storage classes + S3 Object Lock instead.

Storage classes

All classes have 11 nines (99.999999999%) durability. For this exam you mainly need to recognise the classes and know that Lifecycle rules enforce retention/deletion. ▶ #59 05:51

Class Designed for AZs Min duration Min billable size Retrieval / notes
Standard Frequent access (> once a month, even daily); the default and safe choice when unsure ≥3 – – ms; designed for 99.99% availability, 99.9% SLA
Intelligent-Tiering Unknown or changing access patterns; S3 moves objects between tiers ≥3 – – ms; per-object monitoring fee (objects ≥128 KB)
Standard-IA ~once or twice a month; backups and DR files ≥3 30 d 128 KB ms; per-GB retrieval fee; 99.9% availability, 99% SLA
One Zone-IA Re-creatable data, secondary backups; ~20% cheaper than Standard-IA 1 30 d 128 KB ms; 99.5% availability, 99% SLA; lost if the AZ is lost
Glacier Instant Retrieval Archive accessed ~once a quarter ≥3 90 d 128 KB ms; 99.9% availability
Glacier Flexible Retrieval (formerly “Glacier”) Archive ~once a year; backups/DR ≥3 90 d – Expedited 1–5 min, Standard 3–5 h, Bulk 5–12 h; 99.99% availability
Glacier Deep Archive < once a year; compliance retention, tape replacement ≥3 180 d – Standard ≤12 h, Bulk ≤48 h
Reduced Redundancy (RRS) Noncritical, frequent (not recommended) ≥3 – – Legacy: ignore it
  • Standard: used whenever you don’t choose a class. ▶ #59 00:00
  • Intelligent-Tiering: the monitoring charge means that if you already know the access pattern, picking the class yourself is cheaper. ▶ #59 01:00
  • Standard-IA: same durability, throughput and latency as Standard, but lower availability/SLA, a 30-day minimum and per-GB retrieval charges. Cheaper overall unless accessed often. ▶ #59 01:42
  • One Zone-IA: if the AZ is destroyed (earthquake, fire…) the data is lost permanently. ▶ #59 02:42
  • RRS: legacy; Standard is now cheaper and better. “You can probably just forget that this class exists.” ▶ #59 03:51
  • Early deletion is billed for the remaining minimum duration. Restores from Flexible/Deep Archive are temporary copies (RestoreObject for N days).
Glacier classes

The standalone Amazon Glacier vault service is being retired for new customers; archival storage now lives in three S3 storage classes. ▶ #60 00:00

Banner: “Amazon Glacier (original standalone vault-based service) will no longer accept new customers starting on December 15, 2025 … Your existing data will remain secure and accessible in Amazon Glacier indefinitely … we recommend S3 Glacier storage classes which provide a superior experience with S3 APIs, full AWS Region availability, and lower costs.”

  • Glacier Instant Retrieval: significant savings vs Standard-IA, but retrievals are charged, so only for data accessed once or twice a quarter at most. 90-day minimum, early-deletion fees, millisecond access. Use cases: long-lived but rarely used app data, user archives occasionally requested, medical images needed quickly. ▶ #60 00:50
  • Glacier Flexible Retrieval: up to ~10% cheaper than Instant, retrieval in minutes to hours. 90-day minimum, retrieval charges. Use cases: long-term backups and DR, e.g. secondary backups in case primary backups (in a faster class) fail or are compromised. ▶ #60 02:11
  • Glacier Deep Archive: the lowest-cost class, ~75% cheaper than Flexible. At most ~once a year, 180-day minimum, retrieval in hours. Use cases: data kept for years for compliance (financial services, healthcare, media, public sector); replacement for on-prem physical tape. ▶ #60 03:21

Lifecycle rules

Use lifecycle when objects should move e.g. Standard → Standard-IA → Glacier as they age (without Intelligent-Tiering), or be deleted after a set period (e.g. 30 days). ▶ #59 04:10

  • Storage class is per object, but lifecycle configuration is set at the bucket level. Rules run once per day.
  • Scope: filter by prefix, object tags, object size, or all objects. ▶ #59 05:00
  • Actions: ▶ #59 05:10
    • Transition current versions between storage classes
    • Transition noncurrent versions between storage classes
    • Expire current versions
    • Permanently delete noncurrent versions
    • Delete expired object delete markers or incomplete multipart uploads
  • Transitions are a waterfall: you can’t go back up to Standard.
  • On versioned buckets, expiring a current version only adds a delete marker: add NoncurrentVersionExpiration to actually remove data.
  • Security relevance: cost and data hygiene, not keeping data longer than needed. ▶ #59 05:41

The Management tab → Create lifecycle rule; columns show rule name, status, scope, current and noncurrent version actions, expired delete markers, incomplete multipart uploads. Replication rules live on the same tab.

Replication (CRR/SRR)

  • Needs versioning on both buckets.
  • KMS-encrypted objects replicate only if you enable it in the config and give the replication role decrypt on the source key and encrypt on the destination key.
  • Can change replica ownership to the destination account.
  • Replication Time Control (RTC): SLA of 99.99% of objects within 15 minutes.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • ACLs are disabled by default and discouraged. Block Public Access overrides permissive bucket policies and ACLs; accidentally public buckets are a leading cause of breaches. ▶ #51 01:50
  • Best way to learn S3 access: practice the different methods and see what works. ▶ #51 02:20
  • Presigned URLs share objects without credentials or IAM permissions for the recipient, but links can be forwarded or leak, and you can’t control access until expiry. ▶ #52 00:40
  • Access points ≠ VPC endpoints. VPC-only network origin blocks non-VPC traffic even if policies are too permissive. ▶ #53 04:30
  • Clients must use the access point ARN/alias; going to the bucket directly bypasses the access point policy. Deleting an access point is an instant kill switch. ▶ #53 03:40
  • Access Grants maps external identities directly to S3 prefixes without large, repetitive policies; designed for many human users in a corporate directory. ▶ #54 05:41
  • “If you have a scenario about evaluating who or what can access your S3 buckets and their objects, the answer is probably IAM Access Analyzer.” ▶ #55 08:12
  • External access analysis is free; internal and unused access cost money. Archive intended findings to reduce noise. ▶ #55 01:01
  • MFA Delete protects versioning settings and permanent version deletion; CLI/API only. ▶ #57 00:50
  • “If the exam question mentions strict retention with tamperproofing or that not even the root user can delete … it’s going to be compliance mode. If the scenario mentions being able to override settings, it’s probably governance mode.” ▶ #58 02:10
  • Object Lock requires versioning; retention periods and legal holds can both be set. ▶ #58 05:21
  • “You just need to be aware that there are different storage classes and that you can use S3 lifecycle policies.” ▶ #59 05:51
  • Map scenarios to a class by “retrieval time requirements, compliance retention, access frequency, and also cost sensitivity”. ▶ #60 04:21

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Prevent any object ever being public across the org Account-level BPA + SCP denying s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock changes
Objects uploaded by another account are inaccessible to the bucket owner Object Ownership Bucket owner enforced (or require bucket-owner-full-control)
Serve content publicly without a public bucket CloudFront + OAC
Presigned URL stopped working after 1 h although expiry = 7 days It was signed with role/STS credentials
Temporary access to a private object without AWS credentials Presigned URL
Restrict premium content globally / many files / paths CloudFront signed URLs or cookies
Browser form upload with size/content-type limits Presigned POST with policy conditions
Cap presigned URL lifetime centrally Bucket policy Deny on s3:signatureAge
Revoke presigned URLs already issued Remove the signer’s permission or deactivate its key
Bucket reachable only from specific VPCs, even if a policy is too permissive Access point with VPC network origin (+ deny on s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin)
Many apps share one bucket, bucket policy near 20 KB Access points
Transform data on read Object Lambda access points
Single global endpoint with failover across Regions Multi-Region Access Points
Thousands of corporate-directory users need prefix-level access with per-user audit S3 Access Grants
Table/column-level data lake access Lake Formation
Evaluate who or what can access S3 buckets and objects IAM Access Analyzer
Who actually accessed CloudTrail data events
Find sensitive data in S3 Macie
WORM; even admins and root must not delete for 7 years / SEC 17a-4 / immutable / tamper-proof Object Lock compliance mode
WORM, but a special team can delete in emergencies / test retention first Governance mode
Retain until the litigation ends (unknown date) Legal hold
Protect CloudTrail logs even if the central account is compromised Dedicated log-archive bucket + Object Lock compliance + retention
“Users can still delete Object Lock objects” (distractor) They only add a delete marker; the locked version survives
Prevent anyone from permanently deleting versions Object Lock compliance (more often than MFA Delete)
KMS throttling / high KMS cost on S3 S3 Bucket Keys
Other account gets AccessDenied on KMS-encrypted objects Grant cross-account decrypt on a CMK; aws/s3 objects can’t be shared
Must survive an AZ failure / only copy of critical data Not One Zone-IA
Delete logs after N days Lifecycle Expiration
Keep logs N years cheaply Transition to Glacier / Deep Archive
7–10 year regulatory retention, 48 h retrieval acceptable Deep Archive
Millisecond retrieval, accessed quarterly Glacier Instant Retrieval
Occasionally need data within minutes Flexible Retrieval Expedited
Updates since the videos
  • Object Ownership: “object permissions apply only to objects the bucket owner creates” (▶ #51) was true with ACLs enabled. With Bucket owner enforced (default since April 2023) the bucket owner owns every object, so the bucket policy applies to all of them.
  • Presigned URLs carry no JSON policy (▶ #52): they’re SigV4-signed with the creator’s credentials and inherit its permissions, max 7 days. The JSON-policy-with-expiry model is CloudFront signed URLs/cookies.
  • Bucket policy vs access point policy (▶ #53): you don’t need identical policies. Both must allow; AWS recommends delegating from the bucket policy with s3:DataAccessPointAccount.
  • Object Lock (▶ #58): “not even root can delete” is true only in Compliance mode.
  • S3 Standard availability (▶ #59): designed for 99.99%, with a 99.9% SLA (the spoken “99.9% availability” was a slip).
  • Amazon Glacier (standalone vaults) stops accepting new customers on 15 Dec 2025. Use S3 Glacier storage classes + S3 Object Lock; Vault Lock may still appear for legacy vaults.

Real-world practice

  • Public access: keep BPA on at account level in every account; put anything that must be public in a separate “public assets” account or behind CloudFront OAC. Check aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status / Access Analyzer findings in CI. Avoid object-level ACLs entirely: they’re hard to audit at scale.
  • Baseline bucket policy: deny non-TLS, deny unencrypted uploads (or rely on default SSE-KMS with Bucket Keys), restrict to org principals.
  • Presigned URLs: generate them server-side with a dedicated, narrowly scoped role (s3:GetObject on one prefix) and a short expiry (minutes). Validate uploads afterwards (S3 event → Lambda type check, GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3). Never log full presigned URLs: they’re bearer tokens. CloudTrail attributes presigned requests to the signer, so log the end user in the application.
  • Access points: in data lakes, one access point per consumer team scoped to its prefix, VPC origin for in-AWS consumers, bucket policy only delegates. Name them after the consuming app and tag for ownership. Access Analyzer evaluates access point policies too. SDKs accept ARNs; older tools may need the alias. Names are part of DNS (<name>-<account>.s3-accesspoint.<region>.amazonaws.com): no sensitive info in names.
  • Access Grants: grant to groups, not users, so joiner/mover/leaver is handled in the IdP. EMR, Glue, Athena, SageMaker Studio, the Hadoop/Spark plugin and the SDK credentials provider call GetDataAccess transparently. Keep the location role scoped to the registered prefix (it caps every grant there). Watch GetDataAccess volume per user in CloudTrail as an exfiltration signal.
  • Access Analyzer: create an organization external analyzer in the delegated admin (security tooling) account in every Region and route findings to Security Hub. Use tight archive rules (principal account + resource) so new unexpected grants still alert. Scope paid internal-access analysis to crown-jewel buckets/KMS keys. Account-level analyzers show Identity Center and StackSets roles as “external”; an org-zone analyzer removes that noise.
  • Versioning: enable it on all non-ephemeral buckets via IaC plus the Config rule s3-bucket-versioning-enabled (Security Hub control S3.14). Always pair it with noncurrent-version lifecycle rules. Point-in-time restore of many objects needs scripting (list-object-versions + copy) or AWS Backup for S3.
