Console demo: create a service-managed StackSet ([▶ #76](https://youtu.be/d1r5etG-feU))
  1. Access portal → management account (cybr_demo_management) → AdministratorAccess → CloudFormation → StackSets.
  2. Activate trusted access. Note Register delegated administrator.
  3. Edit s3.yaml: BucketName: !Sub this-is-an-example-s3-bucket-${AWS::AccountId}.
  4. Create StackSet → Service-managed → Template is ready → Upload s3.yaml → Next.
  5. Name s3-stackset, description “StackSet that deploys an S3 bucket” → (no parameters) → Next.
  6. No tags, Managed execution Inactive → Next.
  7. Deploy new stacks → Deploy to OUs → Sandbox OU (ou-limh-1tzth5z3, 3 accounts) → filter None → Automatic deployment Activated, removal Delete stacks → us-east-1 → defaults (1 concurrent account, tolerance 0, sequential, strict) → Next.
  8. Review → Submit → watch Stack instances deploy one account at a time.
  9. Member account (ReadOnly): check the IAM roles, the stack instance and the bucket with the account ID.
  10. Keep the resources for the drift lesson; otherwise delete the StackSet from the management account. ▶ #76 14:20

Drift detection and remediation

Drift = any change outside your IaC. “Drift is a major problem… I guarantee it’s something you’ll run across.” ▶ #77 00:51 A colleague makes a bad security change to your secure bucket via CLI or console; CloudFormation doesn’t tell you, and your IaC is out of sync with reality. That leads to shadow IT and technical and security debt. ▶ #77 01:10

The demo switches from ReadOnly to AdministratorAccess in a member account (ReadOnly’s benefit is that it prevents accidental changes) ▶ #77 00:11 and suspends versioning on the StackSet bucket (“preserves any existing object versions”). MFA delete is only changeable via CLI/SDK/API. ▶ #77 01:30

What drift detection checks:

  • Only properties explicitly set in the template, and only for resource types that support it. Resources created outside the stack are not drift; they’re “unmanaged” (find them with the IaC generator or Config).
  • Results have a detection status and a drift status separately: SUCCEEDED + DRIFTED = the check worked and found drift. ▶ #77 03:01
  • Per resource: IN_SYNC / MODIFIED / DELETED / NOT_CHECKED, with expected vs actual values. APIs: DetectStackDrift, DetectStackResourceDrift, DescribeStackResourceDrifts, DetectStackSetDrift.
  • Classic drift detection only detects. Re-deploying the same template doesn’t fix it, because CloudFormation only acts on template changes.

Detecting on a StackSet (management or delegated admin account): select s3-stackset (SERVICE_MANAGED, drift NOT_CHECKED) → Actions → Detect drift. ▶ #77 02:12 The DETECT_DRIFT operation takes about 1.5 minutes, not “a few seconds”. ▶ #77 02:41

The StackSet info tab and the Stack instances → Drift status column tell you which account drifted. ▶ #77 03:30 After a console refresh, the panel showing which resource and property drifted is no longer under the StackSet operation (“I think they killed it”). ▶ #77 04:12

Remediation options (AWS docs, Resolve drift with an import operation): ▶ #77 05:52

Option How
Manually revert Undo the change in the console. Simplest here, since one setting changed, not a whole resource ▶ #77 07:31
Keep the change 1) add DeletionPolicy: Retain to the drifted resource and update; 2) remove it from the template and update (resource retained); 3) make the template match the live state → Stack actions → Import resources into stack
Revert via CloudFormation Update the template/stack (removing a resource fits this path, not a single setting) ▶ #77 07:10

Instructor’s opinion: this is where CloudFormation is “a subpar tool”. Terraform is significantly better at resolving drift. ▶ #77 06:20 After the manual revert, Detect drift again → IN_SYNC, 3 in sync, 0 drifted. ▶ #77 08:10

Automate it. Drift can happen at any time, so schedule checks, e.g. a Lambda that triggers detection, checks results and notifies you. Highly recommended. ▶ #77 08:51 Options: the Config rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check (periodic, NON_COMPLIANT on drift) + EventBridge/SNS, or a scheduled EventBridge rule → Lambda calling DetectStackDrift.

Preventing drift: SCPs or permissions boundaries that deny direct changes except via the pipeline/CloudFormation role (e.g. aws:CalledVia = cloudformation.amazonaws.com, or tag-based denies).

Cleanup:

  1. You can’t delete a StackSet with instances: Actions → Delete stacks from StackSet first. ▶ #77 09:20
  2. It asks for the OU ID (ou-limh-1tzth5z3), not the organization ID (o-jqbqypd27k); the StackSet page doesn’t show it, which the instructor finds frustrating. ▶ #77 09:30
  3. “Deleting stack instances from the selected OU does not remove the OU as a target of this StackSet.” Submit → DELETE SUCCEEDED in seconds. ▶ #77 09:52
  4. Actions → Delete StackSet (permanent). Member buckets are deleted. ▶ #77 10:21
  5. IAM roles remain in members: AWSServiceRoleForCloudFormationStackSetsOrgMember (trusted by member.org.stacksets…) and stacksets-exec-… (trusted by the management account 299551924423). Fine for reuse; delete them (after disabling trusted access) only if never needed. ▶ #77 10:40

Console demo: cause, detect and fix StackSet drift ([▶ #77](https://youtu.be/WUiyphsU-XQ))
  1. Demo account → AdministratorAccess → S3 → this-is-an-example-s3-bucket-396212980357 → Properties → Bucket Versioning → Suspend → Save.
  2. Management account → CloudFormation → StackSets → s3-stackset → Actions → Detect drift.
  3. Operations → wait for DETECT_DRIFT SUCCEEDED → View drift details → DRIFTED (2 in sync / 1 drifted).
  4. StackSet info / Stack instances → Drift status column identifies account 396212980357.
  5. Review the AWS doc on resolving drift (revert / keep via import / revert via CloudFormation).
  6. Demo account → CloudFormation stack → Stack actions → Import resources into stack is the “keep” path (not used).
  7. S3 → re-Enable versioning.
  8. Management account → Detect drift again → IN_SYNC (3/3).
  9. Cleanup: Delete stacks from StackSet (OU ID from Organizations) → Submit → Delete StackSet.

Shift-left checks: cfn-lint, cfn-guard, Hooks

Tool What it does Where it runs
cfn-lint Validates template syntax and resource properties. Not a security policy tool Editor / CI
CloudFormation Guard (cfn-guard) Policy-as-code rules, e.g. “every S3 bucket must have encryption”. The same Guard rules power AWS Config custom policy rules CI pipeline
CloudFormation Hooks (Registry) Check resources before create, update or delete. A failed hook blocks the operation (or only warns, if set to warn) Inside CloudFormation 
# rules/s3.guard
let buckets = Resources.*[ Type == 'AWS::S3::Bucket' ]
rule s3_encrypted when %buckets !empty {
  %buckets.Properties.BucketEncryption exists
  %buckets.Properties.PublicAccessBlockConfiguration.BlockPublicAcls == true
}

cfn-lint template.yaml
cfn-guard validate --data template.yaml --rules rules/s3.guard
aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name prod-network
aws cloudformation update-termination-protection --enable-termination-protection --stack-name prod-network
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • IaC’s main benefit: rebuild quickly and exactly, instead of slow, error-prone ClickOps. ▶ #74 00:11
  • StackSets = one operation across many accounts and Regions, e.g. org-wide Config rules. ▶ #74 02:31
  • IaC generator turns ClickOps resources into templates. ▶ #74 04:40
  • The logical ID is not the resource name; YAML indentation is significant. ▶ #75 03:40
  • A stack in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE must be deleted before redeploying. ▶ #75 07:40
  • Updating = edit the template + redeploy; CloudFormation diffs with a change set. ▶ #75 11:50
  • Service-managed permissions are preferred; use a delegated administrator to keep people out of the management account. ▶ #76 01:22 ▶ #76 02:20
  • Hard-coded globally unique names break multi-account deployments: use !Sub with AWS::AccountId. ▶ #76 03:40
  • Failure tolerance 0 halts at the first failure; strict mode caps failures at tolerance + 1. ▶ #76 10:00
  • Detection status and drift status are separate: SUCCEEDED + DRIFTED = check worked, drift found. ▶ #77 03:01
  • Automate drift detection on a schedule. ▶ #77 08:51
  • Delete stack instances (by OU ID) before deleting the StackSet; the StackSet IAM roles stay. ▶ #77 09:20 ▶ #77 10:50

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Deploy a baseline (Config rules, IAM roles, GuardDuty settings) to every new account automatically StackSets, service-managed, automatic deployment on the OU (CfCT also correct if Control Tower is mentioned)
StackSet deployed to the org root, but the management account has nothing Expected: service-managed StackSets skip the management account
Stack instances fail in one Region in member accounts SCP Region deny blocking the stacksets-exec role
Someone changed a security group by hand; find it Drift detection; continuously: Config rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check + EventBridge/SNS, or scheduled Lambda calling DetectStackDrift
Prevent drift on IaC-managed resources SCP/permissions boundary denying direct changes except via the CloudFormation/pipeline role (aws:CalledVia)
Bucket versioning was suspended (specifically) Config rule s3-bucket-versioning-enabled + auto-remediation AWS-ConfigureS3BucketVersioning, faster than IaC drift workflows
Redeploy the same template to fix drift Wrong: CloudFormation acts only on template changes (unless drift-aware change sets are used)
Stop accidental replacement of the prod DB during stack updates Stack policy
Stop deletion of the whole stack Termination protection
Safely review infrastructure changes before applying Change set
Stack is in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, redeploy fails Delete the stack first
Block non-compliant templates before deploy cfn-guard in the pipeline or a Hook (not cfn-lint)
Password visible in the template or console Dynamic reference to Secrets Manager + NoEcho
Bring ClickOps resources under IaC IaC generator (+ resource import)
Updates since the videos
  • Drift-aware change sets (late 2025) compare the template to the live state and can revert drifted properties during deployment. “CloudFormation can’t fix drift” is no longer strictly true; verify current behavior in the docs.
  • 2010-09-09 is the only valid AWSTemplateFormatVersion (not just “the latest”), and the key is optional.
  • aws cloudformation deploy uploads to S3 only with --s3-bucket or when the template exceeds 51,200 bytes. The cf-templates-<random>-<region> bucket is created by the console on template upload. Protect it (block public access, restrict writes): in 2024 researchers showed predictable cf-templates names could be pre-created by attackers in unused Regions (“shadow resources” / bucket sniping) to inject templates.

Real-world practice

  • Keep templates in Git. CI runs cfn-lint, then cfn-guard validate, then deploys a change set. Production changes go through a reviewed change set (aws cloudformation deploy --no-execute-changeset produces one for approval). Block console changes in prod with SCPs, and alert on drift.
  • Deploy the security baseline from a delegated admin account (Security Tooling or Infrastructure) with service-managed StackSets, not from the management account. Control Tower uses StackSets under the hood; CfCT / Account Factory Customization deploy baselines as StackSets.
  • Run deployments through a pipeline with a dedicated CloudFormation service role rather than personal admin SSO sessions.
  • Prefer generated names (or ${AWS::AccountId}-${AWS::Region} suffixes) to avoid collisions and allow replacement updates. Pair predictable bucket names with bucket policies (aws:ResourceAccount / s3:ResourceAccount) and expected bucket owner checks to avoid bucket squatting.
  • For many accounts, set max concurrent accounts as a percentage (e.g. 25%) and a failure tolerance above 0 so one broken account doesn’t stall a rollout. Keep tolerance 0 for security-critical baselines where a partial rollout is worse than none.
  • Use Retain stacks on account removal for resources holding data (log buckets, KMS keys), so moving an account to a Suspended OU doesn’t destroy evidence.
  • stacksets-exec-* roles are trusted by the admin account, have broad permissions (AdministratorAccess by default) and remain after the StackSet is deleted. Protect them with SCPs (deny iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy / iam:DeleteRole on stacksets-exec-* for non-admins) and monitor unexpected AssumeRole calls.
  • Terraform’s plan shows drift on every run and apply reverts it. CloudFormation drift checks are separate API calls, eventually consistent, and can take minutes across many StackSet instances. Schedule StackSet drift checks per OU and route results to Security Hub CSPM (custom findings) or ticketing; pair with read-only-by-default console access.
  • The IaC generator is good for adopting existing resources (with resource import), but review its output: it often includes defaults and hard-coded IDs.
Hands-on lab
  1. Deploy a stack with one security group.
  2. Add an inbound rule to it in the console.
  3. Run drift detection and look at the diff.
  4. Cleanup: aws cloudformation delete-stack (disable termination protection first if you enabled it).

AWS Service Catalog

At a glance

An approved catalog of CloudFormation-based products, grouped into portfolios. Employees self-provision pre-approved, compliant stacks with limits on configuration, without broad IAM rights on the underlying services.

  • Exam skills: share resources across accounts: Service Catalog, RAM (6.2.4) · IaC (6.2.1) · tagging (6.2.2) · least-privilege policies (4.2.3) · service & execution roles (3.2.2) · secure administrative access (3.2.5)
  • Videos: ▶ #78 Service Catalog Part 1 (admin side) · ▶ #79 Service Catalog Part 2 (end-user side)
  • Cost: 0–1,000 API calls free, then $0.0007/call. The resources products deploy (VPC, NAT gateways, bastion EC2…) cost extra; delete them when done. ▶ #78 00:42

Why Service Catalog

You need to give employees access to IT services but control which services they use and how they configure them. Full access to Amazon EC2 is not acceptable; you want configuration options with limitations. So you write CloudFormation templates and publish them through Service Catalog. ▶ #78 00:00 It’s “a powerful way of controlling who can launch what services in your AWS accounts.” ▶ #79 05:41

The security value is least privilege by design: end users only need permission to launch the product, while the deployment permissions sit in a separate, admin-controlled role.

Console layout ▶ #78 01:00

Area Contents Who
Provisioning Products, Provisioned products End users
Administration Getting started library, Product list, Portfolios, TagOptions library, Service actions, Preferences, AWS CodeStar Connections Admins (start here: products and portfolios must exist first)
AppRegistry Introduction, Applications, Attribute groups, Settings

How it compares

Tool Model
RAM Shares existing resources (subnets, TGWs)
StackSets Pushes the same baseline to every account; the central team decides
Service Catalog Users self-serve approved products; users decide when
AWS Proton, Registry modules Other self-service patterns

Control Tower Account Factory is itself a Service Catalog product.

Portfolios and products

  • A portfolio is a collection of products (template versions). It is the unit for access, governance (constraints) and sharing. ▶ #78 01:21
  • Demo portfolio: name Developers Products, description “Products to enable developers to test their applications”, owner IT. Tags were skipped, but use them in production. ▶ #78 01:52
  • Products can be custom or AWS-provided, and can have multiple versions that you deploy separately. ▶ #78 03:10 ▶ #79 05:52

The Getting started library lists 324 pre-built products from AWS (AWS Quick Starts, Service Catalog Reference Architectures). AWS’s four-step flow: ▶ #78 02:06

  1. Search for a product template: start from a well-architected product instead of from scratch.
  2. Add the product to a portfolio: to manage access, govern and share it.
  3. Add constraints and/or tags (optional): make it comply with organization rules.
  4. Grant end users access: they launch it self-service; the portfolio can also be shared across accounts.

The Amazon VPC product ▶ #78 02:31 “builds a multi-availability zone Amazon VPC with an option to include a single instance Amazon Linux bastion instance”. Owner AWS Service Catalog, type CloudFormation template, created May 5, 2020, ARN like arn:aws:catalog:us-east-1:614450566528:product/prod-7hxyzjd3fqeq2. Its support link points to GitHub (aws-samples/aws-service-catalog-reference-architectures/tree/master/vpc) with template code and docs. Clicking the version ID shows the full template (copy, download, or open in Designer). ▶ #78 03:32

The template’s Parameters (what end users fill in):

  • RegionAZ1Name, RegionAZ2Name: type AWS::EC2::AvailabilityZone::Name.
  • VPCCIDR default 10.229.0.0/16, ConstraintDescription “CIDR block parameter must be in the form x.x.x.x/16-28”, validated by an AllowedPattern regex.
  • SubnetAPublicCIDR 10.229.10.0/24, SubnetBPublicCIDR 10.229.20.0/24, SubnetAPrivateCIDR 10.229.30.0/24, SubnetBPrivateCIDR 10.229.40.0/24, each with the same constraint/pattern.
  • Further down: bastion instance type with AllowedValues, EC2 key pair name, latest AMI, whether to enable VPC flow logs, and more. ▶ #78 03:51

The template already restricts input with AllowedPattern / AllowedValues. A template constraint narrows that further per portfolio without editing the template.

Add to portfolio → Select an existing portfolio → Developers Products → “You successfully copied Amazon VPC to your products.” The product is copied into your account; its name and description can’t be edited. ▶ #78 04:21 Two steps remain: governance (constraints) and access (who can deploy). ▶ #78 04:41

Constraints

Created on the portfolio’s Constraints tab, each for one product. Console: “Constraints will be applied to the selected product when it is provisioned. Constraints will not be applied to products that have already been provisioned.” ▶ #78 05:00

Constraint What it does (console text)
Launch Assign an IAM role to the product that is used to provision the AWS resources
Notification Stream product (stack event) notifications to an Amazon SNS topic
Tag Update Allow or block updating tags after the product has been provisioned
StackSet Deploy the product across accounts and Regions using CloudFormation StackSets
Template Limit the options available to end users when they launch the product
Template constraint

JSON with a Rules block (CloudFormation rule functions such as Fn::Contains, Fn::EachMemberEquals), via Text editor or an interactive editor. ▶ #78 05:11 The Samples button offers three: ▶ #78 05:30

  1. Enforce instance type to be either t2.micro or m3.medium.
  2. Enforce every subnet to belong to the VPC specified.
  3. Enforce every subnet-type parameter to belong to the VPC specified.

The demo removes m3.medium and changes "Ref": "InstanceType" to "Ref": "BastionInstanceType". The rule must reference the parameter logical ID used in this product’s template; with the wrong name the launch fails and you troubleshoot back to the template. ▶ #78 06:02 Description: “Enforce small instance sizes”. ▶ #78 06:40

{
  "Rules": {
    "Rule1": {
      "Assertions": [
        {
          "Assert": {
            "Fn::Contains": [
              ["t2.micro"],
              { "Ref": "BastionInstanceType" }
            ]
          },
          "AssertDescription": "…"
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

The on-screen sample had ["t2.micro", "m3.medium"], { "Ref": "InstanceType" } and "AssertDescription": "Instance type should be either t2.micro or m3.medium". The final edited description wasn’t shown in full.

Launch constraint

“A launch constraint specifies the IAM role that AWS Service Catalog assumes when an end user launches a product. Only one launch constraint can be applied to each product.” ▶ #78 06:51 Choose by Select IAM role, Enter ARN or Enter role name. ▶ #78 07:00

  • With a launch constraint, Service Catalog assumes the role, giving complete control over deployment permissions. End users need only Service Catalog end-user permissions (AWSServiceCatalogEndUserFullAccess) plus portfolio access, not EC2/RDS rights. ▶ #78 07:12
  • Without one, Service Catalog provisions with the end user’s own credentials, so the user needs all the underlying permissions.
  • The role needs: ▶ #78 07:21
    • permissions for AWS CloudFormation (it deploys a stack),
    • permissions for the services the template deploys and uses,
    • read access to the template in the S3 bucket where Service Catalog stores it.

The demo policy VPCServiceControlProduct (in the course show notes) allows CloudFormation, EC2, Service Catalog and SSM actions, s3:GetObject and some IAM actions. The instructor says it is not least privilege, only a starting point. ▶ #78 08:22 The role dropdown only lists roles whose trust policy allows Service Catalog. ▶ #78 09:21

Launch role: starting-point permissions policy and trust policy

A typical starting point (adapt to the template; the exact course policy is in its show notes):

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "cloudformation:CreateStack",
        "cloudformation:DeleteStack",
        "cloudformation:DescribeStackEvents",
        "cloudformation:DescribeStacks",
        "cloudformation:GetTemplateSummary",
        "cloudformation:SetStackPolicy",
        "cloudformation:ValidateTemplate",
        "cloudformation:UpdateStack"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:GetObject",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "s3:ExistingObjectTag/servicecatalog:provisioning": "true" } }
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ec2:*Vpc*", "ec2:*Subnet*", "ec2:*Route*", "ec2:*Gateway*", "ec2:RunInstances", "…"],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

Trust policy created by choosing the Service Catalog use case:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "servicecatalog.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" }
  ]
}
Other constraints
  • Notification: stack events to SNS. Tag update: may users change tags after provisioning. StackSet: deploy the product across accounts/Regions. ▶ #79 06:40
  • TagOptions apply standard tags to launched products. Service Catalog also auto-tags provisioned resources (see below).

Access and sharing

The launch role deploys the product, but users still need access to see and launch it. ▶ #78 09:52 Portfolio Access tab → Grant access:

  • IAM principals in this account (groups, roles, users), or
  • Principal Names, used when the portfolio is shared; the names are resolved in each recipient account.

With IAM Identity Center, grant the AWSReservedSSO_... roles that permission sets create. The demo grants the instructor’s own AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_... role for speed; use dedicated permission sets or test users for real testing.

Sharing (Share tab): to individual account IDs or an organizational node (whole organization or an OU). ▶ #78 10:50 The instructor couldn’t use organization sharing from his account (“not in the right account”) and skipped it.

  • Org/OU sharing works only from the management account or a Service Catalog delegated administrator, after enabling AWS Organizations access in Service Catalog settings.
  • Account-to-account: sign into the recipient account and import the portfolio (Portfolios → Local / Imported tabs). Source changes propagate. ▶ #79 06:20
  • The receiving account grants its own principals access and can add its own launch constraints, which keeps local least privilege.
  • You can share with users, groups, roles, other accounts, OUs. ▶ #79 06:10

Portfolios can also be associated with budgets (Current vs. budget / Forecast vs. budget columns).

Console demo: build the admin side ([▶ #78](https://youtu.be/QCzKFcZFDDA))
  1. Console Home → Service Catalog (us-east-1, sandbox account). ▶ #78 00:30
  2. Administration > Portfolios > Create portfolio: Developers Products, “Products to enable developers to test their applications”, owner IT. ▶ #78 01:21
  3. Getting started library → search Amazon VPC → review details, GitHub link and the version’s template. ▶ #78 02:06
  4. Add to portfolio → Select an existing portfolio → Developers Products. ▶ #78 04:21
  5. Portfolio → Constraints > Create constraint → Amazon VPC → Template → Text editor → Samples → “Enforcing instance type to be either t2.micro or m3.medium” → copy, edit, paste → “Enforce small instance sizes” → Create. ▶ #78 05:00
  6. New tab: IAM > Policies > Create policy > JSON → VPCServiceControlProduct. ▶ #78 07:50
  7. IAM > Roles > Create role → AWS service → Service Catalog (default use case) → attach the policy → VPCServiceControlProductRole. ▶ #78 08:50
  8. Service Catalog → refresh → Create constraint → Launch → Select IAM role → VPCServiceControlProductRole. ▶ #78 09:21
  9. Access > Grant access → Roles → AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_… → “You added access for role(s) AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_f5e2808a1e330887.” ▶ #78 10:01
  10. Share tab reviewed but skipped. ▶ #78 10:50

Launching and managing a provisioned product

Prerequisite: the bastion needs an EC2 key pair parameter, so create test-service-catalog. It’s only needed to create the resource; nobody will SSH in. ▶ #79 00:10

Provisioning → Products → Amazon VPC → Launch product. ▶ #79 00:43 Name TestVpcProduct (or Generate name; start with a letter or number, - _ . allowed). ▶ #79 01:00 Version v1.0, ID pa-jyrndy7vakkak, Guidance DEFAULT. ▶ #79 01:11

The parameters come from the template’s Parameters: ▶ #79 01:21

Parameter Value in demo
RegionAZ1Name / RegionAZ2Name us-east-1a / us-east-1b
VPC, public and private subnet CIDRs Defaults (pre-populated) ▶ #79 01:42
Create bastion instance true ▶ #79 01:50
Bastion instance type Only t2.micro, no dropdown, because of the template constraint. With t3.micro also allowed, the user would get a choice ▶ #79 02:01
EC2 key pair Auto-selected (only one exists) ▶ #79 02:31
Bastion SSH access CIDR 0.0.0.0/0 to hide his IP: “you would never do this”; use your IP or corporate range ▶ #79 02:40
Latest AMI ID Default (an SSM public parameter), changeable ▶ #79 03:00
VPC flow logs false ▶ #79 03:10
Manage tags / Enable event notifications (SNS) Options available ▶ #79 03:10

“That’s really one of the powers of Service Catalog. You can give flexibility, but you can also enforce these types of constraints.” ▶ #79 02:20 Limits are “completely configurable by the admins of that product and of the portfolio.” ▶ #79 03:21

Result: status Under change → Available (“Successfully launched TestVpcProduct…”). ▶ #79 03:50

  • Resources (35) with logical/physical IDs: bastion, security groups, internet gateway, NAT gateways (NATGatewayB, NATGatewayBEIP, NATGatewayBRoute), subnets, network ACLs and entries (NetworkAclEntryInPrivateAllowVPC, NetworkAclEntryInPublicAllowAll…), all CREATE_COMPLETE. Physical IDs are prefixed SC-396-…. ▶ #79 04:12
  • Events show CloudFormation information including outputs; Outputs show the same values more neatly. ▶ #79 04:33
  • Tags: Service Catalog automatically injects its own tags even though tagging was skipped (typically aws:servicecatalog:portfolioArn, productArn, provisioningPrincipalArn, provisionedProductArn…). ▶ #79 04:51

Provisioned products (Access filter User) list name, product, version, Type CFN_STACK, status and the user name (SSO role) that launched it. ▶ #79 05:01 Actions: Update, Change owner, Terminate, Import a stack. ▶ #79 05:11

Terminate (type terminate, optional Ignore errors, “This can’t be undone”) so you don’t accrue charges (NAT gateways) or leave a bastion with SSH open to the world, which “isn’t entirely open” because the key pair is still needed. ▶ #79 05:22

Console demo: launch and terminate the product as an end user ([▶ #79](https://youtu.be/5jJFnBmkjGw))
  1. EC2 → Key pairs → Create key pair test-service-catalog.
  2. Service Catalog → Provisioning → Products → Amazon VPC → Launch product.
  3. Name TestVpcProduct, version v1.0.
  4. Parameters: AZ1 us-east-1a, AZ2 us-east-1b, default CIDRs, Create bastion = true, t2.micro (locked), key pair auto-selected, SSH CIDR 0.0.0.0/0 (demo only), default AMI, VPC flow logs false.
  5. Launch product → wait for Available → review Resources (35), Events, Outputs, Tags.
  6. Provisioned products → select → Actions → Terminate → type terminate → Terminate.
  7. Recap in Portfolios (Local / Imported).
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Service Catalog gives employees self-service access with limits on configuration, instead of full service access. ▶ #78 00:00
  • Template constraints must reference the product template’s parameter logical ID (BastionInstanceType, not InstanceType). ▶ #78 06:10
  • With a launch constraint, Service Catalog assumes the role; it needs CloudFormation, the deployed services, and S3 read on the template. ▶ #78 07:12
  • The launch role deploys the product, but users still need portfolio access to launch it. ▶ #78 09:52
  • Constraints offer flexibility while enforcing limits; here exactly one instance type was left. ▶ #79 02:01
  • Never allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 in real environments. ▶ #79 02:50
  • Service Catalog auto-tags provisioned resources. ▶ #79 04:51
  • Sharing to another account requires the recipient to import the portfolio. ▶ #79 06:20
  • Constraint types: launch, template, notification, tag update, StackSet. ▶ #79 06:40

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Developers must launch approved EC2/RDS setups but must not have EC2/RDS IAM permissions Service Catalog + launch constraint
Restrict instance types / parameter values in self-service Template constraint
Enforce tags on everything users launch TagOptions (+ tag update constraint)
Deploy a product into multiple accounts/Regions StackSet constraint
Central team publishes approved products to all accounts Share the portfolio with Organizations
Bastion host with SSH open Anti-pattern: use SSM Session Manager (no inbound ports, no key pairs, logged) or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint
Updates since the videos
  • Constraints apply at provisioning time only; existing provisioned products are not changed retroactively.
  • AWS CodeStar Connections has been renamed AWS CodeConnections; the console link label may differ.
  • CloudFormation Designer has been superseded by AWS Infrastructure Composer (“view in Designer” opens Composer).
  • Organization sharing requires the management account or a Service Catalog delegated administrator, with Organizations access enabled in Service Catalog settings.

Real-world practice

  • The platform team owns the portfolio in a shared-services or delegated-admin account and shares it to workload OUs. Use principal names (e.g. AWSReservedSSO_Developer*, wildcard supported) so access works in every recipient account without per-account grants.
  • Give the launch role only the permissions the template needs: limit CloudFormation actions, scope resource ARNs, and add a permissions boundary if the template creates IAM roles, otherwise the launch role is a privilege-escalation path.
  • For hard enforcement, add an SCP that denies direct ec2:RunInstances outside approved paths. Provisioned products are CloudFormation stacks (SC-<acct>-pp-…): restrict direct CloudFormation access for end users and run drift detection on those stacks.
  • Bake security into products: VPC flow logs on, SSH CIDR not 0.0.0.0/0 (AllowedPattern or a template-constraint rule), IMDSv2-only, encrypted EBS, cfn-guard checks in the product pipeline.
  • Build products from versioned templates in a pipeline (cfn-lint, cfn-guard) rather than copying Getting started library products, which can be old (the demo one dates from 2020, with legacy t2.micro/m3.medium). Manage portfolios as code (AWS::ServiceCatalog::*, Service Catalog Tools/Factory) and deprecate old versions with Guidance: DEPRECATED.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create a portfolio with an “Encrypted S3 bucket” product (a template).
  2. Add a launch constraint role.
  3. Grant access to a test role with only AWSServiceCatalogEndUserFullAccess, then launch the product.
  4. Cleanup: terminate the provisioned product, then delete the product and the portfolio.

AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)

At a glance

Create resources centrally and share supported ones with other accounts, OUs, the whole organization, or (if allowed) external principals, without copying them. Examples: VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, Route 53 Resolver rules, prefix lists, Private CA, Network Firewall policies, IPAM pools, Incident Manager contacts.

  • Exam skills: share resources across accounts: Service Catalog, RAM (6.2.4) · Organizations (6.1.1) · cross-account resource policies (4.2.1) · network segmentation (3.3.4) · response plans & runbooks (2.1.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #81 Using AWS RAM to share resources across accounts
  • Cost: no additional charge, no setup fees. ▶ #81 00:12

How RAM works

RAM shares resources with any AWS account or through AWS Organizations: create them centrally, then share. ▶ #81 00:12

  1. Select resources.
  2. Specify principals: accounts, OUs or the Organization.
  3. Share resources: principals now have access.

The landing page also explains AZ IDs, which identify AZs consistently across accounts (important when sharing subnets). The left nav has Shared by me (Resource shares, Shared resources, Principals), Shared with me (same three), the Managed permissions library and Settings.

Organizations integration:

  • Enable sharing with AWS Organizations once, from the management account (RAM → Settings; greyed out once enabled). It turns on RAM trusted access, and shares inside the org then need no invitation. ▶ #81 00:20
  • You don’t need the management account to share: any account can share resources it owns. Sharing with individual accounts outside the org requires the recipient to accept an invitation.

What can and can’t be shared

RAM can share across accounts, the organization and even external accounts, but doesn’t support all services and resources. Check the resource-type dropdown. ▶ #81 07:52

Shareable via RAM (commonly tested) Not RAM: use resource-based policies
VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, prefix lists, IPAM pools KMS keys (key policy)
Route 53 Resolver rules, DNS Firewall rule groups S3 buckets (bucket policy)
Network Firewall policies Secrets (secret policy)
AWS Private CA, License Manager configurations IAM roles (trust policy)
Aurora DB clusters (cloning), Glue Data Catalog / Lake Formation
SSM Parameter Store advanced parameters, Service Catalog AppRegistry
Incident Manager contacts / response plans, EC2 Image Builder components, capacity reservations

VPC sharing:

  • Participant accounts create their own resources in subnets the owner shares.
  • The owner manages the VPC (route tables, NACLs, flow logs on the subnets). Participants can’t change the VPC, and the owner can’t change participants’ resources.
  • Each account keeps its own ENIs, security groups and billing.

Permissions and guardrails

  • Permissions define which actions principals may perform on a shared resource. Each resource type has an AWS managed permission (e.g. AWSRAMDefaultPermissionSSMContactsContact, SSM = Systems Manager). You can review its policy template or create a customer managed permission for least privilege (e.g. read-only). ▶ #81 04:51
  • Principals: Allow sharing with anyone (accounts, roles or users outside your organization, e.g. an IT consulting/services company) vs Allow sharing only within your organization. Choose organization-only unless you really need external principals. ▶ #81 05:31
  • Condition keys for guardrails: ram:AllowsExternalPrincipals, ram:RequestedResourceType, ram:Principal, ram:ResourceShareName.

Demo: share an Incident Manager contact

1. Create the resource. In RAM’s resource list, type Incident Manager Contacts (also Response plans) shows nothing yet, so create one first in Systems Manager → Operations management → Incident Manager. ▶ #81 01:10

First-time Incident Manager setup (described verbally, his account was already set up): ▶ #81 02:10

  1. Settings → Set up, agree to terms → Next.
  2. KMS encryption: an AWS owned key for the demo; in production use your own CMK.
  3. Service access settings: uncheck creating service roles for findings in this account (covered elsewhere).
  4. Create a contact.

Contacts → Create contact: ▶ #81 03:00

  • Name Christina, unique alias christina (1–50 chars, a-z 0-9 _ -). The name appears in response and escalation plans.
  • Contact channel: type Email / SMS / Voice; name email; detail support@cybr.com (a real person or team in practice). “A contact must have at least one contact channel and an engagement plan to be engaged during an incident. Using more than one contact channel increases the chance that a contact will receive the engagement.”
  • Engagement plan: the channel plus engagement time (min) after the stage starts, here 0. ▶ #81 03:40
  • Create, then activate the channel with the code sent to the email → Finish → “Contact created successfully”. ▶ #81 04:00

2. Create the resource share share-incident-response-contact: ▶ #81 04:21

  • Resources: Incident Manager Contacts → Christina (add tags in production). ▶ #81 04:40
  • Permissions: keep AWSRAMDefaultPermissionSSMContactsContact. ▶ #81 05:02
  • Principals: organization only → Display organizational structure → Sandbox OU → Example account (488075507604). You could share with the whole OU. ▶ #81 06:01
  • Review → Create resource share → “Resource share successfully created”. ▶ #81 06:22

3. Consumer view. In account 488… (listed under Shared principals), RAM defaults to Shared by me (empty). Go to Shared with me → Resource shares: share-incident-response-contact, status Active. ▶ #81 06:51 Opening it shows the ID, ARN, creation time and owner. ▶ #81 07:20 Shared with me → Shared resources lists the contact; clicking it opens Incident Manager → Contacts (URL includes owner account 299551924423 and alias christina). ▶ #81 07:30

Some resources take a few minutes to appear. If missing, check you’re in the right account and the share is active in the owner account. ▶ #81 07:10

Console demo: share an Incident Manager contact org-wide ([▶ #81](https://youtu.be/zk99xtmO0kg))
  1. Management account → RAM → Settings → enable sharing with AWS Organizations → Save.
  2. Systems Manager → Incident Manager → (first time: terms, AWS owned KMS key, uncheck service roles for findings) → Contacts → Create contact: Christina / christina, Email support@cybr.com, engagement 0 min → Create → enter activation code → Finish.
  3. RAM → Shared by me → Resource shares → Create resource share: share-incident-response-contact, Incident Manager Contacts → Christina → Next.
  4. Permissions: keep AWSRAMDefaultPermissionSSMContactsContact → Next.

  6. Consumer account 488… → RAM → Shared with me → Resource shares (Active) → Shared resources → click through to the contact.
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Start from the management account and enable sharing with AWS Organizations first. ▶ #81 00:20
  • Each resource type has an AWS managed permission defining allowed actions; review the template or create a custom one. ▶ #81 04:51
  • Choose organization-only sharing unless you really need external principals (e.g. consultants). ▶ #81 05:41
  • Shares may take minutes to appear; check the account and the share status. ▶ #81 07:10
  • RAM doesn’t support every resource type. ▶ #81 07:52

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Central network team owns the VPC; app teams deploy EC2 into it from separate accounts VPC sharing via RAM
Share a Transit Gateway or Resolver rules with all accounts RAM
Share a KMS key / secret cross-account Key policy / resource policy + IAM, not RAM
Prevent resources being shared outside the org SCP denying ram:CreateResourceShare / ram:UpdateResourceShare when ram:AllowsExternalPrincipals = true (data perimeter)
Workload accounts must engage the central on-call team via shared runbooks Share Incident Manager contacts/response plans via RAM
Updates since the videos
  • You don’t need the management account to share: any account can share resources it owns. Only enabling the Organizations integration needs the management account.

Real-world practice

  • The network account shares subnets per environment OU (prod subnets to the prod OU only). Pattern: a Network account shares VPC subnets/TGW; a Security account shares DNS Firewall rule groups and Network Firewall policies (often via Firewall Manager, which uses RAM); a Shared Services account shares Private CA and AMIs/components.
  • Use an SCP to block ram:CreateResourceShare with external principals (ram:AllowsExternalPrincipals = true).
  • Tag resource shares and manage them as IaC (AWS::RAM::ResourceShare). Audit with GetResourceShares and IAM Access Analyzer, and alert on AcceptResourceShareInvitation / CreateResourceShare with external principals.
  • Sharing Incident Manager contacts and response plans from a central ops account lets workload accounts start incidents that engage the central on-call team, useful for org-wide IR runbooks.
Hands-on lab
  1. In a two-account org, share a subnet to the member account and launch an instance there.
  2. Notice that the owner account sees the ENI but can’t manage the instance.
  3. Cleanup: terminate the instance, then delete the resource share.

AWS Firewall Manager

At a glance

Central management of firewall rules across all accounts in an organization. It applies them automatically to existing and new accounts and resources. Covers WAF, Shield Advanced, security groups, Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, NACLs and third-party firewalls.

  • Exam skills: central policy enforcement: Firewall Manager (6.2.3) · delegated administrators (6.1.4) · detect/remediate noncompliance (6.3.1) · edge protection (3.1.2) · network controls (3.3.1) · prepare services for incidents (2.1.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #80 About AWS Firewall Manager (conceptual, no policy demo because of cost)
  • Cost: $100 per policy per Region per month, plus the resources it creates. ▶ #80 01:41

What it manages

WAF, Network Firewall and security groups can each be configured on their own, but Firewall Manager is the central location to manage all of them. ▶ #80 00:10 You define security policies once and it automatically applies them across services and all accounts, including new accounts and resources as they’re added. ▶ #80 00:41

The slide shows WAF, Network Firewall, Shield and security groups; per the narration, NACLs (“And now also Network ACLs!”), Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall and third-party firewalls (Marketplace) are now included too. ▶ #80 00:33

Policy type Notes
AWS WAF (Regional and CloudFront) Combines first rule groups + customer rules + last rule groups, so the central team enforces baseline rules while app teams add their own in the middle
Shield Advanced Deploys protections; can also enable automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation. Shield Advanced is still licensed per org ($3,000/month, covers all accounts under consolidated billing)
VPC security groups Common (push a primary SG to resources), content audit (SG rules must/must not match an audit SG, e.g. no 0.0.0.0/0 on 22/3389), usage audit (find/remove unused or redundant SGs)
Network Firewall Needs RAM
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall Needs RAM
Network ACLs
Third-party firewalls Marketplace: Palo Alto Networks Cloud NGFW, Fortinet FortiGate CNF

Policies are scoped by account, OU and resource tags (include/exclude). Findings go to Security Hub CSPM. Policies use Config under the hood, which is why Config is a prerequisite. The console menu has Getting started, Security policies, Resource sets, Application lists, Protocol lists and Settings.

Prerequisites

A classic exam question. ▶ #80 00:52

  1. AWS Organizations with all features enabled. ▶ #80 01:01
  2. A Firewall Manager administrator account to manage policies from (the instructor says “main management account”). ▶ #80 01:01
  3. AWS Config enabled in every account and Region in scope, with continuous recording (daily recording breaks it; see ▶ #84 under AWS Config). ▶ #80 01:11
  4. AWS RAM enabled by the management account for all members, for Network Firewall / DNS Firewall policies.
  5. Marketplace subscriptions for third-party firewalls.

Benefits listed on the page: simplify firewall rule management across accounts; ensure compliance of existing and new applications.

WAF & Shield → AWS Firewall Manager → Settings → Create administrator account: enter the account ID; administrative scope Default Administrator. “The first administrator account that you create is the default administrator. The default admin can create all security policy types and manage third-party firewalls, unlike administrators.” ▶ #80 01:31

Policy modes and rollout

Mode Behavior
Automatic remediation Monitors for drift from policy and takes action on non-compliant resources
Manual remediation Monitors for drift but takes no automated action (monitor/report-only) ▶ #80 02:10
  • Start with manual to fine-tune settings and avoid outages, then automate as much as possible over time. ▶ #80 02:20
  • Once enabled, the Security policies tab lists the accounts in scope and whether each is compliant or non-compliant. ▶ #80 02:30
  • Further reading: AWS Security Blog How to continuously audit and limit security groups with AWS Firewall Manager (Feb 2021), which addresses item #4 of AWS CISO Stephen Schmidt’s top-10 list, “Limit Security Groups”, e.g. high-risk ports such as RDP and SSH. ▶ #80 02:40

Cost: $100 per policy per month, per Region. Firewall Manager also creates resources that cost money (WAF web ACLs, Network Firewall endpoints, Config rules), which is why there’s no policy demo. ▶ #80 01:52

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Firewall Manager is the central way to manage WAF, Network Firewall, Shield, SGs, NACLs, DNS Firewall and third-party firewalls across all accounts, including new ones. ▶ #80 00:10
  • Prerequisites: Organizations, a Firewall Manager admin account, AWS Config enabled. ▶ #80 00:52
  • Cost: $100/policy/month/Region plus underlying resources. ▶ #80 01:41
  • Start in manual remediation to avoid outages, then automate. ▶ #80 02:20

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Every ALB and CloudFront distribution in all current and future accounts must have the WAF baseline Firewall Manager WAF policy
Centrally enforce SGs / deploy Shield Advanced / deploy Network Firewall to all VPCs org-wide Firewall Manager (a single-account WAF rule → WAF directly)
Firewall Manager not applying in an account Check Config is enabled there (continuous recording), the account is in scope, and the admin account is set
Find overly permissive security groups org-wide SG content audit policy (detection-only alternative: Config rules / Security Hub CSPM)
Updates since the videos
  • The administrator is normally a delegated administrator member account (e.g. Security Tooling), not the management account; best practice is that it isn’t.
  • Since 2024 you can have multiple administrators with scoped administrative scope (by account/OU, Region, policy type).
  • RAM (Network Firewall / DNS Firewall) and Marketplace subscriptions (third-party firewalls) are also prerequisites.

Real-world practice

  • The Security Tooling account is the Firewall Manager admin.
  • Baseline WAF policy: AWS Managed Rules (Common, KnownBadInputs, IP reputation) plus a rate-based rule, logging to a central S3 bucket or Firehose.
  • An SG audit policy flags 0.0.0.0/0 on admin ports.
  • Cost model is each policy × each Region: a 10-policy, 4-Region rollout is $4,000/month before WAF/Network Firewall charges. Consolidate policies and scope Regions.
  • Roll out in manual (audit) mode first, review non-compliant resources, then enable auto-remediation, ideally with “Replace existing web ACLs” off until teams migrate.
  • Watch for conflicts: app teams’ own WAF associations or SG changes get overwritten or flagged. Communicate the policy, use exclusion tags for exceptions, and track exceptions.
Hands-on lab

Needs an org and costs money (WAF, and Network Firewall especially). Reading the console flow is usually enough.

  1. If you try it, create one WAF policy scoped to a test OU with a single ALB.
  2. Cleanup: delete the policy and choose “delete all policy resources”.

AWS Config

At a glance

Continuously assesses, audits and evaluates resource configurations and relationships over time (configuration items and history), for AWS and some non-AWS resources, and checks them against rules. It is a detective control: it doesn’t block changes.

  • Exam skills: detect & remediate noncompliance (6.3.1) · conformance packs / automated assessments (1.1.5) · automated remediation (2.1.4) · delegated admins & Organizations (6.1.4, 6.1.1) · StackSets (6.2.1) · aggregate security events (1.1.3) · central logging account (1.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #82 About Config · ▶ #83 Delegating Config · ▶ #84 Initial setup · ▶ #86 Remediation with SSM · ▶ #90 Multi-account Config · ▶ #91 Aggregators & advanced queries · ▶ #92 Multi-account conformance packs
  • Related videos elsewhere: ▶ #85 About Systems Manager (see AWS Systems Manager) · ▶ #87 Monitoring Config with EventBridge (see Amazon EventBridge)
  • Cost: per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation

What Config does: the five features

Security monitoring includes watching resource configurations and whether they change outside an acceptable range. Config is the native service for this. ▶ #82 00:10 It also shows how resources relate to one another and how relationships and configurations changed over time, for resources in AWS and outside of AWS. ▶ #82 00:31

Benefits: ▶ #82 00:50

  1. Discover resources you didn’t know existed (less shadow IT), in AWS, on-prem or other clouds.
  2. Record configurations now and as they change over time. ▶ #82 01:00
  3. Easier to evaluate compliance throughout the resource lifecycle. ▶ #82 01:10
  4. Simpler deployment of rules and remediations across Regions, an entire account or multiple accounts. ▶ #82 01:10

When a configuration changes, Config compares it with your desired configuration. If they differ, it can notify you or automatically remediate. ▶ #82 01:21 Remediation runs via SSM Automation or Lambda. ▶ #82 01:31 Integrations: notify via SNS, push events to CloudWatch/EventBridge, store in S3. ▶ #82 01:40

The flow is record → evaluate → package for scale. Aggregators and advanced queries were added to the slide later.

Feature What it does
Configuration recorder Detects configuration changes and captures them as configuration items (CIs). By default records all supported types in the Region. Customize the types to reduce cost. ▶ #82 02:11
Rules Define the ideal configuration. Recorded changes must be evaluated against rules to know if they comply. AWS provides managed rules. ▶ #82 02:31
Conformance packs Bundles of rules deployed as a single entity (across accounts or Regions). Immutable YAML templates: change them only by updating the pack. ▶ #82 02:50
Aggregators Collect configuration and compliance data from multiple accounts and Regions, one account across Regions, or a whole organization, into one view. ▶ #82 03:10
Advanced queries Query a single endpoint with a limited SQL for current resource state. With an aggregator: across accounts and Regions from one central account. ▶ #82 03:40

Recorder and delivery channel

  • Config is Regional: the recorder must be on in every account and Region you want covered.
  • Only one customer-managed recorder per account per Region. Existing ones make StackSet deployments fail. ▶ #90 01:00
  • The delivery channel sends snapshots and history to S3, and optionally notifications to SNS.
  • History in S3: default retention 7 years (configurable 30 days–7 years). Cross-account delivery needs a bucket policy allowing config.amazonaws.com (and a KMS key policy if SSE-KMS). Missing permissions → delivery failures (1.3.1 troubleshooting).

First activation in an account/Region offers Get started (full wizard) or 1-click setup (defaults). ▶ #84 00:10

Recording strategy ▶ #84 00:20

  • All resource types with customizable overrides (default): all current and future supported types in this Region. Overrides change frequency per type or exclude types.
  • Specific resource types: only the types you list.
  • Recommendation: record everything, at least while learning. ▶ #84 00:50
  • Global resource types (RDS global clusters, IAM users, groups, roles, customer managed policies) may be recorded in more than one Region, and you pay per CI recorded.

Recording frequency ▶ #84 00:54

Continuous Daily
Records A CI on every change Once per day, only if something changed
Cost Higher Lower (the reason to pick it)
Firewall Manager Required ▶ #84 01:10 Breaks it

Overrides ▶ #84 01:31

  • A default override exists: “All globally recorded IAM resource types” → Exclude from recording (to reduce cost). Remove it to record IAM resources.
  • Add types (e.g. S3 buckets) and choose daily recording or exclude. Limits: 100 frequency overrides, 600 exclusion overrides.
  • Changing frequency or stopping recording for a type leaves already-recorded CIs unchanged.

  • IAM role: Config needs the service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForConfig to call other services (create it or choose an existing role). ▶ #84 02:29
  • S3 bucket: create one, choose one in this account, or choose one in another account. The ideal is the Log Archive account. ▶ #84 02:41
  • SNS topic: the instructor advises not enabling it, you get flooded. Use CloudWatch and EventBridge for targeted alerts. ▶ #84 03:31

The Config Settings page shows recorder status (“Recording is on”, Edit / Stop recording), recording method, the governance role, and tabs for Customer managed recorder and Service-linked recorders. ▶ #84 10:31

Console demo: first-time Config setup ([▶ #84](https://youtu.be/xWxE7q1OnS8))
  1. Security tooling account → AWS Config → Get started. ▶ #84 00:10
  2. Recording strategy: All resource types with customizable overrides. Frequency: Continuous.
  3. Keep the override All globally recorded IAM resource types → Exclude from recording.
  4. IAM role: Create AWS Config service-linked role.
  5. Delivery channel: Create a bucket config-logs-cybr-demo. SNS topic off. Next.
  6. Rules: browse managed rules (search “waf” → alb-waf-enabled), select none. Next.
  7. Review (4 resource types with overrides, 407 with default settings) → Confirm: SLR created, bucket created, signing up with Config. ▶ #84 05:31
  8. Tour: Dashboard → Conformance packs → Rules → Resources → Aggregators → Advanced queries → Settings. The “Amazon CloudWatch Events rule” link redirects to EventBridge (CloudWatch Events console is deprecated). ▶ #84 10:50

The bucket policy auto-created for Config allows config.amazonaws.com to s3:GetBucketAcl, s3:ListBucket and s3:PutObject to AWSLogs/<account>/Config/*, conditioned on AWS:SourceAccount and s3:x-amz-acl = bucket-owner-full-control.

Auto-generated delivery bucket policy ([▶ #84](https://youtu.be/xWxE7q1OnS8)) 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {"Sid": "AWSConfigBucketPermissionsCheck", "Effect": "Allow",
     "Principal": {"Service": "config.amazonaws.com"},
     "Action": "s3:GetBucketAcl",
     "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::config-logs-cybr-demo",
     "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"AWS:SourceAccount": "851725223689"}}},
    {"Sid": "AWSConfigBucketExistenceCheck", "Effect": "Allow",
     "Principal": {"Service": "config.amazonaws.com"},
     "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
     "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::config-logs-cybr-demo",
     "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"AWS:SourceAccount": "851725223689"}}},
    {"Sid": "AWSConfigBucketDelivery", "Effect": "Allow",
     "Principal": {"Service": "config.amazonaws.com"},
     "Action": "s3:PutObject",
     "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::config-logs-cybr-demo/AWSLogs/851725223689/Config/*",
     "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"AWS:SourceAccount": "851725223689",
                                    "s3:x-amz-acl": "bucket-owner-full-control"}}}
  ]
}

Rules and evaluations

Rule type Notes
AWS managed e.g. s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, restricted-ssh, encrypted-volumes, iam-root-access-key-check, required-tags, ec2-imdsv2-check
Custom Lambda Your code evaluates resources ▶ #84 06:40
Custom policy (Guard) Written in Guard, no Lambda needed
  • Triggers: configuration change or periodic (1, 3, 6, 12, 24 h).
  • Evaluation modes: detective, and proactive (evaluate before provisioning, via CloudFormation Hooks/API) for some rules.
  • Config ships with AWS managed rules (instructor says “over 100”, the wizard shows 154). As Config records configurations, it evaluates them and can trigger remediation or a notification. ▶ #84 04:01
  • Rules page columns: Name, Remediation action, Type, Enabled evaluation mode, Detective compliance. ▶ #84 06:40

Example managed rules from the demo:

  • alb-waf-enabled: NON_COMPLIANT if an ALB has no web ACL. ▶ #84 04:20
  • cloudtrail-cloudwatch-logs-enabled, cloud-trail-encryption-enabled, cloud-trail-log-file-validation-enabled. ▶ #84 04:51
  • RDS backup rules: someone disabling backups in production is “pretty sketchy” and should alert you. ▶ #84 05:01
  • Also visible: account-part-of-organizations, acm-certificate-expiration-check, alb-http-drop-invalid-header-enabled, alb-http-to-https-redirection-check, access-keys-rotated (param maxAccessKeyAge), acm-certificate-rsa-check (≥2048-bit), acm-pca-root-ca-disabled.

Creating a rule (example ec2-imdsv2-check, identifier EC2_IMDSV2_CHECK: “NON_COMPLIANT if the HttpTokens is set to optional”): ▶ #86 01:21

  • Rules → Add rule: AWS managed rule, custom Lambda rule, or custom rule using Guard. ▶ #86 01:00
  • Scope of changes: All changes (any recorded resource) or Resources (only matching types). Choose Resources → pre-populates EC2 Instance. ▶ #86 01:40
  • Resulting rule: mode DETECTIVE, triggers Oversized configuration changes and Configuration changes.

Alerting and integrations

  • EventBridge receives Config Rules Compliance Change events. Route them to SNS or Lambda for alerts (not the delivery-channel SNS topic, which floods).
  • Security Hub CSPM controls are built on service-linked Config rules (securityhub-*, not editable in Config). Config must be enabled for most Security Hub controls, and for Firewall Manager.
  • AWS::Config::ResourceCompliance must be recorded for accurate compliance timelines and queries.

Resource inventory and timeline

  • Dashboard: conformance packs by compliance score, compliance of rules and resources, noncompliant rules by resource count, resource inventory, usage metrics. Takes time to populate. ▶ #84 05:46
  • Resources: all recorded resources, filterable by category, type, compliance status, identifier, “Include deleted resources”. Can take minutes, keep refreshing over ~24 h. ▶ #84 07:11
  • Clicking a resource shows the CI in JSON (how Config sees it), applied rules and tags. ▶ #84 08:20
  • Resource timeline: configuration changes plus related CloudTrail events with user name and event name (e.g. CreateBucket, PutBucketPolicy, PutBucketPublicAccessBlock). If a threat actor later adds a bucket policy, you see exactly which identity did it. ▶ #84 08:40

“What did this security group look like last Tuesday / who changed it?” → Config timeline (CI + linked CloudTrail event). “Who made the API call?” alone → CloudTrail.

Remediation with SSM Automation

Remediation uses SSM Automation documents (e.g. AWS-DisableS3BucketPublicReadWrite, AWS-EnableS3BucketEncryption, AWSConfigRemediation-EnforceEC2InstanceIMDSv2, or custom). It can be manual or automatic, with retries and rate limits. To call Lambda, wrap it in an SSM document (aws:invokeLambdaFunction). Alternative pattern: compliance change → EventBridge → Lambda/SSM.

Example 1: unencrypted EBS volume. Config evaluates new volumes against an encryption rule and marks unencrypted ones NON_COMPLIANT. ▶ #82 04:01 SSM remediation: ▶ #82 05:02

  1. Identify the noncompliant volume.
  2. Create a snapshot (backup, and the source to encrypt).
  3. Create an encrypted volume from the snapshot.
  4. Shut down the instance, detach the unencrypted volume, attach the encrypted one.
  5. Destroy the unencrypted volume.
  6. Log results to an S3 bucket.

Example 2: public S3 bucket. A bucket made public is flagged NON_COMPLIANT and shows on the dashboard. ▶ #82 04:30 A Lambda function calls the API to block public access. ▶ #82 05:30 This can happen before a human even logs in. ▶ #82 05:41

Automatic or manual? Automatic remediation is not always preferable: often you want a manual look first. ▶ #82 05:51 The instructor prefers manual in ~90% of real cases, because auto-remediation is hard to get right and can cause outages unless fully tested. But exam answers lean toward automatic. ▶ #86 02:40

Setting Meaning
Automatic / Manual Fire on noncompliance, or notify and wait (default manual) ▶ #86 02:21
Maximum retry attempts Default 5 (1–25)
Retry time window Default 60 s. “There are costs associated with running a remediation action.”
Rate limits Concurrent execution rate (placeholder 2), error rate (placeholder 5): how many run at once and how many may fail before the whole remediation fails ▶ #86 04:10
Resource ID parameter Which runbook parameter receives the noncompliant resource’s ID (RESOURCE_ID) ▶ #86 04:20

Parameters accept only String and StringList (“custom SSM documents for remediation with other data types are not supported”).

AWSConfigRemediation-EnforceEC2InstanceIMDSv2 uses the ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions API. ▶ #86 03:31

  • AutomationAssumeRole (required): ARN of the role Automation uses.
  • InstanceId (required).
  • HttpPutResponseHopLimit (optional): 2 or more for instances hosting containers; 0 = don’t change (default). Allowed pattern ^([1-5]?\d|6[0-4])$.
  • Output: GetInstanceMetadataOptions.Output (final MetadataOptions).
  • Steps: aws:executeScript sets HttpTokens to required, then aws:assertAwsResourceProperty verifies it.

The AutomationAssumeRole must trust ssm.amazonaws.com and have permission to fix the resource. Missing permissions show as a failed remediation execution status. To find the required actions, search the runbook name in the SSM Automation runbook reference. ▶ #86 05:41

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "Statement1",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ssm:StartAutomationExecution",
        "ssm:GetAutomationExecution",
        "ec2:DescribeInstances",
        "ec2:ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

Use a narrower Resource than * in production. ▶ #86 06:52

Console demo: auto-remediate IMDSv1 instances ([▶ #86](https://youtu.be/WL2GIQWWIVo))

Scenario: hundreds of instances moved from IMDSv1 to IMDSv2. IMDS gives software on the instance temporary credentials. IMDSv2 is session-oriented (PUT/GET token headers), IMDSv1 is request/response. When you require IMDSv2, IMDSv1 stops working. Some teams still launch IMDSv1 instances, so the manager wants auto-remediation. ▶ #86 00:20

  1. Config → Rules → Add rule → AWS managed → ec2-imdsv2-check → scope Resources (EC2 Instance), no parameters → Save. ▶ #86 01:40
  2. Select rule → Actions → Manage remediation → Automatic, retries 5, window 60 s. ▶ #86 02:21
  3. Action AWSConfigRemediation-EnforceEC2InstanceIMDSv2, rate limits default, Resource ID parameter InstanceId. ▶ #86 04:20
  4. IAM → Create role → AWS service → Systems Manager. ▶ #86 05:10 The wizard no longer creates inline policies, so create the customer managed policy SSMRemediationEC2 in another tab. ▶ #86 06:20
  5. Name the role SSMRemediationEC2 (“Allow SSM to call AWS services on our behalf for Config automated remediation”), copy the ARN (arn:aws:iam::851725223689:role/SSMRemediationEC2) into AutomationAssumeRole → Save. ▶ #86 07:40
  6. Launch TestAutomatedIMDSv2Remediation (Amazon Linux 2023, t2.micro, no key pair, default VPC) with metadata version V1 and V2 (token optional). ▶ #86 09:01
  7. Config isn’t instant: rule → Actions → Re-evaluate, set the “Resources in scope” filter to All. Instance shows Noncompliant. ▶ #86 09:41 EC2 → Modify instance metadata options shows IMDSv2 Optional. ▶ #86 10:21 (A Remediate button exists for manual mode.) ▶ #86 10:41
  8. Within about a minute: “Action executed successfully” while still Noncompliant. The instance now shows IMDSv2 Required. ▶ #86 11:40 A few minutes later: Compliant. ▶ #86 12:31
  9. Inspect the resource timeline, then terminate the instance. ▶ #86 15:05

Forcing IMDSv2 can break apps coded against IMDSv1: a concrete auto-remediation risk. The dialog warns to check the MetadataNoToken CloudWatch metric first. ▶ #86 11:50

Timeline, oldest to newest: ▶ #86 13:00

  1. CloudTrail event (launch).
  2. Configuration change (0 field changes).
  3. Rule compliance: 1 Noncompliant rule(s) (red).
  4. CloudTrail events by the Automation principal calling ModifyInstanceMetadataOptions (twice, ~4 minutes apart; reason unknown, check CloudTrail).
  5. Configuration change (1 field change, JSON diff).
  6. Rule compliance: All compliant (green).
Remediation failing? Check these
  • AutomationAssumeRole trust policy must allow ssm.amazonaws.com.
  • The role needs every action the runbook lists (runbook reference) on the target resources.
  • The Resource ID parameter must map to the runbook’s ID input (e.g. InstanceId).
  • At scale, the role must exist in each member account (deploy it with StackSets).
  • Config isn’t real-time: Re-evaluate, set the filter to All, wait a few minutes. ▶ #86 09:41

Delegating Config in an organization

In the AWS Security Reference Architecture (SRA), Config runs in practically every account, but it is administered from the Security Tooling account, which hosts the Config aggregator. ▶ #83 00:20

  • Org Management account: Systems Manager, Artifact, IAM Access Advisor, Control Tower, IAM Identity Center + the per-account baseline (Security Hub, GuardDuty, Config, Access Analyzer, Organization trail).
  • Security Tooling account: CloudTrail, Private CA, Inspector, Artifact, Audit Manager, Config aggregator, EventBridge, Security Lake subscribers, GuardDuty, Security Hub, Firewall Manager, Lambda, Access Analyzer, Macie, Detective, KMS.
  • Log Archive account: central log bucket (CloudTrail org trail, access logs, DNS logs, flow logs) and Security Lake.
  • Infrastructure OU: Network account (inbound/outbound/inspection VPCs, Network Firewall, Route 53, CloudFront, WAF, Shield Advanced, ACM, RAM, Resolver DNS Firewall, Network Access Analyzer) and Shared Services (delegated Identity Center, Systems Manager, Directory Service, Managed Microsoft AD).
  • Workloads OU: application account (EC2 and Aurora in private subnets, ALB, KMS/SSM/S3 endpoints, Secrets Manager, Private CA, CloudHSM, Cognito, Verified Permissions).

Config in member accounts exists to enforce configurations, monitor changes and report to the central aggregator. ▶ #83 00:41 The central account works in a “dual push and pull” model: it pulls data in via the aggregator and pushes conformance packs out. ▶ #83 01:02

Order of operations (any org-integrated service): enable trusted access → register delegated admin (from the management account, CLI/API) → configure from the delegated admin account. Delegation always starts in the management account. ▶ #83 01:20

  • Console: Organizations → Services → Config (listed without the “AWS” prefix) → Enable trusted access. ▶ #83 01:42 This lets Config query the org structure, create service-linked roles in member accounts, and be notified of org changes.
  • Prefer the CLI: registering a delegated admin has no console button on that page anyway. ▶ #83 02:11

Two service principals. Config uses separate principals for org features:

Principal Covers
config.amazonaws.com The organization aggregator ▶ #83 03:00
config-multiaccountsetup.amazonaws.com Organization conformance packs and organization Config rules ▶ #92 07:32

If you register only config.amazonaws.com, put-organization-conformance-pack from the delegated admin fails with OrganizationAccessDeniedException. The instructor: “I have no idea why they set it up that way.” ▶ #92 07:32

CLI demo: trusted access + delegated admin for Config ([▶ #83](https://youtu.be/uBD-wxsc0PE))

  2. Enable trusted access, then verify config.amazonaws.com is in EnabledServicePrincipals (the demo also lists cloudtrail, ec2, iam, member.org.stacksets.cloudformation, ram, sso). ▶ #83 02:40
  3. Register the Security Tooling account (851725223689) as delegated admin, then verify. ▶ #83 03:00
