Enabling Config org-wide with StackSets

Multi-account Config is “an important part of this exam”. ▶ #90 00:00 Config must be enabled in every member account you want covered (should be all), using CloudFormation StackSets. ▶ #90 00:11 To cover future accounts: a service-managed StackSet with automatic deployment (or Control Tower).

  • Delegate StackSets administration so you don’t deploy from the management account. Management account → CloudFormation → StackSets → Register delegated administrator → Security Tooling account ID. ▶ #90 00:40
  • The delegated admin shares admin access for service-managed stack sets. It can deploy to all accounts or specific OUs, and the management account cannot limit it to specific OUs.

Pre-cleanup: conflicts ▶ #90 01:00

  • Delete the recorder from earlier demos (one customer-managed recorder per account per Region). The instructor says the only way is the CLI.
  • IAM roles from earlier demos may conflict with roles the StackSet creates. Delete them, or let the deployment fail, read the role name in the error, delete it, and redeploy. ▶ #90 01:31

aws configservice delete-configuration-recorder \
  --configuration-recorder-name default --profile cybrdemo

Service-managed permissions Self-service permissions
Roles StackSets sets them up via Organizations You create admin/execution roles
New accounts Automatic deployment Manual

Console demo: StackSet + org aggregator ([▶ #90](https://youtu.be/lq7fIedi5D0))
  1. Management account → StackSets → Register delegated admin (Security Tooling). ▶ #90 00:40
  2. Security Tooling: delete the old recorder (CLI) and known conflicting IAM roles. ▶ #90 01:00
  3. StackSets → Create StackSet → Service-managed permissions → sample template Enable AWS Config with central logging (EnableAWSConfigForOrganizations.yml). ▶ #90 02:01
  4. Name enable-aws-config-org (“Enables AWS Config org-wide with centralized logging”). Parameters changed: include global resource types true, SLR Region us-east-1, frequency Continuous (mind cost), SNS false. ▶ #90 02:22
  5. No Log Archive bucket in the demo (it creates one in Security Tooling). In production, point to the Log Archive bucket. ▶ #90 02:50
  6. Options: Managed execution → Active. Deployment: whole org, Region us-east-1 → Submit. ▶ #90 03:11
  7. Failures usually mean resource conflicts: find the name, delete it, Actions → Edit → redeploy. Result: 9 stack instances, all SUCCEEDED. ▶ #90 03:31
  8. Config → Aggregators → Create aggregator (see next topic). ▶ #90 04:02

If the scenario mentions Control Tower, don’t add your own recorders (conflict).

Aggregators and advanced queries

An aggregator is a read-only, multi-account, multi-Region view (inventory + compliance). It lives in one Region but can collect from all Regions. It does not deploy rules, remediate or record anything: each account still needs a running recorder. Aggregators are “really important”. ▶ #84 09:20

Source type Authorization
Organization None per account. Must be the management account or a registered delegated admin for config.amazonaws.com, with all features enabled ▶ #90 04:21
Individual accounts Each source account authorizes it (PutAggregationAuthorization)

Creating one: ▶ #90 04:02

  1. Tick “Allow AWS Config to replicate data from source account(s) into an aggregator account” (required).
  2. Name MultiAccountAggregator (max 64 alphanumeric chars, hyphens/underscores allowed).
  3. Source: Add individual account IDs (comma-separated or file upload) or Add my organization.
  4. Role: existing AWSServiceRoleForConfig (created by the StackSet) or a new one. ▶ #90 04:41
  5. Regions: us-east-1 → Create. Data takes several minutes to arrive. ▶ #90 05:10

What the aggregator shows (data may lag a few minutes, filter by Region or account): ▶ #91 00:00

  • Compliance status: 34.15% (27 noncompliant rules vs 14 compliant). ▶ #91 00:10
  • Resource inventory: 685 resources by type (CodeDeploy DeploymentConfig 170, ECS CapacityProvider 20, Config ResourceCompliance 15, EC2 SecurityGroup 12, Athena WorkGroup 10).
  • Top 5 noncompliant rules, mostly S3: securityhub-s3-bucket-logging-enabled-… (7), securityhub-s3-lifecycle-policy-check-… (6), securityhub-cloud-trail-encryption-enabled-… (2), securityhub-root-account-hardware-mfa-enabled-… (1). ▶ #91 00:21
  • Accounts by resource count (10 accounts, 59–96 each), by noncompliant rules (account 299551924423 with 27), by noncompliant conformance packs (none). ▶ #91 00:31

  • Compliance dashboard: filter by resource type, Region, account, tags, rule, pack. Pie of COMPLIANT vs NON_COMPLIANT. Top 10 resource types by noncompliant resources: AWS::S3::Bucket (7), AWS::CloudTrail::Trail (2), AWS::::Account (account-level settings), AWS::Athena::WorkGroup, AWS::EC2::VPCBlockPublicAccessOptions. Also top 10 accounts and Regions. ▶ #91 00:50
  • Conformance packs (deployed packs across the aggregator), Rules by compliance. ▶ #91 01:22
  • Inventory dashboard: counts by type, by Region (us-east-1 vs global), top 10 accounts, EC2 types (Subnet, SecurityGroup, DHCPOptions, VPCBlockPublicAccessOptions, InternetGateway, NetworkAcl, RouteTable, VPC). ▶ #91 01:42
  • Resources: every resource across the aggregator with identifier, type, Region and account. ▶ #91 01:51

Advanced queries run a SQL-like SELECT over the current configuration (subset: no joins; SELECT/WHERE/GROUP BY/ORDER BY, aggregates), for one account/Region or across an aggregator. ▶ #84 09:51 Historical changes → Config history / S3 snapshots + Athena.

  • 58 AWS sample queries, custom queries, and a natural language query processor (generative AI turns plain English into a query). The instructor calls the feature brand new (Preview) and possibly not in the 2024/2025 exam versions. ▶ #84 09:51
  • Similar in spirit to CloudTrail Lake / Athena.
  • Every aggregator chart has “View and analyze in query editor” showing the query behind it. ▶ #91 02:01

Searching “s3” finds S3 Buckets by versioning state and S3 buckets with no SSE → Copy to editor → scope MultiAccountAggregator → Run. ▶ #91 02:31 The result is an exact checklist of buckets with versioning off to fix. No remediation is configured, but versioning is simple enough to automate. ▶ #91 03:01

-- Active DynamoDB tables (sample, [▶ #84](https://youtu.be/xWxE7q1OnS8))
SELECT resourceId, resourceName, resourceType, tags, configuration
WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::DynamoDB::Table'
  AND configuration.tableStatus = 'ACTIVE'

-- behind "Compliance summary" ([▶ #91](https://youtu.be/N0aenRnwkuA))
SELECT configuration.complianceType, COUNT(*)
WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::Config::ResourceCompliance'
  AND configuration.complianceType IN ('COMPLIANT', 'NON_COMPLIANT')
GROUP BY configuration.complianceType
ORDER BY configuration.complianceType

-- S3 Buckets by versioning state ([▶ #91](https://youtu.be/N0aenRnwkuA))
SELECT resourceId, resourceType,
       supplementaryConfiguration.BucketVersioningConfiguration.status
WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::S3::Bucket'
  AND supplementaryConfiguration.BucketVersioningConfiguration.status = 'Off'

-- unencrypted EBS volumes across the org (aggregator scope)
SELECT accountId, awsRegion, resourceId
WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::EC2::Volume' AND configuration.encrypted = false

Conformance packs

A conformance pack is an immutable YAML bundle of Config rules and remediation actions (AWS::Config::RemediationConfiguration) plus parameters, deployed and scored as one unit: to Regions in one account, across the org, or across Regions. ▶ #92 00:00 One rule only → organization rules (PutOrganizationConfigRule / put-organization-config-rule) push it into every member account.

  • AWS publishes samples (CIS, PCI DSS, NIST, Operational Best Practices) in awslabs/aws-config-rules/aws-config-conformance-packs. ▶ #82 02:50 Examples: AWS-Control-Tower-Detective-Guardrails, Operational-Best-Practices-For-NIST-800-181, …-for-ABS-CCIGv2-Material/Standard, …-for-ACSC-Essential8, …-for-ACSC-ISM, …-for-AI-and-ML, …-for-API-Gateway, …-for-APRA-CPG-234, …-for-AWS-Backup, …-for-AWS-Identity-and-Access-Management, …-for-AWS-Well-Architected-Reliability-Pillar.
  • Org packs deploy service-linked rules that member accounts cannot modify or delete.
  • Packs are Regional. They can’t deploy where Config isn’t enabled.
  • Console gotcha: two menus named “Conformance packs”. The one under Aggregators only lists deployed packs. Deploy from the top-level one. ▶ #92 00:32

Single-account (console) deployment. Deploy conformance pack → Use sample template → Security Best Practices for CloudTrail → name CloudTrailConformancePack → Deploy. ▶ #92 01:11 Rules in it: ▶ #92 02:01

  • cloud-trail-cloud-watch-logs-enabled (CloudWatch Logs integration on trails)
  • cloudtrail-enabled
  • cloud-trail-encryption-enabled
  • cloud-trail-log-file-validation-enabled
  • cloudtrail-s3-dataevents-enabled
  • cloudtrail-security-trail-enabled (checks security best-practice configuration, not just existence)
  • multi-region-cloudtrail-enabled

Result: Completed, compliance score 43%. The compliance score timeline takes a day or two to populate. ▶ #92 03:10

The rule exists only in this account, with ARN …:config-rule/aws-service-rule/config-conforms.amazonaws.com/config-rule-… (service-linked), trigger Periodic: 24 hours, parameter expectedDeliveryWindowAge. ▶ #92 03:51 Multi-account deployment is not possible from the console: use the CLI/API (put-organization-conformance-pack) or Systems Manager (store pack templates as SSM documents). ▶ #92 04:20 Delete the single-account pack first to avoid duplicates. ▶ #92 05:01

Org-wide deployment from the delegated admin hits three classic errors:

  1. OrganizationAccessDeniedException (“only the master account or delegated administrator”): register the delegated admin for config-multiaccountsetup.amazonaws.com too. ▶ #92 07:01

  1. Invalid delivery bucket name (“must starts with awsconfigconforms prefix”): the bucket name must start with awsconfigconforms and its policy must allow every account in the org. ▶ #92 09:32 Fix: the course template aws-config-conforms-bucket-setup.yaml (params OrganizationId, BucketSuffix) → awsconfigconforms-cybrdemo1234. ▶ #92 10:30

  1. Management account stuck in CREATE_IN_PROGRESS: the StackSet targeted OUs, not the management account, so Config wasn’t there. Use --excluded-accounts for it and handle it separately. ▶ #92 13:11

After rerunning (with a fresh SSO login), the call returns OrganizationConformancePackArn arn:aws:config:us-east-1:851725223689:organization-conformance-pack/CloudTrailConformancePack-yipfdzqp. ▶ #92 12:10 Per-account packs are named OrgConformsPack-CloudTrailConformancePack-yipfdzqp and go CREATE_IN_PROGRESS → CREATE_SUCCESSFUL (minutes, longer with many accounts). ▶ #92 12:22 The aggregator then lists the pack per account with drill-down to rule compliance. ▶ #92 14:11

CLI demo: org-wide conformance pack ([▶ #92](https://youtu.be/1O4VVuqmLGA)) 
# 0. confirm you are in the security tooling account
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile cybrdemosecurity

# 1. template
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/aws-config-rules/refs/heads/master/aws-config-conformance-packs/Security-Best-Practices-for-CloudTrail.yaml

# 2. from MANAGEMENT: trusted access + delegated admin for config-multiaccountsetup (see the delegation topic)

# 3. delivery bucket (name must start with awsconfigconforms, org-wide bucket policy)
aws organizations describe-organization --query 'Organization.Id' --output text --profile cybrdemomanagement
aws cloudformation deploy \
  --template-file aws-config-conforms-bucket-setup.yaml \
  --stack-name aws-config-conforms-bucket-stack \
  --parameter-overrides OrganizationId=o-jqbqypd27k BucketSuffix=cybrdemo1234 \
  --profile cybrdemosecurity
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name aws-config-conforms-bucket-stack \
  --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='BucketName'].OutputValue" --output text \
  --profile cybrdemosecurity

# 4. deploy org-wide from the delegated admin (security tooling)
aws configservice put-organization-conformance-pack \
  --organization-conformance-pack-name "CloudTrailConformancePack" \
  --template-body file://Security-Best-Practices-for-CloudTrail.yaml \
  --delivery-s3-bucket awsconfigconforms-cybrdemo1234 \
  --region us-east-1 --profile cybrdemosecurity
#   (should also have added: --excluded-accounts <management-account-id>)

# 5. monitor (empty at first, rerun after ~1 min)
aws configservice get-organization-conformance-pack-detailed-status \
  --organization-conformance-pack-name=CloudTrailConformancePack --profile cybrdemosecurity

The first bucket tried was the StackSet’s stackset-enable-aws-config-org-…-configbucket-…, which failed the prefix check. ▶ #92 06:11

“AWS Config is kind of notoriously hard to set up multi-account.” ▶ #92 11:51 See also ▶ #77 under AWS CloudFormation (rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check) and ▶ #96 under AWS Audit Manager (Config as an evidence source).

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Know the five features: recorder, rules, conformance packs, aggregators, advanced queries. ▶ #82 01:50
  • Customize the recorder’s resource types to reduce cost. ▶ #82 02:11
  • Firewall Manager requires continuous recording. ▶ #84 01:10
  • Send Config data to a bucket in the Log Archive account. ▶ #84 02:50
  • Don’t enable the delivery-channel SNS topic: use EventBridge. ▶ #84 03:31
  • Real life: manual remediation ~90% of the time. Exam: answers lean toward automatic remediation. ▶ #86 02:40
  • Find an Automation role’s permissions in the SSM runbook reference. ▶ #86 05:41
  • Delegate StackSets administration, don’t deploy from the management account. ▶ #90 00:20
  • One customer-managed recorder per account per Region. ▶ #90 01:10
  • Org packs need a delegated admin for config-multiaccountsetup.amazonaws.com, separate from config.amazonaws.com. ▶ #92 07:32
  • Pack delivery bucket must start with awsconfigconforms and allow all org accounts. ▶ #92 09:50
  • Packs can’t deploy where Config isn’t enabled: exclude the management account if the StackSet skipped it. ▶ #92 13:21
  • “AWS Config is definitely a service you can expect to see questions about on the exam.” ▶ #91 03:30

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Detect AND automatically fix public S3 buckets / open SSH / IMDSv1 instances Config rule + automatic remediation (SSM Automation)
Prevent the change from happening Not Config. SCP/RCP, declarative policies, CloudFormation Hook, proactive rules, Guard in CI
Prevent unencrypted volumes SCP on ec2:Encrypted or EBS encryption by default
Enforce IMDSv2 Prevention first: account IMDS defaults (ModifyInstanceMetadataDefaults), AMI ImdsSupport=v2.0, SCP ec2:MetadataHttpTokens = required on ec2:RunInstances, EC2 declarative policies. Config + remediation catches the rest
Single compliance view across 50 accounts and 4 Regions Aggregator in a delegated admin account
Query current config across all accounts (unencrypted EBS, public buckets) Advanced query with aggregator scope
Same rule set org-wide, reported as one score Organization conformance pack. One rule → put-organization-config-rule
Config enabled in all future accounts Service-managed StackSet with automatic deployment (or Control Tower)
Config shows no data for an account Recorder off/not started, delivery bucket policy, or missing AWSServiceRoleForConfig. A disabled recorder silently drops the account from the aggregator (Security Hub control Config.1)
What did this SG look like last Tuesday / who changed it? Config resource timeline (CI + CloudTrail event)
Who made the API call? (only) CloudTrail
Remediation execution failed AutomationAssumeRole lacks trust for ssm.amazonaws.com or action permissions
put-organization-conformance-pack → OrganizationAccessDeniedException Delegate config-multiaccountsetup.amazonaws.com
Org pack stuck in CREATE_IN_PROGRESS for one account Config not enabled there → --excluded-accounts

IMDS detail: hop limit 1 blocks containers from IMDSv2 (use 2 on container hosts) but defends against SSRF from containers. IMDSv2 mitigates SSRF credential theft (GuardDuty UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration).

Updates since the videos
  • AWS has added service-linked recorders (created by other services, e.g. Control Tower manages its own). The one-customer-managed-recorder-per-account-per-Region rule still holds.
  • The delivery S3 bucket for org conformance packs is optional. If you specify one, its name must start with awsconfigconforms and its policy must allow all org accounts.
  • Correction: config.amazonaws.com delegation covers only the organization aggregator. Organization conformance packs and organization rules from a delegated admin also need trusted access + delegated admin for config-multiaccountsetup.amazonaws.com, otherwise put-organization-conformance-pack fails with OrganizationAccessDeniedException.
  • The “Amazon CloudWatch Events rule” link in Config settings now opens EventBridge: CloudWatch Events is deprecated. ▶ #84 10:50

Real-world practice

  • Turn on the recorder in every account and Region (Control Tower does this, with a central bucket in Log Archive and an aggregator in the Audit account). Delegate Config admin to the Security Tooling account (Config allows only a few delegated admins, keep one source of truth). Don’t use the management account day to day, but still record Config there for audit.
  • Run an org aggregator there, deploy conformance packs per OU, and send compliance changes to Security Hub and EventBridge.
  • Cost is per CI recorded and per rule evaluation. High-churn types (ephemeral EC2/ENIs in autoscaling or EKS, Lambda versions) drive cost: use daily recording or exclusions for them, but keep continuous recording for security-relevant types (IAM, SGs, S3, KMS) and don’t exclude types your controls depend on.
  • Record global IAM resources in one Region only, and make sure that Region still includes them.
  • Central Config bucket in Log Archive: SSE-KMS, Object Lock or tight bucket policies, and a bucket policy allowing config.amazonaws.com with aws:SourceOrgID / aws:SourceAccount conditions (the most common cause of org-wide delivery failures).
  • Auto-remediate low-risk, high-certainty fixes (public S3 block, default encryption, versioning). Use manual approval (SSM Automation aws:approve) for disruptive ones (an EBS swap that stops instances, forcing IMDSv2 on IMDSv1 apps). Check MetadataNoToken before enforcing IMDSv2.
  • At scale deploy rule + remediation via conformance pack or organization rules. The AutomationAssumeRole must exist in each member account (StackSets). Tune concurrency/error rate, scope exceptions by tag, keep Automation execution history as audit evidence.
  • Codify the whole chain (delegations, bucket stack, org pack). Org packs auto-deploy to accounts that join later. Monitor get-organization-conformance-pack-detailed-status (or EventBridge) for CREATE_FAILED (missing recorder, SCP blocking config:*, Region not enabled).
  • A low org compliance score right after enabling Security Hub standards is normal: prioritize by severity and account. Save frequent queries and export results for evidence/ticketing, or run them on a schedule via SelectAggregateResourceConfig. Aggregated data lags minutes: for IR on one resource, check the source account’s timeline.
Hands-on lab
  1. Enable Config with the managed rule s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and the automatic remediation below.
  2. Make a test bucket public, then watch it become NON_COMPLIANT and get fixed.
  3. Cleanup: delete the rule, stop the recorder and delete the bucket. Config charges per configuration item and per rule evaluation.
// remediation.json  →  aws configservice put-remediation-configurations --remediation-configurations file://remediation.json
[{
  "ConfigRuleName": "s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited",
  "TargetType": "SSM_DOCUMENT",
  "TargetId": "AWS-DisableS3BucketPublicReadWrite",
  "Parameters": {
    "AutomationAssumeRole": { "StaticValue": { "Values": ["arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ConfigRemediationRole"] } },
    "S3BucketName":         { "ResourceValue": { "Value": "RESOURCE_ID" } }
  },
  "Automatic": true,
  "MaximumAutomaticAttempts": 5,
  "RetryAttemptSeconds": 60
}]

Tagging strategy & Tag Policies

At a glance

Consistent key/value metadata used for cost allocation, automation, access control (ABAC), ownership tracking, detecting unauthorized resources and incident scoping. “The effort-to-value ratio of implementing tagging is really, really high.”

  • Exam skills: organize resources with tags (6.2.2) · detect/remediate noncompliance (6.3.1) · ABAC & RBAC (4.2.2) · prepare for incidents (2.1.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #141 Tagging best practices
  • Limits: 50 user tags per resource, key ≤128 chars, value ≤256 chars; the aws: prefix is reserved. Tag keys are case-sensitive.

Why tag, and what tags enable

Tags help you understand and allocate costs, control access (ABAC), quickly identify what a resource is and who owns it, detect unusual or unauthorized resources, and manage large multi-account environments. ▶ #141 00:00

Use How tags help ▶ #141 02:40
ABAC Grant access to resources based on tags (condition keys aws:PrincipalTag, aws:ResourceTag, aws:RequestTag, aws:TagKeys)
Track ownership Who to contact during a problem or incident
Cost analysis Break down spend by team, project, environment (prod/staging/test) in Cost Explorer
Automation Auto-apply security controls; find untagged resources and notify teams, e.g. “this resource will be deleted in 48 hours unless tagged properly”
Incident response Quickly identify impacted systems and owners during a security event, instead of hunting for who owns a resource

Which tags to use

AWS recommends three required tags on every resource: ▶ #141 00:51

  • Purpose: what the resource is for.
  • Owner: who is responsible.
  • Environment: where it fits (prod vs not).

Example for an IaC-deployed app stack for a dev team in staging:

company:purpose     = <value>
company:owner       = <team/person>
company:environment-type = staging

Additional useful tags: ▶ #141 01:40

Tag Why
Cost center Finance tracks spending accurately
Project ID Spend and ownership for a specific project
Compliance Audits, applying specific guardrails
Data classification Enforce stricter controls on sensitive data
Managed by e.g. CloudFormation / Terraform: you know where the configuration lives and how to change it

AWS-defined tags. Some services apply their own tags. CloudFormation injects aws:cloudformation:stack-name, aws:cloudformation:stack-id and aws:cloudformation:logical-id on every resource it creates, regardless of your tags. That’s why AWS recommends a company: prefix for your tags. ▶ #141 05:21 CloudFormation stack-level tags also propagate to supported resources.

Best practices ▶ #141 06:11

  1. Never store sensitive data in tags. They are not encrypted and show up in APIs, logs and billing data; anyone with Describe* / tag:GetResources can read them. AWS docs: “Do not add personally identifiable information (PII)…” Use Secrets Manager / Parameter Store instead.
  2. Standardize tag keys and values: if you pick lowercase env, everyone uses exactly env, no capitalization variants. ▶ #141 06:31
  3. Enforce tagging early: a few hours up front saves much more later.
  4. Tag everything that supports it: not all services support tags. ▶ #141 07:10

Reference: AWS docs “Tagging AWS Resources and Tag Editor: Best practices and strategies.”

Enforcing tags: tag policies vs SCPs vs Config

Goal Tool
Standardize keys, allowed values and capitalization Tag policies (Organizations policy type). With enforcement on for chosen resource types they block non-compliant tagging operations. They do not force a tag to exist
Require a tag at creation SCP or IAM policy denying the create action when aws:RequestTag/<key> is missing (Null condition). aws:TagKeys restricts which keys can be set
Detect missing tags Config required-tags rule (remediate via SSM Automation)
Protect ABAC tags Deny TagResource / UntagResource on those keys (aws:TagKeys) except for admin roles. Otherwise a principal can retag itself or resources → privilege escalation
Tags in cost reports Activate cost allocation tags in Billing before they appear in Cost Explorer / CUR 
{
  "Sid": "RequireOwnerTagOnRunInstances",
  "Effect": "Deny",
  "Action": "ec2:RunInstances",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*",
  "Condition": { "Null": { "aws:RequestTag/Owner": "true" } }
}

Finding resources by tag

▶ #141 04:20

  • AWS Resource Groups: “Find and group your AWS resources by using queries.” Unlimited, single-Region groups, by resource types + tag queries or by CloudFormation stack. Its left nav has Tagging → Tag Editor, Tag Policies. Tag-based groups are targets for SSM commands and patching.
  • Resource Groups Tagging API: manage tags programmatically.
  • AWS Resource Explorer: centralized search across resources (demo: 442 resources in us-east-1), with a banner to enable cross-Region search via an aggregator index. Query for untagged resources (tag:none) and pair with Lambda or AWS Config to enforce tagging, e.g. a 48-hour or few-day grace period before deletion. ▶ #141 04:41

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Minimum tags: purpose, owner, environment. ▶ #141 00:51
  • Use a company prefix to separate your tags from AWS-injected ones (CloudFormation stack name/ID/logical ID). ▶ #141 05:51
  • Never put sensitive data in tags: unencrypted and exposed in APIs, logs and billing. ▶ #141 06:11
  • Standardize keys/values, enforce early, tag everything supported. ▶ #141 06:31
  • Resource Explorer finds untagged resources; enforce with Lambda or Config. ▶ #141 04:41

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
CostCenter must use only approved values, case-consistent Tag policy
Every EC2 instance must be launched with an Owner tag SCP with aws:RequestTag + Null
Find untagged resources Config required-tags, Tag Editor or Resource Explorer
Cost report doesn’t show the tag Cost allocation tag not activated
Store a secret/API key in a tag Never; use Secrets Manager

Real-world practice

  • During an incident, tag the affected resources, e.g. SecurityIncident=IR-2026-001. IAM can then deny changes to tagged resources for everyone except the IR role. Quarantine-by-tag is a common IR pattern (tag quarantine=true → automation swaps the SG / ABAC denies access).
  • Bake required tags into IaC modules (Terraform default_tags, CDK Tags.of(app).add) so humans rarely tag manually.
  • Use aws:ResourceTag/environment = prod conditions to restrict destructive actions on prod resources.
  • Resource Explorer views can be scoped per team; enable the aggregator index in a central Region and org-wide multi-account search from a delegated admin.
Hands-on lab
  1. Attach the RequireOwnerTagOnRunInstances SCP above to a sandbox OU.
  2. Launch an instance without the tag (denied), then with the tag (allowed).
  3. Cleanup: detach the SCP and terminate the instance.

AWS Audit Manager

At a glance

Continuously collects evidence from your accounts and maps it to compliance framework controls, to prepare for audits. It collects and organizes evidence; it does not assess or certify compliance itself.

  • Exam skills: collect audit evidence (6.3.2) · detect & remediate noncompliance (6.3.1) · Well-Architected review (6.3.3) · delegated administrators (6.1.4) · automated assessments with Config & Security Hub (1.1.5) · CloudTrail Lake (2.2.2)
  • Videos: ▶ #95 About Audit Manager · ▶ #96 Running assessments · ▶ #97 Evidence & reports
  • Cost: resource assessments: first 35,000 per month free, then $1.25 per 1,000 (free tier for the first two months for first-time customers)

What it does (and doesn’t)

Verifying compliance with frameworks and regulations is a lot of work. Audit Manager helps assess risk and compliance of your accounts and workloads by collecting evidence relevant to the frameworks you’re assessed against. ▶ #95 00:00 It does not assess your compliance itself: “a really important distinction”. ▶ #95 00:20 It reduces manual screenshot gathering; it doesn’t replace auditors or legal interpretation. Results vary by time and source: “this is giving you information, you then have to determine what’s going on.” ▶ #97 04:40

Workflow: ▶ #95 01:01

  1. Select prebuilt framework(s) or create a custom framework with custom controls.
  2. Define a scope: the AWS accounts to collect evidence for.
  3. Audit Manager collects evidence from the scoped accounts.
  4. Select which evidence to include in your report.
  5. Generate the assessment report, stored in S3. ▶ #95 01:31

Other integrations: ▶ #95 02:30

  • AWS License Manager: aggregate software license usage.
  • AWS Control Tower: run a Control Tower audit (prebuilt framework for its guardrails).
  • EventBridge: detect Audit Manager events and react automatically.
  • SNS: notifications about assessments. ▶ #95 03:02
  • Supports Organizations with a delegated administrator (same pattern as GuardDuty, Security Hub, Macie).

Frameworks, controls and control sets

  • Frameworks are prebuilt or custom. Out of the box: AWS Well-Architected, CIS AWS Benchmark, FedRAMP, GDPR, HIPAA, NIST, PCI, SOC 2, AWS best practices and many more. ▶ #95 00:31
  • Frameworks are made of controls grouped into control sets. Controls define the evidence collected. ▶ #95 00:50
  • Slide example (Well-Architected → controls): Operational Excellence (83), Security (65), e.g. SEC01-BP01 Separate workloads using accounts, SEC01-BP02 Secure account root user and properties, SEC01-BP03 Identify and validate control objectives.
  • You create assessments from a framework, scoped to accounts and services, with an audit owner.

Framework library (left menu: Dashboard, Assessments, Delegations, Evidence finder, Download center, Framework library, Share requests, Control library, Settings, Notifications): ▶ #96 04:11

  • 32 standard frameworks at the time, e.g. AWS Audit Manager Sample Framework, AWS-WAF-v10, ACSC Essential Eight, ACSC ISM, AWS Control Tower Guardrails, AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (31 control sets), AWS Generative AI Best Practices v2, AWS License Manager, AWS Operational Best Practices, CCCS Medium Cloud Control (175), FedRAMP Moderate, GLBA, NIST 800-53 Rev 5 (1007 controls).
  • CIS AWS Benchmark v1.2.0 / v1.3.0 / v1.4.0, each in Level 1 and Level 1 and 2 variants (Level 2 = more stringent).
  • Create custom framework from scratch or as a copy of an existing one.

Evidence sources

Data source type From Evidence type Verdict
Compliance check AWS Config rule evaluations (e.g. unencrypted EBS volumes) Compliance check Pass / Fail
Compliance check Security Hub findings Compliance check Pass / Fail
User activity CloudTrail (who did what) User activity —
Configuration data AWS API call snapshots (describe-* results) Configuration data Inconclusive
Manual Uploaded files (policies, procedures) or text responses Manual —

The four automated sources are covered in ▶ #95 01:40.

  • Audit Manager depends on Config and Security Hub being enabled in the scoped accounts. They’re “recommended”, not required, but “you’re going to miss a lot of evidence if you don’t enable it”: a soft requirement. ▶ #96 01:21 Missing evidence → check those services.
  • Inconclusive vs 0 issues: the issue count reflects Security Hub and Config results. API-call evidence (e.g. iam:GenerateCredentialReport) can’t produce pass/fail → Inconclusive. Security Hub evidence can, e.g. Pass: no root access key exists. ▶ #97 03:00
  • Active assessments collect daily. First evidence can take up to 24 h. ▶ #96 07:20 Evidence retention default 2 years.

Setting up Audit Manager

Step What to know
1. Permissions A service-linked role (“no action is required by default”). Its policy is mostly Get*, List*, Describe*: essentially read-only. ▶ #96 00:10
2. Data encryption Default: a key AWS owns and manages (the transcript says “AWS managed KMS key”). Customize encryption settings (advanced) → your customer managed KMS key for full control of key and key policy. ▶ #96 00:41
3. Delegated administrator (optional) 12-digit account ID → Delegate. Required for multi-account support with Organizations. ▶ #96 01:11
4. Config & Security Hub (recommended) Used to collect evidence. Both cost extra. ▶ #96 01:21

Enabling Config from the setup page used 1-click setup in the demo (in production use Get started and review each setting). The review showed: record all resource types with customizable overrides, Continuous frequency, 4 types with overrides and 405 with defaults, delivery bucket config-bucket-<account-id>, 0 rules. Confirm creates the SLR and bucket (“Signing up with AWS Config”).

Enabling Security Hub ▶ #96 02:40

  • It warns you must first enable Config resource recording in every account/Region where you use standards: Security Hub relies heavily on Config. ▶ #96 03:02
  • Pricing shown: $0.0010 per check for the first 100,000, $0.0008 for 100,001–500,000, $0.0005 above. 30-day free trial.
  • Default standards: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices v1.0.0 and CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.2.0. Others: AWS Resource Tagging Standard v1.0.0, CIS v1.4.0, CIS v3.0.0, NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5, PCI DSS v3.2.1, PCI DSS v4.0.1. “Just remember the names of these.” ▶ #96 03:21
  • Results can take up to 2 hours to appear.

Creating an assessment

From the framework library, select CIS AWS Benchmark v1.2.0, Level 1 and 2 → Create assessment from framework. ▶ #96 05:22

  1. Assessment details: name ExampleAssessment, optional description (up to 1000 chars).
  2. Reports destination: the S3 bucket where Audit Manager saves assessment reports (S3 URI, Browse S3 or Create new bucket). Demo bucket cybr-demo-audit-manager-example with defaults (Block Public Access on, SSE-S3, versioning off).
  3. Framework: you can select more than one per assessment.
  4. Accounts in scope: with Organizations you’d see all member accounts.
  5. Audit owners: an IAM user or role that manages the assessment, so the audit can be delegated to someone other than the person who set it up.
  6. Review and create: “evidence will be available within 24 hours”.

The owner list showed Identity Center roles (AWSReservedSSO_AdministratorAccess_…, …_SecurityAdmin_…, …_SecurityAnalyst_…, …_SecurityBreakGlass_…). The demo picked AdministratorAccess.

Delegations assign control sets to reviewers.

Console demo: setup and first assessment ([▶ #96](https://youtu.be/JDaKwmiMMR4))
  1. Audit Manager → Set up AWS Audit Manager. ▶ #96 00:00
  2. Permissions: accept the service-linked role (read-only Get/List/Describe).
  3. Data encryption: default (optionally Customize encryption settings → CMK).
  4. Delegated administrator: skipped (single account).
  5. Enable AWS Config → 1-click setup → Confirm (SLR + S3 bucket, continuous recording of all types).
  6. Enable Security Hub → keep FSBP v1.0.0 + CIS v1.2.0 → Enable.
  7. Complete setup → Framework library → CIS AWS Benchmark v1.2.0, Level 1 and 2 → Create assessment from framework. ▶ #96 04:11

Reviewing evidence

After ~12 h the dashboard shows a daily snapshot (“daily” is key: an active assessment re-collects every day): 27 controls with noncompliant evidence, 27 noncompliant evidence, 1 active assessment. ▶ #97 00:21

Controls with noncompliant evidence are grouped by control domain, up to 10 per domain (download CSV for all). Shown: 2.7 CloudTrail logs encrypted with KMS CMKs, 2.4 CloudTrail integrated with CloudWatch Logs, 3.2 metric filter/alarm for console sign-in without MFA, 3.11 NACL changes, 3.6 console auth failures, 1.8/1.6 password policy, 1.14 hardware MFA for root, 3.1 unauthorized API calls, 3.13 route table changes. ▶ #97 00:40

  • Assessment ExampleAssessment: compliance type CIS-AWS-Benchmark-v1.2, total evidence 676, destination s3://cybr-example-assessment, status Active. ▶ #97 00:51
  • Control status summary: Total 49, Reviewed 22, Under review 27, Inactive 0. Reviewed isn’t default: the instructor marked control sets with “Complete control set review”. ▶ #97 01:00
  • Control 1.12 Ensure no root account access key exists: description, status, tabs Evidence folders, Details, Evidence sources, Comments, Changelog. ▶ #97 01:41

Evidence folders: one per day (collection continues daily unless you pause or stop the assessment). ▶ #97 02:01

  • Folder summary: date, total evidence, resources, evidence by type (User activity, Configuration data, Compliance check, Manual), compliance check status. ▶ #97 02:10
  • Evidence rows: time, compliance check, evidence type, data source (e.g. Security Hub), event name, event source, report selection.
  • Add manual evidence: upload from S3, from the browser, or a text response. ▶ #97 02:31
  • Select evidence → Add to assessment report / Remove from assessment report. ▶ #97 03:50

Second example: control 2.9 Ensure VPC flow logging is enabled in all VPCs (Under review), folder 2024-12-13: 3 evidence, 3 compliance checks, 1 issue found: Security Hub on AWS EC2 VPC failed, others passed. ▶ #97 04:10

Evidence finder searches and filters evidence instead of browsing (assessment, date range, compliant/non-compliant/ inconclusive, grouping). It relies on CloudTrail Lake event data stores: enable it in Settings, attach the required permission policy (Audit Manager creates and manages an event data store), optional S3 export. Extra cost. The delegated admin can query aggregated evidence for all member accounts. Not demonstrated. ▶ #97 07:10

Assessment reports and integrity

  • Reports go to an S3 bucket you choose. The bucket must be in the same Region. With a customer managed KMS key, the key must be in the same Region and the Audit Manager/user roles need key permissions (the classic “report generation fails” question).
  • Assessment → Assessment report selection tab (folders 2024-12-15: 1, 2024-12-14: 1, 2024-12-13: 3) → Generate assessment report. ▶ #97 05:00 Name ExampleAssessmentReport2. ▶ #97 05:20
  • Download center (Assessment reports / Exports tabs): In progress → Ready → Download (zip). ▶ #97 05:40

Report contents (folder ExampleAssessmen-1edeb71c): ▶ #97 06:01

File Purpose
README.txt File structure and what each folder/file means
digest.txt Integrity: JSON with signatures and SHA-384 hashes of every file. Invalidated if anything is altered
AssessmentReportSummary.pdf Overview, linked TOC, control descriptions, testing info, evidence per date (“1 issues found out of 2 evidence”)
Evidence folders By control (1.12Ensurenoroot-…, 2.9EnsureVPCflow-…) → data source → date → one PDF per evidence ▶ #97 06:40

“Prove the report wasn’t tampered with” → validate with ValidateAssessmentReportIntegrity. Compare CloudTrail log file validation and S3 Object Lock.

Console demo: review evidence and generate a report ([▶ #97](https://youtu.be/Tx7LSMimCh4))
  1. Dashboard → review the daily snapshot and noncompliant controls. ▶ #97 00:00
  2. Assessments → ExampleAssessment → Controls → IAM control set → 1.12 → evidence folder → Security Hub row (Pass) → Add to assessment report. ▶ #97 01:41
  3. Logging set → 2.9 VPC flow logs → folder with 1 issue → add evidence. ▶ #97 04:10
  4. Assessment report selection → Generate assessment report → name/description (“Just an example of exporting an assessment report for Cybr course”) → Download center → Download. ▶ #97 05:00

Notifications and settings

  • Notifications page lists sent notifications. Settings → Assessment tab → choose an SNS topic (e.g. a dedicated audit topic). EventBridge can also react to Audit Manager events. ▶ #97 08:01
  • Settings also shows the delegated administrator, AWS Config – recommended and Security Hub – recommended (both incur charges), and Disable Audit Manager: evidence is retained 2 years by default, with a “Delete all data” option. ▶ #97 07:41

Exam tips

From the instructor

  • Audit Manager collects evidence; it does not determine compliance. ▶ #95 00:20
  • Know the four data sources: Config, Security Hub, CloudTrail, API calls. ▶ #95 01:40
  • Reports are generated and stored in S3. ▶ #95 01:31
  • Config and Security Hub are “recommended”, not required, but without them you miss a lot of evidence. ▶ #96 01:21
  • Both cost money after the free trial: disable them after a lab. ▶ #96 02:40
  • Security Hub relies heavily on Config. ▶ #96 03:02
  • Remember the default Security Hub standards: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v1.2.0 and AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. ▶ #96 03:21
  • Active assessments collect daily. Evidence can take up to 24 h. ▶ #97 00:00
  • Inconclusive = the source can’t give a verdict (API snapshots). Config/Security Hub give pass/fail. ▶ #97 03:00
  • The report includes a digest file for integrity. ▶ #97 06:21
  • Evidence finder needs CloudTrail Lake (extra setup and cost). ▶ #97 07:10
  • Notifications via SNS, automation via EventBridge. ▶ #97 08:01

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Auditor needs continuous evidence collection mapped to PCI controls Audit Manager
Need AWS’s own SOC 2 / PCI report, or a BAA AWS Artifact, not Audit Manager
Check current resource compliance with rules Config or Security Hub (Audit Manager consumes them as evidence)
Evidence shows Inconclusive API-snapshot evidence has no compliance verdict
Prove the assessment report wasn’t tampered with digest.txt + ValidateAssessmentReportIntegrity
Report generation fails S3 bucket or CMK in a different Region, or missing KMS key permissions
Missing evidence for many controls Config / Security Hub not enabled in scoped accounts
Search evidence across accounts Evidence finder (CloudTrail Lake)
Updates since the videos
  • In 2025 the original Security Hub was renamed AWS Security Hub CSPM, with a new unified Security Hub on top. Consoles may differ from the videos.
  • Check service availability notices for lesser-used compliance services. Audit Manager remains in the SCS-C03 skill list (6.3.2).

Real-world practice

  • Enable Audit Manager from the Organizations management account, delegate admin to the Security or Audit account, and enable Config and Security Hub first (org-wide Config aggregator + Security Hub central configuration): they are the richest evidence sources.
  • One assessment per audit scope. Export reports to a locked, encrypted S3 bucket.
  • Evidence volume (and cost) grows with scope and controls: scope to in-scope accounts (e.g. the PCI cardholder OU), tailor custom frameworks (copy a standard one, drop irrelevant controls), and keep assessments active only for the audit window.
  • CIS v1.2 is old: prefer CIS v1.4/v3.0 or AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. Many CIS metric-filter/alarm controls fail in setups that use EventBridge/Security Hub instead: document compensating controls as manual evidence.
Hands-on lab
  1. Create an assessment from the “AWS Foundational Security Best Practices” framework for one account.
  2. Wait for evidence to collect, then generate an assessment report.
  3. Cleanup: delete the assessment and disable Audit Manager (it charges per evidence collected). Disable Config and Security Hub too if enabled only for the lab.

AWS Artifact

At a glance

AWS’s free, self-service compliance document library: AWS’s own compliance reports (SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS AOC, ISO certificates, FedRAMP…) and agreements such as the BAA for HIPAA. Nothing to deploy or architect. “You’re not going to see that many questions about it”, but know what it is and why it exists. ▶ #98 00:00

  • Exam skills: collect audit evidence: Audit Manager, Artifact (6.3.2) · Organizations (6.1.1)
  • Videos: ▶ #98 AWS Artifact
  • Cost: free.

What Artifact is for

When auditors or your compliance team need proof that AWS meets certain standards, you get the documents here. ▶ #98 00:11 Console: “No cost, self-service portal for on-demand access to compliance reports and for entering into select online agreements.” Menu: Agreements, Reports, Notification.

Need Service
Proof of AWS’s compliance (SOC 2, PCI AOC, ISO 27001 certificate) Artifact Reports
Legal agreement with AWS (BAA) Artifact Agreements
Evidence of your own controls Audit Manager
Check your resources against PCI/CIS Security Hub / Config conformance packs
  • Access is controlled with IAM (artifact:* actions, e.g. artifact:GetReport, artifact:AcceptAgreement).
  • Some third-party (ISV / Marketplace vendor) reports are also available.
  • Notifications (optional) alert you when new reports or agreements are published; otherwise there’s nothing to configure. ▶ #98 02:10

Reports

AWS compliance certifications and audit reports: SOC 1, SOC 2, PCI DSS attestations, ISO certifications, FedRAMP and many others (the console shows 380). ▶ #98 00:30 They are evidence of AWS’s side of the shared responsibility model; they don’t certify your workload.

  1. An auditor asks whether AWS is SOC 2 compliant.
  2. Find System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2 Report (period Oct 1 2024 – Sep 30 2025, category Certifications and Attestations, series SOC) → Download report. ▶ #98 01:01
  3. Accept the terms (NDA-style, because the documents contain sensitive information about AWS infrastructure): “I have read and agree to the terms” → “Accept terms and download report”. ▶ #98 01:11 A “Copy report URL” option also exists.

Agreements

Accept legal agreements with AWS (not downloads). ▶ #98 01:21

  • AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA) (also an Australian BAA variant) covers AWS services used with personal health information (PHI) under HIPAA / HITECH. ▶ #98 01:30
  • Handling healthcare data under HIPAA → you must have a BAA in place: review and accept it for your account, or at the organization level from the management account. ▶ #98 02:01
  • On-screen BAA text: it is account-specific, so if several accounts hold PHI, accept a BAA in each (or org-level). With PHI in the account you must use only HIPAA Eligible Services and encrypt all PHI in transit and at rest. Status shown: Inactive (not yet accepted).
Exam tips

From the instructor

  • “AWS Artifact is where you get compliance reports and where you accept agreements like the BAA for HIPAA.” ▶ #98 02:20
  • Reports need terms/NDA acceptance before download. ▶ #98 01:01
  • Agreements can be accepted per account or org-wide. ▶ #98 02:01

Keyword → answer

If the question says… Answer
Auditor wants proof AWS data centers are SOC 2 compliant / PCI AOC / ISO 27001 certificate Artifact Reports
Must sign a BAA before storing health data, for all accounts Artifact org agreement from the management account
Collect evidence of our controls Audit Manager
Check our resources against PCI/CIS Security Hub / Config conformance packs

Real-world practice

  • Grant the compliance team a read-only Artifact role. Accepting agreements is a legal act: limit artifact:AcceptAgreement to legal/compliance roles.
  • Track agreement acceptance as part of onboarding a regulated workload. Accept the BAA at org level only if you intend PHI anywhere; otherwise scope it to the PHI accounts and enforce HIPAA-eligible services with SCPs.
  • Artifact Notifications alert the compliance team when new SOC/PCI reports are published, useful for annual vendor-risk reviews.
Hands-on lab
  1. Open Artifact and download one SOC report.
  2. Review the Agreements tab.
  3. Nothing to clean up.
